One of the largest and best-preserved private houses in Pompeii, c. 1,100 sq m, originally built in the 2nd century BCE and lavishly redecorated in the elaborate Fourth Style after the 62 CE earthquake for its owners, the freedmen brothers Aulus Vettius Restitutus and Aulus Vettius Conviva. Sealed under ash in 79 CE with its frescoes almost intact, making it one of the most-studied domus in the Roman world. New category "house" introduced for this feature (domus) since none of the existing categories fit a private residence; logged per shift convention of introducing categories freely. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

ancient_sources.author: CIL IV 3509
ancient_sources.note: Painted election notices on the house's own facade name Aulus Vettius Conviva, one of its two freedman owners, by his title as an Augustalis — the priesthood of the imperial cult freedmen could hold.

ancient_sources.author: CIL IV 3522
ancient_sources.note: A second painted notice on the same facade has Aulus Vettius Restitutus, the house's other owner, canvassing support for a candidate for aedile.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy, c. 400 m northwest of the walls near the Herculaneum Gate
properties.notes: A suburban villa just outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, built in the 1st century BCE and famous for the near-life-size Dionysiac frieze (c. 60 BCE) painted around its triclinium (Room 5), thought to depict a woman's initiation into a mystery cult of Dionysus/Bacchus. Because it lay outside the town walls it took relatively light structural damage in 79 CE, which is why its frescoes survive so completely. New category "villa" introduced (distinct from in-town "house") for this and the Villa of the Papyri entry, following the shift log's precedent of adding categories freely. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.
properties.image_credit: Villa of the Mysteries, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Exterior view of the Villa of the Mysteries at Pompeii

properties.notes: One of Pompeii's seven city gates, on the western wall near the ancient shoreline, connecting the town to its harbor and the Bay of Naples; its double-arched, barrel-vaulted form (a wide arch for animals/carts, a narrow one for pedestrians) is largely a Sullan-colony-era (post-80 BCE) rebuild of an older opening in the Samnite walls. Buried in 79 CE and not fully excavated until 1861 under Giuseppe Fiorelli. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.image_alt: Overview of the ancient city of Herculaneum
properties.image_credit: General view of the Herculaneum excavations · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: A smaller, wealthier seaside town of perhaps 4,000-5,000 people on a coastal spur of Vesuvius, about 8 km southeast of Neapolis. Spared the initial ash-fall that struck Pompeii (giving most residents time to flee toward the shore) but destroyed the following night and morning by a series of pyroclastic surges and flows that buried the town up to 20 m deep, carbonizing (rather than burning away) organic material — wood, food, papyrus, even some human tissue — far more completely than at Pompeii. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as a general wayfinding/city-center pin, same reasoning as the Pompeii city pin.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16 and 6.20 (to Tacitus)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-32623-3 (Scientific Reports, 2023, on the pyroclastic surge sequence at Herculaneum)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the town on its headland above the sea, held in turn by Oscans, Etruscans and Samnites, with air the writer thought unusually healthy.

properties.notes: Meeting hall and shrine of the Augustales, a civic college mostly of wealthy freedmen tasked with maintaining the imperial cult of Augustus (the priesthood was formalized under Tiberius in 14 CE, though this building's core dates slightly earlier, funded by patrons A. Lucius Proculus and A. Lucius Iulianus). Decorated with Fourth-Style frescoes of the labors of Hercules, the city's mythic founder. Rediscovered in 1740 by early Bourbon tunnel excavations. New category "collegium" introduced since this is a civic/cult association's meeting hall rather than a standalone temple; logged per shift convention. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

ancient_sources.author: AE 1979, 169
ancient_sources.ref: marble plaque, cella of the Augustales' hall
ancient_sources.note: Two brothers, Aulus Lucius Proculus and Aulus Lucius Iulianus, funded a dinner for the town councillors and the Augustales to mark the dedication of a monument to the deified Augustus, commemorated on this plaque still fixed inside the hall.

properties.image_alt: Exterior of the Suburban Baths at Herculaneum
properties.image_credit: Suburban Baths of Herculaneum, exterior · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Built in the early 1st century CE as a gift to the town by its greatest benefactor, Marcus Nonius Balbus (ex-tribune, ex-consul, ex-proconsul of Crete), who split the complex off from his own adjoining residence; damaged in the 62 CE earthquake and subsequently expanded with an open-air pool and nymphaeum. Widely regarded as the best-preserved Roman bath building anywhere, buried by the 79 CE pyroclastic flows and only fully excavated/opened in the 20th-21st centuries. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Describes the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius burying the cities of Herculaneum and Pompeii whole.

properties.name_english: House of the Deer (Casa dei Cervi)
properties.notes: The grandest excavated house in Herculaneum, a two-story waterfront residence built/rebuilt under Claudius (41-54 CE) and expanded by absorbing a neighboring property; named for two marble sculptures of deer attacked by hounds found in its garden, and noted for well-preserved still-life frescoes. Street-facing rooms were converted to shops after the 62 CE earthquake. Fully uncovered by Amedeo Maiuri's open-air excavations of 1929-1932. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Ercolano, Campania, Italy, northwest of the main excavated town, mostly still unexcavated/underground
properties.notes: A vast luxury villa on the coast northwest of the town center, plausibly linked (unconfirmed) to Julius Caesar's father-in-law L. Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus; famous for its library of over 1,800 carbonized papyrus scrolls, discovered by Bourbon tunneling from 1750, mostly Epicurean philosophical texts including many works of Philodemus of Gadara. COORDINATE/EXTENT CAUTION: only a fraction of the villa has ever been excavated (much still lies under modern Ercolano and below the water table), so its full footprint and this point's precision are both genuinely uncertain — the coordinates mark the excavated atrium/peristyle area reached by 18th-century tunnels and 20th-century open-air digs, not a confirmed full-villa centroid. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.
properties.image_credit: Excavated ruins of the Villa of the Papyri, Herculaneum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated remains of the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum

properties.notes: Legio I Adiutrix was raised from marines of the Ravenna fleet in the civil war year of 68 CE, and moved to Brigetio on the Danube bend under Domitian, where it stayed for the next three centuries. In August 117 CE the fortress is its home but the legion is not in it: I Adiutrix went east with Trajan for the Parthian war and returns to Pannonia only under Hadrian, in 118. The garrison holding Brigetio at the moment of this snapshot is Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix, which took the place over in 105 and hands it back when I Adiutrix marches home.
sources: https://www.livius.org/articles/legion/legio-i-adiutrix/ (cross-referenced via search synthesis, direct fetch blocked)
properties.image_credit: Plan of the Brigetio legionary fortress, Komarom (Legio I Adiutrix base) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio I Minervia was levied by Domitian in 82-83 CE for the Chattian War and based at Bonna (Bonn) from its founding; it remained the legion's home fortress for the rest of its existence (with a brief detachment fighting for Trajan in the Dacian Wars). The legion's legate c. 101-106 CE was the future emperor Hadrian. By 117 CE the legion had long since returned to and was firmly garrisoned at Bonna.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tacitus describes Bonna as a legionary camp fought over during the Batavian revolt of 69-70 CE, recounting the clash there between Civilis's forces and Roman troops.

properties.image_credit: Roman altar found near Bonn Munster, within the Bonna (Legio I Minervia) fortress site, LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio I Italica, raised by Nero in 66-67 CE from Italian recruits, was posted to Novae on the lower Danube by Vespasian in 69-70 CE and remained there for the rest of its long service (into the 5th century). Its timber-and-earth camp was rebuilt in stone during the Trajanic period (98-117 CE), so by the 117 CE snapshot the legion occupied a substantially stone fortress. Detachments served in Trajan's Dacian and Parthian campaigns, but the main base stayed at Novae throughout.

ancient_sources.author: Procopius
ancient_sources.note: Procopius lists Novae among the Danube-line fortresses in Moesia that Justinian's engineers repaired and strengthened.

properties.image_credit: Ruins of the principia (headquarters) of the Novae legionary fortress, Svishtov, Bulgaria (Legio I Italica) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio II Adiutrix, like I Adiutrix raised from fleet marines (68-70 CE), fought in Trajan's Dacian Wars based temporarily at Singidunum, then was permanently transferred to Aquincum in 106 CE once the new province of Pannonia Inferior was organized, becoming that province's senior garrison and the anchor of what grew into Aquincum's civilian town (later Pannonia Inferior's capital). Its earlier wood-and-earth camp was under stone reconstruction during Hadrian's reign, begun essentially at the 117 CE snapshot.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of Pannonia Inferior lists Aquincum among the province's towns with coordinates — a bare place-name entry rather than a narrative description.

properties.image_credit: Aquincum military amphitheatre, Budapest, built by Legio II Adiutrix · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Legio II Augusta, one of Claudius's original invasion legions of 43 CE, moved to a new purpose-built fortress at Isca Silurum (Caerleon) in South Wales c. 74-75 CE under governor Sextus Julius Frontinus, replacing timber defenses in stone c. 99-100 CE per a Trajanic building inscription. The legion was still garrisoned there in 117 CE and would remain for roughly two more centuries.

ancient_sources.author: Antonine Itinerary
ancient_sources.note: Records Isca (Legio II Augusta's fortress at Caerleon) as a station on several road routes through Roman Britain, under the name Isca Leg. II Aug.

properties.image_credit: Artist's impression of the Roman amphitheatre at Isca (Caerleon), Legio II Augusta fortress · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_english: Camp of Legio II Traiana Fortis (Judaea)
properties.modern_location: Kefar 'Otnay / Legio junction, near Megiddo, Israel
properties.notes: Legio II Traiana Fortis was raised by Trajan c. 101-105 CE for the Dacian Wars and fought in his Parthian campaign (114-117). Multiple sources place it 'in Iudaea, to ensure peace' specifically in 117 CE, immediately after the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt (115-117) — i.e. present in the same province, and very plausibly the same Jezreel Valley camp at Caparcotna/Legio, as VI Ferrata (see that entry) during this transitional year. GENUINE UNCERTAINTY: the legion's permanent post-117 home was Nicopolis near Alexandria, Egypt, but sources disagree on whether it arrived there by c. 119-120 or only by 125 CE. Pinned here at the Judaean camp for the 117 CE snapshot specifically, distinct from its later Egyptian base (not shown, since it postdates 117).
properties.image_credit: Excavation of the Roman legionary camp at Legio/Kefar Otnay, near Tel Megiddo (garrisoned by Legio II Traiana Fortis) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio III Augusta is the only legion in Africa, and by 117 CE it is at Lambaesis in the northern foothills of the Aurès. It had moved up from Ammaedara to Theveste under Vespasian and on to Lambaesis around 100 CE, each step pushing the garrison closer to the mountain and desert country of the Musulamii, whose seasonal movements Rome wanted watched and taxed. The camp at this date is earth and timber. The great stone fortress, and the parade ground where Hadrian addressed the assembled troops in a speech they cut into a pillar, come later, in the 120s.
properties.image_credit: The Praetorium of Lambaesis, headquarters of Legio III Augusta, Tazoult, Algeria · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio III Cyrenaica moved from Egypt to garrison the newly annexed province of Arabia (106 CE) after Trajan's peaceful annexation of the Nabataean kingdom, founding a fortress at Bostra, the new provincial capital. GENUINE UNCERTAINTY FOR THE 117 CE SNAPSHOT: sources indicate the legion (or a large detachment) was pulled back to Egypt around 116-117 CE to help suppress the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt, is attested together with XXII Deiotariana in Egypt in 119 CE, and only clearly returned to Bostra c. 120-127 CE. It is therefore genuinely unclear whether the legion's main body was physically at Bostra or in Egypt at the exact moment of Trajan's death in August 117. Pinned at Bostra as its official provincial post (both immediately before and after this disruption).
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre at Bostra (Busra al-Sham), seat of Legio III Cyrenaica · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio III Gallica, an old Caesarian-era legion long stationed in Syria, was based at Raphanaea (modern Rafniye) in the Orontes valley through the late Republic and into the imperial period, continuing under Trajan and Hadrian. The site is only lightly excavated (limited visible remains, walled-enclosure traces from 1930s aerial survey), so the coordinate is a settlement-level approximation rather than an excavated principia point.
properties.image_credit: Oblique aerial view of the Raphanée (Raphanaea) region, Hama Governorate, Syria — Institut français du Proche-Orient (Ifpo) archive · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio IV Flavia Felix (Singidunum)
properties.notes: Legio IV Flavia Felix was raised by Vespasian in 70 CE from the cadre of the disbanded IV Macedonica, and was moved to Singidunum (modern Belgrade) by Domitian in 86 CE to shore up the Danube frontier after the Dacian invasion that destroyed V Alaudae. Its fortress, the first stone fort at Belgrade, had ramparts up to 3 meters thick with corner and interval towers. German occupation troops first excavated part of its northwest rampart and ditch during the Second World War; postwar digs by archaeologists Marko Popovic and Dragoljub Bojovic, within today's Kalemegdan park, uncovered the fort's northwest and southeast gates. It remained Singidunum's garrison through 117 CE and for centuries after (into the 5th century).

ancient_sources.author: Priscus of Panium
ancient_sources.ref: fragment on the 441 CE Hunnic invasion
ancient_sources.note: Priscus, a 5th-century Byzantine historian, names Singidunum among the Danube cities sacked by Attila's Huns in 441 CE, alongside Viminacium and Margus — a genuine literary description, though written centuries after 117 CE.

properties.image_credit: Kalemegdan Fortress, Belgrade, built over the Singidunum legionary fortress (Legio IV Flavia Felix) · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.notes: Legio IV Scythica was stationed at Zeugma, guarding the strategic Euphrates crossing on the Syria-Parthia frontier, from 66 CE onward for roughly a century, including through Trajan's Parthian War (114-117), in which the legion took part. Recent excavation (Zeugma archaeological project) places the actual legionary camp on the plateau west of the town proper (the 'Meydani' sector), rather than directly on the riverbank city site itself; the point given here marks the town/site as commonly plotted, with that camp-vs-town nuance noted.
properties.image_credit: Roman mosaic from Zeugma (Legio IV Scythica garrison town), Zeugma Mosaic Museum, Gaziantep · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio V Macedonica, veteran of Trajan's Dacian Wars, marched to Troesmis on the lower Danube in 107 CE to guard against the Roxolani Sarmatians and the Black Sea Greek cities' hinterland. Its earthen and timber fortress covered most of the plateau overlooking the river, a stretch later subdivided between two separate stone fortresses once the legion moved on. Around its walls grew a canabae, a civilian settlement of traders and veterans' families governed by its own annually elected magistrates and quinquennial officials, attested in inscriptions the soldiers left behind. The legion remained based at Troesmis through 117 CE and on into the 160s, though a vexillation was pulled east that same year for Trajan's Parthian campaign.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of Moesia Inferior lists Troesmis among the region's towns with coordinates — a bare place-name entry.

properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Troesmis legionary fortress, Romania, base of Legio V Macedonica · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio VI Ferrata was brought into Judaea as its second permanent legion (alongside X Fretensis at Jerusalem) in the aftermath of the Kitos War, founding a camp on a hill above the Jezreel Valley near Kefar 'Otnay/Caparcotna (which gave the later settlement its name, 'Legio', and eventually modern Lajjun/Megiddo). Sources consistently cite 117 CE for this establishment, though the user's brief flags — and archaeological/epigraphic work (Tel Aviv University/Jezreel Valley Regional Project excavations) leaves open — that the stone fortress construction and full garrison strength may date slightly later, c. 117-120 CE, into Hadrian's reign. May have briefly overlapped in the area with II Traiana Fortis (see separate entry) during this same transitional year before that legion moved on toward Egypt.
properties.image_credit: Excavation of the Legio VI Ferrata camp at Legio/Kefar Otnay, near Tel Megiddo · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio VI Victrix came up from Novaesium to the single-legion fortress at Vetera on the lower Rhine around the turn of the century, and it is still there in 117 CE. With Legio X Gemina downriver it holds this stretch of the frontier, quiet enough by now that the veterans' colony beside it is the busier place. In 122 Hadrian takes the legion to Britain to build the wall that carries his name, and Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix moves into the empty fortress behind it — five years after the date of this map.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tacitus gives an extended narrative of the siege of the legionary camp at Vetera during the Batavian revolt, covering Civilis's blockade, the failed relief efforts, and the garrison's eventual surrender.

properties.image_credit: Reconstructed Roman amphitheatre, Archaeological Park Xanten (Vetera), Legio VI Victrix base · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Legio VII Claudia had been in the Moesian theatre since the mid-1st century and became the fixed garrison and namesake military anchor of Viminacium once Domitian split Moesia into two provinces in 86 CE, with Viminacium as Moesia Superior's capital and governor's seat. The legion was still there in 117 CE (Viminacium was elevated toward municipium status right around Hadrian's accession) and remained for centuries.

ancient_sources.author: Priscus of Panium
ancient_sources.ref: fragment on the 441 CE Hunnic invasion
ancient_sources.note: Priscus describes the Huns under Attila destroying Viminacium in 441 CE, naming the city directly among the Danube settlements sacked — written centuries after 117 CE.

properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of the Viminacium legionary fortress, Serbia, base of Legio VII Claudia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio VIII Augusta made Argentorate its permanent base from around 90 CE, guarding a strategic Rhine crossing at what is now Strasbourg, and the legion never really left, remaining garrisoned here for over three centuries. Excavations beneath the Place du Chateau, four meters under the modern street, uncovered the canabae legionis, the sprawling civilian quarter of shops and huts that grew up around the fortress to house merchants, craftsmen, and soldiers' families, along with painted wall fragments from the house of a Roman officer. By 117 CE the defenses were being reinforced as part of a broader strengthening of the German limes. Two and a half centuries later, this same ground hosted one of the Late Empire's decisive battles, when Julian's army crushed the Alamanni here in 357 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Ammianus gives a detailed narrative of the 357 CE Battle of Argentoratum (Strasbourg) between Julian's Roman army and the Alamanni, fought at this fortress site.

properties.image_credit: Roman legionary tombstone found at Koenigshoffen, the Argentoratum fortress site (Strasbourg), Musee archeologique de Strasbourg · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio IX Hispana founded the legionary fortress at Eboracum (York) in 71 CE and was recorded rebuilding it in stone in 107-108 CE. It was still based there in 117 CE; a later, much-debated tradition (going back to Mommsen) has the legion wiped out fighting a Brigantian/Caledonian uprising around 117-120 CE, but this is now widely doubted — inscriptions from Nijmegen suggest elements of IX Hispana were redeployed to the Rhine by c. 120 CE rather than destroyed, with the legion's actual disappearance from the record more plausibly explained by later events (a Rhine posting, or loss during the Parthian War of Lucius Verus or the Bar Kokhba Revolt). FLAGGED PER BRIEF: this entry reflects only the well-attested 117 CE status (still garrisoned at York); its subsequent fate is a genuine, unresolved scholarly dispute, not a 117 CE fact.
properties.image_credit: The Multangular Tower, surviving corner of the Eboracum (York) legionary fortress walls, Legio IX Hispana base · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio X Fretensis garrisoned the ruins of Jerusalem continuously from the city's destruction in 70 CE, encamped on the southwestern hill (the former Herodian Upper City), incorporating the Phasael/Hippicus/Mariamne towers of Herod's palace into its camp wall. It was still Jerusalem's sole legionary garrison in 117 CE; the refoundation of the city as the colony Aelia Capitolina is usually dated c. 130 CE under Hadrian (one late source, Epiphanius, gives 117, but mainstream scholarship treats that as a chronological error), so at the 117 CE snapshot this is still a legionary camp on Jerusalem's ruins, not yet the colonia.

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Titus levels the city but leaves the towers and part of the west wall standing, to quarter the Tenth Legion behind and to show what had been taken.

properties.image_credit: Phasael Tower, Citadel of Jerusalem, used as the Legio X Fretensis camp headquarters after 70 CE · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

properties.notes: Legio X Gemina, long stationed at Noviomagus (Nijmegen) in Germania Inferior from 71 to 103 CE, was transferred east to Aquincum and then to a new permanent fortress at Vindobona (Vienna) in 114 CE, where it remained the garrison through 117 CE and for centuries afterward. The fortress covered some 20 hectares and housed roughly 6,000 men on the ground where Vienna's first district now stands. Around its walls grew the canabae legionis, a sprawling settlement of traders, veterans, and soldiers' families that would later be granted municipal rights as a full town in the early third century. In 117 CE the legion anchored the Danube frontier here, its watch posts facing the Marcomanni and Quadi across the river.

ancient_sources.author: Aurelius Victor
ancient_sources.note: Aurelius Victor states that Marcus Aurelius died at Vindobona in 180 CE — though other ancient authors instead give Sirmium, so the site of his death is itself disputed among ancient sources.

properties.image_credit: Roman excavation site at Hoher Markt, Vienna (Vindobona), Legio X Gemina fortress · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio XI Claudia carries its title from the revolt of 42 CE, when it stayed loyal to Claudius. It transferred from Brigetio to Durostorum on the lower Danube sometime between 104 and 114, and in 117 CE it garrisons the fortress there, watching the river crossings against the Getae and the Roxolani beyond. It will still be at Durostorum three centuries later. A civilian town has grown along the road outside the walls, and the legion's veterans settle in it rather than going home.

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Ammianus names Durostorum in his geographic survey of the lower Danube/Black Sea region; Ptolemy's Geography also lists the town among Moesia Inferior's settlements.

properties.image_credit: Panorama of the ruins of the Durostorum Roman fortress, Silistra, Bulgaria, base of Legio XI Claudia · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY)

properties.notes: Legio XII Fulminata was posted to Melitene on the upper Euphrates after the First Jewish-Roman War (from 71-72 CE), guarding the crossing into Armenia and the end of the road east from Caesarea. It took part in Trajan's Armenian campaign (114) and remained based at Melitene through 117 CE and for centuries after (attested there in the Notitia Dignitatum). The legionary fortress itself has never been conclusively excavated: archaeologists presume it lies beneath modern Eski Malatya, but the fortification walls still standing there today were built centuries later, under Justinian, so no confirmed trace of the Roman-period camp has yet been found.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Tacitus describes Corbulo massing allied cavalry, infantry, and legionary detachments at Melitene before crossing the Euphrates into Armenia during the Parthian War of the early 60s CE.

properties.notes: Legio XIII Gemina stayed behind in newly conquered Dacia after Trajan's Second Dacian War, founding its fortress at Apulum, modern Alba Iulia, in 106-108 CE and becoming the province's senior garrison. Enclosing roughly 37 hectares behind walls some 750 by 500 meters, it ranks as the largest legionary fortress ever built in Romania. Excavations in its southeastern sector in 2010 uncovered a bronze breastplate scratched with a graffito of the goddess Victoria, alongside stamped roof tiles naming individual soldiers of the legion, the first such personal epigraphy found in Dacia. The fortress remained Dacia's principal legionary base through 117 CE, even as detachments were pulled away for Trajan's simultaneous Parthian campaign of 115-117.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's gazetteer of Dacia lists Apulum among the province's towns with coordinates — a bare place-name entry.

properties.image_credit: Porta Principalis Dextra, gate of the Apulum legionary fortress, Alba Iulia, Legio XIII Gemina base · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio XIV Gemina was sent to Pannonia in 92 CE to replace the destroyed XXI Rapax, initially camping at Vindobona, then relocated to Carnuntum after Trajan's Dacian Wars. Sources vary on the precise year of the Carnuntum move (given variously as 106, 114, or 117-118), but agree the legion was there by, or essentially at, the 117 CE snapshot and remained for the next three centuries as the provincial capital's garrison and headquarters of the Pannonian fleet.
properties.image_credit: Heidentor triumphal arch at Carnuntum, near the Legio XIV Gemina legionary fortress · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Legio XV Apollinaris fought in Trajan's Parthian War (114-117) and was in Egypt in the war's immediate aftermath; scholarship on its movements (Speidel) dates its departure for its new permanent post at Satala, on the Cappadocian-Armenian frontier, to around August 117 CE (i.e., essentially at Trajan's death/Hadrian's accession), arriving and establishing its castrum stativum there by summer 118. At the exact 117 CE snapshot the legion was thus most likely already marching toward, or just arriving at, Satala rather than fully garrisoned in its permanent stone fortress — flagged accordingly.
properties.image_credit: Surviving fortress-wall remains at Satala, Sadak, Turkey, base of Legio XV Apollinaris · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio XX Valeria Victrix (Chester)
properties.notes: Deva was first built by Legio II Adiutrix around 70 CE, but II Adiutrix left Britain in the mid-80s and Legio XX Valeria Victrix took over the fortress around 88 CE, rebuilding it in local sandstone. At roughly 20 percent larger than any other legionary base in Britain, Deva stood out further for a unique elliptical building discovered in 1939 behind the modern market hall: two oval structures, one built atop the other, each with its own bathhouse and storerooms, found nowhere else in the Roman army. The oversized scale fed a longstanding theory that Rome intended to launch an invasion of Ireland from here, or even make Deva the future capital of the province. XX Valeria Victrix remained Deva's garrison through 117 CE and for the following two centuries.

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Ptolemy's Geography lists Deva among the towns of the Cornovii and explicitly identifies it as the camp of Legio XX Victrix.

properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre at Deva (Chester), base of Legio XX Valeria Victrix · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

properties.modern_location: Sidi Gaber area, east Alexandria, Egypt
properties.notes: Legio XXII Deiotariana (descended from client-king Deiotarus of Galatia's forces, absorbed by Augustus) was one of Egypt's two permanent legions, based with III Cyrenaica at the double-legion fortress of Nicopolis just east of Alexandria. Elements were used to suppress the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt in Egypt and Cyrenaica (115-117), so the legion (or most of it) was in the immediate Alexandria area through 117 CE; it is attested there again with III Cyrenaica in 119. It was later destroyed or disbanded during the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132-136 CE), long after this map's snapshot. No visible remains of the fortress survive and its precise footprint is unexcavated, so the point is a settlement-level approximation.
properties.image_credit: Richard Pococke's 1743 plan of the castrum at Nicopolis, Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 18th-century engraved plan showing the Roman castrum at Nicopolis near Alexandria

properties.notes: Legio XXII Primigenia, raised by Caligula in 39 CE, was stationed at Mogontiacum (Mainz) from 92 CE onward (having shared earlier Rhine postings with other legions), guarding the Rhine and the Mainz bridge. Recent excavation has traced the fortress through at least three building phases, from a wood-and-earth predecessor camp dated to around 17 BCE — one of the earliest Roman military sites on the Rhine — through to the stone-walled fortress standing in Trajan's day. It remained Mainz's garrison through 117 CE and for the following two centuries; the future emperor Hadrian served as one of its military tribunes in 97-98 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Cassius Dio recounts the revolt of Lucius Antonius Saturninus, governor of Germania Superior, who rose against Domitian at Mogontiacum in 89 CE with the two legions stationed there.

properties.image_credit: Roman legionary tombstone from Mogontiacum (Mainz), Landesmuseum Mainz, fortress city of Legio XXII Primigenia · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix (Brigetio)
properties.notes: Trajan raised Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix for the Dacian wars — the thirtieth legion, hence the number, and Ulpia for his own family name. When Legio XI Claudia left Brigetio for Durostorum on the lower Danube, XXX Ulpia Victrix took the vacated Pannonian fortress in 105 CE, and it holds the place through the whole of 117. It moves on only in 122, to Vetera on the Rhine, as part of a three-way shuffle: Hadrian sends Vetera's Legio VI Victrix across to Britain to build his wall, and Legio I Adiutrix comes back from the East to reclaim Brigetio.
properties.image_credit: Plan of the Brigetio legionary fortress, Komarom, later base of Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Misenum was home to the classis Misenensis, the senior fleet of the Roman navy, founded by Augustus in 27 BCE to command the western Mediterranean. Up to 10,000 sailors and marines were based on the peninsula, drawing fresh water from the vast vaulted cistern known as the Piscina Mirabilis. Pliny the Elder commanded the fleet from here in 79 CE and sailed from this harbor to his death during the eruption of Vesuvius. In 2023 archaeologists uncovered a monumental harborside villa believed to belong to the fleet's prefect.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Sets out the standing fleets of the empire — one at Misenum for the western sea, one at Ravenna for the Adriatic.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: His uncle is in command of the fleet at Misenum when Vesuvius erupts, and orders the ships out towards the shore to take people off.

properties.image_credit: The Piscina Mirabilis cistern, Bacoli, which supplied the Misenum fleet · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Interior of the Piscina Mirabilis, the great cistern that supplied the Roman fleet at Misenum

properties.notes: Classe was the harbor of the classis Ravennas, the second of Augustus's two main Italian fleets, guarding the Adriatic. The base held up to 250 ships and 10,000 marines, linked to Ravenna itself and to the Po by the Fossa Augusta canal, with naval yards and docks stretching some 22 kilometers along the waterway. Silting has since pushed the coastline nine kilometers east of the ancient shoreline.

Forum Iulii's stone harbor, nicknamed Claustra Maris or Sea Bolt, was built by Octavian after Actium as a third great naval base alongside Misenum and Ravenna, guarding the northwest Mediterranean. Its fleet, the classis Gallica, stayed active through the Julio-Claudian era but lost its standing amid the civil wars of 69 CE, after which its ships were reassigned toward Misenum and the Adriatic. The hexagonal harbor basin, once ringed by warehouses and now landlocked more than a kilometer from the sea, still survives as the Lanterne d'Auguste monument marking its ancient entrance.

Founded in 30 BCE after Actium to guard Rome's most vital grain route, the classis Alexandrina escorted the Alexandrian corn fleet across the Mediterranean and patrolled the Nile. Its Liburnian biremes moored in the Great Harbor below the royal quarter on the Lochias peninsula, close by the Pharos lighthouse that already marked the port for the ancient world. Command fell to a procurator paid 60,000 sesterces a year, one rung above ordinary fleet prefects, reflecting Alexandria's importance to the grain supply. Unusually for a Roman fleet, its rowers had to hold Alexandrian or full Roman citizenship rather than being drawn from the wider Egyptian population, a filter meant to keep the corn route in trusted hands. It still sailed unbroken in 117 CE.

Seleucia Pieria served as the seaport of Antioch and home of the classis Syriaca, the Roman navy's main eastern fleet. Vespasian rebuilt the harbor around 70 CE with an inner and outer basin fed by a canal cut partly through solid rock, a feat of engineering still visible today as the Titus Tunnel, designed to flush silt from the port entrance.

Gesoriacum was the Channel headquarters of the classis Britannica, the fleet Claudius built to launch and then supply the conquest of Britain from 43 CE onward. The fortified port sat on the cliff above the Liane estuary, doubling as the customs post for cross-Channel trade and the usual embarkation point for emperors and officials bound for Britannia. A tall lighthouse crowned that same cliff, built around 39 CE on Caligula's orders according to Suetonius — a rare structure predating the fleet itself. Known later as the Tour d'Ordre, it still guided ships in 117 CE and kept working for over a millennium more before coastal erosion finally toppled it into the sea in 1644.

Founded in 12 BCE by Drusus at Castra Vetera to support his campaigns beyond the Rhine, the classis Germanica moved south around 30 CE to a new base at Alteburg, a fort on a low bluff south of Cologne, then the largest of Rome's provincial navies. More than a thousand marines were garrisoned here, organized into centuries under trierarchs and commanded overall by an equestrian praefectus classis answering directly to the provincial governor. Its standard vessel was the Liburnian galley, a fast two-banked warship built for river patrol rather than the open sea. The fleet policed the Rhine from the Rhine-Meuse delta up past the legionary fortresses, keeping supply lines and dispatches moving. In 117 CE it remained Rome's principal instrument of control over the river.

Taurunum stood at the meeting point of the Sava and Danube rivers and served as the main base of the classis Flavia Pannonica, the fleet that patrolled the upper and middle Danube from Regensburg down to Belgrade. Tradition traces its origins to Augustus's Pannonian campaigns around 35 BCE, and the fleet is certainly attested by 45 CE, earning the honorific Flavia under the later Flavian emperors. When Trajan split Pannonia into two provinces in 107 CE, the fleet was formally assigned to Pannonia Inferior with its permanent base fixed here at Taurunum. Flotillas based at this river junction ferried troops and supplies to the string of forts strung along the Danube frontier.

Noviodunum guarded the last narrow crossing of the Danube before the river fans into its delta and the Black Sea beyond. Rome took the site in 46 CE, and it grew into the most important military and commercial town on this stretch of the frontier, eventually rising to municipium status. It headquartered the classis Flavia Moesica, the fleet that policed the lower Danube from the Iron Gates to Crimea, and gained extra importance as a logistics hub during Trajan's Dacian campaigns; the fleet's two-banked liburnian galleys, ferrying troops and supplies across the river, are carved into the reliefs of Trajan's Column in Rome, the clearest surviving picture of what its ships actually looked like.

Pike Hill stood on high ground overlooking the Stanegate road, one of a chain of signal towers built in the early second century to watch the frontier before Hadrian's Wall existed. Its foundations run unusually deep for a 6-meter-square tower, suggesting real height, and the site kept turning up soldiers' gear into the fourth century. When the Wall was built two decades later, its line was bent slightly off-axis just to incorporate this older tower.

ancient_sources.author: Historia Augusta
ancient_sources.note: Records Hadrian's construction of an eighty-mile wall across Britain to separate Romans from barbarians, the frontier system this tower belonged to.

properties.notes: Set on the western end of an Iron Age hillfort above Vindolanda, this signal post let the Stanegate garrison relay messages by direct line of sight to Housesteads and Vindolanda, predating Hadrian's Wall by decades. Excavations in 1939 and again in 1950 uncovered a limestone-flagged rampart base 4.2 meters wide, cut directly into the older Iron Age earthwork it reused. The 1950 dig also found a small oven in the hillfort's northeast corner along with quantities of first-century Roman pottery and charcoal, evidence of a manned watch rather than a bare tower. In 117 CE the post remained active, part of the frontier's still-forming signal network, years before the Wall replaced it with a fixed line of stone.

Mains Rigg's watch tower sat roughly halfway between the Stanegate forts at Nether Denton and Throp, its turf-covered stone footings tracing a tower about six and a half meters square with walls a meter thick. It formed part of the relay of signal posts that let messages travel the length of the frontier road faster than any horse could ride it.

Watchtower 4/49 stood on the Wetterau stretch of the Limes Germanicus, part of a chain of roughly nine hundred wooden lookout posts spaced under a kilometer apart along the cleared frontier road between the Rhine and the Danube. Its original timber tower predates Hadrian's later wooden palisade by two decades; a full-scale reconstruction now stands on the excavated stone footings near Giessen.

properties.modern_location: Chesterholm, near Bardon Mill, Northumberland, England
properties.notes: Vindolanda anchored the Stanegate frontier decades before Hadrian's Wall was built alongside it. Its timber-and-turf forts were rebuilt at least nine times, and the waterlogged ground beneath preserved hundreds of ink writing tablets from around 100 CE, including a soldier's letter recording the oldest known handwritten Latin by a woman, Claudia Severa's birthday invitation to a friend. Archaeologist Robin Birley found the first tablets in March 1973 while digging a drainage ditch outside the stone fort's southwest corner, and went on to direct excavations at the site for nearly fifty years. More than 1,700 Vindolanda tablets are now held in the British Museum, with new ones still turning up as digging continues each season.

ancient_sources.author: Claudia Severa
ancient_sources.note: A birthday invitation from the wife of a nearby commander, written on wood in the 90s CE — the earliest known writing in a woman's hand in Latin.

properties.image_credit: The excavated fort and vicus at Vindolanda · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Aerial view of the excavated Roman fort and civilian settlement at Vindolanda
Excavated remains of Corbridge Roman fort and town
properties.image_credit: Corbridge Roman Site (Coria), Northumberland · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Corbridge guarded the point where the Stanegate road crossed the River Tyne, on the main route north into Scotland. A Trajanic coin sealed beneath its rampart dates this second fort on the site to 103 CE or later, built just as Trajan was pulling troops out of Britain for his second Dacian campaign. The fort later grew into one of the best-supplied garrison towns on the whole northern frontier.

ancient_sources.author: Antonine Itinerary
ancient_sources.note: Lists the station Corstopitum (Corbridge) on the road route through northern Britain, situated between Vindomora and Bremenium.

properties.notes: This small fortlet guarded the crossing where the Stanegate road forded Haltwhistle Burn, holding a single century of about eighty men behind an earth rampart faced with a stone wall roughly three feet thick. Antiquarians J. P. Gibson and F. G. Simpson excavated it carefully in 1907-08, measuring the interior at about 212 feet long by a mean 185 feet wide, wider at its east end than its west. It was one of the first fortlets built anywhere in Roman Britain, part of a new tactic of splitting garrisons into small posts to watch the frontier road closely.
properties.image_credit: Site plan of the Haltwhistle Burn fortlet, 2nd century · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological site plan of the Haltwhistle Burn Roman fortlet

properties.notes: Throp's fortlet sat on a spur above the Poltross Burn, its square turf-and-stone ramparts enclosing barely a quarter of a hectare. Like its sister post at Haltwhistle Burn, its whole purpose was watching a single river crossing on the Stanegate road, decades before Hadrian's Wall's own milecastles took over the job a few hundred meters to the north. F. G. Simpson excavated the fortlet for the Cumberland and Westmorland Antiquarian and Archaeological Society in 1910, uncovering timber gateways and a paved interior. Pottery from the dig showed it was first garrisoned during the building of Hadrian's Wall, then briefly reoccupied in the 4th century.
sources: Transactions of the Cumberland and Westmorland Antiquarian and Archaeological Society, n.s. vol. 13 (1913)
properties.image_credit: Site plan of the Throp fortlet · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological site plan of the Throp Roman fortlet

properties.notes: Newbrough's fortlet sat on the Stanegate road between Corbridge and Vindolanda, roughly equidistant from both, its earthwork enclosure measuring about 195 by 190 feet and holding a small garrison of around 160 men. It went up around 103 CE, when Rome pulled back from Scotland and the Stanegate became the de facto frontier, with Newbrough built alongside Magnis and Brampton Old Church to cover the road at half-day marching intervals. St Peter's church now occupies the site of its later stone-built successor in the village churchyard. The site has been excavated only once, in 1930, leaving much of its interior layout still unrecorded.
properties.image_credit: Site plan of the Roman forts at Newbrough · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological site plan of the Newbrough Roman fortlets

properties.notes: Boothby's fortlet, also known as Castle Hill, overlooked the River Irthing from a scarp edge, built in the late first or early second century when the river itself still marked the edge of Roman control in this sector. It belonged to the Stanegate frontier system alongside the confirmed fortlets at Haltwhistle Burn and Throp. A single ditch and clay rampart enclosed just under half a hectare, big enough for a small detachment watching the crossing below. Aerial photography revealed below-ground traces later confirmed by limited excavation under F.G. Simpson in 1933, though a landslip has since carried away part of the northern half of the site. In 117 CE the fortlet still anchored this stretch of the Stanegate line, five years before Hadrian's Wall would be built a few miles north and make the position obsolete.

properties.modern_location: Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, Germany
properties.notes: The Saalburg guarded a key pass through the Taunus hills on the Limes Germanicus, built up from earlier Domitianic earthworks into a timber-and-earth numerus fort around 90 CE. It housed roughly 160 auxiliary troops through Trajan's reign. Hadrian rebuilt it in stone as a full cohort fort a generation later, and it stands today as the most completely reconstructed Roman fort anywhere on the former frontier.
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed Porta Praetoria, Saalburg Fort · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Reconstructed main gate of the Saalburg Roman fort

properties.notes: Zugmantel sat on the western Taunus stretch of the limes, built under the Flavians around 90 CE as a small numerus fort of just 0.7 hectares, later enlarged to 2.1 hectares and rebuilt in stone through four distinct phases over the century and a half it stayed garrisoned. Units posted here included the Numerus Treverorum and, later, the mounted Cohors I Treverorum equitata. It anchored one end of a dense chain of wooden watchtowers running through the forest toward Saalburg, and its surrounding vicus grew large enough to support two amphitheaters, whose earthwork banks are still traceable in the forest today. The site has carried UNESCO World Heritage status since 2005.
properties.image_credit: Kastell Zugmantel archaeological site · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains at the Zugmantel Roman fort site

properties.notes: Arnsburg held the northernmost bend of the limes as it curved through the Wetterau plain, built under Domitian before 90 CE to anchor the frontier's most exposed salient. A cohort of auxiliary infantry, the Cohors I Aquitanorum, was based here for the better part of two centuries, watching the open farmland beyond the frontier line. Excavations begun in 2020 in the fort's southern cemetery uncovered a richly furnished bustum burial, a grave where the body was cremated directly in the pit it was buried in, which archaeologists identify as the grave of one of the cohort's own commanding officers. The exceptional grave goods recovered there have opened a rare window onto funerary ritual on this stretch of the northern Wetterau frontier.
properties.image_credit: Aerial view of the Arnsburg fort site · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Aerial photograph of the Roman fort site at Arnsburg

properties.notes: Echzell was one of the largest auxiliary forts on the Wetterau limes, its earth-and-timber defenses enclosing more than five hectares on the edge of the modern village that still bears its name. Cavalry units including the Ala Moesica, Ala I Flavia gemina, and Ala I Indiana Gallorum garrisoned it in turn, watching the open frontier plain that Domitian's campaigns against the Chatti had brought under Roman control a decade earlier. Excavators recovered painted wall fragments from the fort's headquarters building and from an officer's dining room, now on display at the Saalburg museum, and traced the fort's own bathhouse beneath the cellar of the modern Protestant parish church that stands on part of the site today.
properties.image_credit: Bathhouse remains, Echzell Roman fort · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the fort bathhouse at Echzell

properties.notes: Markobel held the southeastern end of the Wetterau limes near where it met the Main valley. Pottery finds and brick stamps from Legio XIIII Gemina, withdrawn from Mainz to the Danube around 97 CE, point to an early foundation date under Domitian or Trajan, making it one of the first forts built along this stretch of frontier. Its stone fort measured about 198 by 164.5 meters (3.3 hectares), close in size to the fort at Saalburg — big enough that archaeologists infer a mounted garrison, either a cohors equitata or a 500-strong ala, though no surviving inscription names the actual unit stationed there.
properties.image_credit: Bathhouse of Kastell Marköbel, Limes survey (ORL) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman bathhouse remains at the Markobel fort

properties.notes: Ruckingen held the southeastern corner of the Wetterau limes where it met the River Kinzig, its roughly 140 by 180 meter stone walls replacing an older fort at Salisberg six kilometers southwest as the frontier line moved forward. Garrison was Cohors III Dalmatarum pia fidelis, a 500-strong infantry unit raised in Roman Dalmatia. Archaeological dating places construction somewhere between 110 and 125 CE, a window that straddles Trajan's death on 11 August 117 CE. The site's bathhouse was already being excavated as early as 1802-04, making it one of the earliest Roman military sites dug in the region. Since the fort cannot be confirmed complete by that date, it is marked absent from this snapshot rather than assumed finished.

Kapersburg sheltered a mounted scout unit on the Taunus limes, in front of a hill the locals called the Sow's Head. While a Roman military presence in this sector goes back to the first century, the numerus fort whose stone walls are visible today belongs to the limes reinforcement of the later second century, after Trajan's death, so it is excluded from this 117 CE snapshot pending firmer dating of an earlier phase.
properties.image_credit: Stone building remains, Kapersburg fort · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Stone foundations at the Kapersburg Roman fort

properties.notes: Munningen anchored the Alblimes, the chain of forts Domitian pushed north of the Danube into the Nordlinger Ries basin after his Chattian campaigns, and excavations date its founding to around 90 CE, among the earliest Roman military footholds in this stretch of Raetia. The earth-and-timber fort covered 2.7 hectares, built to house a five-hundred-strong auxiliary cohort with a mounted contingent. Antiquarians first identified the site in 1906, and further excavations in 1930 and 1971 traced its ramparts and uncovered wooden barrel- and box-built wells from the vicus that grew up alongside them. That civilian settlement went on to outlast the fort's own garrison, continuing as a roadside community after the soldiers themselves had moved elsewhere.

Biriciana was raised in timber around 90 CE to hold the ground Domitian had newly won north of the Danube, garrisoning roughly three hectares behind earth ramparts. The fort was rebuilt in stone in the mid-second century, well after the 117 CE snapshot, and its museum today displays one of the best-preserved collections of Roman cavalry parade armor ever found.
properties.image_credit: Biriciana fort remains, Weißenburg in Bayern · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman fort remains at Weißenburg, ancient Biriciana

properties.notes: Mediana was among the oldest forts on the Raetian limes, raised in wood and earth under Domitian in the late first century at the northern foot of the Hahnenkamm ridge, some six kilometers behind the frontier line it helped guard as a rear-guard post. Its ancient name survives on the Tabula Peutingeriana, the Roman road map that recorded troop stations across the empire. A military diploma confirms a cavalry cohort, the Cohors V Bracaraugustanorum, raised generations earlier in Lusitania, garrisoned here by 107 CE. Its stone rebuild, dated by inscription to 144 CE and garrisoned afterward by the Cohors III Thracum, came decades after the 117 CE snapshot, when the fort's timber-and-earth defenses and Lusitanian horsemen were still in place.
properties.image_credit: Terra sigillata pottery from Kastell Gnotzheim, Römisches Museum Weißenburg · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman terra sigillata pottery excavated at Gnotzheim fort

properties.notes: Gerulata held a bend of the Danube just downstream from Carnuntum, its earth-and-timber fort raised under Domitian in the late first century. During Trajan's reign the cavalry unit Ala I Cannanefatium took over the garrison, part of the general strengthening of the Danube frontier during the Dacian Wars. Excavations across four cemeteries and the fort's civilian quarter have recovered tombstones, altar stones, coins, and a Roman officer's helmet, its dome crushed by a hard blow, along with sandstone ballista projectiles from the vicus. In 2018, work beneath the grounds of the Rusovce manor house uncovered a 2nd-century aqueduct, the first Roman-era water supply system ever identified in Slovakia.
properties.image_credit: Gerulata archaeological site, Rusovce · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman fort site at Gerulata, Rusovce

properties.notes: Solva watched a strategic bend of the Danube on the Pannonian frontier, garrisoned by the thousand-strong Cohors I Ulpia Pannoniorum. More than twenty altars dedicated by that unit to Jupiter Optimus Maximus turned up reused as building rubble in a late Roman brick kiln near the fort, a haul that gives a rare, near-complete picture of the garrison's official religious life. The civilian settlement that grew up around the camp prospered enough that Hadrian granted it town status in 121 CE, a step that presumes a well-established fort and vicus already standing here by 117 CE, just a few years before that promotion.

Ad Maiores was built in 104 or 105 CE on the orders of Minicius Natalis, legate of the Third Augustan Legion, to anchor the desert edge of Numidia's frontier southeast of the Aures mountains at Henchir Besseriani, on the Saharan piedmont of the Nemencha massif some five kilometers south of the oasis of Negrine. Two inscriptions recorded in the Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum, CIL VIII 2478-2479, once stood on triumphal arches, one near the camp's west gate and another at a gate of the civilian settlement that grew up beside it. It marks the Trajanic-era origin of the fortified line that would later be extended and consolidated as the Fossatum Africae, and in 117 CE its garrison still watched the same stretch of desert edge.

Gemellae was the best-studied strongpoint of the Fossatum Africae, its ditch and rampart mapped in detail by aerial photography on the edge of the Sahara. French aerial archaeology pioneer Jean Baradez surveyed and partly excavated the site at mid-century, publishing his findings in Fossatum Africae (1949); he measured the fort's enclosure walls at 190 by 150 meters and its ditch cut two to three meters deep, widening toward the top. It was established around 126 CE under Hadrian, roughly a decade after Trajan's death, so it falls outside this snapshot even though it anchors the frontier system the Trajanic sections fed into.

Buridava was raised soon after Trajan's First Dacian War, part of the new chain of forts strung along the east bank of the Olt river to hold the freshly won province. Two of its auxiliary garrisons are named on finds: cohors II Flavia Bessorum and cohors IX Batavorum, part of three successive units posted there over the following decades. It briefly served as headquarters for the governor of Moesia Inferior's forces during the Dacian campaigns, complete with his personal guard, the pedites singulares. Romanian archaeologist Dumitru Berciu began excavating the site in 1950, uncovering a bronze statue of an emperor and coins ranging from Caligula's reign to Justinian's, testament to how long the settlement endured.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Castra Buridava, Stolniceni, Romania · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated remains of the Roman fort of Buridava, Stolniceni, Romania

properties.notes: Castra Traiana takes its name directly from its builder: an earthwork fort with double ditches raised between 102 and 105 CE during Trajan's Dacian Wars, part of the Limes Alutanus running up the Olt river valley in what is now Valcea County, Romania. Brick stamps from the Cohors Hispanorum mark its first garrison. Excavations carried out between 1981 and 1994 traced the eastern rampart for a stretch of nearly 70 meters and uncovered a furnace built into the fort for smelting iron ore, evidence the garrison processed its own metal on site. The fort would later be rebuilt in stone during the first half of the 2nd century, but in 117 CE its ramparts were still raw earth and timber, freshly dug during the conquest itself.

Pons Aluti controlled a crossing of the Olt river on the new Dacian frontier road, its name meaning simply Bridge over the Aluta, roughly halfway between the forts of Buridava and Castra Traiana. An inscription dated to 102 CE names it as a customs post, making it one of the earliest firmly dated points on the entire Limes Alutanus. Brick stamps from the Cohors III Gallorum mark one of its garrisons, and excavators recovered a hoard of coins cached in a corner tower on the fort's northwest side. Within a few years of 117 CE, frontier reorganization would shift a garrison unit here into the newly split province of Dacia Inferior.

Pons Vetus sat on the left bank of the Olt at the mountain gateway into Dacia, recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana and by the geographer of Ravenna as a customs station. Its name, meaning Old Bridge, points to a crossing the Romans found already standing here, built by the local Dacian population before the conquest rather than raised by Roman engineers themselves. An inscription of 102 CE naming it a statio vamalis, a customs post, places it firmly in the opening years of Trajan's Dacian frontier, and by 117 CE it had spent over a decade taxing traffic moving along the Limes Alutanus into the newly annexed province.

Rusidava held the southern stretch of the Limes Alutanus where the Olt valley opens onto the Wallachian plain, part of the same wave of fort-building that followed Trajan's conquest of Dacia. Its precise foundation year is not pinned down as tightly as its neighbors up the valley, but it belongs to the same early Trajanic chain along the river. The 4th-century Tabula Peutingeriana names Rusidava directly, placing it on the Olt valley road 24 Roman miles from Acidava and 14 miles from Pons Aluti — official confirmation of its place in the empire's Dacian road network.

Praetorium reinforced the Limes Alutanus roughly midway up the Olt valley, garrisoned by the numerus Burgariorum et Veredariorum, a unit of couriers and border guards. Built in 138 CE, it was strengthened with two additional corner towers two years later, and a civilian settlement with its own bathhouse grew up alongside it by the third century. The Olt has since eroded away roughly two-thirds of the fort, and what survives sits barely half a kilometer from its sister post, Praetorium II at Racovita. In 2024 UNESCO inscribed the site as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage listing for Dacia. Construction here postdates Trajan's death by two decades, so despite anchoring the same Trajanic-era frontier line, it did not yet exist in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Site plan of the principia of the Praetorium fort at Copaceni, Romania · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological plan of the principia (headquarters building) of the Praetorium Roman fort

properties.notes: Arutela stood on the Olt river's left bank near modern Calimanesti-Caciulata, a strongpoint on the Limes Alutanus where the valley narrows into the Carpathian foothills. It was built in 137-138 CE on the orders of Titus Flavius Constans, procurator of Dacia Inferior, and garrisoned by a numerus of Syrian archers recruited for their skill with the composite bow. Excavators uncovered an attached bath complex and a small chamber first identified as a Mithraeum, though it lacked the altars typical of Mithraic sanctuaries and more likely served another cult purpose. Despite anchoring the same river-line frontier that Trajan had begun, Arutela did not yet exist at the 117 CE snapshot; the valley crossing it would guard still lay twenty years in the future.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Roman fort of Arutela, near Calimanesti, Romania · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated walls of the Roman fort of Arutela on the Limes Alutanus

properties.notes: A small, exact temple on a podium at the head of the forum of Nemausus: six Corinthian columns across the front, the rest engaged in the wall of the shrine behind. The dedication is to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus' grandsons and intended heirs, both dead young — the building is a memorial to a succession that never happened. Its proportions were copied from the Augustan temples of Rome and cut in local limestone by local masons, which is the colonial programme in a single object. In 117 CE it is a little over a century old and in daily use at the centre of a rich Gallic city.
properties.image_credit: Maison Carrée, Nîmes · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: CIL XII 3156
ancient_sources.quote: C. Caesari Augusti f. co(n)s.; L. Caesari Augusti f. co(n)s. designato; principibus iuventutis
ancient_sources.note: Dedicated to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus's grandsons and heirs. The bronze letters are long gone; the text was reconstructed from the nail-holes that once held them.

properties.notes: Heliopolis' second great temple doesn't exist yet in 117 CE — construction won't begin for another generation, around 150 CE under Antoninus Pius, tucked behind Jupiter's colossal precinct. When it finally rises, forty-two Corinthian columns will screen a podium carved almost everywhere a chisel can reach: vines and poppies in the ceiling coffers, a doorway framed in grapes and wheat, lions' heads along the cornice. The dedicatee is usually taken to be Bacchus, though nothing on the building says so outright, and the imagery would suit the young god of the local triad just as well.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Bacchus, Baalbek · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Macrobius
ancient_sources.note: Describes the great oracular sanctuary of Jupiter Heliopolitanus at Heliopolis (Baalbek), including the prophecy the god gave Trajan in 114 CE about his Parthian campaign. The Temple of Bacchus stood within this same sacred precinct, though Macrobius does not name it separately.

properties.notes: Fifty-four columns ring this temple and each stands about twenty metres tall — the tallest in the Roman world. They rest on a podium built from limestone blocks so large that three of them, laid side by side in a single course, weigh several hundred tonnes apiece; the quarry is less than a kilometre away, and they were brought in on rollers by rope and muscle. The god is Jupiter Heliopolitanus, a Roman name laid over a much older local weather god who is still worshipped in the old way. In 117 CE the temple is finished and the vast forecourts in front of it are still being built.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Jupiter, Baalbek · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Macrobius
ancient_sources.note: Macrobius gives a detailed description of the cult of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Heliopolitanus at Heliopolis (Baalbek), including the gold cult statue said to have been brought from Egypt, its iconography, and the statue-borne oracle by which the god's will was divined, citing a 114 CE prediction to Trajan.

properties.notes: Palmyra's greatest sanctuary was dedicated on 6 April 32 CE and fills a walled precinct two hundred metres across, big enough to hold the whole civic body at festival. The temple inside quietly breaks the classical rules it borrows: the door is on the long side, and there are two shrines rather than one, at either end, the northern reached by a stair for carrying the god out in procession. Bel is worshipped here with the sun god Yarhibol and the moon god Aglibol. Ceiling beams show veiled Palmyrene women and a camel bearing a shrouded litter. In 117 CE the cult is at its height.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Bel, Palmyra (pre-2015) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Palmyra set apart by its soil and its water in a great circuit of sand, and by a position that leaves it courted by Rome and Parthia both.

properties.notes: Two thousand years of building stand on this one site, and none of it is Roman. The hypostyle hall alone carries a hundred and thirty-four columns, the tallest of them twenty-one metres, set so densely that the roof slabs need almost no span. Obelisks of Hatshepsut and Thutmose rise beyond it, and a sacred lake lies to the south. Amun-Ra has been worshipped here since the Middle Kingdom, and under Roman rule the priesthood carries on, funded and supervised from Alexandria. Emperors' names go on being cut into these walls in cartouches. In 117 CE Karnak is old, working, and the largest temple complex in the world.
properties.image_credit: Great Hypostyle Hall, Karnak · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Thebes seen as a scatter of villages among enormous temples; Strabo measures the surviving avenues of sphinxes and the halls of columns.

properties.notes: The great temple of Hathor at Tentyra rises inside a mudbrick enclosure on the west bank, its hypostyle hall carried on twenty-four sandstone columns whose capitals all wear the goddess's face. Building began around 54 BCE and never really stopped: the hall was finished under Tiberius, and in 117 CE masons are still cutting reliefs that show Roman emperors dressed and titled as pharaohs, making offerings to Egyptian gods. A birth house for Hathor's son is going up at the front of the site. Crypts below hold the cult statues, and a sanatorium beside the sacred lake takes pilgrims hoping for a cure.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Hathor, Dendera · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo describes Tentyra (Dendera) and its people's ritual hostility toward crocodiles, unlike neighboring Egyptians, and notes that at Tentyra the goddess Aphrodite (Hathor) is worshipped, with a temple of Isis behind her shrine.

properties.notes: Egypt's most complete temple sits in the middle of Apollonopolis Magna, its pylon towers rising thirty-six metres over the town. Work ran from 237 to 57 BCE, and the walls carry the fullest surviving account anywhere of how an Egyptian temple was founded, consecrated and run. The falcon god Horus of Behdet lives here, in a polished granite shrine older than the building around it. Once a year his image travels downriver to meet Hathor of Dendera; priests stage the killing of Seth as a hippopotamus in front of the crowd. In 117 CE the rituals are still kept, in Egyptian, by Egyptian priests.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Horus, Edfu · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: Plutarch describes the custom at Apollonopolis (Edfu) of hunting and ritually killing crocodiles every year and casting the carcasses down opposite the temple, explained through the myth of Typhon (Set) escaping Horus in crocodile form.

properties.notes: The temple of Athena Parthenos has stood on the Acropolis rock for five and a half centuries by 117 CE, and Rome has left it very nearly as it found it. Inside is Pheidias' Athena, twelve metres of gold and ivory, the gold plates made removable so they can be weighed as a reserve of the city's treasure. Around the top of the shrine wall runs a continuous carved procession of horsemen, girls and cattle. The one Roman mark on the building was a line of bronze letters fixed to the east front honouring Nero, taken down again after his fall; the holes are still there.
properties.image_credit: The Parthenon · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Works through the pediments — Athena's birth, her contest with Poseidon — and the gold and ivory statue standing inside with a Victory in her hand.

properties.notes: Athens' best-preserved temple stands on the low hill of Kolonos Agoraios, looking down over the Agora. It went up from about 449 BCE in Pentelic marble, six columns across the front and thirteen down each side, and it honours Hephaestus alongside Athena Ergane — the right pair for a district packed with bronze foundries and potters' workshops on the slope below. Carved panels across the east front show the labours of Herakles and the deeds of Theseus. In 117 CE it is close to six centuries old and entirely intact, one of the few Greek temples Rome found no reason to touch.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Hephaestus, Athens · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The temple above the Kerameikos holding Hephaestus and, beside him, Athena — placed together, he says, because of the story of Erichthonius.

properties.notes: The largest temple in the Peloponnese, and everything about it is scaled to the statue inside. Pheidias' Zeus sits enthroned in gold and ivory, roughly twelve metres high and so close to the ceiling that visitors come away saying the god could not stand without lifting the roof off. Olive oil is poured on the floor in front of him to keep the ivory from cracking in the damp of the Alpheios valley. The east pediment shows Pelops readying the chariot race that gave the games their founding story. Every fourth summer the sanctuary fills; in 117 CE the festival is still running on its ancient count.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Olympia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Built from the spoils of Pisa, roofed in Pentelic marble cut to look like tiles, and holding Pheidias's seated Zeus — a god who, if he stood, would take the roof off.

properties.notes: Aphrodisias took its name from its goddess, and this Ionic temple is the reason the city mattered. Columns ring the shrine eight across and thirteen deep, many of them carrying the names of the citizens who paid for them. The Julian house claimed descent from Venus, so Augustus and his successors treated the sanctuary as family business: the city holds a grant of freedom and exemption from tax, carved up on a wall in public for anyone to read. White marble from quarries an hour's walk away feeds a school of sculptors whose signed work travels the empire. In 117 CE the cult is thriving.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Aphrodite, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Aphrodisias comes before the Senate in 22 CE to defend its temple's right of asylum, producing decrees going back to the dictator Caesar.

properties.notes: The largest temple the Greeks ever attempted, and after four centuries of work it is still not finished — many of its hundred and twenty-two columns stand unfluted and the pediment was never built. You do not so much enter it as pass through it: two vaulted tunnels lead down into a roofless court where laurel grows around a spring, and a small shrine there holds the bronze Apollo. A prophetess takes the water and answers the questions the priests put to her. The paved Sacred Way running the sixteen kilometres up from Miletus was rebuilt by Trajan in 101 CE. In 117 CE the oracle is busy.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Didyma · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The temple left without a roof because of the sheer size of it, with a sacred grove inside and out, and works of art the writer rated the finest in Asia.

properties.notes: A small temple to Isis stood in Pompeii's theatre quarter, rebuilt from its foundations after the earthquake of 62 CE at the expense of a freedman's six-year-old son — the boy was enrolled in the town council in return. Steps led up to a podium shrine; behind it a sunken basin held Nile water for purification, and a side room was painted with Egyptian scenes for initiates. The cult drew servants, freedmen and women in numbers no civic temple matched. Vesuvius buried the building in 79 CE. In 117 CE it lies under several metres of ash, its walls and paintings intact and unreachable.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Isis, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 846
ancient_sources.quote: N. Popidius N. f. Celsinus aedem Isidis terrae motu conlapsam a fundamento p(ecunia) s(ua) restituit
ancient_sources.note: Numerius Popidius Celsinus, a boy of six, rebuilt the temple from its foundations at his own expense after the earthquake of 62 CE, and the council enrolled him free of charge in thanks — the money, of course, was his father's.

properties.notes: The oldest sanctuary in Pompeii stood just west of the forum, a colonnade of forty-eight columns enclosing a raised temple reached by a broad flight of steps. Worship on the spot goes back to the sixth century BCE, when Greek and Etruscan traders were already dealing along this coast. A bronze Apollo drawing his bow faced a bronze Diana across the court, and a sundial on a column kept the sanctuary's hours. Vesuvius buried the whole city in 79 CE. In 117 CE the temple lies under several metres of ash and pumice, its roof gone and its columns snapped.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 787
ancient_sources.note: The magistrates Marcus Holconius Rufus and Gaius Egnatius Postumus paid 3,000 sesterces for precinct works, by decree of the council; the text names the town 'Colonia Veneria Cornelia'.

properties.notes: The Proserpina Dam held back a reservoir north of Emerita Augusta, an earthen embankment fronted by stone buttresses that still stretches 427 meters across the valley. Water released from its sluices fed the Aqueduct of the Miracles into the city below. Roman engineers built it in the first or second century CE alongside the nearby Cornalvo dam, and it has never stopped holding water since. Local swimmers still use its reservoir as a summer bathing spot today.
properties.image_credit: Embalse de Proserpina, Mérida · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: The Cornalvo Dam still backs a reservoir east of Merida behind packed earth and rubble faced with dressed stone, standing 194 meters long and up to 24 meters high. It formed a second water source for Emerita Augusta alongside Proserpina, feeding the city through its own aqueduct and a sluice tower that still works. Most scholarship dates it to the first or second century CE, though a few Spanish studies argue for a later Hadrianic date near 130 CE. Water still flows to Merida from it today.
properties.image_credit: Roman Cornalvo dam, Extremadura · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Nero dammed the Aniene river in three places above Subiaco, creating the Simbruina Stagna lakes that fronted his 75-hectare villa in the gorge. The tallest of the three dams reached roughly 50 meters, briefly the highest dam in the Roman world, and it kept holding its lake for over a millennium after Nero's death. Even after the emperor's fall in 68 CE, the lakes stayed intact in 117 CE. The largest dam finally failed in a 1305 flood; only Lago di San Benedetto survives today.
properties.image_credit: San Benedetto, Subiaco (site of Nero's dammed lakes) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Roman engineers raised this dam across the Aguasvivas river under Augustus or Tiberius, building it 34 meters tall, the tallest Roman dam known to survive anywhere. It stored water for irrigation across the dry Aragonese plain and remained Spain's tallest dam for over 1,500 years, only surpassed in 1590. Its rubble-and-mortar core, faced with cut stone, was already a century old by 117 CE and still holding back its reservoir, showing how far provincial engineers pushed dam technology.
properties.image_credit: Roman dam at Almonacid de la Cuba · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Nabataean engineers built this dam across the Siq's mouth around the mid-first century BCE, sealing Petra's main entrance from flash floods and diverting water through a tunnel cut nearly 90 meters through rock. Standing about 13 meters high, it protected the processional approach for centuries. Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom as Arabia in 106 CE, just eleven years before this map's snapshot, so by 117 CE the dam guarded a new Roman province rather than an independent kingdom.
properties.image_credit: Petra Dam at entrance to the Siq · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sixteen waterwheels arranged in two rows down a hillside at Barbegal drove what is considered the largest concentration of mechanical power in the ancient world, grinding flour for a small city. A dedicated aqueduct branch fed the wheels in sequence, each turning a pair of millstones before passing water on.
