Carbonate deposits point to that branch being built around 120 to 130 CE, just after Trajan's death, though a Trajanic coin found on site keeps the exact date genuinely debated.
properties.image_credit: Barbegal aqueduct and mill remains, Fontvieille · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Seventeen barrel-vaulted cisterns lie beneath a colonnaded plaza at Ptolemais known as the Square of the Cisterns, together holding some 7,000 cubic meters of water for a city with no spring of its own. Roman engineers carried water in from the surrounding hills to fill them, expanding what may have begun as a smaller Hellenistic reservoir. A 2025 excavation even found a human face carved into the plaster on one wall. The system was already old and in continuous use by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ptolemais archaeological site, Tolmeita · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: At least two dozen vaulted cisterns once stood in a line at La Malga, each roughly 130 Roman paces long, storing tens of thousands of cubic meters piped in from the Zaghouan aqueduct to supply Carthage and its baths. Hadrian ordered that aqueduct built starting around 128 CE, so these cisterns could not yet have held water at this map's 117 CE snapshot. Carthage instead relied on wells and smaller cisterns at Trajan's death. The ruins, later stables, are now overgrown with fig trees.
properties.image_credit: Roman cisterns of La Malga, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Carved into volcanic tuff above Misenum, the Piscina Mirabilis held up to 12,600 cubic meters of fresh water under a vaulted roof on 48 cross-shaped pillars in five aisles. Augustus had it built between 33 and 12 BCE as the final reservoir of the Aqua Augusta, giving the navy's fleet at Misenum water for its base and ships. Sailors nicknamed it the water cathedral, and by 117 CE it had supplied the fleet for over a century. It remains one of Rome's largest cisterns.
properties.image_credit: Piscina Mirabilis, Bacoli · photo by RaBoe, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Names Misenum as home port of one of Rome's two main imperial fleets, the naval base this cistern supplied with fresh water.

properties.notes: Gaius Julius Lacer built this granite bridge across the Tagus between 104 and 106 CE, financed by eleven nearby Lusitanian towns and dedicated to Trajan. Its six arches carry the roadway 194 meters across the gorge and rise 45 meters above the water, fitted from massive blocks without mortar. An inscription boasts its builder raised a bridge that would last forever, and in 117 CE it was barely a decade old, already carrying imperial traffic. It still carries traffic nineteen centuries later.
properties.image_credit: Alcántara Bridge over the Tagus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL II 759-760
ancient_sources.quote: Imp. Caesari divi Nervae f. Nervae Traiano Aug. Germ. Dacico pontif. max. trib. potes. VIII imp. V co(n)s. V p. p.
ancient_sources.note: Twin texts on both faces of the bridge's own arch name Trajan by his full titles. A separate verse inscription nearby (CIL II 761) names the architect, Gaius Julius Lacer.

properties.notes: Apollodorus of Damascus built this bridge across the Danube in just two years, finishing in 105 CE so Trajan's legions could cross freely during the Dacian conquest. Twenty stone piers over 40 meters tall carried wooden arches spanning 1,135 meters in total, the longest bridge built anywhere for a thousand years afterward. It still stood at full length in 117 CE. Hadrian later dismantled its wooden superstructure, but the stone piers endured, and several still break the Danube's surface today.
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Bridge over the Danube, 1907 reconstruction drawing by E. Duperrex · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Twenty piers of squared stone carrying arches across the Danube — the work Dio rates above everything else Trajan built, given the depth and the current.

properties.notes: Augustus's engineers tore this mountainside apart to reach its gold, following the region's conquest in the Cantabrian Wars around 25 BCE. They channeled water for miles — a network of more than 300 kilometers of leats and channels, some single runs stretching over 100 kilometers from mountain reservoirs — before releasing it in one collapsing torrent Pliny called ruina montium. Five tons of gold came out of these red cliffs over two centuries of mining. In 117 CE the works were still running at full capacity, decades before exhaustion finally closed them.
properties.image_credit: Panoramic view of the Las Medulas mining landscape · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: The ruina montium in detail — galleries driven in, the hill brought down by its own weight, and water run in from miles off to wash the gold out of the debris.

properties.notes: Roman engineers arrived within a year of Trajan's conquest of Dacia and drove galleries deep into these gold-bearing hills, importing Illyrian miners as an entire transplanted community. Waxed writing tablets left underground recorded contracts, wages, and burial-club dues from the settlement above the shafts. By 117 CE the mine was eleven years into what became a century and a half of continuous extraction.
properties.image_credit: Roman gallery at the Rosia Montana gold mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Tabulae Ceratae Dacicae (Dacian wax tablets, private legal documents)
ancient_sources.note: A set of wax-coated wooden writing tablets recovered from Roman gold-mining galleries at Alburnus Maior (Rosia Montana) since the 19th century, recording everyday legal acts of the mining settlement: labor contracts, loan and sale agreements, and the charter of a funerary collegium. One well-known tablet records the founding statutes of the collegium of Jupiter Cernenus, naming officers whose dues funded members' funeral expenses.

properties.notes: Copper had been smelted in this valley south of the Dead Sea since the Chalcolithic, but Rome turned Phaeno into an industrial-scale operation, damming wadis to cool furnace slag by the ton. Watchtowers of dressed stone still guard the approaches to the mines. The site's grim later reputation as an exile camp for condemned Christians was still two centuries away in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at Khirbat Faynan, ancient Phaeno · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Roman engineers cut miles of leats across the Cothi valley to feed hydraulic mining at Britain's only known Roman gold mine, sluicing hillsides much as Las Medulas was worked in Spain. The longest of these channels ran roughly seven miles from the River Cothi, with a second leat drawing extra water from the River Annell to power the hushing that stripped soil from the gold-bearing rock. A fort called Luentinum stood guard nearby from around 78 CE, its garrison overseeing convict labor in the shafts until the post was abandoned around 125 CE. Mining here had been underway for more than forty years by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Pithead gear at Dolaucothi Gold Mine · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0, Geograph)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: States that Britain produces gold, silver, and other metals, the province's mineral wealth that mines such as this one extracted.

properties.notes: Copper cementation tanks at Algares turned scrap iron and mine water into usable metal on an industrial scale at this Lusitanian mining district. Bronze tablets found here preserved the actual mining code Rome used to regulate leases, wages, and bathhouse fees at state-run mines. The workings had been active for decades by 117 CE, well before Hadrian's administration later formalized the regulations found inscribed on those tablets.
sources: Claude Domergue, La mine antique d'Aljustrel (Portugal) et les tables de bronze de Vipasca, 1983
properties.image_credit: Mining landscape of the Parque Mineiro de Aljustrel · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Lex Metalli Vipascensis (anonymous, Roman imperial mining regulation)
ancient_sources.note: Two bronze tablets found at Aljustrel (ancient Vipasca) in 1876 and 1906 preserve mining regulations for an imperial metalla district. One concrete surviving provision fixes bathhouse admission fees and hours: men pay half an as and may bathe from the eighth hour until the second hour of night, while women pay a full as and bathe from daybreak to the seventh hour. The tablets also regulate leases (conductores), the status of coloni, slaves and free wage-laborers (mercenarii), and the sale or transfer of mining claims.

properties.modern_location: Charterhouse, Mendip Hills, Somerset, England, United Kingdom
properties.notes: Roman lead ingots stamped from this Somerset hillside reached the legionary fortress at Chester within six years of the invasion of Britain, making Charterhouse one of the empire's fastest industrial start-ups. Silver skimmed from the ore helped pay soldiers' wages. A small amphitheatre built for the mining workforce is the only one of its kind linked to a Roman mine anywhere in southwest Britain.
properties.image_credit: Panorama of the Charterhouse lead mines, Mendip Hills · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Notes that in Britannia lead is found so near the surface, and in such quantity, that a law had to be passed limiting how much could be produced.

properties.notes: Lead pigs stamped DECEANGL after the local tribe left this Flintshire mountain and turned up at the legionary works in Chester, proof that Rome had the district under military control within two decades of conquest. A private smelter run by one C. Nipius Ascanius operated alongside the army's own works. Both lead and its telltale traces of silver kept the mountain in production through 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: View of Halkyn Mountain · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0, Geograph)

properties.notes: Pliny called this the empire's most valuable mine for the revenue it brought the treasury, and its cinnabar ore supplied nearly all the vermilion pigment used to redden Roman walls, cosmetics, and ceremonial togas. A leasing company called the societas sisaponensis ran the works on the state's behalf. The deposit here remains the largest mercury reserve ever found on Earth.
properties.image_credit: View of Almaden, site of the ancient mercury mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Cinnabar from Sisapo is a state monopoly: the ore is sealed at the mine, refined only at Rome, and the price is fixed by law to stop adulteration.

properties.notes: Augustan-era coins turned up alongside Roman wells and Archimedes-screw drainage systems at this pyrite-belt mine, the second-largest mining basin in Huelva province after Rio Tinto. Slaves worked the galleries in punishing conditions, laboring by lamplight in heat and dust, some spending their entire lives underground turning the tiered water wheels, or noria, that lifted drainage water up through as many as nine levels to an outflow adit. Spain's mines were the empire's single largest silver source, feeding an output that peaked at roughly 200 tons of silver a year across the whole Roman world in the first and second centuries CE. Copper, iron, and silver came out of the same red-stained ground worked here for nineteen more centuries after Rome fell silent. Germanic invasions, not exhaustion, eventually shut the Roman works down.
properties.image_credit: Reservoir and slag heaps at the Tharsis mines · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.modern_location: Villanueva del Rio y Minas, Seville Province, Spain
properties.notes: Iron and copper drawn from the hills around this Baetican hill town paid for a hillside sanctuary to Fortuna and Hercules so grand it remains the largest terraced temple complex outside Italy. Rome granted Munigua municipal status under Vespasian in recognition of its wealth. Its mines kept supplying the empire with metal until a wave of closures swept Hispania's mining districts in the late second century.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Roman mining town of Munigua, Baetica · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: Preserves the emperor Titus's letter of 79 CE responding to Munigua's appeal over a civic debt, addressed directly to the town.

properties.notes: A bronze hydraulic pump recovered from these Huelva copper workings, now displayed in Madrid's national archaeological museum, shows Roman engineers draining shafts here with the same screw technology used at Rio Tinto. One surviving Archimedes screw measured 3.6 meters long and 48 centimeters across, one of a set of three installed in series to lift water stage by stage from one sump to the next, deep below the surface. Tartessian miners had worked this ground centuries before Rome arrived, and Roman-era slag heaps called teleras still mark the district today, alongside shafts that plunged far enough underground to require exactly this kind of relay pumping to keep them dry.
properties.image_credit: Roman bronze hydraulic pump from Sotiel Coronada, Museo Arqueologico Nacional · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: CIL III 25 = ILS 2612 = I.Pan 39
ancient_sources.work: Dedicatory inscription of the centurion Annius Rufus
ancient_sources.note: This inscription records that Annius Rufus, a centurion of Legio XV Apollinaris, was placed in charge of the quarrying works at Mons Claudianus by "the best emperor" Trajan.

properties.modern_location: Eastern Desert, Red Sea Governorate, Egypt
properties.notes: Named for the emperor Claudius who opened it, this Eastern Desert quarry supplied the gray granodiorite columns that still stand in the Pantheon and in Hadrian's villa at Tivoli. A fortified settlement housed the quarry workforce ninety miles from the Nile, supplied along a road guarded by watchtowers. Ostraca left by the garrison recorded rations, wages, and water deliveries in exacting detail.
properties.image_credit: View of the Mons Claudianus quarry site · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Numidian kings quarried this yellow marble a century before Julius Caesar's ally Lepidus first shipped blocks of it to Rome for his own doorsills. Augustus later paved his forum with giallo antico from these same Tunisian hills. A joint German-Tunisian excavation, running since 1965 under the German Archaeological Institute's Friedrich Rakob and Tunisia's National Heritage Institute, has uncovered the quarry town's Numidian-era royal monument alongside its Roman forum, temples, and bath complex, mapping how the settlement grew up around the marble trade. By 117 CE, Simitthus had held colonial status for nearly a century and its quarries remained under direct imperial administration.
properties.image_credit: Ancient marble quarry at Chemtou (Simitthus) · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny records that this Numidian yellow marble was first brought to Rome by the consular Lepidus, who used it for door-sills in his house — the earliest reference to the marble later called giallo antico that modern scholars trace to the Simitthus quarries.

properties.notes: Ships loaded at the nearby port of Luna carried this white and blue-grey marble to build the Pantheon, Trajan's Column, and dozens of other monuments across the capital. Large-scale quarrying began under Augustus and never really stopped for the next two centuries. More marble has come out of these Apuan Alps than any other quarry district on Earth. Each of the 19 marble drums forming Trajan's Column's shaft weighed close to 32 tons, and masons shipped roughly 1,100 tons of dressed Luna marble downriver to Rome to build that single monument.
sources: McMaster University Trajan's Column digital edition, Introductory Essays
properties.image_credit: Marble quarry (cave di marmo) at Carrara · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The quarries above Luna, worked in blocks and slabs of white and blue-grey marble, loaded straight onto ships in the harbour below for Rome.

properties.notes: A single abandoned obelisk still lies fused to its Aswan bedrock, cracked before workers could free it, and would have stood 137 feet tall had it ever been finished. Roman quarrymen reused these same pink granite pits, leaving wedge-and-water cracking marks unlike the hammer-dressed grooves of their pharaonic predecessors. Granite from here traveled the length of the Nile to build across the empire.
properties.image_credit: The Unfinished Obelisk in the Aswan granite quarries · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Marble cut from this coastal peninsula on Thasos loaded directly onto ships without ever touching a cart, a logistical advantage that kept the quarry in business for twelve straight centuries. Extraction here began in the Archaic period and only intensified as Roman demand grew. Much of the ancient quarry now lies underwater, submerged along the shoreline it once supplied by sea.
properties.image_credit: Ancient marble quarry on Thasos island · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny names Thasian marble, alongside Cycladic and Lesbian marble, among the stones ancient sculptors worked — naming Thasos as a marble source, though not describing the Aliki quarry face itself.

properties.notes: Roman soldiers built watchtowers and a fortified well along this desert road to protect greywacke quarry convoys hauling bekhen-stone the ninety miles from the Nile to the Red Sea coast. Watchtowers stood at intervals close enough for signal fires to pass from one to the next, and many still crown the barren hilltops flanking the road today. The well itself, known as Bir Hammamat, ran 34 meters deep with a winding staircase cut into its shaft so guards and travelers could reach the water table safely. Graffiti left by travelers here name emperors from Augustus to Antoninus Pius. Quarrying at Hammamat had already run for nearly three thousand years by the time Trajan died.
properties.image_credit: View of Wadi Hammamat in Egypt's Eastern Desert · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY, MediHAL)

properties.notes: A dozen salting workshops packed the shoreline of this Baetican port town, their stone vats still holding traces of the tuna-belly garum that made Baelo Claudia's fortune. Archaeologists working the site in 2015 found tuna skin fragments preserved intact in the bottom of a vat, the first such find anywhere in the empire. The Strait of Gibraltar's seasonal tuna runs kept the factories running for centuries.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Baelo Claudia, including the salting factories · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The port opposite Africa where the crossing to Tingis is made, on a stretch of coast whose towns live off tunny fishing and salting.

properties.notes: Salting tanks here could hold more than a million liters of fish at once, making Lixus the largest garum producer anywhere in the western Mediterranean. The factories sat inside the lower town gate, within sight of an amphitheatre and bathhouse the fish-salters' profits helped pay for. Production peaked under Claudius and was still running strong when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at the Lixus archaeological site · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo describes Lixus as a Mauretanian town on the Atlantic coast opposite Gades, linking it to the legendary Garden of the Hesperides and the palace of Antaeus.

properties.notes: Twenty-five separate workshops packed the Troia peninsula with 182 salting tanks between them, an industrial concentration UNESCO calls unmatched anywhere else in the Roman world. The workshops varied hugely in scale: the largest topped 1,000 square meters and held 19 tanks on its own, while the smallest ran to just 135 square meters and nine tanks. Tuna and sardines came out of the Sado estuary and went into amphorae as garum bound for the length of the empire. Production here ran continuously from the 1st century into the 6th.
properties.image_credit: Fish-salting tanks (cetariae) at the Roman ruins of Troia · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Caetobrix among the coastal towns of Lusitania south of the Tagus, the ancient name conventionally identified with the fish-salting settlement on the Troia peninsula opposite Cetobriga.

properties.notes: Strabo singled out this Baetican port for its salt, meat, and fish trade, and its very name comes from the Phoenician word for salt. Excavations under the University of Malaga's rectorate building, carried out between 1998 and 2002 while the old post office was being converted, uncovered twenty-seven separate salting vats lined with waterproof opus signinum plaster. Those vats once cured anchovy and sardine into garum shipped across the Mediterranean, and the surrounding slope down from the Alcazaba appears to have been terraced with still more basins. The industry had already defined the city's economy for centuries before Rome absorbed it.
properties.image_credit: Roman fish-salting pools beneath the University of Malaga rectorate · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Malaca, laid out in the Phoenician manner, with large works for salting fish serving the trade with the African coast.

properties.notes: A fishing settlement called Caetaria on the Strait of Gibraltar took its very name from the salting vats, or cetariae, that anchored its economy. Founded around the 1st century BCE near the mouth of the Picaro River, the settlement's name survived antiquity, softening through the Middle Ages into Xetares and then the modern Getares, the bay where the ruins sit today. The surviving tanks, now preserved in a public park, cured fish caught in the same strait that fed Baelo Claudia's factories just up the coast. Spain declared the site a protected cultural asset, a Bien de Interes Cultural, on 27 June 2002.
properties.image_credit: Salting vats (piletas) of the Roman fish factory, Parque Smith, Algeciras · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.name_english: Cerro da Vila Roman Villa and Fish Factory
properties.notes: A wealthy family from nearby Ossonoba built salting tanks and a garum warehouse into this Algarve coastal estate, curing tuna blood, roe, and liver into a delicacy prized across the empire. The estate had already stood for over a century by 117 CE and would keep expanding for two more, adding mausoleums for its owners. Purple-dye production ran alongside the fish trade on the same grounds.
properties.image_credit: Watercolour reconstruction of the fish-processing tanks at Cerro da Vila · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Garum from this Phoenician-founded port carried its own brand name, garum sociorum, and fetched a thousand sesterces for barely two liters according to Pliny, more than three years of a legionary's pay. Martial name-dropped the sauce in his poetry as a status gift for Saturnalia. Excavators uncovered the salting vats at El Majuelo park in 1970, nineteen centuries after they last cured a fish.
properties.image_credit: Fish-salting factory (Firmum Iulium Sexi) tanks at El Majuelo, Almunecar · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo names Sexi among the Phoenician-founded coastal towns of southern Iberia noted for large fish-salting establishments.

properties.notes: Salt pans on this Adriatic lagoon gave the town its very name, changed from Ficocle to Cervia after the acervi, or great heaps, of salt piled up in its evaporation ponds. Pliny catalogued Adriatic salinae like this one among the empire's standard methods of harvesting sea salt. Archaeologists date the excavated Roman-era saltern here to the second half of the 1st century CE.
properties.image_credit: Cervia salt pans, Emilia-Romagna · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Stone-lined evaporation tanks stretching over half a mile of the ancient Vigo coastline made this the most sophisticated salt-works excavated anywhere in Roman Galicia. Southern Galicia holds a denser concentration of confirmed Roman salinae than any other stretch of the empire's Atlantic coast. Production here ran through the first three centuries CE before the marsh reclaimed the site. Workers uncovered the saltworks by accident in 1998 while building a health center in Vigo. The site fed the region's fish-salting industry, producing salt for garum and salsamenta as Atlantic Iberia's salted-fish trade expanded through the 1st to 3rd centuries.
properties.image_credit: Excavated Roman salinae at O Areal, Vigo · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.modern_location: Ses Salines, Ibiza, Balearic Islands, Spain
properties.notes: Phoenician settlers first worked these salt flats on Ibiza's southern tip, and Rome kept the evaporation ponds running after making Ebusus a municipality under Vespasian in 70 CE. Ships from across the Mediterranean once queued to load salt harvested from these same pans, a trade that outlasted the empire itself by well over a thousand years. Flamingos now nest where Roman salt-rakers once worked.
properties.image_credit: Ses Salines salt flats, Ibiza · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Brick stamps bearing the name of Legio XIII Gemina turned up at this Dacian salt works, proof the Roman army itself ran production here to keep its garrisons supplied. Rome founded the site as Salinae within a decade of conquering Dacia in 106 CE, exploiting a salt dome nearly half a mile across. Wooden tools pulled from the old workings survive today in Alba Iulia's museum.
properties.image_credit: Roman wooden tools used for salt mining at Ocna Mures, National Museum of the Union, Alba Iulia · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Names a Dacian town called Salinae in his list of the province's settlements, conventionally identified with the salt-producing site at modern Ocna Mures.

properties.notes: A single kiln at this Gallic pottery town could fire forty thousand vessels at once, making Condatomagus the largest ceramics factory the Roman world ever built. Terra sigillata stamped here has turned up as far away as Britain and the Danube frontier. By 117 CE the workshops had passed their peak, with the rival center at Lezoux drawing away trade, but production continued for decades more.
properties.image_credit: The great kiln (Grand Four) and baths at La Graufesenque · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.ref: R. Marichal, Les graffites de La Graufesenque, Gallia Supplément 47 (1988), ~250 texts
ancient_sources.note: Potters scratched bilingual Latin-and-Gaulish tallies onto unfired dishes before each kiln load, naming vessel types and counting them with native Gaulish numerals — cintus, allos, tritios, petuarios — the single richest surviving body of written Gaulish.

properties.notes: Fine red-gloss Arretine ware first made this Etruscan hill town famous across the Roman world, its potters' stamped molds still filling the local Maecenas museum. Emigrant potters had already carried the technique to Lyon and Pisa under Augustus, and by the Flavian dynasty the industry that made Arretium's name had largely moved on. In 117 CE the city's great pottery boom was history, not headline news.
properties.image_credit: Arretine ware potter's stamp (poincon) · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Arretium among the towns whose tableware is famous, in a passage arguing that earthenware still outranks silver at most Roman tables.

properties.notes: By the early 2nd century this Gallic town had overtaken La Graufesenque as the empire's leading source of fine red terra sigillata tableware, its sherds so distinctive they can date an archaeological layer to within a few decades. Pottery from Lezoux turned up as far as Roman Dacia, making up over half the fine ware at one excavated fort there. Production here was near its peak in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Lezoux plate, Musee departemental de la Ceramique · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Terra sigillata from this Rhineland town would eventually reach markets from Britain to Crimea, fired in kilns hot enough to reach a thousand degrees Celsius. The great pottery works that made Rheinzabern's name as Tabernae did not begin until roughly 150 CE, more than three decades after Trajan's death. In 117 CE this stretch of the Rhine frontier had not yet become an industrial center.
properties.image_credit: The Terra-Sigillata-Museum building in Rheinzabern · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Itinerarium Antonini
ancient_sources.note: Lists 'Tabernis' as a station 13 Roman miles from Saletio and 11 from Noviomagus on the Rhine valley road — the waystation that grew into the great terra-sigillata-producing town of Rheinzabern.

properties.notes: Slave gangs on this Etruscan estate pressed wine and processed grain across workshops arranged around a terraced courtyard, following the model Roman agronomists Varro and Columella prescribed in their farming manuals almost to the letter. Built by the wealthy Sestii family in the mid-1st century BCE, it stood just three miles from the port town of Cosa that shipped its produce onward. Excavations here in the 1970s helped found modern Roman villa archaeology.
properties.image_credit: Lower terrace wall of the Roman villa of Settefinestre · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Eighteen wine vats filled this Campanian farmhouse's cella vinaria, the working heart of a busy wine-producing estate outside Pompeii. Mount Vesuvius buried the whole property under volcanic ash and pumice on 24 August 79 CE, entombing its dolia and its wine press mid-operation. By 117 CE the villa had lain sealed underground for thirty-eight years, its productive life already over.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Villa Regina at Boscoreale · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Colonnaded promenades stretched nearly a kilometer along this Istrian bay, linking a senatorial family's seaside villa to temples of Neptune, Venus, and the Capitoline Triad. The Laecanii family, who also ran a major amphora workshop nearby at Fazana, owned the estate before it passed into imperial hands under the Flavians. Its private beach still shows traces of the multicolored mosaics that once decorated it.
properties.image_credit: Brijuni National Park, site of the Verige Bay Roman villa · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny names the Insulae Pullariae (the Brijuni islands) among the notable islands off the Istrian coast near the mouth of the Timavus river.

properties.notes: Highway construction crews accidentally uncovered this senatorial estate in 1962 while building a tollbooth outside Rome, revealing one of the most completely excavated great villas in Italy. The powerful Volusii Saturnini family ran productive farmland here alongside a lavish peristyle residence, next to the sanctuary town of Lucus Feroniae on the Via Tiberina. Its cryptoporticus and storage ranges still stand largely intact.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Villa dei Volusii Saturnini at Lucus Feroniae · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Records the death at ninety-three of Lucius Volusius Saturninus, head of the senatorial family that owned this villa, and praises his long-accumulated wealth.

properties.notes: A soaring drum-shaped tomb raised at the third milestone of the Appian Way for Caecilia Metella, daughter-in-law of the general who crushed Spartacus. Its 20-meter cylinder of travertine once carried a marble frieze of ox skulls and garlands, giving the road below the nickname Capo di Bove. Sitting on a square base of solid concrete, it was built to be seen from far down the road toward Rome. By 117 CE it had already loomed over Appian traffic for close to a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Tomb of Cecilia Metella, Via Appia Antica, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Cylindrical stone tomb of Cecilia Metella beside the Via Appia

ancient_sources.author: Inscription
ancient_sources.note: Names her as Caecilia, daughter of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus and wife of a Crassus — the text carved into the drum that has identified the tomb ever since.

properties.notes: A cylindrical mausoleum crowning Monte Orlando above the Gulf of Gaeta, built for Lucius Munatius Plancus, the consul and general who founded the colony of Lyon. Its drum spans nearly 30 meters and originally carried a stepped conical roof visible far out at sea. Its entrance inscription lists his offices as consul, censor, and triumphator over the Raetians. Ships rounding the cape had used it as a landmark for well over a century by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Mausoleum of Lucius Munatius Plancus, Monte Orlando, Gaeta, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Drum-shaped Roman tomb of Munatius Plancus on a hilltop above the sea

ancient_sources.author: Funerary inscription of L. Munatius Plancus
ancient_sources.note: The inscription on Plancus's mausoleum at Gaeta lists his career: consul, censor, imperator acclaimed twice, septemvir of the epulones, triumphator over the Raetians, builder of the Temple of Saturn from war spoils, and founder of the colonies of Lugdunum and Colonia Raurica.

properties.notes: A wedge-shaped tomb built by a freed slave who made his fortune baking bread under state contract, standing where two busy roads met outside the city walls. Its frieze carved rows of round openings to mimic the mouths of dough-mixing machines, a boast in stone about the trade that made him rich. An inscription names him Marcus Vergilius Eurysaces, baker and contractor, beside his wife Atistia. Already close to two centuries old by 117 CE, it stood as a freedman's answer to senatorial tombs.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Tomb of Eurysaces the Baker, near Porta Maggiore, Rome, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Travertine tomb of the baker Eurysaces with rows of circular relief openings

ancient_sources.author: CIL I2 1203-1205 = CIL VI 1958 (Marcus Vergilius Eurysaces, self-composed funerary inscription)
ancient_sources.work: Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum I (2nd ed.) / VI
ancient_sources.note: The inscription, repeated on multiple sides of the tomb, identifies the monument as that of Marcus Vergilius Eurysaces, a baker and public grain and bread contractor.
ancient_sources.quote: est hoc monimentum Marcei Vergilei Eurysacis pistoris redemptoris: apparet

properties.notes: A stepped tower tomb built for Lucius Poblicius, a discharged legionary who settled in the young colony of Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium. Rising close to 15 meters along the road south out of the city, it carried life-sized statues of the family in togas and ranked among the largest funerary monuments raised north of the Alps. By 117 CE it had watched over that approach road for decades, a landmark of Rome's veteran-settled Rhine frontier.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the reconstructed Tomb of Poblicius, Romano-Germanic Museum, Cologne, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Tall stepped Roman tower tomb with statues, reconstructed in a museum hall

properties.notes: An open-air cemetery running along the southern slope of the Vatican Hill, next to the ruins of Nero's circus and its Egyptian obelisk. Roman families had begun raising rows of small brick mausolea here by the start of the 2nd century CE, each fronted with a doorway naming the dead inside. A modest grave among these tombs is traditionally linked to the apostle Peter, two centuries before any basilica rose above it. In 117 CE it was still an ordinary pagan burial ground.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Vatican Necropolis beneath St. Peter's Basilica, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Row of small brick mausolea in the Vatican Necropolis

properties.notes: A mile-long avenue of tombs and carved stone sarcophagi lining the road just outside the walls of Roman Arelate. Wealthy citizens of the busy river port had lined the way with monuments since Julius Caesar planted a colony of veterans here, giving the cemetery its later name, the Elysian Fields. Rows of coffins stretched toward the horizon, a sight that centuries later drew painters like Van Gogh. By 117 CE it had already served as Arelate's main burial ground for well over a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Les Alyscamps necropolis, Arles, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Tree-lined avenue of ancient stone sarcophagi at the Alyscamps

properties.notes: An underground family tomb cut into volcanic rock beside the Via Appia, holding generations of the Cornelii Scipiones, the clan that produced the general who first fought Hannibal in Spain. Four square pillars left in the living rock divided the burial chamber, later enlarged with a brick gallery and its own facade on the road. Burials there had stopped roughly 150 years earlier, but the carved chamber remained intact. By 117 CE the once-famous tomb sat quiet beside the city's busiest road.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the entrance to the Tomb of the Scipios, Rome, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Entrance to the rock-cut underground Tomb of the Scipios

properties.notes: The largest tomb standing along the Appian Way, a drum of concrete and stone 27 meters across at the sixth milestone south of Rome. It originally rose in a cone ringed by stone seats and a carved frieze of weapons and garlands, long since built over by a small medieval farmhouse. Roman tradition connected it to the family of orator and general Valerius Messalla Corvinus, though the burial was never confirmed by inscription. By 117 CE it had watched over Appian traffic for over a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Casal Rotondo, Via Appia Antica, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Large circular Roman tomb mound topped by a small farmhouse

properties.notes: A steep marble-clad pyramid built as a tomb for Gaius Cestius, a magistrate on the priestly board that ran Rome's ritual feasts. Standing 37 meters tall and finished within 330 days by its own inscription, it borrowed the pyramid form from Rome's fascination with conquered Egypt. Its builders sealed the burial chamber with painted frescoes and left no visible door, so it stayed hidden for centuries. By 117 CE it had already stood beside the road to Ostia for over a century.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Pyramid of Cestius, Rome, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: White marble pyramid tomb of Gaius Cestius in Rome

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Names Gaius Cestius, the praetor and priest whose tomb this pyramid became, decades before it was built — the closest thing to a literary trace of the man himself.

properties.notes: A towering tomb facade cut into rose sandstone at the entrance to Petra, capital of the Nabataean kings. Its columned front rises some 40 meters, blending Hellenistic style with Nabataean tradition, carved for royalty rather than built from blocks. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom only eleven years before 117 CE, folding this tomb and its caravan city into the new province of Arabia. Legend later credited the stone urn on its facade with hidden treasure, giving the monument its modern name.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), Petra, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Rock-cut facade of Al-Khazneh at Petra, carved into pink sandstone cliffs

properties.notes: One of Petra's grandest royal tombs, cut into the cliff face of Jabal al-Khubtha above a broad forecourt on stone arches, with a facade rising some 17 meters. A large stone urn carved atop its pediment gave the tomb its name and may mark the resting place of a Nabataean king. Vaulted chambers built beneath the terrace served for storage or further burials. Only eleven years into Roman rule over Arabia Petraea by 117 CE, it remained one of the most striking monuments in the new province.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Urn Tomb, Petra, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Rock-cut Urn Tomb facade above a vaulted terrace at Petra

properties.notes: Sacred grove of Zeus at the heart of Olympia, enclosed by a wall on three sides and open to the Hill of Kronos on the north. Priests, athletes, and pilgrims packed the 200-yard precinct every four years for the Olympic Games, sacrificing oxen on the great ash altar of Zeus. By 117 CE the Altis held the temples of Zeus and Hera, dozens of treasuries, and centuries of victor statues. Trajan's own coins had circulated among the crowds here in the years before his death.
properties.image_credit: Plan of the Olympia sanctuary (Altis) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The Altis itself: the great altar built up from the ash of burnt thighbones, the treasuries in their row, and the rule about who may climb to the top.

properties.notes: Built around 590 BCE, the Heraion is the oldest standing temple at Olympia and one of the earliest Doric temples in Greece. Its original wooden columns were replaced one by one with stone over centuries, so no two columns fully match. The temple held the discus used to light the Olympic flame and hosted the footrace of the Heraean Games for women. It still stood in active cult use when Trajan died in August 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Hera, Olympia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The oldest temple in the sanctuary, with one oak column still standing in the rear chamber in his day — the last of the originals, replaced in stone as each decayed.

properties.notes: Small Doric temple built around 400 BCE for Rhea, mother of the gods, and repurposed under Roman rule for the imperial cult. By 117 CE its cella held statues of Roman emperors rather than the old Anatolian goddess, including an oversized Augustus posed as Zeus with a thunderbolt. The switch turned a centuries-old temple into a showcase for Rome's living rulers. Six by eleven Doric columns still framed the small shrine at Trajan's death.
properties.image_credit: Metroon, Olympia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: A Doric temple of the Mother of the Gods that by Roman times held statues of emperors instead.

properties.notes: Doric temple built around 330 BCE to host the Nemean Games, one of the four Panhellenic 'crown' festivals. Argos moved the games permanently to its own stadium in 271 BCE, and Nemea's sanctuary slid into agricultural obscurity soon after. By 117 CE the temple's roof had already failed and its cult statue was gone, the ruin the traveler Pausanias later confirmed on his visit. Thirty-two Doric columns once ringed a shrine that a farming valley had long since stopped worshipping at.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Nemea · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Greece's oldest oracle, where priests read the rustle of a sacred oak's leaves and the clang of bronze cauldrons to hear the will of Zeus. Homer already knew the shrine by the 8th century BCE, long before Epirus's King Pyrrhus gave it a 17,000-seat theater and grander temple in the 3rd century BCE. Croesus of Lydia and generations of Greek states sent envoys here before major decisions. The oracle still answered questions in the mountains of Epirus when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Zeus, Dodona · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Two accounts of the founding side by side: the priestesses' black dove that spoke from an oak, and the Egyptian priests' woman carried off from Thebes.

properties.notes: Seat of the Pythia, the trance-speaking priestess whose cryptic verses steered Greek colonization, war, and politics for over a thousand years. The temple standing in 117 CE dated to about 330 BCE, the third rebuild after fire and earthquake destroyed its predecessors. The priest Plutarch served on staff here around this time, later writing candidly about the oracle's fading but still-real power. Pilgrims still climbed Parnassus to question Apollo the year Hadrian took the throne.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Delphi · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The maxims cut in the forecourt, the stone called the navel of the earth, and the inner room where the prophetess gave her answers.

ancient_sources.author: SIG³ 801d
ancient_sources.note: Marble fragments found by the temple preserve a rescript of the emperor Claudius naming 'Lucius Junius Gallio, proconsul of Achaia' — the same Gallio before whom the apostle Paul was brought at Corinth.

properties.notes: Circular marble shrine built around 380 BCE in the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, the goddess who guarded Delphi's approach. Twenty Doric columns ringed the outside and ten ornate Corinthian columns lined the inside of a building whose exact purpose no ancient source explains. Standing half a mile from the main oracle, it was already three centuries old and still admired for its craftsmanship in 117 CE. Fire would gut its roof only in the following century.
properties.image_credit: Tholos of Delphi, Marmaria · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Vitruvius
ancient_sources.note: Listed among buildings whose own architects wrote them up — Theodorus of Phocaea on the round temple at Delphi.

properties.notes: Ionia's rival to Delphi, where a priest, not a priestess, drank from a hidden spring and delivered verse oracles to pilgrims waiting outside. The marble Doric temple, begun in the late 4th century BCE, was still unfinished when Trajan died, completed only later under Hadrian. The oracle kept operating throughout construction, answering cities across Asia Minor from a crypt finished generations earlier. Colophon's harbor sent a steady stream of anxious questioners up this valley in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Ionic temple ruins comparable to Claros's Doric sanctuary · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative)

properties.notes: Desert oracle so respected that Alexander the Great crossed 300 miles of Egyptian sand in 331 BCE just to ask Amun-Ra if he was a god's son. Built in the 6th century BCE atop an earlier shrine, the temple sat on Siwa's only natural hill, ringed by nothing but oasis palms and salt flats. Its priests answered by nodding or tilting a ceremonial barque rather than speaking outright. The oracle still drew travelers crossing the western desert when Rome ruled Egypt in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of the Oracle of Amun, Siwa · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Arrian
ancient_sources.note: Alexander's march across the desert to the oracle, the rain and the guides, and a consultation whose answer he told no one.

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Places the sanctuary in its oasis and gives the Theban account that a priestess carried off from Egypt founded it.

properties.notes: One of Greece's five great oracles, consulted by rulers from Croesus to the Persian general Mardonius. Petitioners drank from two springs, Lethe and Mnemosyne, to forget their worries and remember the vision to come, before being lowered into a cave shaped like a bread-oven to meet the hero Trophonios. Visitors climbed out unable to laugh for weeks. Plutarch, writing a generation after Trajan's death, confirmed the oracle still spoke when other Boeotian oracles had gone silent.
properties.image_credit: Otto Magnus von Stackelberg, artist who documented the Trophonios oracle site in the 1830s · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative portrait, not a site view)

properties.notes: Sanctuary of the seer-hero Amphiaraos, swallowed alive by the earth at Thebes and reborn as a healing and dream oracle on Attica's coast. Pilgrims slept in a 360-foot stoa hoping the hero would prescribe a cure or send an answer in a dream. Sulla had granted the shrine tax-free sacred status in 73 BCE, and its theater and baths still functioned under the empire. By 117 CE crowds had thinned from the sanctuary's 3rd-century-BCE peak, but its spring still drew the sick.
properties.image_credit: Amphiareion of Oropos · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The rite in full: purify yourself, sacrifice a ram, sleep on its skin on the ground, and wait for the answer to come in a dream.

properties.notes: The most famous healing sanctuary in the Greek world, where the sick slept in a colonnaded hall hoping Asklepios himself would appear in a dream and cure them. Its Doric temple, built around 375 BCE, stood beside inscribed stone tablets recording hundreds of claimed miracle cures, from blindness to tapeworms. Roman patrons and physicians alike sent gifts and visits to the sanctuary under the empire. In 117 CE pilgrims from across the Roman world still queued for a night in Asklepios's dormitory.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Asklepios, Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The sacred grove with its boundary marks, the rule that no one may be born or die inside it, and the slabs recording who was healed and of what.

properties.notes: Enigmatic round building designed by Polykleitos the Younger around 360 BCE, its foundations concealing a spiral maze of six concentric walls that no surviving ancient text explains. Doric columns encircled the outside and Corinthian columns lined an inner ring, one of the earliest uses of that order anywhere in Greek architecture. Snakes, sacred to Asklepios, were kept in the maze below the floor. The Tholos still stood within the healing sanctuary when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Tholos of Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: A round building of white marble by Polykleitos, worth going to see for the painting of Drunkenness drinking from a glass cup.

properties.notes: Older than the Asklepios cult it eventually shared a hilltop with, this sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas centers on a 6th-century-BCE archaic temple built over Mycenaean cult remains dating back to roughly 1500 BCE. Epidaurus's healers worshipped Apollo here for centuries before Asklepios, his mythological son, took the valley below. Excavated animal-bone deposits show near-continuous ritual use across two millennia. The temple still crowned the ridge above Epidaurus's crowded sanctuary in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas, Epidaurus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Healing sanctuary built around a spring where patients drank sacred water, bathed, and walked a tunnel meant to carry them symbolically toward the god. Founded near 400 BCE, its earliest buildings were a modest temple of Asklepios Soter, a treatment hall, and a fountain house. The sprawling complex with theater and library that visitors picture today did not exist in 117 CE; that rebuild began only under Hadrian. The sanctuary was respected but still generations from its greatest fame.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Birthplace-by-legend of the physician Hippocrates and one of the ancient world's premier medical sanctuaries, built in stacked terraces on a pine-covered hillside. King Eumenes II of Pergamon funded its grand Doric temple in the 2nd century BCE, modeled on the sanctuary at Epidaurus. A fourth building phase was underway under Roman rule as Trajan's reign ended, adding terraces to a site already four centuries old. Physicians here used methods later cited by the doctor Galen.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Kos · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: A famous sanctuary outside the town, hung with votive tablets recording cures — the same tablets Hippocrates was said to have learned from.

properties.notes: Healing sanctuary at the north edge of Corinth, built beside a spring that patients believed carried curative power. Excavators recovered hundreds of terracotta votives shaped like the body parts pilgrims hoped to heal, from hands to organs. Its four-columned temple, late 4th century BCE, was rebuilt after an earthquake and stood alongside dining rooms for patients. Corinth, refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BCE, still kept the Asklepieion running when Trajan died in 117.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of ancient Corinth near the Asklepieion · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Founded in 420/19 BCE on the Acropolis's south slope, after a priest smuggled the healing snake of Asklepios into Athens during a wartime plague. Its terrace held a temple, altar, sacred spring, and stoas where patients slept awaiting a healing dream, wedged between the Theatre of Dionysos and the Acropolis rock above. The sanctuary had run continuously for over five centuries by the time Trajan died in 117 CE. Its cure-tablets remain prime evidence for ancient medical practice.
properties.image_credit: Asklepieion of Athens, south slope of the Acropolis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: The sanctuary on the south slope of the Acropolis, with its spring and the statues of the god and his children.

properties.notes: Gallo-Roman healing sanctuary built around a sacred pool fed by underground springs, dedicated to Apollo Grannus, a Gallic curative god Rome folded into its own Apollo. A processional road nearly 900 meters around encircled the precinct, drawing pilgrims from across Gaul to a site later tradition claims even emperors visited. The 1st-century sanctuary sat in the territory of the Leuci, in what is now the Vosges. By 117 CE Andesina's spring-fed shrine was an established stop for the sick.
properties.image_credit: Inscription to Apollo Grannus, Roman Grand (Andesina) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Healing shrine at the actual source of the Seine, dedicated to Sequana, the river's own goddess, whom pilgrims believed could cure whatever ailed them. Gauls built a wooden shrine here by the 2nd century BCE; Rome then raised masonry temples and a pool over the springs around 50 CE. Excavators recovered over a thousand votive offerings, carved eyes, limbs, and organs, left by pilgrims seeking cures. The sanctuary was still drawing the sick to Burgundy's source-country in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Bronze statuette of Sequana from Fontes Sequanae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sanctuary of Diana on the volcanic crater lake the Romans called the 'Mirror of Diana,' guarded by a priest-king who won the post by killing his predecessor in single combat beside a sacred tree. Caligula would later sink two huge pleasure barges in the lake, raised again only in the 1930s, but in 117 CE the cult still ran on its old, violent rules. Slaves and freedwomen alike could serve as priestesses here. Pilgrims carried torches to the lakeshore each August for the Nemoralia.
properties.image_credit: Statue of Diana Nemorensis from her sanctuary at Nemi · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The priest of Diana at Aricia is a runaway slave who won the office by killing the last priest, and holds it with a drawn sword against the next.

properties.notes: Classical temple raised around 60-70 CE over Britain's only natural hot spring, merging the Celtic goddess Sulis with Rome's Minerva into a hybrid deity. Only one other truly classical temple existed anywhere else in Roman Britain, Claudius's shrine at Colchester. Visitors dropped curses etched on lead sheets into the sacred spring, some naming thieves who stole their bath towels. By 117 CE the temple had been drawing pilgrims to Aquae Sulis for roughly half a century.
properties.image_credit: Gorgon's Head pediment, Temple of Sulis Minerva, Bath · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Solinus
ancient_sources.note: Britain's hot springs, fitted out for bathing and set under the protection of Minerva, where the fire in the temple burns coal rather than wood.

properties.notes: Home of the Eleusinian Mysteries, secret initiation rites into the cult of Demeter and Persephone that even Roman emperors sought out. The Telesterion, a columned initiation hall built around 435 BCE under the architect Iktinos, could hold roughly 3,000 initiates under one roof each year. Hadrian would later fund the sanctuary's grand marble gateway, but that lay years ahead. In 117 CE Eleusis already had six centuries of secrecy behind it, its rites unrevealed to this day.
properties.image_credit: Telesterion, Sanctuary of Demeter, Eleusis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: He reaches the wall of the sanctuary and stops: a dream forbade him to write down what is inside, and the uninitiated may not ask.

properties.name_english: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace
properties.notes: Mystery sanctuary on a remote Aegean island where sworn-to-secrecy initiates sought protection from shipwreck through rites Roman writers described only in riddles. Philip II of Macedon commissioned its earliest monumental building around 340 BCE; construction continued for centuries under the Ptolemies and Rome. The Winged Victory statue would later crown a fountain here, well after this snapshot. In 117 CE the altar court and theater already drew initiates from across the Greek world.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Diodorus Siculus
ancient_sources.note: The island's mysteries, open to anyone including slaves, and the belief that initiates come off better in storms at sea.

properties.notes: Largest round building ever raised in the Greek world, a gift from Ptolemaic queen Arsinoe II to the Samothracian mystery cult around 285 BCE. A ring of pilasters supported a marble roof spanning 20 meters, sheltering theoroi, sacred delegates sent from Greek cities to attend the mysteries. An early Roman-era earthquake forced repairs to its roofline, converting it to an octagonal tile pattern. The rotunda was still the sanctuary's grandest structure when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Rotunda of Arsinoe II, Samothrace · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Vast sandstone temple built by Amenhotep III around 1400 BCE for the annual Opet Festival, when statues of Amun, Mut, and Khonsu traveled by barge from Karnak to be reunited here. Ramesses II later added the towering entrance pylon and colossal statues that still guard the gate. Under Rome the forecourt held a shrine honoring the emperors, soldiers' graffiti scratched beside 3,000-year-old reliefs. In 117 CE the temple had stood in continuous ritual use for over 1,500 years.
properties.image_credit: Luxor Temple · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo, describing Thebes (Diospolis) which he visited under Roman rule, notes the city's ruins extended some eighty stadia and that several of its temples — damaged earlier by Cambyses — still stood alongside colossal statues and obelisks; a general eyewitness account of the great Theban temple precinct spanning the Luxor/Karnak area.

properties.notes: Isis's holiest shrine, built on a granite island in the Nile's First Cataract and finished under Ptolemy III after his father broke ground around 280 BCE. Pilgrims from as far as Meroe and Rome sailed here to petition the goddess, leaving Greek and Demotic graffiti across its walls. Roman emperors kept enlarging it; Trajan's own kiosk, with 14 unfinished columns, already stood on the island by 117. Philae's cult outlasted nearly every pagan temple, closing only under Justinian.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Isis, Philae · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: The island above the First Cataract, shared by Egyptians and Ethiopians, with a temple of Isis reached by ferry from the rocks below.

ancient_sources.author: CIL III 14147
ancient_sources.note: A stele in hieroglyphic, Latin and Greek set up by Gaius Cornelius Gallus, the first Roman prefect of Egypt, recording his suppression of a revolt and an embassy received from the king of the Ethiopians.

properties.notes: Unique double temple sharing one roof between two gods, crocodile-headed Sobek on one side and falcon-headed Horus on the other, with mirrored sanctuaries and courts in parallel symmetry. Ptolemy VI began construction around 180 BCE on a Nile bend once thick with crocodiles kept as sacred animals. Later Ptolemies and Roman-era builders kept adding to the complex for two more centuries. By 117 CE the temple's twin cults still drew worshippers to this stretch of Upper Egypt.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Kom Ombo · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Juvenal
ancient_sources.note: Juvenal's Fifteenth Satire recounts a real, violent religious riot between the neighboring Egyptian towns of Ombos (crocodile-worshippers) and Tentyra (crocodile-hunters), including a notorious act of cannibalism during the clash — cited as an eyewitness-adjacent account of the crocodile cult centered on this temple.

properties.notes: Temple to the ram-headed creator god Khnum, believed by Egyptians to have shaped humanity on a potter's wheel from Nile clay. Its hypostyle hall, still visible today nine meters below the modern town, was raised under Roman rule beginning around the reign of Claudius. Decoration of its 24 columns continued for generations, running well into the 3rd century CE. In 117 CE the hall's columns were already carved and standing, part of a program that kept adding inscriptions for another 150 years.
properties.image_credit: Roman-period hypostyle hall, Egyptian Nile temple · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative)

properties.notes: Sandstone temple to Mandulis, a Lower Nubian sun god merged with Egyptian and Greek solar imagery, built around 30 BCE under Augustus near Egypt's southern frontier. Roman governors used its forecourt for imperial ceremonies, decorating the gateway with reliefs of Augustus offering to Mandulis. Its decoration was never entirely finished. It still marked Rome's Nubian border sanctuary in 117 CE, centuries before 1960s engineers dismantled it to save it from Lake Nasser's floodwaters.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Kalabsha (relocated to New Kalabsha) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Small sandstone temple that Augustus commissioned around 23 BCE for two deified Nubian brothers, Pedesi and Pihor, alongside the goddess Isis. Roman governor Petronius built it barely a generation after Actium, at Egypt's new southern frontier. Egyptian priests still tended its shrine when Trajan died in 117 CE, one of the smallest and most personal temples Rome ever funded. Egypt later gave the structure to the United States; it now stands reassembled in New York's Metropolitan Museum.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Dendur, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Nubian temple begun as a one-room chapel to Amun by the Kushite king Adikhalamani around 200 BCE, then expanded by Ptolemaic pharaohs and finished with Roman-era carvings under Augustus and Tiberius. Positioned near Philae on Egypt's southern frontier, it absorbed three dynasties' worth of religious patronage in under two centuries. By 117 CE its Roman decoration was complete. Egypt gifted the structure to Spain in 1968, and it now stands reassembled in a Madrid park.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Debod, now in Madrid · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Healing shrine built into the ruins of Queen Hatshepsut's 1,300-year-old mortuary temple, where Ptolemaic and Roman-era pilgrims sought cures from the deified sages Amenhotep son of Hapu and Imhotep. Sufferers slept inside hoping for a healing dream, exactly as at Epidaurus, a case of Greek and Egyptian medicine merging into one practice. Surviving graffiti record visitors thanking the gods for cures found nowhere else. By 117 CE the shrine had treated the sick for roughly four centuries.
properties.image_credit: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sacred precinct where Carthaginians cremated and buried infants beneath stone markers dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit, in continuous use from the 8th century BCE until Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. Caesar's colonists, refounding the city a century later, built workshops, kilns, and housing directly over the sacred ground. By 117 CE the tophet's stelae lay buried under a Roman neighborhood, its rites gone, Baal Hammon's identity quietly folded into Rome's cult of Saturn.
properties.image_credit: Stelae at the Tophet of Salammbô, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Syria's grandest sanctuary to Atargatis, the fish-tailed mother goddess, its walls stretching over 600 feet according to the 2nd-century writer Lucian, who left the fullest surviving account of any pagan temple's daily rituals. A sacred lake inside the precinct, said to be bottomless, held fish so holy that only priests could touch them, some wearing gold rings. The sanctuary was already ancient, ruled by Commagenian and Seleucid kings before Rome, when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Coin of Atargatis, goddess of Hierapolis Bambyce · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Phoenicia's most sacred temple, built for the god-king Melqart under King Hiram in the 10th century BCE and known even to Herodotus, who described its two pillars, one gold and one of glowing emerald-green glass. Alexander besieged Tyre for seven months in 332 BCE partly because its priests refused him the right to sacrifice inside. Romans equated Melqart with Hercules and kept the cult running. In 117 CE the thousand-year-old sanctuary still anchored one of Rome's wealthiest Phoenician cities.
properties.image_credit: Melqart, god of Tyre · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Phoenician sanctuary to Melqart, worshipped by Romans as Hercules, founded by Tyrian colonists on the southern tip of Cadiz's island as early as the 8th century BCE. Ancient writers described bronze gate-columns engraved with the labors of Hercules and an eternal flame priests tended day and night. Julius Caesar wept before a statue of Alexander here, envying his youthful conquests. Roman coins from Gades still carried Melqart-Hercules's image when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Votive statuettes from the Temple of Hercules Gaditanus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Maltese hilltop sanctuary with four thousand years of sacred use, from a Neolithic megalithic temple through a Phoenician shrine to Astarte and finally a Roman-era temple of Juno. Cicero denounced governor Verres in 70 BCE for looting ivory tusks the sanctuary displayed as an offering, proof of its reach. Sailors and even pirates respected the shrine's sanctity passing Malta's coast. By 117 CE the temple had worshipped Juno, heir to Astarte's identity, for two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Punic votive stelae, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons (illustrative Punic-Phoenician material culture, not Tas-Silġ itself)

properties.notes: Best-preserved freestanding temple in Petra, built around 30 BCE for Dushara, the Nabataean kingdom's chief god, standing over 75 feet tall at the end of the city's colonnaded street. Nabataean kings funded it in the same building boom that produced Petra's rock-cut Treasury facade. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom peacefully in 106 CE, turning Petra into the province of Arabia without a fight. In 117 CE the temple was barely a decade into Roman rule, still the city's religious heart.
properties.image_credit: Qasr al-Bint, Petra · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Petra reported at second hand from Athenodorus, who lived there: a rock plateau ringed by cliffs, with springs inside, and a people so orderly they barely go to law.

properties.notes: Palmyra's temple to Baalshamin, lord of the heavens and storms, traced to a small shrine of the late 2nd century BCE that gained a new altar in 115 CE, two years before Trajan died. The grand cella that later defined the site, funded by the Palmyrene Male 'Agrippa' to mark Hadrian's visit, was not dedicated until 131 CE. In 117 CE worshippers still used the older, smaller sanctuary, not the monument photographs later showed. Militants destroyed that later temple with explosives in 2015.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Baalshamin, Palmyra, before its 2015 destruction · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Palmyrene inscription
ancient_sources.note: A bilingual Greek and Palmyrene-Aramaic text by Malé son of Yarhai, a temple official. The Greek pairs Baalshamin with 'Zeus Oromasdes'; the Aramaic dedicates the building to Baalshamin alone.

properties.notes: Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushed three Roman legions marching through the forest, wiping out roughly 20,000 men over three days. Governor Varus fell on his own sword rather than be captured. Excavations at Kalkriese since 1987 have recovered some 5,000 to 6,000 Roman objects and 2,000 coins, including eight gold pieces found clustered together in 2016, likely spilled from a dying officer's leather pouch, and coins bearing the countermark VAR that Varus himself had issued. A silvered iron cavalry mask, its face serene and eyes closed, once graced a parade helmet rather than battle gear. Rome never again pushed its permanent frontier east of the Rhine. Emperor Augustus reportedly banged his head on doors crying, 'Quintili Vare, legiones redde!'
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed defensive wall at the Kalkriese battlefield site, photo by Markus Schweiß · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Germanicus's men reach the field six years on and bury what is left: the half-ruined rampart, the bones lying where the ranks had stood, skulls nailed to trees.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The fullest narrative of the ambush — the broken country, the rain, and three legions destroyed over several days of march.

properties.notes: Governor Agricola pushed deep into Caledonia and crushed a coalition of Caledonian tribes led by Calgacus, killing a claimed 10,000 warriors for only 360 Roman dead. It was the northernmost Roman battlefield victory in Britain. Tacitus, Agricola's own son-in-law, put a defiant speech in Calgacus's mouth before the fighting began, condemning Roman conquest in words that still echo: 'where they make a desert, they call it peace.' Rome still never permanently held the ground it won that day, and the site itself remains unidentified among dozens of candidate hills across northeast Scotland. By 117 CE, three decades on, the empire's real frontier in Britain sat far to the south, nowhere near the battlefield's forgotten ground.
properties.image_credit: Map of Agricola's campaigns, 80-84 CE · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Hannibal's double-envelopment trapped and annihilated a Roman army twice the size of his own, killing an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 men in a single day. It remains one of history's bloodiest one-day battles. Rome lost more citizens here than on any other day in its history, yet refused to negotiate and eventually won the war. Military academies still teach the maneuver.
properties.image_credit: John Trumbull, "The Death of Paulus Aemilius at the Battle of Cannae," 1773 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: The line that bows forward and then folds in, the cavalry closing the back, and a casualty figure the author says he took from men who were there.

properties.notes: Scipio Africanus finally beat Hannibal on African soil, breaking Carthage's war elephants with disciplined gaps in the Roman line and finishing the fight with Numidian cavalry. The defeat ended the Second Punic War and Carthage's status as a great power for good. Hannibal survived and fled into exile. The battle is often staged as ancient history's classic general-versus-general showdown. Polybius recorded that Hannibal massed more than 80 war elephants at the front of his line, backed by 12,000 mercenary infantry. Scipio broke from Rome's standard checkerboard formation and arranged his maniples in open lanes, funneling the elephant charge harmlessly through to his rear ranks.
properties.image_credit: Cornelis Cort, "The Battle of Zama," 1567 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: Scipio opens lanes through his maniples to let the elephants run through, then re-forms; the two commanders meet before the battle and neither gives ground.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar trapped Vercingetorix's Gallic army inside the hilltop fortress with a double ring of siege works, then held off a Gallic relief force of some 250,000 warriors from the outside at the same time. Vercingetorix surrendered in person, laying his weapons at Caesar's feet. The siege effectively ended organized Gallic resistance to Rome. It remains one of history's most studied feats of military engineering.
properties.image_credit: Lionel Royer, "Vercingetorix Throws Down His Arms at the Feet of Julius Caesar," 1899 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: His own account of the double ring of works — one facing the town, one facing the relief army — with the ditches, stakes and pits described piece by piece.

properties.notes: Julius Caesar, outnumbered roughly two to one, crushed Pompey the Great's larger army on 9 August 48 BCE by anticipating a cavalry flanking move and countering it with a hidden fourth line of veteran cohorts posted behind his right flank. Caesar fielded nine legions, worn thin by years of campaigning, against Pompey's fresher 45,000 legionaries backed by 7,000 cavalry. Pompey's forces suffered roughly 6,000 dead against Caesar's few hundred, and thousands more surrendered in the following days. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered on arrival and presented to Caesar as a trophy. The battle effectively decided the Roman civil war and Caesar's path to dictatorship, a settlement still shaping the empire Trajan ruled in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Apollonio di Giovanni, "The Battle of Pharsalus and the Death of Pompey," 15th century · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Mark Antony and Octavian fought Caesar's assassins Brutus and Cassius in two engagements three weeks apart on the plain west of Philippi. Cassius, wrongly believing the battle lost, took his own life; Brutus followed after the second defeat. The Liberators' cause died with them, clearing the way for the Second Triumvirate to carve up the Roman world. Tens of thousands of veterans were later resettled at the city as a reward.
properties.image_credit: Map of the first Battle of Philippi, 42 BCE · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Appian
ancient_sources.note: Two engagements three weeks apart on the marshy plain, and the deaths of Cassius and Brutus, each after mistaking how his own wing had fared.

properties.modern_location: Gulf of Ambracia, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: Octavian's admiral Agrippa outmaneuvered the combined fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off the Ambracian Gulf, and Cleopatra's squadron broke and fled mid-battle with Antony following. The naval defeat ended their bid for power and left Octavian sole master of Rome. Within a year both Antony and Cleopatra were dead by suicide in Egypt. Octavian founded the victory city of Nicopolis on the spot and became Augustus four years later.
properties.image_credit: Lorenzo A. Castro, "The Battle of Actium," 1672, National Maritime Museum · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: The fleet undermanned and burning its surplus ships, and the moment Cleopatra's squadron turns for open water with Antony following.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: The line of battle off the promontory and the fighting at close quarters between heavy ships and light.

properties.notes: Parthian horse-archers and cataphracts under the general Surena wore down and destroyed seven legions under Marcus Licinius Crassus, killing roughly 20,000 Romans and capturing the legionary standards. Crassus himself died in the aftermath, reportedly with molten gold poured down his throat. It was Rome's worst defeat since Cannae and left the eastern frontier an open wound for a century. Trajan's ongoing Parthian War answers that old humiliation.
properties.image_credit: "Death of Crassus in the Battle of Carrhae," Cassell's Illustrated Universal History, 1882 · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: The Parthian horse archers and the camel train that kept them supplied with arrows, and the retreat that ended with Crassus dead under a truce.

properties.notes: Roman legions under Titus Quinctius Flamininus caught Philip V of Macedon's phalanx on broken hilly ground where it could not hold formation, and flanked it with a detached maniple for a decisive win. Macedonian losses ran to roughly 8,000 dead against a few hundred Romans. The battle proved the flexible legion could beat the rigid Macedonian phalanx on uneven terrain. Flamininus later declared the Greek cities free at the Isthmian Games to wide applause.
properties.image_credit: Battle plan diagram, Battle of Cynoscephalae · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Polybius
ancient_sources.note: Two armies collide in fog on the ridge; Polybius uses the day to argue why a phalanx cannot hold formation on broken ground.

properties.notes: A Roman army under Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with his famous brother Africanus advising, smashed the huge Seleucid army of Antiochus III, including his scythed chariots and war elephants. Roman losses were light against tens of thousands of Seleucid dead and captured. The defeat broke Seleucid power west of the Taurus Mountains for good. Rome walked away the unrivaled power of the eastern Mediterranean.
properties.image_credit: Illustration of the Battle of Magnesia, 190 BCE · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Livy
ancient_sources.note: The Seleucid line with its elephants between the phalanx blocks, and the scythed chariots that break back into their own cavalry.

properties.notes: Consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus lured the Macedonian phalanx onto broken ground and picked it apart in gaps with sword-armed legionaries, killing an estimated 20,000 men in an afternoon. King Perseus fled and was later paraded in Paullus's triumph. The victory ended the four-century Antigonid dynasty and Macedon as an independent kingdom. Rome split the territory into four puppet republics rather than annex it outright.
properties.image_credit: Andrea del Verrocchio, "The Battle of Pydna," 15th century · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: The phalanx advances, the Roman line gives, and gaps open in the pike wall as the ground breaks up — the fighting decided in under an hour.
