Excavators uncovering it in 1831 found the stucco and mosaic decoration almost perfectly preserved. It remains one of the best-preserved columbaria in Rome.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Mosaic dedicatory inscription, Columbarium of Pomponius Hylas, Rome
ancient_sources.note: A colored mosaic inscription set into the entrance stairway names Gnaeus Pomponius Hylas and Pomponia Vitalinis, freedwoman of Gnaeus. A V for vivit over Pomponia's name shows she was still alive when it was added; Hylas had purchased the pre-existing early-1st-century CE chamber and installed this panel.

properties.modern_location: Between Via Appia and Via Latina, Rome, Italy
properties.notes: Three vast underground burial chambers stood between the Appian and Latin Ways, their brick vaults lined floor to ceiling with niches for cinerary urns. The oldest of the three belonged to freedmen and slaves of Marcus Claudius Marcellus, brother of Tiberius, and dates to the Augustan era. Excavated in the mid-19th century, the chambers held thousands of urns for imperial household staff who could never afford solo tombs. They remain among the largest columbaria found in Rome.

properties.modern_location: Via Labicana, near Porta Maggiore, Rome, Italy
properties.notes: A family of builders raised this tomb along the Via Labicana around 100-120 CE and covered it with marble reliefs advertising their own trade. One panel shows a giant treadwheel crane hoisting stone blocks, the clearest surviving depiction of Roman construction machinery. Another shows the funeral bier of Hateria, a freedwoman and priestess, lying in state inside a miniature temple. The reliefs, unearthed in 1848, now hang in the Vatican Museums.
properties.image_credit: 19th-century plate reproduction, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription associated with the Tomb of the Haterii, Rome
ancient_sources.note: Names Quintus Haterius Tychicus, a freedman public building contractor, and is the textual basis scholars use to link the tomb's ownership to a Haterii family of builders -- consistent with the tomb's marble reliefs depicting monuments they built, including the Colosseum. The inscription is a scholarly attribution rather than a label found in situ on the monument itself; the tomb's own on-site inscription, if any, is lost.

properties.notes: Dozens of tombs lined the Via dei Sepolcri just outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, built between the colony's founding in 80 BCE and the eruption of 79 CE. Freedmen, magistrates, and merchants competed for plots visible to everyone entering the city, filling the road with altars, exedra benches, and aedicula shrines. Vesuvius buried the entire street under ash and pumice in 79 CE, sealing it exactly as it stood. Excavation from the 18th century onward has recovered it intact.
properties.image_credit: 19th-century watercolor by Luigi Bazzani, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Seneca
ancient_sources.note: Describes the earthquake of 62 CE that struck Pompeii, the city outside whose walls this necropolis lies.

properties.notes: A 250-meter stretch of road outside Pompeii's Nocera Gate held hundreds of tombs belonging to freedmen, local elites, and at least one military veteran. The priestess Eumachia received an exedra-shaped monument here, and nearby stood the high-podium tomb of magistrate Publius Vesonius Phileros. Founded when Pompeii became a Roman colony in 80 BCE, the cemetery was still filling with new burials the day Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. Volcanic ash sealed it in that instant.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Describes the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius burying Pompeii, the city outside whose walls this necropolis lies.

properties.notes: Pompeii's city council granted this prime plot to Mamia, a public priestess, so she could build her tomb in the form of a semicircular stone bench facing the road. Her inscription records that she paid for a temple to the emperor's Genius in the forum, generosity the decurions repaid with this burial site by public decree. Archaeologist Karl Weber uncovered it between 1758 and 1764. Vesuvius had buried it under ash in 79 CE, thirty-eight years before this map's date.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Metropolitan Museum of Art collection, via Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 998 (unknown/anonymous, funerary inscription)
ancient_sources.note: The inscription records that Mamia, daughter of Publius, public priestess, was given the burial place by decree of the town councillors.
ancient_sources.quote: Mamiae P(ubli) f(iliae) sacerdoti publicae locus sepultur(ae) datus decurionum decreto

properties.notes: Pompeii's leading fish-sauce manufacturer got a public monument here, his father having spent it building on land the town councilors voted him. Scaurus's name appeared on roughly 29 percent of garum jars found across Pompeii and Herculaneum, making him the city's dominant exporter of the pungent condiment. The councilors also authorized 2,000 sesterces toward his funeral and a bronze equestrian statue in the forum. The 79 CE eruption sealed the tomb decades before this map's date.
properties.image_credit: Tomb of Aulus Umbricius Scaurus, Porta Ercolano necropolis, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the tomb of Aulus Umbricius Scaurus in the Herculaneum Gate necropolis at Pompeii

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 1024 (unknown/anonymous, funerary inscription)
ancient_sources.note: The inscription, set up by his father, records that the town decurions voted Aulus Umbricius Scaurus a burial monument site, 2,000 sesterces toward his funeral, and an equestrian statue in the forum.

properties.notes: A freedwoman named Naevoleia Tyche commissioned this monument for herself, her husband Gaius Munatius Faustus, and their own freed slaves while she was still living. One relief carved into the altar shows a full-sailed merchant ship with a woman at the helm, likely Tyche herself advertising the seaborne trade that made her fortune. The inscription spells out exactly who earned the right to be buried there. Vesuvius's ash sealed the tomb in 79 CE, before this map's snapshot date.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0

ancient_sources.author: CIL X 1030 (unknown/anonymous, funerary inscription)
ancient_sources.note: The inscription records that the freedwoman Naevoleia Tyche built this monument, while still living, for herself and for Gaius Munatius Faustus, and for their own freedmen and freedwomen.
ancient_sources.quote: Naevoleia L(uci) lib(erta) Tyche sibi et C(aio) Munatio Fausto ... hoc monimentum Naevoleia Tyche libertis suis libertabusque et C(ai) Munati Fausti viva fecit

properties.notes: Gaius Vestorius Priscus died in office as a Pompeian aedile at just 22 years old, and his mother paid for a tufa-stone tomb near the Vesuvius Gate to mark it. Painted walls inside show him entering through a doorway, a table stacked with writing tools and coin, and a pair of gladiators he had sponsored in the amphitheater. The city had voted two thousand sesterces toward his funeral. The 79 CE eruption buried the tomb, decades ahead of this map's 117 CE date.
properties.image_credit: Tomb of Vestorius Priscus, Porta Vesuvio necropolis, Pompeii · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the painted tomb enclosure of Gaius Vestorius Priscus at Pompeii

ancient_sources.author: AE 1911, 72 (unknown/anonymous, funerary inscription; the tomb was excavated in 1908, after CIL X's 1883 publication, so it first appeared in L'Annee epigraphique rather than CIL)
ancient_sources.note: The inscription records that Gaius Vestorius Priscus, aedile, died at 22; the town decurions granted the burial place and 2,000 sesterces toward the funeral, and his mother Mulvia Prisca built the tomb at her own expense.
ancient_sources.quote: C. Vestorio Prisco Aedili vixit annis XXII locus sepulturae datus et in funere (sestertium) duo milia d(ecreto) d(ecurionum) Mulvia Prisca mater pecunia sua

properties.notes: Five walled burial enclosures belonging to Aquileian families lined a secondary road outside the city, used from the 1st century CE onward for both cremation and inhumation. Excavators recovered 87 tombs here, packed with glass balsam-jars, stamped oil lamps, and pottery imported from the eastern Mediterranean. Roman law barred burial inside the walls, so wealthy families competed for visibility along this road instead. It remains the only Aquileian necropolis still visible in situ.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aquileia as a Roman fortress and trading emporium on the River Natiso.

properties.notes: Fourteen barrel-vaulted columbaria lined the start of the consular road out of Puteoli toward Capua, most built in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. Niches inside held cremation urns for the dead, and some chambers still carry traces of their original stucco and mosaic decoration. One building has been read as the seat of a burial club, a collegium funeraticium, that pooled dues so ordinary members could afford a decent send-off. Rediscovered in the 1930s, it opened fully to the public only in 2022.

A local Gallo-Roman family called the Julii built this three-tiered tomb outside Glanum around 30-20 BCE to honor their father and grandfather. A square base carved with battle and hunt scenes supports a miniature triumphal arch, topped by a round temple sheltering two standing statues of the deceased. It stands roughly 18 meters tall and counts among the best-preserved Roman funerary monuments anywhere. Paired with a nearby arch, the site is still known locally as Les Antiques.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Carole Raddato, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: The mausoleum carries its own dedicatory inscription naming Sextus, Lucius, and Marcus Julius as the sons who raised the tomb to their forebears.

properties.notes: Numidian kings raised this circular royal tomb near Batna in the 3rd century BCE, ringing its drum with sixty engaged Doric columns beneath an Egyptian-style cornice. Its exact occupant is unknown, though historians link it to the Numidian king Massinissa or one of his Massylian predecessors — either way, its tumulus form and scale mark it as North Africa's oldest surviving royal mausoleum. It still stood as a recognizable landmark under Roman rule in the province of Africa two centuries later. Its diameter runs about 59 meters.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: King Juba II and Queen Cleopatra Selene II, daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony, were said to be entombed beneath this vast circular monument between Tipaza and Cherchell. Sixty engaged columns ring its drum, which rises in a stepped cone roughly 40 meters high on a base over 60 meters wide. No royal remains have ever been found inside, likely lost to ancient tomb raiders. Arabic tradition later renamed it Kbor er Roumia, the tomb of the Christian woman, for the cross-shaped lines on its false door.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

ancient_sources.author: Pomponius Mela
ancient_sources.note: Marks the common tomb of the royal house on the coast road west of Icosium.

properties.notes: A bilingual inscription in Punic and Libyan once crowned this 21-meter royal tomb, naming the Numidian prince Ateban, son of Lepmatath, as its occupant. Built in the 2nd century BCE, it blends Numidian and Hellenistic design across three stacked levels ringed with Ionic pilasters. The inscription was so prized that a British consul dismantled part of the monument in 1842 to carry it off to the British Museum. French archaeologists rebuilt the mausoleum between 1908 and 1910.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

ancient_sources.author: Libyco-Punic bilingual dedicatory inscription, Mausoleum of Ateban, Dougga
ancient_sources.work: KAI 100 (Punic text; the parallel Libyan/Numidian text is KAI 101)
ancient_sources.note: Bilingual Punic/Libyan inscription from the podium frieze of the mausoleum, naming the Numidian prince Ateban son of Lepmatath as honoree; it was a key text used to decipher the Libyco-Berber script. British consul Thomas Reade removed part of it in 1842, damaging the monument, and it is now held in the British Museum.

properties.notes: A 30-meter tower rises on a square plan outside El Khroub, near ancient Cirta, built in the second half of the 2nd century BCE by Greek and Carthaginian masons working for the Numidian court. Tradition names it for King Massinissa, though the balance of evidence points to his son and successor Micipsa as the actual occupant. Its mixed Greco-Punic style reflects the cosmopolitan workforce Numidian kings employed at their capital. It still stood as a visible landmark under Roman rule.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

properties.notes: A three-tiered funerary tower rose beside the Via Augusta six kilometers from Tarraco, built in the early 1st century CE for a family that owned the surrounding land. Two carved figures on its face were mistaken for the Scipio brothers by writers from the 15th to 19th centuries, giving the tower its lasting name even though the real Scipios died a century earlier. Twentieth-century research settled the dating and cleared up the misidentification. It ranks among the best-preserved Roman funerary towers on the Iberian Peninsula.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes Tarraco, near which this tower stands, as a colony founded during the Second Punic War.

properties.notes: Wealthy families of Carmo lined this hillside along the Via Augusta toward Hispalis with rock-cut chamber tombs during the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. Cremation dominated the burial rite here, with ashes placed in holes cut directly into the bedrock beside elaborate underground chambers. Accidental discovery in 1830 led to full excavation from 1882 onward, uncovering one of the largest and best-preserved Roman burial grounds on the Iberian Peninsula. It opened to the public in 1885, the first Spanish site of its kind to do so.
properties.image_credit: Tomb of the Elephant, Carmona Roman Necropolis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Interior of the rock-cut Tomb of the Elephant in the Carmona Roman necropolis

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes Carmo (Carmona) as by far the strongest community in the province of Baetica.

properties.notes: The grandest tomb in the Carmona necropolis was built to resemble a complete Roman villa, with a colonnaded courtyard surrounded by family burial rooms. It takes its name from a statue pedestal found inside inscribed to Servilia, daughter of Lucius, marking it as the mausoleum of an aristocratic family in the 1st century CE. Excavators recovered several statues from its porticos, now displayed in Carmona's own archaeological museum. Its Hellenistic design set it apart from every other tomb on the site.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes Carmo (Carmona), the city whose necropolis holds this tomb, as by far the strongest community in Baetica.

properties.notes: A multi-chambered crypt cut deep into the rock at Carmona takes its popular name from a small stone elephant statue found inside, now kept in the site museum. A window aligned to the equinox sun points to an original use as a shrine to Mithras or to Cybele and Attis, before it was pressed into use for ordinary burials alongside the rest of the necropolis. Its dual life as sanctuary and tomb makes it one of Carmona's more unusual monuments.

Two Roman families, the Voconii and the Julii, built open-air cremation columbaria in this funerary district southeast of Emerita Augusta. Small above-ground chambers held rows of niches for cinerary urns, several of which survive today alongside a painted family portrait of the Voconii. The site grew up around the same time as a nearby luxury villa, the House of the Mithraeum, built for the colony's upper class in the late 1st or early 2nd century CE. It now forms part of Merida's UNESCO World Heritage listing.

Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism who moved her royal household to Jerusalem, was buried in this rock-cut funerary complex after her death around 50-56 CE. A monumental staircase and courtyard lead to a 28-meter facade that the historian Josephus said was once crowned by three pyramids. Underground chambers and passages inside could hold up to fifty burials, cut for her family from Assyria's Adiabene kingdom. A massive rolling stone still seals part of the original entrance.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Queen Helena of Adiabene is buried in the three pyramids she had built three stades outside Jerusalem.

properties.notes: A 20-meter monolithic tower rises from the floor of the Kidron Valley, its lower half carved from solid rock and its upper half built up in ashlar masonry to a concave conical roof. Tradition long linked it to Absalom, King David's rebellious son who died a thousand years earlier, but its Egyptian, Persian, and Hellenistic architectural blend points instead to the 1st century CE. Vaulted chambers cut into its square base held actual burials. It stands just meters from the tombs of Zechariah and the Bnei Hezir family.
properties.image_credit: Historic photograph, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Josephus records that Absalom built himself a marble pillar/monument in the King's Dale two stadia from Jerusalem, which by his own day (1st century CE) was popularly called 'Absalom's Hand' or monument, matching the traditional identification of this Kidron Valley tomb.

properties.notes: This solid, uncarved block of limestone stands cut directly into the cliff face of the Kidron Valley, facing the Temple Mount from across the ravine. Jewish tradition names it for the priest Zechariah ben Jehoiada, though the monument itself is a monolith carved from the rock rather than a hollow chamber, meaning it never actually held a burial. Architectural analysis points to construction sometime in the 1st century BCE or CE. It sits just six meters from the neighboring Tomb of Benei Hezir.

A Hebrew inscription carved above the entrance identifies this as the burial cave of the Benei Hezir, a family of priests who served in the Jerusalem Temple. Two rock-cut columns stand between pilasters below a Doric frieze, making it the oldest of the four monumental Second Temple-era tombs clustered in the Kidron Valley. Scholars date its excavation to the Hasmonean period, roughly the 2nd or early 1st century BCE. It remains a burial complex rather than a solid monument like its neighbors.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Hebrew funerary inscription, Tomb of Benei Hezir, Kidron Valley
ancient_sources.work: CIIP I/1 (Corpus Inscriptionum Iudaeae/Palaestinae, vol. I: Jerusalem, Part 1), no. 137
ancient_sources.note: Inscription carved on the architrave above the tomb's facade naming Eleazar, Hania, Jo'azar, Judah, Shimon and Johanan, sons of Joseph son of Oved, and Joseph and Eleazar sons of Hania, as priests of the sons of Hezir -- identifying the tomb as belonging to a priestly family active in the Second Temple period.

properties.notes: King Herod built himself an elaborate three-story mausoleum on the slope of his hilltop fortress south of Jerusalem, its circular tholos ringed with an Ionic colonnade beneath a conical roof. Archaeologist Ehud Netzer identified its remains in 2007, along with fragments of a reddish limestone sarcophagus smashed into pieces. Jewish rebels who despised Herod's memory tore the tomb apart during the revolt of 66-72 CE, decades before this map's 117 CE date. No trace of Herod's actual remains has ever been found.

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: The funeral procession from Jericho: the bier of gold, the guard in arms, and eight miles' march to burial at Herodium.

properties.image_credit: The Tomb of Herod, Herodium · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The excavated tomb structure identified as the Tomb of Herod at Herodium

properties.notes: Queen Artemisia II built this towering tomb for her husband and brother Mausolus around 350 BCE, stacking a colonnaded temple and stepped pyramid roof atop a massive podium roughly 45 meters tall. Ancient writers counted it among the Seven Wonders of the World, and its scale gave the world the word mausoleum. The monument still stood largely intact under Roman rule in 117 CE; only earthquakes centuries later, between the 11th and 15th centuries, brought it down. Crusader knights then quarried its stones to build a nearby castle.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction painting by Ferdinand Knab, 1886, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Gives the tomb its measurements and the four sculptors who each took a side, and says the fourth was still working when the queen who commissioned it died.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (tomb facade)
ancient_sources.note: A merchant's tomb in the necropolis records that he built it for himself and his sons after sailing round Greece's dangerous Cape Malea to Italy seventy-two times over his trading career.

properties.notes: More than 1,200 tombs stretch across two kilometers on the slopes north and south of Hierapolis, making it the largest ancient burial ground in Asia Minor. Tumuli, house-shaped tombs, and elaborately carved sarcophagi span the late Hellenistic period through the early centuries of Roman rule. Visitors traveled here for the city's hot mineral springs, believed to have healing power, and many chose to be buried within sight of the sacred waters. The necropolis remains one of the best-preserved of its kind anywhere in the ancient world.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Palmyrene inscription, Tower of Elahbel
ancient_sources.note: A carved Aramaic inscription on this Valley-of-the-Tombs tower records that it was built by the Palmyrene citizen Marcus Ulpius Elahbel and his three brothers as a family funerary tower.

properties.notes: West of Palmyra, a narrow valley filled with tower tombs rising four and five stories against the desert cliffs, the tallest funerary architecture anywhere in the Roman world. Wealthy Palmyrene families built these sandstone towers between roughly 9 BCE and 128 CE, packing each level with loculi for hundreds of family members across generations. Corinthian columns and painted coffered ceilings decorated the more elaborate interiors. Many of these towers stood until ISIL destroyed several with explosives in 2015.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.modern_location: Valley of the Tombs, Palmyra, Syria
properties.notes: Four Palmyrene brothers, Elahbel, Shagai, Mogimo, and Maani, finished building this four-story sandstone tower tomb in 103 CE, an exact date recorded in its dedicatory inscription. Corinthian pilasters and painted coffered ceilings decorated burial chambers that together held more than 300 bodies across the tower's levels. It stood as one of the tallest and best-preserved tower tombs in the Valley of the Tombs for nearly two thousand years. ISIL destroyed it with explosives in August 2015.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Elahbel and his brothers
ancient_sources.ref: Greek and Palmyrene text, Seleucid Era 414 (103 CE)
ancient_sources.note: The tower's own foundation inscription records that Marcus Ulpius Elahbel and his brothers, sons of Wahballat, built it as a family tomb in 103 CE — fourteen years before this map's snapshot.

properties.notes: Carved into Petra's eastern cliff face between 40 and 70 CE, this tomb takes its name from capitals loosely resembling the Corinthian order, though they're actually Nabataean floral horn designs. Its facade spans nearly 28 meters wide and 28 meters tall, modeled on the design of the famous Treasury nearby. The layout borrows heavily from Ptolemaic architecture that had developed in Alexandria. It stands directly beside the even larger Palace Tomb along the same royal cliff.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Petra, the Nabataean capital, as a fortified rock city with abundant springs, drawing on the eyewitness account of Athenodorus. A general description of the city, not this specific tomb facade.

properties.notes: The largest rock-cut facade in Petra spans 49 meters wide and 46 meters tall, carved into the eastern cliff toward the end of the 1st century CE. Its top story breaks with every other tomb in the city by extending beyond the cliff face as freestanding built masonry rather than carved rock. Four wide entrances on the ground floor lead into separate burial chambers behind the towering facade. Its scale and unusual construction mark it as one of Petra's grandest Nabataean monuments.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Petra, the Nabataean capital, as a fortified rock city with abundant springs, drawing on the eyewitness account of Athenodorus. A general description of the city, not this specific tomb facade.

properties.notes: Swirling bands of pink, purple, gold, and orange run across this tomb's sandstone facade, carved sometime in the first half of the 1st century CE. Iron and manganese oxides trapped in the rock, polished smooth by centuries of wind and water, produced the vivid marbled effect that gives the tomb its modern nickname. Compared with its grander neighbors along the Royal Tombs cliff, its facade is modest and unadorned by columns. The colors alone have made it one of Petra's most photographed monuments.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: Four elongated pyramids carved above this facade at Petra's entrance represent nefesh, Nabataean markers for the souls of the dead, with a worn figure of a cloaked man niched between them. Most scholars date it to the reign of Malichos II, between 40 and 70 CE, built directly above a separate dining hall known as the Bab as-Siq Triclinium. An inscription at the site records details connecting the two structures. Visitors today pass beneath it on the walk into Petra's main canyon.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0

properties.notes: A carved figure wearing a muscled cuirass decorated with flowers stands at the center of this facade in the Wadi Farasa valley, its armor style so distinctly Roman that early visitors assumed it marked a soldier's grave. Archaeologists now date the complex to the third quarter of the 1st century CE, decades before Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE. A carved triclinium banquet hall sits directly across a courtyard from the tomb facade. The figure was almost certainly a Nabataean official, not a Roman legionary.

Rock-cut tombs spread across the hillsides ringing Cyrene, one of the largest burial landscapes to survive from the Greek and Roman world, with graves ranging from the 6th century BCE through the Roman period. The Western Necropolis holds the most monumental examples, its facades carved with Doric and Ionic porticoes along a dedicated funerary road. Temple-tombs and painted chamber tombs with rock-cut sarcophagi honeycomb the surrounding cliffs. Italian archaeologists continue to uncover previously unrecorded tombs here.
properties.image_credit: 19th-century illustration, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the founding of Cyrene by settlers from Thera under the leader Battus, naming the city whose extensive rock-cut necropolis surrounds its ruins.

properties.notes: An Ionic temple facade with columns carved straight out of the cliff, rather than built up in front of it, marks this rock-hewn tomb above ancient Telmessos. A Greek inscription beside the entrance names it for Amyntas, son of Hermagios, and dates the monument to around 350 BCE. It remains the grandest of a whole cliffside cluster of Lycian house-tombs overlooking the harbor. The city below, later renamed Fethiye, remained a landmark of Lycian territory throughout Roman rule.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor, CC BY-SA 4.0

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Dedicatory inscription, Tomb of Amyntas, Telmessos
ancient_sources.note: The Greek inscription carved beside the tomb's entrance names its occupant — Amyntou tou Hermagiou, "[tomb] of Amyntas, son of Hermagias" — and its letterforms date it to around 350 BCE, which is how the monument got its name.

properties.notes: More than 100 rock-cut tombs honeycomb the cliffs above Myra, most carved in the 4th century BCE in the distinctive Lycian house-tomb style that mimics timber architecture in solid stone. Stonemasons reproduced beams, joists, and doors down to the smallest detail, and traces of the original red and blue paint still survive on several facades. The River Necropolis holds the famous Painted Tomb, decorated with life-sized carved figures on both its interior and exterior walls. Myra remained a major Lycian city throughout Roman rule of the province.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Myra as one of the six leading cities of the Lycian League, entitled to three votes.

properties.notes: Lycian ruler Arbinas built himself a Greek temple in miniature atop an 8-meter podium at Xanthos around 390-380 BCE, its columns framing statues of sea nymphs that gave the monument its modern name. Two carved friezes wrapped the podium with scenes of sieges and battles, part biography and part legend. The design later influenced the far larger Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. Only stone blocks of the podium remain in place today, the sculpted superstructure having been removed to the British Museum in the 19th century.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction drawing, Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.ref: Greek text SEG 28.1245, Lycian text N 311
ancient_sources.note: A bilingual Greek-and-Lycian text on the monument's statue base survives in fragments, invoking Artemis the huntress alongside what scholars read as a record of the dynast Arbinas's campaigns.

properties.notes: An ordinary pagan cemetery grew up on the northern edge of Salona from the 2nd century BCE onward, filling with cremation and inhumation burials for the provincial capital's residents over the following centuries. By 117 CE it functioned as a typical extramural Roman burial ground outside Dalmatia's chief city, undistinguished from dozens of similar cemeteries across the empire. Its later fame as a Christian pilgrimage site, built around the martyred bishop Domnius, only began after his execution in 304 CE. Stone sarcophagi from the Roman-era burials still scatter the site today.
properties.image_credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons contributor

properties.notes: The largest of Rome's four imperial gladiator schools, built by Domitian directly east of the Colosseum and linked to it by an underground tunnel so fighters could reach the arena unseen. Its own small oval training ground, ringed by barracks and cells, could hold roughly 2,000 gladiators at full capacity. Excavated remains are still visible today just off the Via Labicana. In 117 CE it was Rome's premier gladiatorial training ground, fully staffed and in daily use.
properties.image_credit: Ludus Magnus, Rome, photographed 2006 by Jastrow - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodian
ancient_sources.note: Recounts that the emperor Commodus, in his obsession with gladiatorial combat, wanted to abandon the imperial palace and live instead in the gladiators' barracks (the Ludus Magnus) next to the Colosseum.

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy, near the Caelian Hill
properties.notes: Founded under Domitian and completed under Trajan to train gladiators drawn from Dacian prisoners, its fighters specialized in the falx, the curved blade that had cut through Roman shields on the Danube frontier. It stood on the slope of the Caelian Hill east of the Colosseum, alongside Rome's three other imperial schools, though its exact footprint has never been pinned down by excavation. Trajan's Dacian triumph of 106 CE kept it freshly supplied with captives in the years just before 117 CE.

One of Domitian's four imperial gladiator schools, training fighters in the heavy-armored style associated with Gallic warriors, whose bulky equipment was prized for spectacle even as it slowed a fighter's footwork in the arena. Ancient sources place it in Rome's Regio II near the Colosseum alongside the Ludus Magnus, Dacicus, and Matutinus, but unlike the Ludus Magnus its precise site has never been excavated. It was still functioning as one of the four state-run schools in 117 CE.

The fourth of Domitian's imperial schools, training bestiarii, the men who fought and hunted wild animals in the morning program before the afternoon's gladiator bouts, hence its name. Topographers have placed it between the Claudianum and the Vicus Caput Africae, but like the Gallicus and Dacicus, no excavated structure has been firmly identified as this school. It was one of four functioning state schools supplying the Colosseum's beast hunts in 117 CE.

The most famous gladiator school outside Rome, and the oldest one on record: a lanista named Aurelius Scaurus was training state gladiators here around 105 BCE. It became infamous in 73 BCE when roughly 70 gladiators, led by the Thracian fighter Spartacus, broke out and touched off the Third Servile War. Its ruins lie beside Capua's amphitheater, second in size only to the Colosseum. The school was still operating, and the amphitheater still hosting games, in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Santa Maria Capua Vetere, adjacent to the gladiator school site - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: Describes the gladiatorial school at Capua run by Lentulus Batiatus, where about 70-78 gladiators including Spartacus broke out with kitchen implements in 73 BCE, sparking the Third Servile War.

properties.notes: Ravenna hosted one of the handful of gladiator schools outside Rome brought under direct state administration by the early empire, alongside Praeneste, Alexandria, and Pergamon. Its exact site within the ancient city has not been located archaeologically, and its history survives mainly through epigraphic and literary mentions rather than excavated remains. Ravenna's standing as home port of Rome's Adriatic war fleet made it a natural garrison town for a state-run school of this kind.

Alexandria's gladiator school was one of a small group of provincial ludi absorbed into direct imperial administration by the late 1st century CE, training fighters for Egypt's amphitheaters. Its physical location within the ancient city is not archaeologically fixed, and it is known chiefly through literary references grouping it with the state schools at Pergamon, Praeneste, and Capua. Alexandria's rank as the empire's second city made it a natural site for imperial investment in the games.

Pergamon's gladiator school was another of the provincial ludi brought under state control in the early empire, training fighters in a city also renowned for a great school of medicine. Its exact location has not been excavated or identified, and it is attested mainly alongside the other named state schools at Alexandria, Praeneste, and Capua. Pergamon sat in a province where Greek athletics, not gladiatorial games, remained the dominant public spectacle.

Begun under Caligula on his family's estate on the Vatican Hill and finished under Claudius, this circus is separate from the Circus Maximus across the river, best known as the site of Nero's persecution of Christians after the fire of 64 CE. Its spina carried an Egyptian obelisk from Heliopolis, the same one standing today in St Peter's Square since 1586. Still active in 117 CE, it later gave its ground to the basilica of St Peter's.
properties.image_credit: Vatican Obelisk, originally the spina obelisk of the Circus of Nero - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Nero's persecution of Christians after the Great Fire of 64 CE, including executions staged as spectacles in the circus on the Vatican hill where Nero's family had an estate (Pliny the Elder, Natural History 36.74, separately describes the obelisk erected there by Gaius and Nero).

properties.notes: Built over a former necropolis at the end of the 1st century CE, Carthage's circus stretched more than 470 meters, about a third the length of the Circus Maximus, and could seat roughly 45,000 spectators for chariot races. It ranked among the largest circuses anywhere outside Rome and Antioch, reflecting Carthage's status as Africa's leading city. In use and hosting races by 117 CE, it remained active for centuries afterward, with further building work added in the early 3rd century.

ancient_sources.author: Salvian
ancient_sources.note: Describes Carthage's citizens still packing the circus and shouting for the races as the Vandal army closed in on the city in 439 CE, calling it a mark of how far the city's morals had fallen even in its last hours.

properties.image_credit: The Circus of Carthage site · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving traces of the Circus of Carthage

properties.notes: Carthage's amphitheater went up west of the Byrsa hill at the end of the 1st or start of the 2nd century CE, with an inscription confirming it was already in service by 133-139 CE, just after this map's snapshot. It seated around 30,000, one of the largest arenas in Roman Africa. Christian tradition later placed the martyrdoms of Perpetua and Felicity here in 203 CE. Under construction or newly finished as Trajan's reign closed in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Carthage, interior view - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous (redactor, incorporating Perpetua's own prison diary)
ancient_sources.note: Early-3rd-century (c. 203 CE) martyrdom account that narrates in detail the execution of Perpetua, Felicity, and companions by beasts and sword in the amphitheatre of Carthage.

properties.notes: Long before the massive amphitheater that made El Djem famous, Thysdrus already had a much smaller arena, an earthen structure excavated in 1973 with a capacity of around 6,000, dated by specialists to the 1st century CE. A second, intermediate amphitheater followed on the same site before the great stone amphitheater seen today rose around 238 CE, over a century after Trajan's death. In 117 CE it was this small first-generation arena serving Thysdrus, not the monumental one tourists visit now.

Built under the Flavian emperors in the closing decade of the 1st century CE, Nimes's amphitheater could seat around 24,000 spectators and remains one of the best-preserved Roman arenas anywhere, still hosting events today nearly two thousand years later. Its two tiers of arcades in dressed limestone reflect the wealth Nemausus drew from its position on the road linking Italy to Spain. Fully operational and hosting games in 117 CE, a generation or so after its completion.
properties.image_credit: Arena of Nimes - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL XII 3316
ancient_sources.note: A text on the podium wall reserves places for the guilds of Rhône and Saône boatmen, by decree of the town council of Nîmes.

properties.notes: Raised around 90 CE under Domitian, not long after the Colosseum in Rome, Arles's amphitheater measures 136 by 107 meters across two levels of arcades, 60 arches below and 34 above, and could hold roughly 20,000 spectators for gladiatorial combat, beast hunts, and public executions. Arelate's wealth as a Roman colony and river port on the Rhone funded a building program on a scale that rivaled cities twice its size. Fully active and staging games in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Arenes d'Arles (Arles Amphitheatre) - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Arelate as a Roman colony settled by veterans of the Sixth Legion, one of the leading towns of Gallia Narbonensis where this amphitheater stood.

properties.notes: Raised outside Verona's walls in the early 1st century CE, most likely around 30 CE, in pink and white limestone, the Verona Arena could seat around 30,000, one of the largest amphitheaters in Roman Italy after the Colosseum and Capua's arena. Its outer ring mostly collapsed in a 12th-century earthquake, but the inner structure survives intact enough to still host opera today. In full use for games nearly a century before Trajan's reign closed in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Verona Arena - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Pliny writes to Maximus praising him for giving a gladiatorial spectacle to the people of Verona as a memorial to his late wife, a Veronese woman; the letter does not name the amphitheater building itself but is about games staged at Verona.

properties.notes: Begun under Augustus as a smaller structure, then enlarged for gladiatorial games under Vespasian from 79 CE and finished under Titus around 81 CE, the amphitheater at Pula in Istria could hold about 23,000 spectators. Its full limestone outer wall survives intact, unlike most Roman amphitheaters, making it one of the six largest and best-preserved arenas from the ancient world. Actively hosting games as a fully finished, mature amphitheater in 117 CE, roughly one generation after completion.
properties.image_credit: Pula Arena, Croatia - Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Pola as a city on a sheltered natural harbor on the Istrian coast, with a legendary founding by Colchian exiles sent in pursuit of Medea, the city where this amphitheater was built.

properties.notes: Docimium's quarries had been worked on imperial account since the 1st century BCE for their prized purple-veined marble, and would go on to become one of the empire's great sarcophagus-carving centers, exporting garland- and column-decorated coffins as far as Rome and Africa. In 117 CE that specialty hadn't started yet: the earliest dated garland sarcophagi belong to the Hadrianic period beginning in the 130s CE. Docimium was already a mature imperial marble exporter, just not yet a sarcophagus workshop.

Athens became one of the Roman world's three major sarcophagus-exporting centers, its workshops carving Pentelic marble coffins shipped across the eastern Mediterranean. But the dating is unambiguous: surviving Attic sarcophagi run from roughly 130 to 260 CE, with output really taking off only after 200 CE. In 117 CE this industry had not yet started. Athens under Trajan still cremated its dead, a full generation before its famous sarcophagus workshops carved their first pieces.

Aphrodisias already had a thriving marble-sculpture export trade by 117 CE, with signed work by its sculptors turning up in Rome, Greece, and Africa on the strength of local quarries and a renowned sculpture school. Its columnar sarcophagi, an architectural facade with figures between the columns, are a later specialty documented from the 2nd century, with nearby Goktepe marble spreading Mediterranean-wide only from the mid-2nd century. In 117 CE it stood on the edge of its own sarcophagus boom.
properties.image_credit: Aphrodisias, site of the city's marble workshops - Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Aquileia's forum anchored the colony's public life at the junction of the Via Iulia Augusta and the Via Sacra. Workers paved the square with pale Aurisina limestone slabs quarried from the nearby Karst hills, replacing the timber-and-rubble forum that had served the colony since its founding in 181 BCE. A civil basilica closed the square's south side, housing courts and the city council, while merchants kept shops along its east and west flanks. A canal ran beneath the pavement, channeling river water toward the port. By 117 CE the forum had stood at the heart of Aquileia for over a century, hosting markets, trials, and the colony's public assemblies beneath the Alpine sky.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum, Aquileia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: AE 1996, 685
ancient_sources.note: An honorific elogium for one of the colony's founding triumvirs recorded the powers granted him to draft Aquileia's laws, enroll its senate, and dedicate a temple during the colony's 169 BCE reinforcement.

properties.notes: Marcus Agrippa financed the theatre for the new colony of Augusta Emerita, and builders finished it in 16 BCE. A two-story colonnaded stage backdrop rose behind the orchestra, its columns and marble statuary framing performances for an audience of six thousand. Veterans of the Roman legions who settled the colony filled its semicircular tiers for comedies, tragedies, and public ceremonies alike. Under Trajan, workers refaced the stage building's facade in marble and fenced a sacred precinct into the front seating rows with a marble railing. Cut into a hillside above the Guadiana River, the theatre stood 132 years old in 117 CE, still the beating heart of the colony's cultural life.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre, Merida · Hakan Svensson (Xauxa), Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL II 474
ancient_sources.note: A lintel inscription over the theatre's side passages named Marcus Agrippa, three times consul, as its builder, opening with the same 'M AGRIPPA L F COS' formula he later used on Rome's Pantheon.

properties.notes: Trajan founded Timgad in 100 CE as a colony for army veterans, laying the city out as a nearly perfect grid centered on its forum. Porticoes and rows of shops framed the paved square, with the curia and a basilica standing at its heart and a small temple to Victory tucked into one corner. Retired soldiers of the Third Augustan Legion walked its colonnades to conduct civic business and hear public announcements. A dedicatory tablet found near the forum commemorated the emperor's foundation of the colony and the legionary legate who oversaw the work. Seventeen years old in 117 CE, the forum still smelled of new-cut stone from a city built at Trajan's order in the empty steppe.
properties.image_credit: Forum of Timgad · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII 2355
ancient_sources.note: A fragmentary tabula found near the forum and west gate commemorated Trajan's founding of the colony of Thamugadi, carried out through his legate and the Third Augustan Legion; scholarship places it tentatively in this area rather than on any specific standing arch.

properties.notes: The Cavaliere wreck sank in the cove of Le Lavandou around 100-90 BCE with its oak hull sheathed in lead and its mast still standing on the seabed. Its hold mixed amphorae and black-gloss pottery with cuts of salted pork, plus coins from Numidia, Spain, and Massalia tracing the ship's trading circuit across the western Mediterranean. Excavators also raised seven bronze helmets of different styles, suggesting an armed escort rode along to guard the cargo. The wreck sank as Rome was actively Romanizing the Ligurian coast, two centuries before Trajan's empire reached its territorial height.

The Planier 3 wreck lies at the base of a drop-off on the Pierre-de-la-Bague reef off Marseille, found in 1961 in the strong currents that have claimed several ships at this single point. Chemical residue analysis of its amphorae detected grape and fermentation markers, confirming the ship carried wine rather than oil or fish sauce when it sank. The find sits among a cluster of wrecks at Planier that map directly onto the shipping lanes converging on Massalia, ancient Marseille's harbor. It offers direct chemical proof, not just jar shape, of what a Roman wine ship actually carried to market.

Bulldozers building Rome's Fiumicino airport in 1958 struck the hulls of five Roman vessels preserved in the silt of the harbor basin built under Claudius and later expanded under Trajan. The find included three flat-bottomed river barges that ran cargo up the Tiber to Rome, one seagoing merchant ship, and a rare fishing boat fitted with a 300-liter tank to keep its catch alive. Marble and amphorae recovered inside the hulls show these boat types were still working the harbor-to-city supply chain into the early second century CE. The fleet captures the exact logistics of feeding Rome at the height of imperial Portus traffic.
properties.image_credit: Museo delle Navi Romane, Fiumicino · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Strait of Sicily, between Sicily and Tunisia
properties.notes: Deep-sea survey in the Strait of Sicily located Wreck B eighty kilometers northwest of Sicily at a depth of roughly eight hundred meters, undisturbed since it sank in the last quarter of the first century CE. Its amphorae came from four different origins on one voyage — Campania, Egypt, Crete, and Tripolitania — showing a single ship loading cargo across multiple ports. The 1988-97 survey that found it used deep-submergence technology more commonly associated with Titanic research to map the largest concentration of ancient shipwrecks ever found at such depth. The wreck proves Roman captains sailed the open central Mediterranean directly rather than always hugging the coast.

A storm drove this Greek-built ship onto rocks near Mahdia around 80-70 BCE while it hauled looted Athenian art to Italy, spoils from Sulla's sack of the city in 86 BCE. Its hold carried more than sixty marble columns weighing some 200 tons combined, together with bronze statues including a herm signed by the sculptor Boethos of Chalcedon. Salvage divers recovered the wreck's contents between 1907 and 1913, and most of the finds now fill galleries at the Bardo National Museum in Tunis. The cargo shows how thoroughly Rome's elite were draining Greece's art markets a generation after Sulla's legions marched through Athens.
properties.image_credit: Mahdia shipwreck finds, Bardo National Museum · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Spargi Island, La Maddalena archipelago, Sardinia, Italy
properties.notes: The Spargi wreck sank around 120-100 BCE near La Maddalena with its thirty-five-meter oak hull sheathed in lead, carrying wine amphorae, pottery, and furniture. Excavators eventually recovered roughly 400 amphorae from the site, enough to reconstruct a full cross-section of the original hold now on permanent display in the local museum. One bronze helmet turned up still holding a skull, a grim hint the ship went down in a fight rather than a simple storm. The wreck marks a well-traveled corridor through the Strait of Bonifacio linking Italy, Sardinia, and Corsica generations before Trajan's Mediterranean.

properties.modern_location: Lavezzi Islands, Strait of Bonifacio, Corsica, France
properties.notes: The Sud-Lavezzi 2 wreck sank in the Strait of Bonifacio between 22 and 25 CE hauling a genuinely mixed Baetican cargo: olive oil, wine, and fish sauce packed across at least six distinct amphora types, plus raw copper and lead ingots. That range of goods on one ship shows how thoroughly southern Spain's Guadalquivir valley had industrialized its exports by the early first century CE. The wreck sits in the same strait where the Spargi ship also went down, a genuine bottleneck for ancient Mediterranean shipping. It captures Baetica functioning as one of Rome's most productive single-province economies less than a century before Trajan's reign.

properties.modern_location: Between Cap Corse, Corsica and Capraia Island, Italy
properties.notes: Divers found the Capo Corso 2 wreck in 2012 lying 350 meters deep in the channel between Corsica and the island of Capraia, dated to around the turn of the first and second centuries CE. Its hold was stacked almost entirely with glass — raw glass blocks meant for reworking plus thousands of finished bowls, cups, jugs, and bottles, some still stacked as loaded. Only one other known Roman wreck in the Mediterranean has carried a cargo this dominated by glass rather than amphorae. It documents the raw-material glass trade that fed Italian glassworking workshops in the decades just before Trajan's empire reached its greatest extent.

The Diano Marina wreck sank about half a mile offshore in the mid-first century CE, its hold packed with Dressel 2/4 wine amphorae loaded in and around Roman Barcino, modern Barcelona. Part of its cargo also included massive dolia, ceramic vats holding roughly 3,000 liters apiece, stacked to carry wine in bulk rather than jar by jar. Divers found the wreck lying forty meters deep, and part of its amphora cargo is now on permanent display in Diano Marina's civic museum. It shows Catalonia already exporting wine westward across the Ligurian Sea two generations before Trajan's death.

A police patrol boat's sonar found this wreck in 2023 sitting 160 meters down off Civitavecchia, roughly eighty kilometers northwest of Rome, its hold still packed with hundreds of intact amphorae. Archaeologists dated the more-than-twenty-meter hull broadly to between the first century BCE and the first century CE based on the recovered amphorae. Italian authorities kept the exact coordinates secret after the discovery specifically to keep looters away from the intact site. The wreck marks the deep shipping lane that fed cargo up the Tyrrhenian coast toward Rome's harbors at Ostia and Portus.

The Chretienne H wreck sank off the Golfe-Juan coast around 15-20 CE carrying Pascual 1 amphorae, a distinctive wine-jar type produced in Hispania Tarraconensis in northeastern Spain. Its cargo forms part of a documented pattern of Augustan-era wrecks tracing Tarraconensian wine into Gallia Narbonensis just as Rome was consolidating its hold on southern Gaul. The reef here, La Chretienne, has claimed enough ships across the centuries that archaeologists now catalog its wrecks by letter. It captures Spanish wine displacing Italian exports along the French Riviera trade routes within a generation of Augustus's death.

Construction crews building a rail link at Pisa's San Rossore station struck a buried ship hull in 1998 and kept striking more for the next eighteen years, eventually uncovering thirty-nine vessels preserved in the silted-up channel of Pisa's ancient river harbor. The ships span roughly nine centuries of continuous use, from the second century BCE into the early medieval period, alongside ceramics, glass, rope, tools, and even human skeletons preserved by the waterlogged mud. Archaeologists nicknamed the site the 'Pompeii of the sea' for how completely the silt sealed in organic material that almost never survives elsewhere. The harbor was a working river port in continuous operation through the exact period this map depicts, though no single hull is dated precisely to the year 117 CE.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Nave I Museo delle Navi Antiche di Pisa.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Hull from the Pisa San Rossore ship graveyard · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Augustus's engineers finished this bridge around 27 BCE to carry the Via Flaminia across the Nera river gorge on four soaring arches, reaching 30 meters at its highest point and stretching some 160 meters end to end, making it one of the largest bridges the Romans ever built. Its ruins later amazed the painter Corot so much that he sketched them again and again in the 1820s. Only the southernmost arch still stands today, but in 117 CE all four carried the empire's main road north from Rome toward the Adriatic. Every courier and legion marching from Rome toward Ariminum crossed this exact span leaving Umbria.
properties.image_credit: Bridge of Augustus, Narni · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Martial
ancient_sources.note: Closes a poem to a friend detained at Narnia by invoking the town's bridge over the sulfurous river Nar, wishing it to stand forever.

properties.notes: Roman engineers raised this limestone bridge around 3 BCE to carry the Via Domitia, the oldest Roman road in Gaul, across the seasonal Calavon river. Three arches span 85 meters, with the central arch alone stretching over 16 meters, and the builders cut rectangular openings straight through the piers so floodwater could pass without toppling the structure. The design worked so well that the bridge still carried ordinary car traffic until 2005, more than two thousand years after the last Roman legionary crossed it. Travelers moving between Italy and Spain along the Via Domitia in 117 CE would have crossed this exact span west of Apt.
properties.image_credit: Pont Julien, Bonnieux · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Apta Iulia among the towns with Latin rights in Gallia Narbonensis, near which this bridge carries a Roman road across the Calavon river.

properties.notes: A local Gallo-Roman notable named Lucius Donnius Flavos left money in his will around 12 BCE for this single-arch bridge over the Touloubre river, and his family carried out the plan, adding a matching triumphal arch at each end in his memory. Each gate stands about 7 meters tall in the Corinthian order and was originally topped with stone lions, turning an ordinary river crossing into a ceremonial gateway. It carried the Via Julia Augusta, the coastal road linking Italy to Spain through Gallia Narbonensis, and it remains the only Roman bridge anywhere still flanked by both of its original triumphal arches. Traffic used the span continuously for nearly two thousand years until a wartime bombing finally forced its closure to vehicles in 1944.
properties.image_credit: Pont Flavien, Saint-Chamas · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription
ancient_sources.note: Records that L. Donnius Flavus, priest of the imperial cult at Rome and Augustus, funded the bridge by testamentary bequest around 12 BCE, built under two named supervisors.

properties.notes: Lucius Fabricius, curator of Rome's roads, built this bridge in 62 BCE to replace an older wooden crossing lost to fire, linking the Campus Martius to Tiber Island on two wide arches braced by a central pier. At 62 meters long it is the oldest Roman bridge still standing anywhere in the world, and Fabricius's own inscription is still legible on the stonework today. Later generations nicknamed it Ponte dei Quattro Capi after four-headed marble herms added at one end centuries afterward. By 117 CE it had already carried foot traffic over the Tiber's eastern channel for nearly 180 years without ever needing to be rebuilt.
properties.image_credit: Pons Fabricius, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription
ancient_sources.ref: carved four times on the bridge itself
ancient_sources.note: Records L. Fabricius, curator of roads, overseeing the bridge's construction in 62 BCE, with a later restoration notice added under consuls Lepidus and Lollius in 21 BCE.

properties.notes: A Roman magistrate named Lucius Cestius built this bridge in the mid-40s BCE to link Tiber Island to the Trastevere bank, completing the island's connection to both shores alongside its older sister crossing, the Pons Fabricius. Legend held that a sacred serpent from Epidaurus had swum ashore on the island during a 3rd-century BCE plague, prompting Rome to build a temple to the healing god Aesculapius there, and this bridge became the main route pilgrims used to reach it. The bridge would eventually need a full imperial restoration under Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian in 370 CE, but through Trajan's reign it still stood on its original Republican-era masonry. Trastevere's residents crossed it daily to reach the heart of the city.
properties.image_credit: Ponte Cestio, Rome · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Augustus's veterans founded Emerita Augusta in 25 BCE as a retirement colony for soldiers of the Cantabrian Wars, and builders soon raised this bridge across the Guadiana to link the new Lusitanian capital to the southern road network. Including its approaches it ran nearly 790 meters on more than 60 granite arches, making it one of the longest bridges the Romans ever built and still the longest surviving bridge from the ancient world today. Trajan himself was born a few days' ride away at Italica, and by his reign the bridge had already carried Lusitania's capital's traffic for well over a century. The dams at Proserpina and Cornalvo that fed Emerita Augusta's own aqueducts stood just outside the city this bridge served.
properties.image_credit: Roman Bridge over the Guadiana, Mérida · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Names Augusta Emerita as a city jointly settled by military veterans in the territory of the Turduli, the city this bridge connects across the Guadiana river.

properties.notes: Roman engineers built this dam in the 1st century BCE across the Vallon de la Baume gorge just south of Glanum to store water for the growing Gallo-Greek town below, making it the earliest known arch dam anywhere in the ancient world. Standing 12 meters high and 18 meters long, it curved against the water pressure the way modern arch dams still do, a principle later Roman engineers in Spain and North Africa would reuse for centuries. Glanum had grown up around a sacred healing spring, and this dam let the town keep both its ritual pool and its everyday water supply flowing through dry Provençal summers. The dam survived close to two thousand years before a modern replacement destroyed its remains in 1891.

properties.name_latin: Ermita de la Virgen del Pilar Dam
properties.name_english: Ermita de la Virgen del Pilar Dam
properties.notes: Roman hydraulic engineers built this gravity dam in the 1st or 2nd century CE across a stream near modern Alcotas, part of a wider Roman push to dam and irrigate the drier interior valleys of Hispania Tarraconensis. Centuries later a small hermitage dedicated to the Virgen del Pilar was built directly against its ancient stonework, which is how the dam earned the name it carries today. Unlike the curved dams at Glanum or Petra, it worked as a plain gravity dam, holding back its reservoir through sheer mass and thickness rather than an arched shape. It belongs to a scattered family of small Roman dams across inland Aragon that together show how systematically Rome managed water even far from its famous city aqueducts.

Roman administrators expanded the ancient copper mines at Phaino, tucked into the rugged Wadi Faynan south of the Dead Sea, into one of the empire's largest copper-producing districts after annexing the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE. Engineers built a reservoir and dam here to store enough water for cooling and processing smelted ore, since the wadi itself ran dry for most of the year. Convicts and forced laborers, Christians exiled here for their faith among them in later centuries, kept the smelting furnaces running on water this system supplied. Dark slag heaps still blanket the valley floor today, physical evidence of just how much copper Rome pulled out of this remote corner of Arabia.

Builders at Bulla Regia raised eight massive vaulted cisterns side by side at the edge of town to store water for a wealthy trading city that shipped wheat, olive oil, and exotic circus animals to Rome. The cisterns doubled as a passive cooling system: shafts let attendants sprinkle water down onto the mosaic floors of the town's famous half-underground villas, and the evaporating water pulled the worst of the North African heat out of the rooms below. Bulla Regia's elite built their houses with an entire sunken story specifically to escape the summer sun, something almost no other Roman city bothered to do. The cisterns still stand today as the first structure visitors see walking into the site.

Nabataean traders carved and plastered rock-cut cisterns into the hillside at Avdat generations before Rome ever ruled the region, capturing the Negev's scarce winter rain to keep caravans supplied on the long haul between Petra and the Mediterranean port of Gaza. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom outright in 106 CE and folded Avdat into the new province of Arabia without tearing down the water system that already worked, so Roman soldiers stationed there simply kept drawing on the same cisterns their Nabataean predecessors had built. The site sits in a region that receives less than 150 millimeters of rain a year, which made every cistern the difference between a functioning waystation and an abandoned ruin. Incense and spice caravans still watered here on the road north through Arabia in the years after Trajan's death.

Nabataean settlers built the first cisterns at Mamshit in the mid-1st century CE, turning a stop on the Petra-to-Gaza incense route into a real town rather than just a caravan halt. After Trajan's annexation of Arabia in 106 CE the town grew quickly under Roman rule, and residents cut new cisterns and stone channels to keep pace, catching rainwater that ran off the surrounding hillsides through carefully graded conduits. Mamshit had no natural spring of its own, so every drop its people drank had to be caught, stored, and rationed through systems exactly like these. The Negev's caravan cities depended on this kind of engineered water harvesting far more than on any river or masonry aqueduct.

Trajan opened the Aqua Traiana in 109 CE to serve both drinking fountains and industry, channeling fresh water down the steep slope of the Janiculum hill above Trastevere. Archaeologists excavating under the American Academy in Rome in the 1990s found a multi-wheeled flour-milling complex built astride that channel, but the mills themselves date to the late 3rd century CE, roughly a century and a half after Trajan died in 117 CE. The aqueduct he built kept powering Rome's grain mills for centuries afterward regardless: the mills became so vital to feeding the city that the Ostrogoths deliberately cut the Aqua Traiana in 537 CE hoping to starve Rome out, forcing the general Belisarius to improvise floating mills anchored in the Tiber instead. On 11 August 117 CE the aqueduct's water was already running past this exact hillside; the wheels that would one day turn on it were still a century and a half away.

ancient_sources.author: Procopius
ancient_sources.note: Procopius describes the grain mills powered by the Aqua Traiana on the Janiculum falling silent when the Goths cut the aqueduct during the 537 CE siege, prompting Belisarius to rig replacement mills on boats in the Tiber.

properties.notes: A warm, mildly sulfurous spring called Efqa rose from a cave deep inside a mountain west of Palmyra's center and had watered the oasis for millennia before Rome ever reached the Syrian desert, but Palmyrene engineers under Roman rule refined it into a working qanat system, channeling the flow through a 400-meter hand-cut tunnel and nine wells out to the gardens and palm groves below. The spring never let up, producing roughly 5,000 cubic meters of water a day at a nearly constant rate year-round, which is exactly what let a caravan city thrive in the middle of an otherwise waterless desert. Palmyra's merchants grew enormously wealthy in the decades around Trajan's reign taxing the silk and spice caravans that crossed the desert, a business only possible because this single spring made a stopover here viable at all. Inscriptions treated Efqa as sacred, and religious rites at the spring continued alongside its everyday use for irrigation and drinking water throughout the Roman period.
properties.image_credit: Efqa Spring, Palmyra · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Pliny praises Palmyra for its location, the richness of its soil, and its pleasant springs amid a vast surrounding sea of sand, the oasis water that made the desert city possible.

properties.notes: Rome's senate raised this marble arch on the mole of Ancona's harbor in 115 CE to thank Trajan for paying out of his own pocket to expand the port, calling the improved crossing a safer gateway to Italy. Apollodorus of Damascus, the same architect behind Trajan's Column and Forum, designed it: a single arched passage on a tall limestone podium, faced in imported Greek marble and originally topped with six bronze statues of the emperor's family, long since stripped for their metal. By 117 CE the arch was barely two years old, the newest monument on a harbor Trajan had just finished remaking.

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: The arch's own surviving inscription honors Trajan for making 'the entrance to Italy safer' (tutiorem accessum Italiae) and names his wife Plotina and sister Marciana alongside him.

properties.image_credit: Arch of Trajan, Ancona · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

properties.notes: Ancona's amphitheater rose on the hill the cathedral now occupies, its long elliptical wall built up in alternating bands of opus reticulatum and brick that still stand near Piazza del Senato. Augustan builders raised the first arena to hold a few thousand spectators, and later enlargement under Trajan pushed capacity toward ten thousand, tying the games here directly to the same imperial patronage rebuilding the harbor below. By 117 CE it had hosted the city's spectacles for close to a century and a half, only recently expanded to match Ancona's growing importance as an eastern gateway.
properties.image_credit: Roman Amphitheatre of Ancona · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Juvenal
ancient_sources.note: Opens the satire of the giant turbot by describing Ancona and its hilltop shrine to Venus, naming the city where this amphitheater was built.

properties.notes: The Senate and People of Rome dedicated this triumphal arch in 114 CE to mark the opening of Trajan's new road to Brindisi. Carved from Parian marble, the 15.6-meter gate rose exactly where the Via Traiana split from the Via Appia at the town's edge. Its reliefs show Trajan founding colonies, funding the alimenta child-support program, and receiving Dacia's submission. Only three years old at Trajan's death, it survives today essentially untouched by time.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Trajan, Benevento · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Dedicatory inscription
ancient_sources.note: The arch's own attic inscription titles Trajan with his full imperial style — Germanicus Dacicus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the eighteenth year — and records the Senate and People of Rome as dedicators.

properties.notes: Hadrian inaugurated this theatre in 126 CE, nine years after Trajan's death, on ground that held no such building in 117 CE. Its finished cavea spanned 90 meters and sat up to 15,000 spectators, rivaling any stage in southern Italy. Caracalla enlarged it further between 200 and 210 CE, an expansion recorded on a stone at the stage entrance. Buried for centuries, it was rediscovered in 1890 and reopened to the public in 1957.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre, Benevento · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Horace
ancient_sources.note: Recounts a kitchen fire at an inn in Beneventum during Horace's journey to Brundisium. A passing anecdote about the town, not a description of the theatre.

properties.notes: Nero paused at Beneventum in 63 CE to watch a gladiator show staged here by the courtier Vatinius. Built at the city's edge for fast crowd access, the arena measured roughly 160 by 130 meters, rivaling the amphitheatres of Capua and Verona. A detached branch of Rome's own gladiator school trained fighters on site. Its buried remains stayed hidden until archaeologists uncovered them in 1985.
properties.image_credit: Roman Amphitheatre of Benevento · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Nero, travelling south, paused at Beneventum to watch a lavish gladiatorial show that the courtier Vatinius was staging there.

properties.notes: Domitian founded this sanctuary to Isis around 88 CE, shipping in genuine Aswan granite rather than local stone. Twin obelisks carved with hieroglyphs flanked its entrance, one hailing the goddess as Lady of Beneventum. The find makes Beneventum home to the largest collection of original Egyptian antiquities anywhere outside Egypt. One obelisk still stands in Piazza Papiniano, moved there in 1872, while its broken twin sits in the Museo del Sannio.
properties.image_credit: Egyptian obelisk of the Temple of Isis, Piazza Papiniano, Benevento · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Beneventum's Via Appia crossed the Sabato River on this bridge, raised around the colony's founding in the 3rd century BCE. Six stone arches originally carried the road; four still stand today. Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored the span in 202 CE after centuries of heavy traffic. Its ancient paving stones stayed in use as the working roadbed into the 20th century.
properties.image_credit: Ponte Leproso, Benevento · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Rome's Latin colony at Beneventum, founded in 268 BCE, ringed its hilltop with a defensive circuit running roughly 2,100 meters around a pentagon-shaped town of nearly 30 hectares. The walls climbed the high ground between the Calore and Sabato rivers, guarding the point where the Via Appia entered from the west. Medieval fortifications nearly two miles long later rose along much of the same ancient line. Sections of the original masonry still surface beneath today's city center.

Beneventum's forum anchored the Latin colony founded on this ground in 268 BCE, sitting where the town's decumanus crossed its cardo. By Trajan's reign brick civic buildings and shrines to the imperial cult ringed the square on every side. The complex sat roughly 300 meters from the new Arch of Trajan, at the heart of the colony. Wartime bombing later exposed massive brick foundations that archaeologists have only partly excavated.

A monumental bath complex once filled the ground beneath today's Piazza Cardinal Pacca, steps from Beneventum's forum. Brick walls and floor remains uncovered there date to the first and second centuries CE, the decades of the city's building boom under Trajan. Medieval nuns later built a convent chapel directly into one of the bathing halls, preserving its walls through reuse. Excavators have since found a mosaic floor and bathing pools beneath the piazza.

Six Doric columns anchor each short end of this temple, raised around 450 BCE from local travertine and ranked among the best-preserved Greek buildings on earth. Its interior colonnade rises in two stacked tiers, carrying the roof without a single central support. Eighteenth-century excavators who uncovered the ruins mistook them for a shrine to Neptune, and the name never left. By 117 CE it had already stood watch over the coastal plain for more than five centuries.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Neptune (Hera II), south facade, Paestum · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Places Poseidonia (Paestum) near the mouth of the Silarus river, noting the nearby sanctuary of Argive Hera and the city's founding by colonists from Sybaris. Describes the city's setting rather than this specific temple.

properties.notes: Nine columns line each short end of this temple instead of the usual even number, an odd count builders used nowhere else at Paestum. Raised around 550 BCE, it is one of the oldest Greek temples still standing anywhere in Italy, its columns swollen with the heavy archaic curve typical of the earliest Doric style. Eighteenth-century antiquarians mistook the roofless ruin for a Roman civic hall and called it the Basilica, a name that stuck for good. It still carried its full colonnade in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: First Temple of Hera (the Basilica), Paestum · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Paestum, called Posidonia by the Greeks, among the towns of Italy's third region (Lucania). A geographic notice of the city rather than a description of this temple.

properties.notes: Builders set this temple on the highest ground in the city and blended two architectural orders in a single design, running Ionic details along a Doric frame. Finished around 500 BCE, it is the smallest and latest of Paestum's three great temples. Excavators found dozens of small terracotta statuettes of Athena buried near its altar, evidence strong enough to overturn its old mislabeling as a temple of Ceres. Christians later used its cella as a church without tearing the columns down.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Athena (formerly called Temple of Ceres), Paestum · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Paestum, called Posidonia by the Greeks, among the towns of Italy's third region (Lucania). A geographic notice of the city rather than a description of this temple.

properties.notes: Rome laid this rectangular civic square directly over the southern half of the old Greek marketplace within a few years of planting a Latin colony here in 273 BCE. A colonnade wrapped all four sides, fronting shops, the comitium, the curia, and a row of small shrines packed shoulder to shoulder along the south end. Magistrates conducted the colony's business here for four centuries straight, and by 117 CE the square still anchored daily life in a quiet but fully functioning provincial town.
properties.image_credit: Capitolium temple standing in the Roman forum of Paestum · Wikimedia Commons (Wiki Loves Monuments)
properties.image_alt: Roman-era Capitolium temple in the forum of Paestum

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Places Poseidonia (Paestum) near the mouth of the Silarus river and describes its founding by colonists from Sybaris. Describes the city's setting, not the forum specifically.

properties.notes: Three parallel naves divided this rectangular hall on the forum's north side, where the colony's magistrates kept their archives and heard petitions. It stood beside the comitium as part of one continuous complex, built within a generation of Rome founding its Latin colony at Paestum in 273 BCE. A row of decurions sat here to run local government the same way the Senate ran Rome, just at a fraction of the scale. The building remained the seat of that local government through the reign of Trajan.

properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman amphitheater at Paestum
properties.image_credit: Amphitheater of Paestum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Cut into the ground around 50 BCE, this amphitheater is one of the oldest surviving examples of the form anywhere in the Roman world, built decades before Rome's own Colosseum. A modern highway sliced straight through the site in the eighteenth century and still buries roughly half the arena today.
