Builders added an outer ring of seating near the end of the first century CE to pack in a bigger crowd for the gladiator games. By 117 CE it stood as the entertainment hub of a modest colonial town.

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Praises the rose gardens of Paestum that bloomed twice each year, naming the city that later built this amphitheater.

properties.image_alt: Section of the ancient city walls of Paestum
properties.image_credit: City walls of Paestum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Nearly 5 kilometers of limestone fortification ring the entire city, punctuated by 28 towers and four gates set at the cardinal points. Lucanian builders raised the earliest stretches in the fourth century BCE, and Roman colonists repaired and extended the circuit after taking the city in 273 BCE. Forty-seven small sally ports pierce the walls at irregular intervals, narrow enough for a single soldier to slip through on a raid. The full circuit still stood intact in 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Paestum, called Posidonia by the Greeks, among the towns of Italy's third region (Lucania). A geographic notice of the city, not a description of its walls.

properties.notes: This eastern gate takes its name from a carved relief of a two-tailed siren set into its keystone, still legible after more than two thousand years of weather. It formed the main approach from the inland hills, funneling traffic from the Lucanian countryside straight toward the forum. Builders cut it into the fourth-century BCE circuit and Roman engineers kept it in service without major rebuilding. Of Paestum's four gates it survives today in the best original condition, arch and all.

This western gate opened straight onto the road to the harbor, a fifteen-minute walk from the shoreline in antiquity. It carried the heaviest commercial traffic of any gate in the circuit, funneling grain, fish, and the city's famous roses in from the coast. The gate keeps its original Hellenistic-era masonry better than any other entrance in the wall, arch and flanking towers intact. Merchants and sailors still passed through it daily when Trajan died in 117 CE.

The southern gate in Paestum's circuit stood where the road toward the Roman colonies of Lucania left the city, opposite Porta Aurea on the northern side. Together with three companion gates it gave access through nearly 5 kilometers of unbroken fortification. Builders set it into the fourth-century BCE Lucanian wall and Roman colonists kept it standing after 273 BCE without major redesign. It remained one of the city's four working entrances throughout the Trajanic era.

Set at the northern point of the city walls, this gate carried its name from a golden hue ancient writers attributed to its stonework at sunrise. It anchored the northern approach along nearly 5 kilometers of fortification studded with 28 towers. Centuries of stone-robbing after antiquity left it the most fragmentary of Paestum's four gates, reduced today to scattered foundation blocks. In 117 CE it still stood as a functioning entrance in the working city wall.

Greek colonists built this small underground shrine around 510 BCE as a symbolic tomb honoring the city's founding hero. Inside, excavators found eight bronze vases still holding traces of honey, six water amphorae, and five long iron spits laid out as an untouched funerary offering. Roman colonists buried the structure under a mound of earth around 273 BCE, sealing it out of use for over two thousand years. It stayed hidden until archaeologists reopened it in 1954.
properties.image_credit: Heroon, underground founder's shrine, Paestum · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Praises the twice-blooming rose gardens of Paestum, naming the city where this shrine to the settlement's legendary founder was built.

properties.notes: Workers cut this circular assembly hall straight into the natural rock around 480 BCE, ringing it with stone benches that seated up to 1,700 citizens for civic votes. An Oscan inscription dedicated to Zeus Agoraios found inside shows the hall stayed in use through the later Lucanian period. Roman colonists deliberately buried the whole structure around 273 BCE, erasing the city's old assembly ground rather than adapting it. It stayed sealed underground through Trajan's reign.

This paved street ran the full length of the city as its main north-south axis, linking the Temple of Athena at one end to the two temples of Hera roughly a kilometer away. Roman surveyors laid it out fresh when they founded the colony in 273 BCE, cutting through ground that had carried no road under the Greeks. Wheel ruts worn into its paving stones still mark the routes carts took past the forum on market days. It remained the city's main thoroughfare in 117 CE.

Colonists raised this podium temple on the forum's north side to honor Mens Bona, goddess of sound judgment, after Paestum stayed loyal to Rome through Hannibal's invasion. Six columns crossed its facade and eight ran down each flank, set atop a tall platform reached by one central stairway. The temple's builders sliced directly into the old comitium's seating to fit it in, crowding out a piece of the colony's civic space. It still stood in active cult use in 117 CE.

Nerva's veteran colonists walled their new town the moment they broke ground on its rocky spur between two ravines, ringing barely 7 hectares with a polygonal defensive circuit. The south gate, still standing in large dressed blocks, anchored one end of the cardo maximus and controlled every approach from the Sitifis road. Later prosperity outgrew this modest perimeter entirely, and by the Severan era the city had spilled far beyond it into unwalled southern suburbs. What survives is the skeleton of the original military-grade settlement plan, built for veterans who expected trouble on the Numidian frontier.

This roughly 2,000-square-meter square sat at the crossing of the cardo and decumanus and served as the sole civic heart of Cuicul for its first century, laid out as essential founding infrastructure alongside the town's ramparts and earliest temples. Colonnaded walks and regular paving framed a space built for a walled town of barely 7 hectares, planned on a scale that fifty years of prosperity would soon outgrow. A monumental altar and further sculptural embellishment were added here more than a century later, but the pavement and portico lines a visitor walks today trace the square that Nerva's colonists actually used. It stands now as the oldest surviving public space of Roman Djemila, humbler and more compact than the grand Severan forum built beside it.

A square temple with six internal chambers and a sacrificial altar stood close by the Old Forum, dedicated to the Capitoline Triad of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva that every Roman colony was expected to honor. A torso from a cult statue of Jupiter, recovered on the spot, confirms the identification of the god the building served. Raising a Capitolium was one of the first acts of civic religion for a new veteran colony, marking Cuicul's formal membership in the Roman world within a generation of its founding under Nerva. It remains one of the few religious buildings at the site whose core construction plausibly predates the great Antonine and Severan expansions that transformed the rest of the city.

Granite columns and a porticoed courtyard still mark this small temple on the cardo maximus, whose surviving dedication preserves only the single word Genetrix. Its cult likely rode a wave of imperial favor under Antoninus Pius, whose court repeatedly cast the empress Faustina the Younger as an incarnation of Venus Genetrix on coinage circulating across the empire. That places its construction in the mid-2nd century, decades after Trajan's death, tucked beside an arch on the same colonnaded street. Nothing about its modest footprint hints that it once anchored one of the most photographed corners of the ancient city.

Two brothers, Lucius and Gaius Cosinius, paid 30,000 sesterces of their own money to give Cuicul this market under Antoninus Pius, and an inscribed measuring table for grain still sits where merchants once checked their weights. Eighteen shops ringed a colonnaded courtyard whose centerpiece was a circular tholos, with stone counters carved with animal heads and garlands fronting each stall. It was a private benefaction on a civic scale, the kind of gift that let a provincial family's name outlast the empire itself. The building postdates Trajan's reign by a full generation and belongs squarely to the city's mid-2nd-century boom.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII
ancient_sources.work: Career and building dedication of L. Cosinius Primus
ancient_sources.note: A stone inscription records the career of the local aedile and duumvir L. Cosinius Primus, who built the market's colonnades, statues, weighing-station, and central tholos together with his brother.

properties.image_credit: Measuring table, Market of Cosinius, Djemila · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Carved directly into the hillside above the eastern ravine, this theatre seated roughly 3,000 people arranged strictly by rank, with senators and knights in a continuous front block of six rows and ordinary citizens climbing fifteen rows split into six wedges above. Two civic benefactors, Caius Julius Crescens and Caius Julius Didius Crescentianus, financed its construction and dedicated it in 161 CE, the same year Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus took the throne jointly. Its stone cavea remains one of the best-preserved Roman theatres in North Africa. It rose nearly half a century after Trajan's death, well outside the city's founding generation.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre of Cuicul, Djemila · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII 8300 = ILS 368
ancient_sources.note: The dedication, opening "to the Harmony of the Emperors," names local patrons Gaius Julius Crescens and Gaius Julius Didius Crescentianus and dates the theatre's construction to the joint reign of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.

properties.notes: Built in 183 CE under Commodus, Cuicul's largest bathing complex once carried the emperor's name much as its counterpart in Rome did. Fragments of marble revetment and figured mosaic floors still lie in situ across its hot, warm, and cold rooms, while the finest sculpture recovered here now stands in the site museum. It gave the growing city, by then well beyond its original walls, the kind of full-scale public bathing establishment a prosperous 2nd-century provincial capital was expected to offer. The complex belongs entirely to the later Antonine building boom, more than sixty years after Trajan's death.
properties.image_credit: Great Baths of Djemila · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII
ancient_sources.note: Two inscriptions found at the Great Baths date their dedication to the reign of Commodus, recording that the town itself, the Respublica Cuiculitanorum, paid for the complex.

properties.notes: This roughly 532-square-meter hall off the Old Forum served as courtroom and exchange, funded by the city priest Caius Julius Crescens Didius Crescentianus in the year of Lucius Verus's death. Litigants and merchants shared one long colonnaded space where a magistrate could hear a property dispute in the morning and grain brokers could strike deals by afternoon. Its construction rounded out the forum precinct with the last major public building the founding-era square would ever receive intact. It arrived more than half a century after Cuicul's colonists first broke ground under Nerva.
properties.image_credit: Arch on the Cardo Maximus beside the Basilica Julia, Djemila · photo by Carole Raddato, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)
properties.image_alt: The Cardo Maximus arch next to the Civil Basilica at Djemila

properties.notes: Cuicul's population had so far outgrown its original walls by the early 3rd century that the city built an entirely second forum outside them, an irregular quadrilateral of some 3,200 square meters framed by porticoes on two sides. It gave the expanded southern districts their own civic and religious center, anchored by a monumental arch and a dynastic temple rather than retrofitting the cramped Old Forum a mile of streets away. The project reflects Cuicul near its demographic peak, a boomtown of some 12,000 people sprawling well past its founding-era footprint. It postdates Trajan's reign by nearly a century.
properties.image_credit: Panorama of the Severan Forum and Temple of the Gens Septimia, Djemila · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Standing 12.5 meters tall astride the road to Sitifis, this single-span arch formed the ceremonial gateway into Cuicul's new Severan forum. Its attic inscription, dedicated in 216 CE, honored the reigning Caracalla, his mother Julia Domna, and his deified father Septimius Severus, with pedestals on the facade once carrying their statues among Corinthian columns and niches. Townspeople raised it as a direct statement of loyalty to the ruling dynasty rather than to commemorate any local military victory. It rose exactly a century after Nerva's veterans first settled the site, making it one of the latest, not earliest, of Cuicul's great monuments.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Caracalla, Cuicul (Djemila) · photo by Carole Raddato · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII.1, 8321 + 20137
ancient_sources.note: The arch's attic inscription reads "the town council decreed and the community built this triumphal arch from the ground up," dedicating it to Caracalla, his mother Julia Domna, and his deified father Septimius Severus.

properties.notes: Raised on a high podium behind rows of massive Corinthian columns, this temple in the Severan Forum was dedicated in 229 CE by Emperor Alexander Severus to the Gens Septimia, his own ruling dynasty. Dedicating a temple to a living imperial family, rather than to a traditional god, was an unusually direct piece of political theater even by the standards of Roman provincial religion. It closed out Cuicul's greatest wave of monumental construction, capping a southern forum built to display loyalty to Rome's ruling house. Its dedication falls more than a century after the city's founding under Nerva.
properties.image_credit: Temple of the Gens Septimia, Cuicul (Djemila) · photo by Carole Raddato · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII
ancient_sources.note: A fragmentary inscription found at the temple dates its dedication, under Severus Alexander, to the Severan imperial dynasty, the Gens Septimia.

properties.notes: In the far south of the expanded city, late Roman Christians built a walled precinct holding three basilicas, a cathedral, a bathhouse, and a baptistery ranked among the largest of the early Christian period in North Africa. The baptistery's circular basin sat beneath a stone canopy on columns, ringed by 36 stucco seats where catechumens waited to be received into the faith. Construction clustered at the very end of the 4th century, as Christianity moved from tolerated cult to the city's dominant religion within a single lifetime. It stands about 280 years after Cuicul's founding as a pagan veteran colony under Nerva, on ground the earliest colonists never even walled.

One of the wealthy peristyle townhouses that spread through Cuicul's central district as the city prospered through the 2nd and 3rd centuries, taking its modern name from a figured mosaic of Europa and the bull found in one of its rooms. That mosaic was actually laid centuries after the house was first built, when a room was remodeled into a formal dining triclinium in the 5th century, showing how long these grand African townhouses stayed in fashionable use. Rich mosaic pavements throughout the house display the domestic opulence that Cuicul's merchant and landowning families could afford at their height. Neither the house's construction nor its famous decoration belongs to the city's founding decades under Nerva and Trajan.
properties.image_credit: Rape of Europa mosaic from the House of Europa, now in the Djemila Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Mosaic of the Rape of Europa, House of Europa, Djemila

properties.notes: The forum served as the civic and commercial heart of Roman Volubilis, raised during Nero's reign over the remains of the earlier Mauretanian-era town center. Colonnaded porticoes lined three sides of the open square, framing the space where the city's duumvirs and town council conducted public business. By the time Trajan died in 117 CE the forum anchored a functioning municipium of citizen-farmers, oil merchants, and Romanized Mauretanian elites. The basilica and Capitol that now flank it were still a century away, so in 117 the forum stood essentially alone as the town's monumental core.
properties.image_credit: View across the forum toward the basilica ruins, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Volubilis built two public bathing complexes during its first Roman century, and one of them went up under the Flavian emperors in the later first century CE. Bathers moved between hot, warm, and cold rooms heated by underfloor hypocaust systems, a standard Roman comfort planted on the empire's western frontier. This Flavian-era bath predated the city's better-known Baths of Gallienus by well over a century. By 117 CE it had already served two generations of Volubilis's citizens and their Romanized Mauretanian neighbors.

The House of Orpheus went up in the second half of the first century CE as one of Volubilis's substantial townhouses, later celebrated for one of the finest figural mosaics on Rome's African frontier. Its dining room floor eventually depicted Orpheus playing his lyre to a circle of six animals, from elephant to bear to bird, charmed into stillness by the music. Craftsmen set the scene in tesserae roughly one centimeter square, fine enough to render convincing muscle and shading. That famous mosaic was laid a generation later, but the house's walls and plan already stood complete when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Orpheus mosaic, House of Orpheus, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Volubilis among the towns of Mauretania; the passage describes the town, not this specific house.

properties.notes: The House of Venus went up in the second half of the first century CE as one of Volubilis's grand Roman-era residences, built around a private suite of baths that set it apart from ordinary townhouses. Its dining room later gained a mosaic showing Venus riding a ship escorted by the Three Graces and nymphs on sea-horses, one of the most admired images ever pulled from Volubilis's soil. That mosaic was a second-century addition, but the house itself, its walls, baths, and plan, already stood complete when Trajan died in 117 CE. The residence anchored a quarter of the city where Volubilis's oil-wealthy elite kept building increasingly showy homes.
properties.image_credit: Diana mosaic, House of Venus, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman mosaic of Diana bathing with a nymph, from the House of Venus at Volubilis

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Volubilis among the towns of Mauretania; the passage describes the town, not this specific house.

properties.notes: Volubilis grew along two separate street grids laid at different orientations, evidence of a town that expanded in phases from its Mauretanian core into a full Roman street plan. The Decumanus Maximus, the city's principal east-west thoroughfare, took its paved and porticoed form under Trajan and Hadrian in the early second century CE, lined with shops sheltering beneath covered walkways. It linked the city's northern gate to the forum at the town's heart. By 117 CE the street's early paving was already carrying the daily traffic of a prosperous provincial capital.
properties.image_credit: The Decumanus Maximus, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: In 44 CE, Emperor Claudius rewarded Volubilis's loyalty during the revolt of Aedemon with an edict granting its people Roman citizenship, the right to intermarry with non-citizens, and claim to the estates of residents who died without heirs. The city's council had these privileges inscribed and paired them with an honorific stela to Marcus Valerius Severus, a native Mauretanian who had commanded auxiliary units in that same war and later served as duumvir. His wife, Fabia Bira, raised the monument in his honor. The inscription stands as one of the clearest records of a Berber-Punic elite family converting local prestige into Roman citizenship within a single generation of annexation.
properties.image_credit: Inscription recording Volubilis's transformation into a Roman municipium · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: ILAfr
ancient_sources.note: Preserves the privileges the emperor Claudius granted to Volubilis, including Roman citizenship and ten years' tax immunity, for its loyalty during Aedemon's revolt.

properties.notes: The sanctuary on Volubilis's eastern rise began as a Punic precinct sacred to Baal, one of the oldest cult sites in the city, reaching back to the settlement's pre-Roman centuries. Romans rededicated it to Saturn, the common fate of Punic gods across Roman North Africa. An inscription dated 218 CE records the sanctuary's rebuilding, and by then the site had grown to include four smaller attendant shrines, one of them dedicated to Venus. This structure as it stands today postdates the 117 CE snapshot by a full century, even though worship on the same ground reached back to Volubilis's Punic origins.

Volubilis raised its great defensive circuit in 168 and 169 CE under Marcus Aurelius, a direct response to the pressure Berber tribes from the Atlas Mountains kept putting on the city's Roman rulers. The rubble-and-ashlar rampart ran 2,613 meters around the city, enclosing 40 hectares and studded with six main gates and 24 towers. Builders recycled stone blocks pulled from older structures to raise it quickly. Because it postdates 117 CE by half a century, the early Roman municipium under Trajan and Hadrian actually stood open and unfortified on its Mauretanian frontier.
properties.image_credit: Volubilis archaeological site, Morocco · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Wide view of the Volubilis ruins including the city's Roman-era walls

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Volubilis among the towns of Mauretania; the passage describes the town, not its walls specifically.

properties.notes: The Tangier Gate formed the northern entrance through Volubilis's city wall, one of six main gates built into the 168-169 CE defensive circuit raised under Marcus Aurelius. Travelers and merchants passed beneath its arch on the road linking Volubilis to the coastal city of Tingis, modern Tangier, from which the gate took its name. Flanking towers gave defenders a clear line of sight down the approach road. Since the gate belongs to a wall system built roughly half a century after Trajan's death, no fortified northern entrance existed at Volubilis in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Decumanus Maximus leading toward the Tangier Gate, Volubilis · photo by Christian Rosenbaum, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Volubilis's main street looking toward the Tangier Gate

properties.notes: Volubilis raised its civil basilica beside the forum in the Severan era, finishing construction under Emperor Macrinus in the early third century CE. The two-story building measured 42.2 meters long and 22.3 meters wide, giving the city's magistrates a covered hall for legal proceedings and business that no open-air forum could match through Morocco's rainy winters. Its scale ranks it among the finest Roman basilicas built anywhere in Africa. This building postdates the 117 CE snapshot by roughly a century; in Trajan's day, Volubilis conducted its legal business without it.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the civil basilica, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Volubilis among the towns of Mauretania; the passage describes the town, not this specific building.

properties.notes: The Capitolium of Volubilis went up in 218 CE, a tetrastyle temple raised on the city's ceremonial high ground and dedicated to the Capitoline Triad of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. Four columns fronted its podium, marking a temple type every Roman citizen would have recognized from a hundred provincial cities across the empire. A stork's nest now tops one of its surviving columns, a small irony atop a monument built to project Roman religious authority on the empire's western edge. Because construction began a full century after Trajan's death, Volubilis had no Capitoline temple at all during the 117 CE snapshot.
properties.image_credit: The Capitoline temple, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Volubilis among the towns of Mauretania Tingitana in his survey of the province. A geographic notice of the city, not a description of the Capitolium.

properties.notes: Volubilis's council raised the Arch of Caracalla between December 216 and April 217 CE, honoring the emperor for extending Roman citizenship to the province's free population and easing certain taxes. Its dedicatory inscription named Caracalla holder of tribunician power for the twentieth time and praised his mother Julia Domna as mother of the camp, the senate, and the country. Before construction finished, both Caracalla and Julia Domna had been murdered, turning a monument to a living emperor into one honoring the dead. This arch, the site's best-known landmark today, postdates Trajan's death in 117 CE by exactly a century, making it the clearest example of a Volubilis monument that falls outside this map's snapshot.
properties.image_credit: The Arch of Caracalla, Volubilis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Locates Volubilis as a free town in Mauretania Tingitana, equidistant from the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, the city where this arch was later erected.

properties.notes: Gerasa's oldest monumental sanctuary spread over a lower terrace 100 by 50 metres, laid out in 27/28 CE by a local architect who cut his own name into the stone. Caravan merchants paid for the work, and the vaulted substructures swallowed an older Hellenistic shrine whole. In 117 CE this terrace and its first-century naos crowned the hill above the theatre. The towering peripteral temple that replaced the shrine came 45 years later.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek dedicatory inscription of the lower terrace, Sanctuary of Zeus, Gerasa
ancient_sources.note: Records the enclosure of the sanctuary under Diodoros son of Zebedas, an architect of Gerasa.

properties.notes: Domitian's governor of Syria dedicated this 3,000-seat theatre in 91/92 CE, and the donors who paid for it had their names carved straight into the seating. Greek numbering still marks the ringside blocks, and two vaulted passages funnelled crowds beneath the tiers. In 117 CE Gerasenes packed it, eleven years after Rome annexed Arabia. Trajan and Hadrian later dressed up the stage wall with Corinthian columns.
properties.image_credit: South Theatre, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek dedicatory inscription of the South Theatre, Gerasa
ancient_sources.ref: year 154 of the local era, 91/92 CE
ancient_sources.note: Dedicates the theatre to Domitian by order of the legate Lappius Maximus.

properties.notes: An inscription on the northwest gate recorded these walls complete in 75/76 CE, a circuit of about 3.5 kilometres looping around both banks of the Chrysorhoas. Roughly 120 towers studded the line, and the masons ran it straight across abandoned quarries and rock-cut tombs. In 117 CE the circuit already fixed limits Gerasa never outgrew. Later emperors thickened and patched it, but the Flavian trace held.

ancient_sources.author: Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Records a Roman force under Lucius Annius storming Gerasa in 68 CE, shortly before the walls were finished.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Gerasa among the cities of the Decapolis.

properties.notes: A dedicatory inscription of 115 CE hails Trajan as founder and saviour of the city, dating this gate two years before the emperor died. Its builders gave it a trapezoidal plan, wedging the road in from the northwest so it lined up dead straight with the Cardo. In 117 CE it was the newest monument in Gerasa and the main entrance from Pella. The trick of the skewed walls stays invisible until you stand inside the passage.
properties.image_credit: North Gate of Gerasa, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman North Gate of ancient Gerasa (Jerash), Jordan

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek dedicatory inscription of the North Gate, Gerasa
ancient_sources.note: Names Trajan as founder and saviour of the city.

properties.notes: Gerasa's spine ran some 800 metres from the oval plaza to the north gate, colonnaded in the late first century CE with Ionic shafts. Chariot ruts still score paving laid at a diagonal to grip iron-shod wheels, and manholes along the kerb drop into a sewer running the full length. In 117 CE shoppers walked the Ionic version. The taller Corinthian colonnade and the widening of the roadway both came later in the second century.
properties.image_credit: Cardo maximus, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Gerasa buried its dead beyond the south gate along the road to Philadelphia, sinking shaft tombs into worked-out limestone quarries. The cemetery stretched more than a mile and held intact skeletons, skull-less burials and cremated bone in the same ground. In 117 CE it was still in daily use. Hadrian's builders closed quarry and necropolis together in the 130s and drove new foundations through the tomb chambers.

The great peripteral temple on the upper terrace was inaugurated in 162/163 CE, reached by a grand staircase cut into the west face of the older terrace below. Columns nearly 15 metres tall fronted a chamber that stared straight down at the oval plaza. This building postdates the 117 CE snapshot by some 45 years, when the hilltop still carried only the first-century sanctuary. An earthquake later dropped its drums in neat rows where they lie today.
properties.image_credit: The Temple of Zeus, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek building inscription of the Temple of Zeus, Gerasa
ancient_sources.note: Marks the inauguration of the rebuilt temple on the upper terrace.

properties.notes: Gerasa's showpiece piazza measured about 90 by 80 metres and swung an oval colonnade between the Cardo's grid and the skewed axis of the Zeus sanctuary. Engineers filled a deep hollow between two hills to flatten the ground. The plaza belongs to the great early second-century rebuilding around Hadrian's visit, so it postdates the 117 CE snapshot. Its paving curves in concentric rings toward a central pedestal.
properties.image_credit: Oval Plaza, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: The city raised this triple arch in 129/130 CE for Hadrian's winter visit, 37 metres wide and 21 metres tall. Its Greek inscription counts the year 192 of the local era and names Flavius Agrippa as the man who willed it. Acanthus wreaths bulge from the column bases, a local flourish found nowhere in Italy. It postdates the 117 CE snapshot by twelve years and stood half a kilometre outside the walls, waiting for a city that never grew to meet it.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Hadrian, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek dedicatory inscription of the Arch of Hadrian, Gerasa
ancient_sources.ref: year 192 of the local era, 129/130 CE
ancient_sources.note: Dedicated by the city of the Antiochenes on the Chrysorhoas, formerly the Gerasenes, for Hadrian's safety.

properties.notes: Gerasa's southern entrance copied the acanthus-wreathed column bases of Hadrian's arch downhill and went up around 130 CE, fifteen years after the north gate. A single arched passage pierced the wall and fed traffic straight into the oval plaza. It postdates the 117 CE snapshot. Olive presses later crowded the ground just inside the threshold, turning the ceremonial entry into a working yard.
properties.image_credit: Steffen 962, South Gate at Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.notes: Gerasa's largest temple honoured the city's patron goddess and rose between 150 and 170 CE on a huge artificial terrace. Twelve Corinthian columns front the ruin, and eleven still stand; slide a blade into a drum joint and you can watch the shafts rock in the wind. Only twelve of the thirty-two planned columns were ever raised. The whole complex postdates the 117 CE snapshot by more than three decades.
properties.image_credit: The Temple of Artemis, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Welles 1938, no. 60
ancient_sources.note: An inscription on the monumental gateway into the sanctuary records its formal dedication under Antoninus Pius, matching this site's own dating - the temple did not yet exist at this map's 117 CE snapshot.

properties.name_english: Propylaea of the Sanctuary of Artemis
properties.notes: A dedicatory inscription dates this monumental gateway to 150 CE under the governor Attidius Cornelianus. Three doorways opened off the Cardo onto a stair of seven flights of seven steps that climbed to the goddess's terrace. The processional route behind it ran more than 400 metres back from a bridge over the wadi. It postdates the 117 CE snapshot by a generation, and its carved door frames still stand nearly full height.
properties.image_credit: Gateway to the Temple of Artemis, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek dedicatory inscription of the Artemis propylaea, Gerasa
ancient_sources.note: Names Attidius Cornelianus, legate under Antoninus Pius, as patron of the gateway.

properties.notes: Gerasa's council met here from about 135 CE in a roofed chamber whose lower seats carry Greek inscriptions naming the city's voting tribes. Builders converted it into an odeon for music and recitation in 165 CE, then enlarged it again in 235. Every phase, the original council house included, postdates the 117 CE snapshot. Carved theatrical masks and acanthus from the collapsed stage wall still litter the orchestra floor.
properties.image_credit: Carved detail, North Theatre, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek architrave inscription of the North Theatre, Gerasa
ancient_sources.note: Names the building an odeon and ran along the stage front.

properties.notes: Gerasa finished this grand public fountain in 191 CE at the city's own expense, a two-storey facade with a half-domed apse opening onto the Cardo. Water spilled from seven carved lion heads into a basin at street level. Marble sheathed the lower storey and painted stucco covered the upper, traces of which survive. It postdates the 117 CE snapshot by 74 years, and the half-dome still holds its scalloped shell carving.
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Greek dedicatory inscription of the Nymphaeum, Gerasa
ancient_sources.note: Names the city itself as the body that commissioned the fountain.

properties.notes: Gerasa's circus was the smallest in the Roman world, a track 245 metres long by 52 wide holding about 15,000 spectators. Work began around the middle of the second century and finished before 212 CE, so it postdates the 117 CE snapshot by decades. Its foundations cut straight through the rock-cut tombs of the earlier necropolis. By the late third century potters had moved in and were mass-producing pottery between the starting gates.
properties.image_credit: Hippodrome, Jerash · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: A Roman temple to Dionysos crowned this terrace above the Cardo from the mid-second century CE, taking over a spot sacred to the Nabataean god Dushara. Christians cut it down to the podium in the fourth century and reused its columns in the basilica now called the Cathedral. The temple postdates the 117 CE snapshot; in 117 the Nabataean shrine still held the ground. A triple-arched gateway on the Cardo marks the old approach.

The forum spread 275 by 135 meters across three city blocks, one of the largest public squares north of the Alps. Traders from the Moselle, the Rhine and inner Gaul struck deals under its porticoes while the procurator governing three provinces worked alongside. A modest Augustan square grew into this monumental market by the end of the first century, so anyone crossing it in 117 CE walked a finished forum. Fourth-century emperors rebuilt it yet again.
properties.image_credit: Plan of Roman Trier showing the forum insulae · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: The Treveri worshipped their healing war-god Lenus Mars on the west bank of the Moselle, on a terrace fed by a spring that drew pilgrims from across Gallia Belgica. A walled precinct with two cult buildings already stood here in the first century CE, so visitors in 117 found the sanctuary busy. Parents dedicated small statues of hooded children in hope of cures. The grand 28 by 32 meter temple and its semicircular cult theater arrived later, in the second century.
properties.image_credit: Site of the Lenus Mars temple precinct at Irminenwingert, Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: More than 5 hectares of the Altbach valley held dozens of small shrines packed shoulder to shoulder, the densest cult site in Roman Trier. Treveran deities such as Ritona and Aveta kept their own temples with courtyards laid out for ritual banquets and offerings. Worship ran here from the first century CE for some three hundred years, so pilgrims in 117 already climbed these slopes. Excavators in the 1920s lifted a relief of Mithras being born from the rock out of the rubble.
properties.image_credit: Grounds of the former Altbachtal temple precinct, Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Engineers drove fresh oak into the Moselle in 71 CE, replacing the crossing of 17 BCE whose timbers effectively founded the city. Tree-ring dating pinned the new piles to that single year. The deck carried the great highway from Lyon to Cologne straight toward the forum, and it was still the working river crossing under Trajan in 117 CE. Builders replaced it a third and final time with basalt piers in the 140s.

properties.name_english: Roman Road from Trier to Cologne
properties.notes: Agrippa's surveyors laid this highway as part of the network radiating from Lyon, and the Trier to Cologne leg ran 147 kilometers, counted locally as 66 Gallic leagues. It entered Augusta Treverorum from the north and fed straight into the Moselle bridge and the forum. Wine, Treveran cloth and army pay moved along it, and it carried heavy traffic under Trajan in 117 CE. A century later the Porta Nigra rose astride its city entrance.

Seven basalt piers still carry road traffic across the Moselle, quarried from Eifel volcano rock and pointed upstream to split ice floes. Masons raised them between about 144 and 152 CE, the third bridge on the spot and the only one that lasted. It postdates the 117 CE snapshot: under Trajan the crossing was the timber bridge of 71 CE. The piers have stood for more than 1,800 years, the oldest bridge structure in Germany.
properties.image_credit: Roman bridge over the Moselle at Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Ernst Hollstein
ancient_sources.work: Mitteleuropäische Eichenchronologie: Trierer dendrochronologische Forschungen zur Archäologie und Kunstgeschichte (Trierer Grabungen und Forschungen, Band XI)
ancient_sources.note: Foundational tree-ring chronology study for the Rhineland, built from oak piles recovered at the Trier bridge site; it establishes the dated sequence of bridge phases at 17 BCE, 71 CE, and the surviving stone-pier phase of 144-152 CE, fixing the piers as later than the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: The stone arena seated roughly 18,000 and was cut into the Petrisberg slope so the hillside itself carried the seating banks. A vaulted cellar under the sand hoisted animals and fighters up through trapdoors. Older guidebooks assign it to 100 CE, but the masonry building went up in the later second century and postdates the 117 CE snapshot. A timber arena of the later first century occupied the site before it, and Trajan's citizens used that one.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre at Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: Some 7,200 sandstone blocks, the heaviest around six tonnes, were stacked without a drop of mortar and locked together with iron clamps. The gate rose about 170 CE as the northern entrance of the new city wall, so it postdates the 117 CE snapshot by half a century. Rusting clamps and weathering blackened the pale stone and earned it its medieval name. A Greek hermit later walled himself inside it, which is why demolition crews spared it.
properties.image_credit: Porta Nigra, Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the revolt of Julius Florus among the Treveri in 21 CE, naming the tribe whose later capital, Augusta Treverorum, this gate guarded.

properties.notes: Builders under Marcus Aurelius ringed the city with 6.4 kilometers of wall pierced by four main gates and studded with towers. The circuit postdates the 117 CE snapshot: under Trajan, Augusta Treverorum was a rich open town with no defences whatsoever. The line swallowed the amphitheatre, whose outer wall was drafted in as a bastion. Later generations quarried most of it away, leaving only buried footings and the Porta Nigra.

The Barbara Baths covered 42,000 square meters, ranking behind only the great imperial baths of Rome itself. Bathers moved between heated halls above a labyrinth of service tunnels tall enough to walk through upright. Construction fell in the second half of the second century, so the complex postdates the 117 CE snapshot. Stone robbers stripped the ruins for centuries until only the substructures survived.
properties.image_credit: Barbara Baths, Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Michael Dodt
ancient_sources.work: Gestempelte römische Ziegel aus Trier: zu Neufunden aus Kaiserthermen, Barbarathermen und Basilika
ancient_sources.ref: Funde und Ausgrabungen im Bezirk Trier 45 (2013), pp. 40-48
ancient_sources.note: Stamped-brick finds from the Barbarathermen excavation used to place construction in the second half of the 2nd century CE, decades after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: A channel almost 13 kilometers long tapped the Ruwer river and pushed up to 25,000 cubic meters of water a day into the city's baths and fountains. Masons lined it with waterproof opus signinum and vaulted it over a duct barely 78 centimeters wide. It belongs to the second century and postdates the 117 CE snapshot, built to feed the huge new bathhouses. Trajan's Trier still drew on wells and the river.
properties.image_credit: Roman Ruwer aqueduct remains, Waldrach · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The circus stretched roughly 450 meters, long enough for chariot teams to grind out seven laps before crowds banked on the embankments. It took monumental form in the second quarter of the second century, so the building that spectators would recognise postdates the 117 CE snapshot. A plainer racetrack may have marked the same ground from the city's earliest years. Constantius Chlorus rebuilt the whole thing after 293 to serve his imperial residence.
properties.image_credit: Scale model of Roman Trier showing circus and amphitheatre · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

properties.notes: The Secundinii, a family grown rich on cloth, raised this 23 meter sandstone pillar over their tomb around 250 CE, well after the 117 CE snapshot. Reliefs on all four faces show them settling accounts with tax officials, hauling bales of fabric and dining in state, with Jupiter carrying off Ganymede at the summit. It remains the tallest Roman funerary monument standing north of the Alps. Villagers called it a wedding stone, and that legend spared it.
properties.image_credit: Igel Column, funerary monument of the Secundinii · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the fighting around Augusta Treverorum (Trier) during the Batavian revolt of 69-70 CE. Describes the city amid the uprising, not this funerary monument, which was built more than a century later.

properties.notes: Constantius Chlorus began these baths for his new imperial residence at the end of the third century, and work halted around 316 CE with the complex never finished as a bathhouse. The caldarium apses still rise 19 meters, and service tunnels run beneath the entire site like a second city. They postdate the 117 CE snapshot by nearly two centuries. Later builders converted the unfinished shell into barracks and then into a city gate.
properties.image_credit: Imperial Baths, Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Michael Dodt
ancient_sources.work: Gestempelte römische Ziegel aus Trier: zu Neufunden aus Kaiserthermen, Barbarathermen und Basilika
ancient_sources.ref: Funde und Ausgrabungen im Bezirk Trier 45 (2013), pp. 40-48
ancient_sources.note: Stamped-brick evidence from the Kaiserthermen tying the complex to the early 4th-century Constantius Chlorus building program, nearly two centuries after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: Constantine's throne hall ran 67 meters long and 33 meters high inside, roofed in a single clear span with no columns breaking the floor. Hot air circulated under the pavement and inside the walls to warm the whole volume while the emperor received petitioners in the apse. Built about 310 CE, it postdates the 117 CE snapshot by two full centuries. The bare brick surfaces hide the fact that marble and mosaic once covered every inch.
properties.image_credit: Konstantinbasilika, Trier · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Michael Dodt
ancient_sources.work: Gestempelte römische Ziegel aus Trier: zu Neufunden aus Kaiserthermen, Barbarathermen und Basilika
ancient_sources.ref: Funde und Ausgrabungen im Bezirk Trier 45 (2013), pp. 40-48
ancient_sources.note: Brick-stamp finds from the Basilika (Aula Palatina) that anchor its construction to the Constantinian building campaign of c. 310 CE, two centuries after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.image_alt: Colonnaded ruins of the Old Forum at Leptis Magna
properties.image_credit: Old Forum, Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Leptis Magna's original civic square, laid out under Augustus and still the working heart of the city in 117 CE. Three temples line its south side, to Rome and Augustus, to Liber Pater, and to Hercules, patron gods the city had honored since its Phoenician founding. Nearly a century would pass before Septimius Severus, born in this city, gave it a second, grander forum nearby.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Great Leptis (Leptis Magna) along the African coast between the two Syrtes. A geographic notice of the city, not a description of the forum.

properties.notes: Begun under Augustus around 8 BCE and dedicated under Tiberius, this temple anchors the south side of the Old Forum with statues of Roma, Augustus, Tiberius, and Livia inside. Its bilingual Latin and Neo-Punic dedication names two local suffetes, magistrates the city still elected in the old Punic style even as a Roman province. A full century after Tiberius unveiled it, it remains Leptis Magna's grandest imperial-cult shrine in 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Bilingual dedicatory inscription, Temple of Rome and Augustus
ancient_sources.note: Records the temple's completion under two named suffetes and lists statues of Roma, Augustus, Tiberius, and Livia placed inside.

properties.notes: A local benefactor, Annobal Tapapius Rufus, paid for this market out of his own pocket around 9 BCE, giving the city two elegant octagonal pavilions inside a rectangular portico. One held a stone measuring table for grain and produce; the other, built around a small pool, likely sold fish fresh off the boats from Leptis's harbor. Bilingual Latin and Neo-Punic inscriptions over its doors are among the oldest Latin texts found anywhere in the city, already more than a century old by 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Bilingual dedicatory inscriptions, Market of Leptis Magna
ancient_sources.note: Latin over the entrance, Neo-Punic on the architrave of a central pavilion, naming Annobal Tapapius Rufus as founder.

properties.image_credit: Market of Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Dedicated around 1 or 2 CE by Annobal Tapapius Rufus, the same benefactor behind the city's market, this is the oldest stone theatre anywhere in Roman Africa. Its builders cut the curved seating bank straight into a hillside that had previously served as a cemetery. By 117 CE the theatre has staged performances for well over a century, its colonnaded stage building faced in imported marble.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Bilingual dedicatory inscription, Theatre of Leptis Magna
ancient_sources.note: Names Annobal Tapapius Rufus as builder and dedicates the theatre to Augustus.

properties.image_credit: Theatre of Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Suphunibal, daughter of the theatre's founder, funded this small shrine onto the theatre's colonnaded walk in 35 or 36 CE. Its cult statue of Ceres Augusta carried the features of Livia, Augustus's widow and Tiberius's mother, folding an old Roman grain goddess into the imperial family. In 117 CE the shrine has been a fixture of the theatre precinct for eight decades.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Great Leptis (Leptis Magna) along the African coast between the two Syrtes. A geographic notice of the city, not a description of this temple.

properties.notes: Governor Gaius Rubellius Blandus raised this limestone arch across the Cardo Maximus in 35 or 36 CE, marking a street-paving project funded with land confiscated after the Tacfarinas revolt in Numidia. Its bilingual inscription names both the governor and the deputy who oversaw the work. Eighty years on, in 117 CE, the arch still frames the city's main north-south street.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Bilingual dedicatory inscription, Arch of Tiberius, Leptis Magna
ancient_sources.note: Names the governor Gaius Rubellius Blandus and his legate.

properties.notes: A local benefactor built this colonnaded exchange around 11 or 12 CE, dedicating it to the cult of Augustus while the emperor himself was still alive. Its name echoes the arcaded trading halls of the Greek world, though what exactly changed hands inside is still debated. By 117 CE it stands only a few paces from the Arch of Trajan, raised at the very same crossroads just seven years earlier.

properties.image_alt: Aerial view of the Roman amphitheatre at Leptis Magna
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Governor Marcus Pompeius Silvanus dedicated this amphitheatre to the young emperor Nero in 56 CE, cutting a natural depression above the sea into an oval arena for around 16,000 spectators. A decorative tabula ansata inscription names the governor, his deputy, and the emperor it honored. In 117 CE, six decades old, it still stands roughly a kilometer from the city center, near enough for a show and far enough that the Forum barely hears the crowd.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Dedicatory inscription, Amphitheatre of Leptis Magna
ancient_sources.note: Names governor Marcus Pompeius Silvanus, his deputy Quintus Cassius Gratus, and Nero.

properties.notes: Dedicated in 110 CE, this arch is the first monument at Leptis Magna to record the city's promotion to a full Roman colony, Colonia Ulpia Traiana Lepcitanorum, named for the emperor himself. It stood at the northeast corner of the Chalcidicum, over the crossroads of the Cardo and the road to the theatre. Trajan died at Selinus in Cilicia on 11 August 117 CE, just seven years after his name went up here, making this arch one of the newest standing monuments anywhere in the empire on this map's own date.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Dedicatory inscription, Arch of Trajan, Leptis Magna
ancient_sources.note: Names the Colonia Ulpia Traiana Lepcitanorum council and assembly as dedicators, the earliest record of the city's colonial status.

ancient_sources.author: IRT 361
ancient_sources.note: Records the governor Publius Valerius Priscus, acting through his legate Popilius Celer, formally opening the bathhouse under Hadrian.

properties.notes: Hadrian's governor Publius Valerius Priscus dedicated this vast bath complex in 127 CE, the first building at Leptis Magna to use imported marble as a structural material rather than mere decoration. In 117 CE, the year this map is frozen at, the site is still open ground; construction is a full decade away. Later generations would rank it among the largest baths anywhere in Roman Africa.

Septimius Severus, born in Leptis Magna, gave his hometown a second forum nearly twice the size of the old one, faced in imported marble and ringed with carved Medusa heads. Ground for it was not broken until nearly a century after this map's snapshot date. In 117 CE, Leptis Magna's civic life is still entirely confined to its modest Augustan-era Old Forum.
properties.image_credit: Severan Forum of Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Great Leptis (Leptis Magna) along the African coast between the two Syrtes. A geographic notice of the city, not a description of the forum.

properties.image_alt: The tetrapylon Arch of Septimius Severus at Leptis Magna
properties.image_credit: Arch of Septimius Severus, Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: A four-way triumphal arch raised around 203 CE to mark Septimius Severus's visit to his native city as reigning emperor, carved with reliefs of his family and their armies. It rises nearly a century past this map's 117 CE snapshot, when Leptis Magna's grandest arch is still Trajan's, dedicated only seven years before. Severus himself would not be born for another 35 years.

ancient_sources.author: Sallust
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the founding of Lepcis by settlers from Sidon and its later appeal to Rome for protection during the Jugurthine War, the city where this arch honors its native-born emperor.

properties.notes: Local Numidian and Punic craftsmen raised this tower-tomb around the mid-2nd century BCE, more than two centuries before Rome absorbed Sabratha into its African provinces. Its upper story carries reliefs of Bes, a Punic protector-god of the dead, which gave the mausoleum its modern name. By 117 CE the tomb has stood on this ground for close to 300 years, already ancient before Trajan was even born.
properties.image_credit: Mausoleum of Bes, Sabratha · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sabratha's own patron god, Shadrapa, took the Roman name Liber Pater when Augustan-era builders first raised him a temple in the forum. An earthquake around 65 or 70 CE brought that structure down; its builders re-raised it in the ringed-column form still standing in 117 CE. A restoration inscription cut two and a half centuries later still remembered the shrine as toppled by ancient collapse, proof of how old it already felt to Sabratha's own residents.

ancient_sources.author: Anonymous
ancient_sources.work: Restoration inscription, Temple of Liber Pater, Sabratha
ancient_sources.note: A later restoration describes the temple as ruined by ancient collapse, attesting to its earlier, pre-117 origin.

properties.notes: Flavian-era builders raised these baths directly on Sabratha's shoreline, close enough that bathers could hear the surf through the walls. Mosaic floors here depict Oceanus, the sea's personification, giving the baths their modern name. By 117 CE the complex is around a quarter-century old, one of the bathing houses of a Punic trading city that had become fully Roman only a few generations before.
properties.image_credit: Seaward Baths (Baths of Oceanus), Sabratha · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The marble Capitolium standing over Sabratha's forum today is a late-2nd-century rebuilding from the age of the Antonine emperors, roughly six decades past this map's 117 CE snapshot. An earlier, plainer temple to the Capitoline Triad may have stood on the same spot, but no securely dated evidence for it survives. In 117 CE this corner of the forum does not yet hold the building visitors see today.
properties.image_credit: Inscription naming the Capitolium of Sabratha · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Inscribed stone mentioning Sabratha's Capitolium
The restored scaenae frons of the Roman theatre at Sabratha
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Sabratha · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Sabratha's celebrated three-story theatre, one of the largest ever built in Roman North Africa, rose under the later Antonine and Severan emperors and was finished around the start of the 3rd century CE, roughly ninety years after this map's 117 CE snapshot. In 117 CE, the ground where thousands will one day watch tragedies performed is still open land at the edge of the city.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Sabrata among the towns on the edge of the Lesser Syrtis in Roman Tripolitania. A geographic notice of the city, not the theatre.

properties.notes: Built during the reign of Commodus at the end of the 2nd century CE, this oval arena east of the city center held several thousand spectators for beast hunts and gladiator bouts. It postdates this map's 117 CE snapshot by six decades or more. Sabratha's residents in 117 CE would have had to travel to Leptis Magna, or further, for anything resembling a permanent amphitheatre.

Sabratha's forum gained this temple only after Antoninus Pius became emperor in 138 CE, honoring the third of Rome's so-called good emperors. Trajan was already dead by then, and even Hadrian's own sixteen-year reign had years left to run before Antoninus ever took the throne he was building toward. In 117 CE this stretch of Sabratha's forum has yet to be built on at all, still bare ground waiting for a temple nobody has planned yet.

The Byzantine emperor Justinian ordered this basilica built in the 6th century, recycling columns and stone salvaged from Sabratha's older pagan temples into a Christian church. It rises more than four hundred years after this map's 117 CE snapshot, in a North Africa Rome no longer rules directly. Its scavenged marble is the closest thing left standing here to the temples its own builders tore apart to make it.

Sabratha's council chamber, where the city's local senate met, is dated by the one source available to the 4th century CE, roughly two centuries after Trajan died at Selinus, the event this map is frozen at. Whatever building served the city's council under Trajan and Hadrian, if one existed yet, has left no trace that modern archaeologists have managed to recover from the site. Sabratha's civic buildings, like much of its forum, were still taking shape decades after this map's own snapshot date.

Tibur's patron god Hercules received the largest sanctuary built to him anywhere in Italy after the one at Cadiz, a terraced complex nearly 200 meters long carved into the hillside above the Aniene. A covered passage tunneled straight through the foundations, letting the Via Tiburtina run beneath the sanctuary without disturbing pilgrims overhead. By 117 CE the complex has drawn worshippers, including senators with country villas nearby, for close to two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Hercules Victor, Tivoli · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Notes that Tibur has a notable temple of Hercules, naming it alongside the town's famous waterfall on the Anio.

properties.notes: Ten of this small round temple's original eighteen Corinthian columns still ring its drum, perched dramatically on the cliff above the Aniene's waterfalls. Renaissance visitors named it for Vesta, though no inscription confirms which goddess it actually honored, with Hercules and the local nymph Albunea both proposed instead. By 117 CE it has crowned this cliff edge for nearly two centuries, its silhouette already a fixture of the view every visitor to Tibur described.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Vesta, Tivoli · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Horace
ancient_sources.note: Praises Tibur's landscape, singling out the echoing grotto of the Sibyl Albunea by the Anio falls, the site traditionally associated with this round temple, though the building itself is not described.

properties.notes: A smaller rectangular Ionic temple stands beside the round Temple of Vesta on Tibur's acropolis, most likely dedicated to Tiburnus, the legendary founder the city took its name from. Horace, who loved this stretch of the Aniene, wrote of 'the grove of Tiburnus' in the same breath as the roaring river below it. By 117 CE both temples have watched over the falls together for well over a century.

ancient_sources.author: Horace
ancient_sources.note: Names 'the grove of Tiburnus' alongside the headlong Anio and the sanctuary of Albunea.

properties.notes: Marcus Plautius Lucanus gave his name to this stone bridge carrying the Via Tiburtina across the Aniene on the approach to Tibur. Travelers from Rome crossed it for nearly two thousand years afterward; it stayed in use until the mid-20th century. By 117 CE it has carried traffic toward Tibur's sanctuaries for roughly a century, with its builder's family tomb rising beside the road just steps away.
properties.image_credit: Ponte Lucano over the Aniene · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Consul Marcus Plautius Silvanus, a friend of Augustus, raised this cylindrical drum tomb for his family right beside the bridge that already carried his own family's name. Its design echoes the grander imperial mausolea going up in Rome at the same time, a senator's family claiming the same architectural language as the emperor's own house. By 117 CE it has stood watch over travelers crossing the Aniene for well over a century.
properties.image_credit: Tomb of the Plautii, beside Ponte Lucano · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Tibur's Republican-era forum, laid out on the site of today's cathedral square, held a public weigh-house with marble tables carved with cavities for standard weights, and an Augusteum, an imperial-cult building paid for by a local freedman. Merchants settled disputes over measures at the weigh-house while priests tended the emperor's cult a few steps away. In 117 CE both buildings anchor the civic heart of the city.

The poet Statius devoted an entire poem to touring this villa, which spanned both banks of the Aniene and let its owner supposedly listen to the river's roar without it ever disturbing his sleep. Manlius Vopiscus filled it with art and gardens landscaped around the water rather than against it. By 117 CE the villa is a generation old, already famous enough that Statius's poem describing it has circulated for twenty years.

ancient_sources.author: Statius
ancient_sources.note: A full poem describing the villa's position spanning the Aniene, its gardens, and its art collection.

properties.name_english: Aniene Falls and Sanctuary of Albunea
properties.notes: The Aniene river drops in a roaring cascade beneath Tibur's acropolis, a natural spectacle the Romans folded straight into their religious life. Horace called it the echoing home of Albunea, a water nymph some ancient writers counted as a tenth Sibyl, worshipped in a grotto above the falls. In 117 CE the falls and their sanctuary are already old beyond memory, older than Rome's own founding myths.

ancient_sources.author: Horace
ancient_sources.note: Describes 'the echoing home of Albunea' beside the headlong Anio.

properties.image_alt: The Canopus canal and Serapeum at Hadrian's Villa
properties.image_credit: The Canopus and Serapeum, Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The so-called Serapeum, The so-called Serapeum was a monumental summer cenatio with nymphaeum set at the southern end of the Canopus, Hadrian's Villa (37679255384).jpg?width=800
properties.notes: Hadrian would spend the next two decades building the largest and most experimental villa complex the Roman world ever saw, drawing on architecture he had seen touring Egypt, Greece, and the East. On 11 August 117 CE, the day this map is frozen at, Hadrian has just become emperor and not one stone of it has been laid; brickmakers are only beginning to stockpile material nearby. The valley where it will rise is, for now, still open countryside.

ancient_sources.author: Historia Augusta
ancient_sources.note: Describes how Hadrian built his villa at Tibur and named sections of it after famous places he had seen on his travels, including the Lyceum, Academy, Prytaneum, Canopus, and even a Hades.

properties.notes: A local benefactor named Bleso funded this amphitheatre for Tibur sometime during Hadrian's reign, giving the city its own venue for games without a trip to Rome. It rises well after this map's 117 CE snapshot, in the same building boom that produced Hadrian's Villa nearby. In 117 CE, Tibur's citizens still have to travel to see anything resembling a proper arena.

Praeneste's hillside sanctuary to Fortuna Primigenia climbed in terraces so vast that ancient writers claimed it was visible from Rome, more than 30 kilometers away. Republican builders reshaped the entire hillside around 100 BCE, layering porticoes, ramps, and a theater-shaped stairway on top of one another to lift worshippers toward the temple at the summit. By 117 CE it has drawn pilgrims, including emperors and their families vacationing at nearby villas, for well over two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, Palestrina · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Terraced ruins of the Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia at Palestrina (ancient Praeneste)

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the legendary origin of the Praenestine oracle, in which Numerius Suffustius split open a rock to reveal wooden lots inscribed with letters, then argues against the validity of divination by these sortes.

properties.notes: A small round temple crowned the sanctuary's highest terrace, holding a gilded bronze statue of Fortuna shown as a young armed warrior rather than the usual goddess of chance. Its remains would later be built directly into a Renaissance palace, but in 117 CE it still stands alone at the summit, the goal every pilgrim climbing the terraces below was working toward. From here the whole Praenestine plain, and on a clear day Rome itself, spreads out below.
properties.image_credit: Scale-model reconstruction of the Temple of Fortuna Primigenia, Palestrina Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Museum scale model reconstructing the ancient terraced Temple of Fortuna Primigenia complex

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the legendary founding of the oracle of Fortuna Primigenia at Praeneste and the wooden lots (sortes) drawn there by the goddess's priests.

properties.notes: A pit on the Terrace of the Hemicycles held the oak-wood lots that made Praeneste's oracle one of the most consulted in Italy, inscribed slips a boy would draw at random in the goddess's presence. Cicero wrote skeptically about the ritual's origin myth while admitting its enormous popularity. A century later Tiberius grew wary enough of the lots' predictions that he had the entire box brought to Rome, then thought better of it and sent it straight back.
properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, Palestrina (Praeneste) · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0, Ugo Bongarzoni)
properties.image_alt: Terraced ramp of the Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia at Praeneste (Palestrina)

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Describes the founding legend and the ritual of the oak-wood lots, skeptically.

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Records Tiberius's wariness of the Praenestine lots, brought to Rome then returned.

properties.notes: A vast figured floor mosaic once paved a grotto-like hall on the sanctuary's lower terrace, showing the Nile in full flood from its Ethiopian source down to Alexandria, crowded with soldiers, priests, hunters, and exotic animals. Scholars still debate whether the hall it decorated belonged to the sanctuary itself or the adjoining civic forum, but its Republican-era workmanship places it comfortably before this map's 117 CE snapshot. It survives today as one of the largest and most detailed Nilotic scenes to come down from the ancient world.
properties.image_credit: Nile Mosaic of Palestrina · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A grand terrace ringed by porticoes on three sides opened onto a monumental staircase built in the shape of a theater, rising toward the sanctuary's summit terraces. A vaulted passage ran beneath the stairs to carry foot traffic and supplies out of sight of worshippers processing up above. By 117 CE the staircase has funneled pilgrims toward Fortuna's temple for two centuries.

A multi-chambered cistern at the foot of the hillside stored water for the fountains and nymphaea running through the sanctuary's terraces, engineering as ambitious in its own way as the temple above it. Brick-faced concrete construction let Praeneste's builders vault chambers wide enough to hold a real reserve against the dry Italian summer. In 117 CE it still supplies water to a sanctuary drawing pilgrims from across Italy.

A fortified summit above the sanctuary, today the hilltop village of Castel San Pietro Romano, served as Praeneste's ancient citadel, walled like the other old Latin hill towns of Alatri and Segni. Its height let defenders watch the approach from Rome long before an enemy reached the terraced sanctuary below. By 117 CE it has guarded the city for longer than anyone in Praeneste could say.

Praeneste's civic forum and basilica sat on a lower terrace beneath the sanctuary proper, giving the city a working seat of government right at the foot of Fortuna's temple. A medieval cathedral would later rise directly on top of its foundations, but in 117 CE the Roman-era forum still functions as built, roughly two centuries after Praeneste's builders raised it alongside the sanctuary above.

Second in size only to Rome's own Colosseum, this arena seated some 60,000 spectators around a floor spanning 170 meters, its four tiers of seating carried on eighty travertine arches. Underground passages threaded beneath the sand, moving animals and fighters up through trapdoors into the show above. Ancient inscriptions credit Augustus with building it; the city's own heritage authority instead dates it a century later. Either way it was already old and celebrated by 117 CE, and tradition holds Rome modeled its own Colosseum on this one, not the reverse.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Capua · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Argues that Rome's ancestors ranked Capua alongside Carthage and Corinth as one of only three cities in the world grand enough to rival Rome, the city where this amphitheater was later built.

properties.notes: Capua's Capitolium gave the colony its own temple to Jupiter, built to the same pattern every Roman colony carried from Rome itself. Emperor Tiberius traveled down from Rome to dedicate it in person in the year 26, folding the ceremony into the same Campanian trip that consecrated a shrine to Augustus at nearby Nola. Magistrates and priests conducted the colony's official rites here for generations afterward. The temple stood at the heart of the colonia Julius Caesar had refounded with 20,000 resettled plebeians in 59 BCE.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Records Tiberius traveling to Campania in 26 CE 'ostensibly to consecrate a temple at Capua to Jupiter, and a shrine at Nola to Augustus.'

properties.notes: A triple archway spanned the Via Appia at Capua's western approach, greeting travelers as they entered the colony. Three of its pillars and one side archway survive today, once dressed in marble reliefs and statues now lost. Built under the Flavian emperors to mark the city's rise in status, it only picked up the name Arch of Hadrian generations later, from a since-discredited dedication inscription. Locals called it Arco Felice, echoing Capua's own official name, Colonia Iulia Felix Augusta.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Hadrian, Capua · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A temple to Diana crowned the western slope of Monte Tifata above Capua, drawing worshippers from the city below for centuries. Cult activity here reached back to the 6th century BCE, though the monumental temple itself rose two centuries later. The general Sulla loaded the sanctuary with rich votive offerings after defeating a rival army near the mountain in 82 BCE. A carved white doe tied to a local founding legend gave the shrine part of its enduring fame.

Workers cut this 131-meter gallery straight into the tufa flank of Cumae's acropolis, its trapezoidal cross-section engineered to survive the region's frequent earthquakes. Six openings pierced the rock along its length, throwing shafts of daylight across the floor as visitors walked toward a vaulted inner chamber. Legend held that a prophetess spoke Apollo's oracles here in a voice that echoed through a hundred mouths in the stone. Virgil sent his hero Aeneas down this same passage in the Aeneid, and a visitor in 117 CE could still walk its full length, even with the oracle's prophetic heyday long past.
properties.image_credit: Cave of the Cumaean Sibyl · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aeneas entering the Sibyl's cave, its hundred mouths and hundred doors, and her prophetic frenzy.

properties.notes: Cumae's Temple of Apollo crowned a terrace of the acropolis, rebuilt on a grander scale under Augustus after centuries as a Greek-style shrine. Its cella once ran some 34 meters long, facing out over the coastline toward Ischia. Priests here linked the sanctuary to the Sibyl's cave a short walk downhill, and pilgrims arriving by sea climbed the terraced slope to reach its columned front. The temple was still active in 117 CE, its tufa podium already carrying the marks of a rebuild more than a century old.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Cumae · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Describes Daedalus building the temple, its golden doors carved with the story of Minos, Pasiphaë, and the Minotaur.

properties.notes: The Temple of Jupiter occupied the highest terrace of Cumae's acropolis, raised on a Samnite-era foundation and monumentalized after Rome absorbed the city in 338 BCE, likely as its Capitolium. From its platform the sanctuary commanded a sweeping view down the Campanian coast. It served as Cumae's principal civic temple through the Roman period, still a working pagan shrine in 117 CE. Its later life as a Christian church and baptistery lay centuries in the future.

Defenders raised walls of finely cut tufa along the acropolis's southeastern ridge as early as the 6th century BCE, extending the line as the lower city grew. Roman engineers later reinforced sections of the circuit, and its course went on to shape the medieval town centuries afterward. A visitor walking Cumae in 117 CE followed roughly the same defensive perimeter that had protected the city hundreds of years before, tying together the acropolis heights, the temple terraces, and the lower town's forum and harbor.

Roman engineers bored this tunnel nearly a kilometer through Monte Grillo to link Lake Avernus with Cumae, wide enough for two wagons to pass side by side. Agrippa commissioned the work around 37 BCE while converting Avernus into a hidden naval harbor for the war against Sextus Pompeius. Six vertical shafts pierced the hillside for daylight and air, the tallest running more than 30 meters straight up through solid rock. The fleet moved on to Misenum decades before 117 CE, but the tunnel stayed open and in everyday use long after its military purpose had passed.
properties.image_credit: Grotta di Cocceio, the Agrippan road tunnel near Cumae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Domitian's road engineers cut this monumental gateway through Monte Grillo in 95 CE, opening a passage some 20 meters tall for the new Via Domitiana linking Rome to Naples and on to Cumae. Two carriageways ran side by side through the cutting, carrying imperial traffic past the hillside instead of over it. A traveler heading north from Cumae toward Rome in 117 CE passed beneath the same arch, then barely two decades old. Despite later legend crediting it with carrying an aqueduct overhead, no trace of a water channel survives along its crest.
properties.image_credit: Arco Felice, Via Domitiana near Cumae · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Statius
ancient_sources.note: Celebrates the construction of the Via Domitiana past Cumae, the road whose cutting through Monte Grillo this arch spans.

properties.notes: Cumae's forum formed a paved rectangular square ringed by a two-story portico, Doric below and Ionic above. The Lucceii family funded an ornate fountain house on the square once the city tapped into the Aqua Augusta aqueduct feeding water across Campania. Merchants, magistrates, and priests all passed through this plaza, which anchored the lower town beneath the acropolis's temple terraces. The forum still functioned as Cumae's civic heart in 117 CE, roughly four centuries after its first paving.

Cumae's Forum Baths rank among the earliest purpose-built public bathhouses anywhere in the Roman world, tracing back to the city's early years under Roman rule. Bathers passed through a frigidarium fitted with two separate cold-water plunge pools before moving into the complex's warmer rooms. The building sat directly beside the forum, giving citizens easy access on their way through the civic center. Centuries of renovation kept the baths in active use, and Cumae's residents were still bathing on this same spot in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Forum Baths, Cumae · Wikimedia Commons
