properties.notes: Builders cut Cumae's amphitheater into the natural slope of Monte Grillo, banking up an earthen wall on the north side to complete the oval bowl. It ranks among Campania's earliest stone amphitheaters, raised alongside similar arenas at Capua and Liternum around the turn of the 2nd to 1st century BCE. The arena floor sat sunk below ground level, with much of the seating carved directly against the hillside. By 117 CE the structure had already hosted spectacles for close to two centuries.

One of the largest arenas anywhere in the Roman world seated roughly 25,000 spectators, with its lower tiers cut straight into the hillside to save on masonry. Hadrian commissioned it as part of a sweeping expansion of his home city after becoming emperor. Trajan, also born in Italica, never saw it: construction fell entirely within Hadrian's reign, which began the very day this map is set.

Hadrian raised this temple at the center of a vast colonnaded square to worship his predecessor as a god, dressing it in polychrome marble hauled in from imperial quarries across the empire. Only the foundations and scattered sculptural fragments survive above ground today, but they trace out an unusually imposing footprint. A temple to a Divus cannot predate its subject's death and deification, so this one only rose after Trajan died on this map's own snapshot date.

Emperor Vespasian dedicated this Capitoline temple in 73 CE to thank Brixia for backing him against Vitellius. Three parallel cellae honored Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva behind a Corinthian portico, with polychrome marble floors still visible today. A landslide off the Cidneo hill buried the ruins in the Middle Ages, preserving them until excavation began in 1823. It stood at the north edge of the forum, the religious anchor of the whole civic square.
properties.image_credit: Capitolium of Brescia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Colonnaded facade of the Capitoline temple in Brescia

ancient_sources.author: Catullus
ancient_sources.note: Calls Brixia (Brescia) the 'beloved mother' of Verona in a poem about a gossiping door. A passing mention of the city, not a description of the Capitolium.

properties.notes: Built directly east of the Capitolium as part of Vespasian's Flavian-era forum project, this theatre gave Brixia a stage for public performances beside its civic religious center. It was enlarged under Septimius Severus more than a century later, but the Flavian core was already standing and in use by 117 CE. Excavations resumed at the site in the 2020s to bring more of the cavea to light. It sits immediately adjacent to the Capitolium, sharing the same archaeological park.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre, Piazza del Foro, Brescia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman theatre in Brescia's Piazza del Foro

properties.notes: Brixia's forum square existed from the Late Republic and gained a basilica and porticoes under Augustus, but Vespasian rebuilt it wholesale in 73 CE alongside his new Capitolium and theatre. The rebuilt square gave the colony a unified civic center on the model of Rome itself. Its footprint survives in the modern Piazza del Foro, which still carries the ancient name. By 117 CE it had been the city's political and commercial heart for over four decades in its Flavian form.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction of the Imperial forum of Brescia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Reconstruction illustration of the Roman forum of Brescia

properties.notes: This 195-centimeter bronze started life as a Hellenistic statue of Aphrodite admiring her reflection in a shield, then got new wings and an inscribed shield to become a Victory writing a victor's name. Brixians buried it under the Capitolium floor with other precious bronzes ahead of a late-antique threat, which is exactly why it survived. Excavators found it there in 1826, still gleaming under centuries of rubble. It stood on display inside the temple complex through the 117 CE snapshot.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Parco archeologico di Brescia romana Vittoria alata 8 Brescia.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Winged Victory of Brescia · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Bronze Winged Victory statue displayed at the Brescia archaeological park

properties.notes: Four side-by-side cult rooms with their own pronaos porticoes made up Brixia's oldest religious complex, raised around 85 BCE on a terrace above the decumanus. Vespasian's builders buried it under fill in 73 CE to raise the platform for the new Capitolium, ending its life as a standing shrine. That burial accidentally preserved some of the best-conserved Roman wall frescoes in northern Italy. One of its four halls has been open to visitors since 2015 after decades underground.

This was the first large public building the Romans raised at Mediolanum, going up in the Augustan era with room for up to 9,000 spectators. Its stage wall rose 20 meters and its curved cavea spanned 95 meters, a scale meant to announce the colony's ambitions. Performances continued here into the 4th or 5th century before it fell out of use. Its foundations now sit in the basement of Palazzo Turati, home to Milan's Chamber of Commerce.
properties.image_credit: Remains of the Roman Theatre, Milan · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated remains of the Roman theatre beneath Palazzo Turati in Milan

properties.notes: Mediolanum's amphitheatre rose in the Flavian era, construction spanning roughly the second half of the 1st century CE, and reached 150 by 120 meters, third largest in Roman Italy after the Colosseum and Capua. Gladiator bouts and animal hunts filled the arena for over three centuries. Built outside the city walls, it later became a defensible position for attackers and was torn down for stone in the chaos of the 5th century. Excavations that began in 1931 uncovered its outer wall under Via Conca del Naviglio.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/4194 - Milano - Ruderi dell'Arena romana - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto 14-July.2007.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Roman arena, Milan · photo by Giovanni Dall'Orto, Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated foundation ruins of the Roman amphitheatre in Milan

properties.notes: Mediolanum's forum occupied the crossing of the cardo and decumanus, a 160 by 55 meter square laid out as the city grew into its role as a municipium after 49 BCE. It carried the basilica, market stalls, and civic offices that ran the colony's daily business. Excavations in the 1950s under Via Brisa exposed foundations of its reception halls, and paving slabs turned up again beneath the Pinacoteca Ambrosiana. Piazza San Sepolcro sits directly above it today.

Mediolanum got its first circuit of masonry walls in 49 BCE when the town became a Roman municipium, enclosing a roughly square area about 700 meters on a side. These republican walls stayed the city's only fortification until Maximian's much larger extension nearly two centuries later, in 286-305 CE, well after this snapshot. A surviving tower base near the Carrobbio marks where the Porta Ticinensis once pierced this original line. Frederick Barbarossa finally razed the masonry circuit during the 1162 siege of Milan.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Giardinetti con resti di mura nei pressi del Carrobbio, Milano.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Remains of the Roman walls near Carrobbio, Milan · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving fragment of Roman-era wall masonry near Carrobbio in Milan

properties.notes: These sixteen Corinthian columns were carved in the 2nd or 3rd century CE, decades after this snapshot, for a pagan temple or bath complex elsewhere in Mediolanum. Workers salvaged and re-erected them here in the 4th century to front the newly built Basilica of San Lorenzo, giving the church a monumental Roman colonnade it never originally had. They now form the best-known Roman-looking streetscape in modern Milan, along Corso di Porta Ticinese. Because the columns postdate 117 CE, they do not belong on a snapshot of that year.
properties.image_credit: Columns of San Lorenzo, Milan · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Row of ancient Corinthian columns in front of the Basilica of San Lorenzo, Milan

properties.notes: The Roman Senate dedicated this arch to Augustus in 27 BCE for restoring the Via Flaminia, and it stands today as the oldest surviving Roman triumphal arch. Carved from pale Istrian stone, it rises 9.92 meters at the point where the Via Flaminia met the Via Aemilia. Medallions of Jupiter, Apollo, Neptune, and Minerva face outward above its arch. Travelers on foot and horseback still pass beneath it, exactly as they did in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Augustus, Rimini · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman triumphal arch of pale stone with a single archway, Rimini

ancient_sources.author: Julius Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes Caesar occupying Ariminum with his troops immediately after crossing the Rubicon in 49 BCE, the city where this arch was later dedicated to Augustus.

properties.notes: Augustus began this five-arch bridge over the Marecchia in 14 CE, and Tiberius finished it in 21 CE, giving it his name. Cut from solid Istrian stone, it has carried traffic across the river for two thousand years without a single arch collapsing. Blind aedicules frame the piers between its five spans. By 117 CE it had already linked Ariminum to the coastal road toward Ravenna for nearly a century.
properties.image_credit: Ponte di Tiberio, Rimini · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman stone bridge with five round arches spanning the Marecchia river

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: Preserves the bridge's own dedicatory inscription recording its completion under Augustus and Tiberius.

properties.notes: This seaside house did not yet exist in 117 CE; builders raised it in the second half of the 2nd century, decades after Trajan's death. Its last owner was a doctor whose toolkit of over 150 surgical instruments survived a fire that destroyed the house in the mid-3rd century. Excavators uncovered the site in 1989 under a modern piazza. Its mosaics and bronze scalpels now sit inside a glass-walled archaeological park.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Domus del chirurgo, mosaico di 'Orfeo tra gli animali'.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Orpheus mosaic, Domus del Chirurgo, Rimini · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman floor mosaic of Orpheus playing the lyre surrounded by animals, from the Domus del Chirurgo in Rimini

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Describes Caesar's forces reaching Ariminum (Rimini), the city where this house stood, after his crossing of the Rubicon.

properties.notes: Builders raised this amphitheater under Hadrian, so it stood unbuilt on 11 August 117 CE, the day Trajan died and Hadrian succeeded him. A coin bearing Hadrian's portrait, found embedded in its masonry, fixed the date. Two rings of arches once held more than 10,000 spectators near the harbor. Allied bombing in World War Two left only its elliptical outline and a few brick arches standing.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre ruins, Rimini · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Brick ruins of the elliptical Roman amphitheatre at Rimini

properties.notes: Roman colonists built this gate around 82 BCE, in the wall circuit raised after Sulla's civil war, giving Ariminum a fortified southern entrance still standing in 117 CE. Its arch used double rows of stone voussoirs cut from Covignano hillside sandstone. World War Two bombing tore the gate apart, but restorers rebuilt its surviving barrel vault at street level in 2004. It once carried the name Porta Sant'Andrea.
properties.image_credit: Porta Montanara, Rimini · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman stone gate arch of Porta Montanara in Rimini

properties.notes: Colonists laid out this forum in 268 BCE at the crossing of the decumanus and cardo, and by 117 CE it had served as Ariminum's civic heart for nearly four centuries. Tradition holds that Julius Caesar addressed his soldiers here in 49 BCE after crossing the Rubicon. A theater closed the square to the north and an archway marked its southern entrance. A basilica for courts and business stood nearest the sea.

This amphitheater postdates 117 CE; excavators date its construction to the Antonine period, decades after Trajan's death, though older accounts once placed it a century earlier. Once finished, it held about 7,000 spectators for gladiatorial games and animal hunts. Archaeologists uncovered it starting in the 1950s. Its elliptical outline still sits within the walled Roman city near the Magra river mouth.
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre ruins, Luni · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Elliptical ruins of the Roman amphitheatre at Luni

properties.notes: Colonists raised this temple to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva at the forum soon after founding Luna in 177 BCE. Terracotta architectural fragments and black-gloss pottery from the site date its earliest phase to the colony's very first years. Standing on a raised podium overlooking the forum, it anchored civic and religious life in 117 CE. Marble from the nearby imperial quarries later reinforced the site's later buildings.

Colonists first built this temple to the goddess Luna in the mid-2nd century BCE, and Augustan-age builders later rebuilt it completely, wrapping it in a triple portico. A sculpted pediment showing a council of the gods, carved around 175-150 BCE, survives from its earliest phase. The rebuilt sanctuary stood in active use in 117 CE at the city's northwest corner. A cuirassed statue from the renovation may depict Octavian himself.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Frontone A del grande tempio di luni con concilio degli dei, 175-150 ac. ca. 01.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Pediment of the Temple of Luna, Luni · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Carved stone pediment fragment showing a council of gods from the Temple of Luna

properties.notes: Roman colonists enclosed their new town with defensive walls in 177 BCE, the year Luna's colony was founded on land taken from the Ligurian Apuani. The fortified circuit closed off about 39 hectares of the coastal plain along the Magra river. Poets remembered the city for its white walls centuries later. By 117 CE those walls had already sheltered five generations of colonists.

Luna's forum took shape in 177 BCE at the intersection of the cardo and decumanus, and Augustan-age building projects later widened it considerably. The Capitolium closed its north end while a basilica handled courts and commerce nearby. By 117 CE the city drew wealth from Carrara marble quarries just inland, some of which had become imperial property under Augustus. Excavators have since uncovered the forum, theater, and amphitheater.
properties.image_credit: Forum remains, Luni archaeological park · photo by Mediatus, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
properties.image_alt: View of the excavated Roman forum area at the Luni archaeological park

properties.notes: This house's oldest walls date to the 1st century BCE, standing on foundations of river pebbles with a crushed-terracotta floor set in a white-tessera diamond pattern. That Republican-era core already stood in 117 CE, well before the mosaics that later made the house famous. Its celebrated Circus Maximus and Dionysus mosaics belong to renovations three and five centuries after Trajan's death. Excavators still work the site today near La Spezia.

A single red-granite column standing 20 meters tall, one of the largest monoliths Roman engineers ever quarried. Raised around 297 CE by the prefect Publius after Diocletian crushed a local uprising — a garbled reading of his name centuries later gave the column its enduring, entirely wrong link to Pompey. It didn't exist yet in 117 CE: this spot, on the old Serapeum precinct, was still nearly two centuries away from getting its column.
properties.image_credit: Pompey's Pillar, Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A three-level tomb complex cut 35 meters down into the bedrock, mixing pharaonic funerary scenes, Greek columns, and Roman portrait busts in the same burial chamber. What began as one wealthy family's vault grew into a communal necropolis for hundreds of Alexandrians. Archaeological dating puts its start in the second quarter of the 2nd century CE, so this tomb hadn't been dug yet in 117 CE — it was rediscovered by accident in 1900 when a donkey cart broke through its roof.
properties.image_credit: Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Began as a shoreline shrine Cleopatra raised, then was rededicated to the cult of the god Augustus once Egypt became a Roman province. In 13 BCE the prefect Publius Rubrius Barbarus hauled two New Kingdom obelisks — cut a millennium before Alexandria even existed — from Heliopolis to stand in its forecourt; they're known today as Cleopatra's Needles, one in London and one in New York. In 117 CE it still functioned as Alexandria's seat of imperial cult worship, its odd pairing of Ptolemaic temple and pharaonic monoliths overlooking the Great Harbor.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction of the Caesareum of Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Artist's reconstruction of the Caesareum with its two obelisks

properties.notes: Once the largest bath complex in Roman Africa, its frigidarium alone the size of a cathedral nave, held up on towering grey granite columns shipped in from as far as Anatolia. A surviving dedication fixes the start of construction at 145 CE under Antoninus Pius, finished under his successors. In 117 CE this stretch of Carthage's shoreline was still bare — the baths were a full generation away from breaking ground.
properties.image_credit: Antonine Baths, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Alexandre Lézine
ancient_sources.note: The definitive excavation monograph reconstructing the bath complex and publishing the surviving dedicatory inscription that fixes the start of construction at 145 CE under Antoninus Pius, a full generation after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: Cut into a hillside north of the old Byrsa citadel, seating at least 5,000 for tragedy, comedy, and later the novelist Apuleius reading his own work aloud to a Carthaginian crowd. Archaeological dating places its construction around the middle of the 2nd century CE. It hadn't been built yet in 117 CE — the site was still bare ground, decades before Carthage got a stone theatre of its own.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_english: Byrsa Hill and the Roman Forum
properties.notes: Carthage's rebuilt civic heart, planted directly on the ashes of the Punic citadel Rome had razed in 146 BCE. Augustus's engineers shaved roughly 15 meters off the hilltop and hauled away close to a quarter-million cubic meters of rubble to make room for a proper Roman forum. By 117 CE it had been running as the seat of provincial government in Africa Proconsularis for well over a century, government buildings and temples ringing the plateau.
properties.image_credit: The Byrsa hill archaeological site, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Two adjoining harbors on Carthage's old lagoon — a circular naval basin 325 meters across that once sheltered over 200 Punic warships around a central island, paired with a rectangular commercial port beside it. Scipio Aemilianus filled both with rubble when he destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE, but Augustus's refounded colony dug them back out. By 117 CE they were working merchant harbors again, loading North African grain onto ships bound for Rome.
properties.image_credit: The Punic ports, Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A seated bronze goddess crowned with the city's own walls, one foot resting on the shoulder of a swimming youth who personifies the river Orontes, wheat sheaves in her lap. Sculpted around 296 BCE by Eutychides of Sicyon for Seleucus I, she became the most copied civic image in the Greek and Roman world — dozens of later replicas survive as far away as the Vatican and the Louvre. The earthquake of December 115 CE that flattened much of Antioch left her untouched, and she still stood as the city's icon on the day Trajan died.
properties.image_credit: Roman-era copy of the Tyche of Antioch · Louvre Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Small bronze copy of Eutychides' Tyche of Antioch

properties.name_english: The Great Colonnaded Street of Antioch
properties.notes: A shop-lined colonnade running roughly 3 kilometers straight through the city, 27 meters wide and financed in part by Herod the Great and the emperor Tiberius — one of the very first monumental colonnaded streets built anywhere in the Roman world. The earthquake of 13 December 115 CE tore long stretches of it apart, and Trajan himself, wintering in Antioch for the Parthian campaign, barely escaped the collapsing city. On 11 August 117 CE it stood only provisionally patched, its full rebuild still years away.
properties.image_credit: Yakto mosaic border depicting Antioch's colonnaded streets, Hatay Archaeology Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Detail of the Yakto mosaic's topographical border, showing Antioch's streets and buildings

properties.notes: A sprawling imperial residence built on Antioch's river island, eventually the main seat of Roman emperors in the East whenever they campaigned against Parthia. The chronicler Malalas credits the emperor Gallienus with starting it in the mid-3rd century CE, with Diocletian finishing the complex decades later. It didn't exist in 117 CE — the island that year held older, more modest residences instead, over a century before this palace was ever planned.

The largest artificial harbor built in the open sea anywhere in the ancient world, enclosing about 40 hectares behind breakwaters poured from hydraulic concrete shipped over 1,000 kilometers from Puteoli, Italy. Herod built it from nothing in a decade, giving Judaea a deep-water port on a coastline that had none. By 117 CE the harbor was already quietly failing — slow tectonic sinking and weak spots in the underwater concrete had begun pulling sections of both breakwaters beneath the waves.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Sebastos Harbor, Caesarea · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_english: Temple of Roma and Augustus, Caesarea
properties.notes: Stood on a raised platform over twelve vaulted warehouses, positioned so it was the first thing any sailor saw entering the harbor. Josephus describes a colossal cult statue of Augustus inside, rivaling the scale of Olympian Zeus at Olympia, paired with an image of the goddess Roma. Built by Herod as a very public declaration of loyalty, it remained Caesarea's most visible landmark in 117 CE, towering over the harbor entrance.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Roma and Augustus platform, Caesarea Maritima · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Carved from local limestone with seating for roughly 3,500 people, and — unusually for a Roman theatre — built facing straight out to sea instead of inward toward the stage. Herod built it as part of his first wave of construction at Caesarea, connected directly to his palace next door. It was still hosting performances in 117 CE, and the same stage has been restored in modern times to host concerts again, two thousand years later.
properties.image_credit: The Herodian theatre, Caesarea Maritima · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Stretched about 315 meters long with seating for 12,000, its stone starting gates built on the same design as the Circus Maximus in Rome. Herod opened it for the city's grand inauguration with the Actian Games, a festival he founded in Augustus's honor and held every four years with chariot racing, athletics, and combat sport on one program. In 117 CE it was still running in its original Herodian form — its later conversion into a dedicated gladiator arena was still years away.
properties.image_credit: Herod's Hippodrome, Caesarea Maritima · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Herod's palace jutted 100 meters out into the Mediterranean on its own rocky point, a lower terrace built almost at sea level around a large rock-cut swimming pool and an upper terrace centered on a colonnaded courtyard. It became the official residence of Rome's prefects of Judaea after Herod's death — this is very likely where Pontius Pilate governed from decades earlier. In 117 CE it was still functioning as the seat of Roman government on this stretch of coast.
properties.image_credit: Herod's Promontory Palace, Caesarea · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Carried fresh water some 16 kilometers on raised stone arches from springs near Shuni to a city Herod had built on bare sand with no water source of its own. A long row of its arches still marches along the beach at Caesarea today, one of the most photographed Roman ruins in Israel. In 117 CE only Herod's original single channel was running — Hadrian would order a second channel built alongside it later in his reign.
properties.image_credit: High-Level Aqueduct, Caesarea · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Built soon after the city's founding, its timber entrance posts felled by tree-ring dating to 74 or 75 CE. Crowds packed its earthwork banks for gladiator fights and animal baiting for decades before anyone touched it again. Workers rebuilding the Guildhall Art Gallery in 1988 broke straight into its buried arena wall by accident, and its remains now sit on public view in the gallery's basement. In 117 CE it was still the original wooden arena — the stone rebuild was a few years off.
properties.image_credit: London's Roman amphitheatre, Guildhall · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Londinium at the time of the Boudican revolt of 60/61 CE as a town not yet formally a colony but famous for its crowds of merchants and supply traffic, the city where this amphitheater stood.

properties.notes: A small temple to the soldiers' god Mithras rose on the bank of the buried River Walbrook, its nave lined with columns for the cult's secret initiation rites. Worshippers later rededicated it to Bacchus and buried its Mithraic sculptures under the floor rather than hand them to a rival cult. Rediscovered by chance in 1954 during post-war rebuilding, crowds queued for hours to see it uncovered. In 117 CE this spot was still open ground beside the stream — the temple was more than a century away.
properties.image_credit: The London Mithraeum · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Londinium, the city where this mithraeum later stood, as a hub of traders and commerce sacked during the Boudican revolt.

properties.notes: Roman builders raised a defensive circuit three miles around Londinium using an estimated 85,000 tons of quarried Kentish ragstone, one of the largest construction projects anywhere in Roman Britain. Historians tie its building to the power struggle between the usurper Clodius Albinus and Septimius Severus in the 190s CE. Sections still stand several meters high at Tower Hill and the Barbican today. In 117 CE Londinium had no wall at all — it stood open for at least another 75 years.
properties.image_credit: A surviving section of the London Wall · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Londinium around 60/61 CE as a bustling centre of trade and merchants, though not yet a chartered colony. Describes the settlement, not its later stone wall, which was built well after this period.

properties.notes: Lugdunum built an intimate covered concert hall beside its larger open-air theatre, reserved for music and poetry readings rather than mass spectacle, seating roughly 3,000. Its floor was paved in polychrome marble shipped in from Africa, Greece and Asia Minor — an expensive touch for a room this size. Archaeologists still argue over its exact building date, clustering estimates in the Trajanic-to-Hadrianic years just after 100 CE, which puts its construction more likely just after 117 CE than before it.
properties.image_credit: The Odeon of Lyon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Workers cut this arena into the hillside overlooking the Mediterranean, seating up to 15,000 for beast hunts, executions, and gladiatorial combat. A 140-meter inscription later added around 221 CE crowning its podium remains the longest such inscription found anywhere in the empire, and a church was eventually built directly over its sand. Construction began around 122 CE, under Hadrian rather than Trajan — on 11 August 117 CE this hillside was still bare ground.
properties.image_credit: Tarragona Amphitheatre · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Tarraco as a colony founded by the Scipios and the capital of the province of Hispania Tarraconensis, the city where this amphitheater overlooks the sea.

properties.notes: Chariot teams thundered around a 325-meter track built under Domitian, seating up to 30,000 — likely more people than the city itself held. It ran directly beneath the terrace of the provincial forum, letting the governor watch races from his own portico above. In continuous use for chariot racing until the 5th century CE, its vaulted galleries still run beneath the streets and cafes of Tarragona's old town today. By 117 CE it had already been racing chariots for two decades.
properties.image_credit: The Roman Circus of Tarraco · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Tarraco as a colony founded by the Scipios and capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, the city where this circus stood beside the provincial forum.

properties.notes: Roman troops began raising these fortifications in the late 3rd century BCE, making them the oldest Roman walls standing anywhere outside Italy. The 3,500-meter circuit sat on megalithic Iberian foundations dressed with massive, irregular stone blocks, including the Tower of Minerva, home to the oldest Roman inscription found anywhere on the Iberian peninsula. Roughly 1,100 meters survive today along the Passeig Arqueològic. By 117 CE these walls had already guarded the provincial capital for more than three centuries.
properties.image_credit: The Roman walls of Tarragona · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Calls Tarraco (Tarragona) 'the work of the Scipios,' comparing its founding to Carthage among the Carthaginians. Describes the city's origins, not the walls specifically.

properties.name_english: The Provincial Forum and Temple of Divus Augustus
properties.notes: Tarraco's citizens petitioned Tiberius in 15 CE for permission to build a temple to the deified Augustus, and Rome granted it — the first time any province was allowed to worship a dead emperor, a precedent Tacitus singled out as setting the pattern for the whole empire. The temple stood inside a colonnaded square nearly the size of two football pitches, ringed by a wall nine meters high. Hadrian would rebuild it during a stay in Tarraco in the winter of 122/123 CE, but in 117 CE the century-old temple still stood in its original Tiberian form.

Two tiers of stacked arches carry this aqueduct 249 meters across a valley four kilometers north of the city, rising 27 meters at its tallest point, with twenty-five smaller arches sitting atop eleven larger ones. It channeled water from the Francolí river fifteen kilometers away straight into Tarraco's fountains and baths. Locals later nicknamed it the Devil's Bridge, certain no human hands could have built something so precise. Already a century old by 117 CE, it had long outlasted the emperor who built it.
properties.image_credit: Les Ferreres Aqueduct, Tarragona · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Tarraco as a colony founded by the Scipios and capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, the city this aqueduct supplied with water.

properties.notes: King Eumenes II raised this altar on the acropolis to celebrate Pergamon's victories over the Galatians, wrapping its base in a 113-meter marble frieze of gods battling giants — one of the largest sculptural friezes to survive from antiquity. Worshippers climbed a broad staircase on its western face to reach the sacrificial table inside a colonnaded court. It had already stood for nearly three centuries by 117 CE, still in active religious use. Only its foundations remain on the hill today; 19th-century German excavators shipped the sculpted superstructure to Berlin, where it now anchors its own museum.
properties.image_credit: Foundations of the Great Altar of Zeus, Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Compares the ash-built altar of Zeus at Olympia to a similarly ash-constructed altar of Zeus at Pergamon; scholars debate whether he means this monumental altar or a separate, older one on the same acropolis.

properties.notes: Eumenes II built this library beside his Temple of Athena, stacking it with an estimated 200,000 parchment scrolls that made it the greatest rival to the library at Alexandria. Egypt's Ptolemies reportedly banned papyrus exports to starve out the competition, forcing Pergamon's scribes to perfect treated animal skin as a substitute — parchment, pergamena, takes its name from this city. By 117 CE it had operated as one of the ancient world's great centers of learning for roughly three hundred years.
properties.image_credit: The Sanctuary of Athena, Pergamon, where the library stood · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Temple of Athena precinct, adjoining the library's former site

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (temple entrance)
ancient_sources.note: An inscription found by the temple's entrance hails Trajan as "lord of the earth and the sea," part of the imperial-cult honors built into this temple.

properties.notes: Trajan commissioned this podium temple for the highest point of Pergamon's acropolis, ringed by Corinthian columns — six across the front, nine down each side — meant to honor Zeus Philios alongside the emperors themselves. Its platform needed an enormous vaulted substructure just to level the steep hilltop for construction. Trajan never saw it finished: on 11 August 117 CE, the day he died, his temple stood as an active building site. Hadrian completed it roughly a decade later and joined his own cult to his adoptive father's inside it.
properties.image_credit: The Temple of Trajan, Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Builders cut this theatre directly into the acropolis slope at close to 70 degrees, the steepest surviving seating bank from the ancient world. Eighty rows of stone seating for 10,000 spectators climb 36 meters from stage to summit, engineered so tightly against the hillside that its wooden stage building had to be assembled fresh before every performance and dismantled after. By 117 CE it had already hosted plays for roughly 350 years, one of the oldest structures still working on the acropolis.
properties.image_credit: The Hellenistic theatre of Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Pergamon's rise under the Attalid kings and its site on a cone-shaped hill above the Caicus plain. A description of the city, not the theatre.

properties.notes: Raised around 25 BCE as part of Augustus's monumental spring sanctuary, this vaulted hall got its romantic name centuries later from visitors who mistook its coffered ceiling and wall niches for a shrine to the huntress goddess — no ancient inscription ever confirmed it. Its walls run over a meter thick and still stand two stories tall despite Huguenot troops torching it in 1577. Medieval monks folded it into their monastery, probably the only reason it survived at all. By 117 CE it had anchored the sacred precinct beside the city's founding spring for nearly a century and a half.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Diana, Nimes · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Nemausus (Nimes) as the metropolis of the Volcae Arecomici, ruling twenty-four subordinate villages. A description of the city, not this temple.

properties.notes: Standing on the highest point in Nimes, this tower was raised around 15 BCE as the tallest of fourteen towers ringing Augustus's new seven-kilometer city wall, built directly over an older Gallic tower whose height it roughly doubled. It still rises 32 meters today despite losing its upper third to centuries of stone-robbing. In 117 CE it dominated the skyline over the plain toward the Mediterranean, already well over a century old.
properties.image_credit: Tour Magne, Nimes · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Nemausus among the towns with Latin rights in Gallia Narbonensis, the city whose hilltop this tower crowned before Augustus enclosed it within new city walls.

properties.notes: Built around 16 BCE as the grand eastern gateway into Nemausus, this gate greeted every traveler arriving on the Via Domitia from Italy. Two broad carriage arches, flanked by narrower pedestrian passages topped with statue niches, still carry the dedication crediting Augustus's fortification of the colony. It originally carried twin projecting towers and an arcaded upper gallery, both long gone. By 117 CE it had been funneling trade and traffic through those arches for well over a century.
properties.image_credit: Porte d'Auguste, Nimes · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Nemausus among the towns with Latin rights in the territory of the Arecomici, the city whose walls this gate once pierced.

properties.notes: Erected around 15 BCE on the opposite side of the city from the Porta Augusta, this gate carried the Via Domitia west toward Hispania, earning it the old local name Porte d'Espagne. A single semicircular arch, once flanked by two round towers, still frames the street that bears its name today. It's one of only two surviving gates from Augustus's original ring of fourteen towers. In 117 CE it stood as the quieter western counterpart to the Porta Augusta, still funneling travelers toward Spain.

Built around 40-50 CE at the terminus of the fifty-kilometer aqueduct that flowed from a spring near Uzes and crossed the Pont du Gard, this circular stone basin distributed water across Roman Nimes. Water entered through a single channel and left through ten pipes set into the basin wall, each feeding a different quarter of the city. It's one of only two water-distribution tanks of this kind known to survive anywhere from the Roman world, the other at Pompeii. By 117 CE it had quietly done this job for well over half a century.
properties.image_credit: Castellum Divisorium, Nimes · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Gauls gathered at this gushing spring to worship Nemausus, the native god who gave the city its name, since at least the 6th century BCE. Augustus's engineers monumentalized the site around 25 BCE, building a nymphaeum, porticoes, and altar terraces around the water and folding the old cult into the new imperial one. The spring still feeds the same pool today, exactly where the Roman altar terraces once stood. In 117 CE this was the religious and civic heart of Nemausus — the place the city's own name came from.
properties.image_credit: Jardins de la Fontaine, Nimes, site of the spring sanctuary · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The spring and gardens of the Roman sanctuary precinct

properties.notes: Built between 40 and 30 BCE under Augustus, this was one of the earliest stone theatres raised anywhere in Gaul. Its stage wall once stood three stories tall, faced with over a hundred columns of colored marble, of which a single surviving pair — nicknamed "the two widows" — still stands today. Excavators found a colossal statue of Augustus buried near the stage, which is how the theatre's date was pinned down. By 117 CE it had staged performances and public gatherings for roughly a century and a half.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Arles · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Arelate (Arles), the station of the Sixth Legion, among the colonies of interior Gallia Narbonensis. A geographic notice, not a description of the theatre.

properties.notes: Built around 25-10 BCE as the load-bearing foundation for the Forum of Arelate above it, this U-shaped network of vaulted stone galleries covers roughly 3,400 square meters, six meters underground. Its narrow airshafts still ventilate the space exactly as Roman engineers designed them. It likely doubled as a grain store and administrative annex for the bustling forum overhead. By 117 CE it had spent well over a century silently holding up the civic heart of the city above it.
properties.image_credit: The Cryptoporticus, Arles · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Founded as the civic and commercial hub of Arelate around 25-10 BCE, the forum once filled the city center with a temple, porticoes, and a paved plaza. Only two Corinthian columns and a fragment of entablature survive today, built into the corner of a later building. The whole complex sat atop the cryptoporticus, whose vaults absorbed the weight of the sloping ground below. By 117 CE the forum was still the busy administrative and commercial center of the colony, well over a century into daily use.

Quarried from Egyptian granite and never inscribed, this fifteen-meter obelisk was raised in the 4th century CE as the centerpiece of the spina running down the middle of the Circus of Arles. It toppled and snapped in two after the circus fell out of use in the 6th century, then lay forgotten until rediscovered in 1389. The city finally re-erected it in a main square in 1676, topped with a bronze sun. It did not exist in 117 CE — more than two centuries would pass before Constantine's family had it raised.
properties.image_credit: The Obelisk of Arles · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Built around 149 CE on the west bank of the Rhone to host chariot races, this circus stretched 450 meters long and seated roughly 20,000 spectators. Its builders drove some 30,000 wooden piles into the marshy riverbank just to keep the structure from sinking. Its central spina later held the granite obelisk now standing across the river in the city's main square. In 117 CE this stretch of riverbank was still open ground — the circus wouldn't be built for another three decades, under Antoninus Pius rather than Hadrian.
properties.image_credit: Remains of the spina, Circus of Arles · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Arelate as a colony of veterans of the Sixth Legion, one of the leading towns of Gallia Narbonensis where this circus was built along the Rhone.

properties.notes: Built in the early 4th century CE for Constantine's imperial residence at Arelate, these baths still preserve a soaring brick hall and a row of tall arched windows that once lit the hot room. Alternating bands of stone and brick decorate the surviving exterior walls in red and grey. The complex was abandoned by the early 6th century as the city's fortunes declined. In 117 CE this riverside quarter had no baths at all — Constantine wouldn't be born for another century and a half.
properties.image_credit: Baths of Constantine, Arles · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This podium temple rose in the heart of Vienne to honor the emperor Augustus, later rededicated to include his deified wife Livia. Its six Corinthian columns and deep porch still stand almost fully intact, one of the best-preserved Roman temples anywhere outside Italy. Locals turned it into a church, then a Temple of Reason during the Revolution, then a library, before restorers stripped it back to its Roman skin. By 117 CE it had already stood for over a century as the religious anchor of the forum.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Augustus and Livia, Vienne · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Identifies Vienna (Vienne) as the metropolis of the Allobroges on the Rhone. A city-level notice, not a description of this temple.

properties.notes: Carved directly into the slope of a hill overlooking the Rhone, this theatre seated around 13,000 people, making it one of the largest in Gaul after Autun. Its curved seating bank spans some 130 meters across, terraced tier after tier up the hillside. It had been open for entertainment, oratory, and civic gatherings for roughly seventy years by the time Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Vienne · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_latin: Pyramide (local name; no ancient name survives)
properties.notes: A 23-meter stone needle rising from a four-arched base, this is the last standing "Egyptian-style" monument in France and once marked the centerline of Vienne's chariot-racing circus. It stood at the middle of the spina, the raised central barrier chariots looped around, originally flanked by small shrines and fountains. Sources disagree on exactly when the circus and its pyramid went up, with one strand of scholarship placing it after Trajan's reign, so this ships conservatively as not yet standing in 117 CE rather than picking a side in an unsettled argument. Rediscovered by excavators in 1852, it has been a protected monument ever since.

This green square in the middle of modern Vienne preserves the skeleton of the Roman city's forum: two stretches of a sculpted portico decorated with a river-god relief, a massive wall from a municipal assembly hall that once seated 800 magistrates, and the foundations of a wealthy townhouse. It functioned as the administrative, economic, and political heart of the Gallo-Roman city for well over a century by 117 CE. The site's modern name comes from the later cult of Cybele, though the surviving structures are civic rather than religious.

This stone-piered bridge carried Vienne's main east-west road across the Rhone to the settlement on the opposite bank, and stayed in continuous use until the 17th century. Its piers were reinforced with driven wooden piling to anchor them into the riverbed, still visible at low water for centuries after antiquity. Sonar surveys have picked up traces of at least one other Roman-era crossing nearby, suggesting the city needed more than one bridge to manage its Rhone traffic. By 117 CE it had already carried travelers and trade across the river for well over a century.

properties.image_alt: Roman underground warehouse galleries at the Horreum of Narbonne
properties.image_credit: Underground galleries of the Horreum, Narbonne (Narbo Martius) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: Five meters below Narbonne's streets, these vaulted stone galleries once stored the grain, oil, and goods that moved through Rome's first colony outside Italy. It's the only Roman-era structure still visible above ground level in the city, walkable today exactly as ancient dockworkers left it. By 117 CE it had already been in continuous use as a warehouse for roughly a century and a half.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Calls Narbo (Narbonne) the emporium of all Gaul, surpassed by no other port in the volume of traffic it received.

properties.notes: A sunken rectangle of massive limestone paving slabs sits below street level in the middle of Narbonne's main square — a surviving stretch of the actual road surface of the first Roman road built in Gaul. Deep wheel ruts are still cut into the stone from centuries of cart traffic. Uncovered during excavations in 1997, it lets a visitor stand on the same pavement legionaries and merchants used to cross from Italy toward Spain. By 117 CE this road had carried imperial traffic for well over two centuries.
properties.image_credit: Exposed Via Domitia paving, Narbonne · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The Via Domitia crossed the river here on a bridge of six or seven stone arches, carrying Roman traffic straight through the middle of Narbo Martius. Only one arch is still visible today, above a later canal, but it has never stopped being a working bridge — later builders simply buried the rest under dozens of buildings of shops and houses, one of only two inhabited bridges still standing in France. In 117 CE it carried the entire commercial life of the Via Domitia across the water.
properties.image_credit: Pont des Marchands, Narbonne · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Seventy-two arcades and four gated entrances once ringed this amphitheatre, built on flat ground using vaulted ring-walls rather than a natural hillside slope — a genuine feat of engineering. Nothing rises above ground today; the arena's outline survives only as a curve traced by a modern street, pinpointed by land surveys in 1838. It had likely been hosting games for at least two decades by the time Trajan died in 117 CE.

Narbo Martius's grandest temple stood on a marble-clad podium over 3 meters tall and 48 by 36 meters across, ringed by a colonnade enclosing the sanctuary of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. Excavators uncovered it in the late 19th century beneath the site of the city's high school. Both scholarly datings for its construction place it after Hadrian became emperor on 11 August 117 CE, so on the day Trajan died this temple didn't exist yet, even though Narbo's forum itself had already been the city's civic heart for well over two centuries.

properties.image_alt: Excavated Hellenistic-era ramparts of ancient Massalia
properties.image_credit: Jardin des Vestiges — Hellenistic ramparts of ancient Massalia, Marseille · Wikimedia Commons
properties.notes: A gateway flanked by two stone towers standing up to 15 meters tall once guarded Massalia's harbor-side entrance — the oldest visible fortification anywhere in France. Pink limestone curtain walls run alongside it, laid down generations before Rome ever set foot in Gaul. Julius Caesar's legions besieged the city in 49 BCE and stripped it of its fleet and most of its territory for backing Pompey, but never tore down its walls. By 117 CE these Greek-built defenses had stood watch over the port for more than 450 years.

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Gives a detailed account of Trebonius's siege of Massilia on Caesar's behalf, including the city's walls, siege towers, and mines, and a truce broken when the defenders burned the siege works.

properties.notes: This sheltered inlet, fed by a freshwater stream and pinched between two rocky headlands, is the reason Massalia exists at all — Phocaean sailors picked it out around 600 BCE as the perfect natural harbor and built their city on the hills around it. For over seven centuries it drew merchant ships from across the Mediterranean, its quays gradually rebuilt in stone under Roman rule after Caesar curtailed the city's independence in 49 BCE. In 117 CE it was still doing exactly the same job it does today: sheltering boats in the middle of the city.

Rows of dolia — massive ceramic jars taller than a person, used to store wine and oil — still sit sunk into the floor of this Roman commercial warehouse exactly where dockworkers left them. The complex was rediscovered by accident in 1947 while the district was being rebuilt after wartime destruction. Excavators only place its construction broadly in the 2nd century CE, a window that straddles this map's 117 CE cutoff too closely to call with confidence, so it ships conservatively as not yet standing rather than guessing which side of Trajan's death it falls on.
properties.image_credit: Musée des Docks Romains, Marseille · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: In-situ Roman dolia (storage jars) inside the Musee des Docks Romains, Marseille

properties.notes: Stone-lined graves and funerary enclosures uncovered during 20th-century excavations trace Massalia's burial grounds back to the earliest Greek settlers, with burial use continuing straight through the Roman centuries. At least half a dozen sarcophagi containing urns and ashes turned up in the old port district alone. By 117 CE this ground had already received the dead of the city for over seven hundred years, Greek and Roman alike buried close to the same harbor their trade had built.

Roman engineers raised this gate as the eastern threshold of Augustodunum around 15 BCE, cutting four passages through its face: two broad bays for cart traffic and two narrow ones for pedestrians. Large quadrangular limestone blocks from the Chalonnais quarries still lock together without mortar in the surviving arches. No other city in Gaul kept a Roman gate standing this complete above street level, and by 117 CE it had already carried two centuries of traffic in and out of the Aeduan capital.
properties.image_credit: Porte Saint-Andre, Autun · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Vivien Barrière
ancient_sources.work: Aux portes d'Augustodunum: architecture, fonction et histoire des portes de l'enceinte antique d'Autun
ancient_sources.note: Architectural and stratigraphic study of Autun's Roman gates, including the Porte Saint-André, placing its construction in the Augustan/early Julio-Claudian period, roughly a century before the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: This gate marked the northern end of Augustodunum's main street and was one of the very first monuments raised when the city was founded and named for Augustus. Two large arcades once let carts roll through side by side, flanked by two smaller footpaths still visible today. Historians place its completion somewhere in the last decades of Augustus's reign, more than a century ahead of Trajan's death in 117 CE, and it has stood at this river crossing for over two thousand years.
properties.image_credit: Porte d'Arroux, Autun · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Builders raised this theatre on the eastern edge of Augustodunum in the decades after 70 CE, giving it a 148-meter diameter that made it the largest theatre in Roman Gaul. Three semicircular tiers of seating, cut by radiating staircases, once held as many as 20,000 spectators for comedy, tragedy, and civic assembly. When Trajan died in 117 CE the theatre had already been staging performances for roughly two generations.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Autun · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pierre Wuilleumier
ancient_sources.ref: Revue des Études Anciennes, Tome 42 (1940), pp. 699-706
ancient_sources.note: Study of the theatre's 1930s excavation, including a worn as coin of Claudius found in construction fill, supporting a build date in the decades after 70 CE, before the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: A Romano-Celtic sanctuary rose northwest of Augustodunum around the turn of the 2nd century CE, built around a square cella ringed by a covered walkway. Two of its four cella walls still stand more than 20 meters tall today, an unusually complete survival for this style of temple. No inscription has ever confirmed which god the sanctuary actually honored, despite the popular but almost certainly wrong "Janus" label attached centuries later; whichever god it was, the building was already an established local landmark well before Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Janus, Autun · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Set within Augustodunum's Champ des Urnes necropolis, this square-based pyramid rose 22.65 meters on a 10.5-meter base, its outer facing stone long since stripped away. No burial chamber has ever been found inside it, leaving its exact purpose a mystery archaeologists still argue over. Most evidence points to a 1st-century CE build, so it had already watched over the Aeduan dead for decades by the time news of Trajan's death reached Gaul in August 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Pyramid of Couhard, Autun · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A monumental triple archway rose in Durocortorum in the early 3rd century CE, stretching 32 meters long and 13 meters high, the widest triumphal arch to survive anywhere in the Roman world. Carved reliefs along its vault show Romulus and Remus nursed by the wolf and Leda with Jupiter as a swan. Built roughly a century after Trajan's death, it did not yet exist on 11 August 117 CE; later builders folded it into the medieval city wall, where it stayed hidden until demolition work fully re-exposed it in the 1840s and 50s.
properties.image_credit: Porte de Mars, Reims · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Names Durocortorum, the city where this gate stood, as the chief town of the Remi.

properties.notes: Workers cut a U-shaped underground gallery beneath Durocortorum's forum around the turn of the 2nd century CE, its two long arms each running 60 meters and its northern arm 100 meters, all vaulted and once covered in painted plaster. Recent archaeomagnetic testing of the brickwork dates construction to roughly 90-100 CE, so it had already been supporting the forum square above for close to two decades when Trajan died in 117 CE. It survived intact because later residents repurposed it for storage instead of tearing it apart for stone.
properties.image_credit: Cryptoporticus of Reims · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A monumental arch once marked the southern end of Durocortorum's main street, where the road left the city for Rome. Builders raised it in the 2nd or 3rd century CE, well after Trajan's reign had ended, so it was not part of the city Trajan's contemporaries walked through in 117 CE. City authorities tore the arch down in 1752, leaving behind just one pier and a single heavily worn column that still stand inside a school courtyard today.

Roman engineers built a 44-kilometer channel around 20 CE to carry water from springs at Jonchery-sur-Suippe into Durocortorum, feeding the city's public baths and fountains for roughly four centuries. A single arched masonry fragment of that system survives today beside Place Royale, though nearly everything else lies buried under the modern street grid. The channel had already been delivering water to the Remi capital for almost a century by the time Trajan died in August 117 CE.

Forum Iulii raised its amphitheatre to hold roughly 10,000 spectators around an arena floor measuring 69 by 39 meters, ringing it with tiers of Esterel sandstone seating for gladiatorial bouts and public executions. By the time Trajan died in 117 CE the arena had already been staging games for a generation. Centuries later it became a stone quarry and even a rubbish tip before archaeologists finally cleared it in 1960.
properties.image_credit: Roman Amphitheatre of Frejus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Forum Iulii as a strategically important naval colony on the Gallic coast during the civil war of 69 CE, the city where this amphitheater stands.

properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman theatre at Fréjus
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Fréjus (Forum Julii) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Théâtre romain de Fréjus et buste de Léotard.jpg?width=800
properties.notes: Forum Iulii's theatre was the city's first purpose-built entertainment venue, raised in Esterel sandstone on a gentle hillside so around 2,000 spectators could watch actors in full view. By 117 CE it had already hosted a century of performances near the city's Gate of Rome. It later served as a defensive bastion and a stone quarry before archaeologists excavated it in the 1920s.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: States that Agricola was born at Forum Iulii (Fréjus), the city where this theatre stood.

properties.notes: Forum Iulii's western gate opened directly onto the Via Aurelia, the road linking Rome to Gaul, through a monumental semicircle 50 meters across, flanked by round towers and a wide carriageway. It is the best preserved of the four gates that once pierced the city's 4-kilometer circuit wall. In 1919 excavators found the original paving still rutted by Roman cart wheels beneath the arch, which by 117 CE had funneled traffic between Italy and Gaul for roughly a century.
properties.image_credit: Porte des Gaules, Frejus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A 42-kilometer channel once carried water from the Siagnole springs down to Forum Iulii's water tower, crossing 36 separate masonry bridges along the way. By 117 CE the system had been feeding the city's fountains and baths for decades. Geologists have measured the mineral crust left inside the channel to show it stayed in continuous use for roughly three centuries; isolated arches still march across the landscape near the modern town entrance.
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct of Frejus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes Forum Iulii as a fortified naval colony on the Gallic coast, the city this aqueduct supplied with water carried down from the hills above Frejus.

properties.notes: This freestanding arch, popularly called a golden gate, is actually the surviving frigidarium wall of the harbor baths that once served Forum Iulii's fleet quarter. Excavation of an associated drainage sewer dates its construction to the second half of the 2nd century CE, decades after Trajan's death, so no version of it stood on 11 August 117 CE. Coordinates are approximate, placed near the ancient harbor basin the baths served.

A wealthy Santon citizen named Caius Julius Rufus paid for this arch himself, dedicating it to Tiberius, Drusus, and Germanicus to mark the completion of the road linking Lyon to the Atlantic. It originally spanned the Roman bridge over the Charente, carrying traffic for well over a millennium, and by 117 CE had already stood watch over the crossing for a full century. The bridge itself was torn down in 1843 over Victor Hugo's public protest, and the rescued arch was moved stone by stone to its present riverbank site.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Germanicus, Saintes · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: Preserves the arch's own dedicatory inscription honoring Tiberius, Drusus Caesar, and Germanicus.

properties.notes: Saintes built this amphitheatre around 40 CE by cutting directly into a natural hillside, letting the terrain itself carry much of the seating for a crowd of up to 15,000 -- one of the oldest amphitheatres in Roman Gaul, predating the Colosseum by roughly 40 years. Its arena floor stretches 66 by 39 meters, ringed by underground galleries that once held animals and gladiators before their entrances. It already stood as a mature, decades-old landmark of Mediolanum Santonum by the time Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman Amphitheatre of Saintes · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Mediolanum Santonum as the chief town of the Santones tribe in Gallia Aquitania, the city where this amphitheater was built.

properties.notes: These public baths once covered 8,000 square meters, making them one of the largest thermal establishments in Roman Aquitania, complete with a monumental caldarium and its own fountain. Bathers were already using the complex for decades by 117 CE, more than a century before the city abandoned it as Saintes drew back within tighter walls in the 3rd century. A Christian shrine to Saint Saloine later rose on the ruins. Coordinates are an approximate placement within the ancient city, pending a precise site geocoding.

Saintes drew its water from springs up to 15 kilometers away, and its most dramatic surviving link is the Pont des Arcs, a 160-meter masonry bridge whose 27 arches once carried the channel 16 meters above a valley floor. The system delivered as much as 120,000 cubic meters of water a day to the fountains and baths of Mediolanum Santonum, and had already been running for the better part of a century when Trajan died in 117 CE. Coordinates mark the surviving arcaded piers near Fontcouverte; farmland has swallowed most of the rest of the line.

The Great Bath channeled over a million litres of naturally hot, mineral-rich water a day into a lead-lined pool 1.6 meters deep, sheathed in 45 sheets of Roman-cut lead that still line its floor today. Bathers descended four wide steps into steam rising off water heated by nothing but the earth itself. By 117 CE, the year Trajan died, the pool had already been drawing sick and hopeful travelers from across Britannia for two generations.
properties.image_credit: The Great Bath, Bath · Diliff, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

ancient_sources.author: Solinus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the hot springs at Aquae Sulis as sacred to Minerva, with a flame on her altar that never turns to ash.

properties.notes: Roman engineers tamed a wild geothermal spring surging up at 46 degrees Celsius inside a lead-lined stone wall built over oak piles driven into the mud. Pilgrims threw curse tablets and coins into the water as offerings to the goddess Sulis, dozens of which archaeologists later pulled from the silt. By 117 CE the reservoir had stood for roughly half a century, already the ritual heart of Aquae Sulis.

Underfloor hypocaust channels drove heat from wood-fired furnaces beneath a raised floor, warming bathers through rooms running from tepid to scorching hot. Water drawn straight from the adjoining Great Bath fed a lukewarm pool here before visitors worked up to the sweat rooms proper. The suite's original timber-roofed form already stood by 117 CE, part of the same first-generation building campaign as the Great Bath itself.

A stone wall two meters thick eventually rose around the temple and baths, enclosing 23 acres of sacred and civic ground, though historians still argue whether it served real defense or simply dignified a famous religious site. It came more than a century after Trajan's death; in 117 CE, Aquae Sulis's bathing precinct still stood open and unwalled. Only fragments survive today, folded into Bath's later medieval fortifications.

properties.image_alt: Reconstruction illustration of the Roman forum at Verulamium
properties.image_credit: Artist's impression of the Forum of Verulamium · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Artist impression of the Forum of Verulamium (16207649850).jpg?width=800
properties.notes: A monumental dedication slab over four meters long once announced the completion of Verulamium's civic heart, credited to the governor Julius Agricola. The basilica anchored the largest building in Roman Britain's third city, a hall where magistrates heard cases beneath a forum lined with shops and colonnades. Already 38 years old by the time Trajan died in 117 CE, it stood as the undisputed administrative center of one of Britain's most Romanized towns; its foundations still lie beneath St Michael's Church.

ancient_sources.author: RIB
ancient_sources.note: Preserves the forum and basilica's own dedicatory inscription to the emperor Titus, erected under governor Agricola.

properties.notes: Unusually for Roman Britain, this theatre was built with a raised stage rather than as a simple amphitheatre, hosting religious processions and armed combat before its auditorium was enlarged decades later. It rose beside the great road of Watling Street, on the site of an older Celtic shrine. It did not yet exist in 117 CE; construction began roughly a generation after Trajan's death, and today it remains one of only a handful of purpose-built theatres known from Roman Britain.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Verulamium · Rob Hinkley, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the sack of the municipium of Verulamium during the Boudican revolt, where only the temple held out under a two-day siege before the town was plundered and burned.

properties.name_english: Roman Wall of Verulamium and the London Gate
properties.notes: Mortared flint rubble banded with red brick rose five meters high around a two-mile circuit, pierced by the London Gate's four separate passages where Watling Street, the great road from Dover to Chester, entered the city. This fortification belongs to the anxious, embattled Britain of the later 3rd century; in 117 CE, at the height of Trajan's empire, Verulamium had no stone walls at all. Its foundations are still walkable today in Verulamium Park.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the sack of the municipium of Verulamium during the Boudican revolt, where only the temple held out under a two-day siege before the town was plundered and burned.

properties.notes: Roughly 200,000 individually cut tesserae form a mosaic floor laid directly over a hypocaust system whose brick pillars once channeled hot air beneath a wealthy townhouse's reception rooms. Excavators in the 1930s chose to leave it exactly where the Romans built it, now sheltered by a museum building. This particular house did not yet stand in 117 CE; it belongs to Verulamium's later, more prosperous 2nd-century building boom.
properties.image_credit: Verulamium hypocaust and mosaic · Przemyslaw Sakrajda, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

properties.notes: The Temple of the Deified Claudius rose as Roman Britain's largest classical temple, its podium alone measuring 32 by 24 meters. Colonial elites built it to honor Rome's new god-emperor, and Boudica's rebels found it so hateful a symbol of occupation that they besieged the last defenders inside for two days before torching it in the winter of 60-61 CE. The colony rebuilt the temple on its surviving podium within a year or two, and by 117 CE it had served as Camulodunum's ceremonial heart for more than five decades; its massive foundation still survives, buried beneath Colchester Castle.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Claudius, Colchester · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Diagram of the Temple of Claudius podium underlying Colchester Castle

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the temple as a hated symbol of servitude to the Britons and records its destruction during Boudica's revolt in 60/61 CE.

properties.notes: Britain's largest surviving Roman gateway opened where the road from Londinium met the town's western wall. A freestanding triumphal arch marked the new colonia around 50 CE, then was folded into a far bigger structure, two carriageways and two footways spanning 33 meters, once the town wall rose after the Boudican revolt. By 117 CE the gate had carried traffic in and out of Colonia Claudia Victricensis for decades, and its western arches still stand today as the best-preserved Roman gateway in Britain.
properties.image_credit: Balkerne Gate, Colchester · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

properties.notes: Colchester's defenders built Britain's first town wall after Boudica's rebels burned the undefended colonia to the ground in 60-61 CE. Legionary engineers raised a 2.8-kilometer circuit of rubble and brick, standing nearly six meters high in places, over roughly two decades starting around 65 CE. By 117 CE the completed wall had ringed the colony with six gates for a generation, guaranteeing nothing like the Boudican sack could happen again; long stretches still stand today, making it the oldest complete town-wall circuit surviving in Britain.

Duncan's Gate pierced the northeastern stretch of Colchester's new town wall, one of six gateways built into the circuit after the Boudican revolt. Unlike the grand Balkerne Gate, this was a modest single-arched entrance with a small guardroom above it, built from the same rubble as the rest of the wall in the decades after 60-61 CE. It had stood as a working gate for roughly 50 years by the time Trajan died in August 117 CE, and survives today, rediscovered in 1853, as one of only two Roman gates in Colchester still visible above ground.

Britain's only known Roman chariot-racing circus stretched about 450 meters long and up to 74 meters wide just south of Colchester's walls. Archaeologists found its buried foundations by accident in 2004 during redevelopment of a former army barracks, making global headlines as the first circus ever confirmed in Roman Britain. Dating evidence points to construction around 120-130 CE, roughly a decade after Trajan died in 117 CE, so the circus had not yet been built at this map's snapshot moment; its outline is preserved beneath a housing estate today.
properties.image_credit: Reconstruction of the Roman Circus of Camulodunum · Carole Raddato, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the unfortified veteran colony of Camulodunum, resented by the dispossessed Trinobantes, and its fall to Boudica's forces after the statue of Victory there fell face-down as an omen.

properties.notes: The largest theatre yet found in Roman Britain was a banked earthwork auditorium seating roughly 5,000 spectators around a semicircular stage, standing beside Colchester's most important native temple complex. Excavation found that an earlier timber theatre had stood on the site before being demolished and rebuilt as a turf-and-clay bank held by a stone wall; a coin of Hadrian and pottery found in that rebuild date it to the later 2nd century, decades after Trajan's death. The site is marked out in the grass at Gosbecks Archaeological Park today.

Gosbecks' temple sat inside a monumental covered portico roughly 100 meters square, wrapped around a small cella barely 13.5 meters on a side, on ground that had served as a religious center for local Britons for a century before the Roman conquest. Excavation dates the grand stone-built portico to the mid-2nd century CE, roughly a generation after Trajan's death, so the temple in its known monumental form was not yet complete in 117 CE. Its outline, like the neighboring theatre's, is marked out in the grass of Gosbecks Archaeological Park today.

Builders raised Calleva's first earthen rampart around 200 CE and faced it in flint and stone roughly seventy years later, eventually enclosing 2.4 kilometers of the town in a wall line that still runs almost unbroken through the Hampshire fields today. When Trajan died in 117 CE none of this existed; Calleva sat open and undefended, decades away from its first bank and ditch. Visitors today can walk the near-complete circuit past the recessed sockets where its timber gates once hung.
properties.image_credit: Silchester Roman town walls · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Workers cut this oval arena into the earth just outside Calleva's northeast corner sometime between 55 and 75 CE, banking the spoil into raised seating that still rings the field today. By the time Trajan died on 11 August 117, this amphitheatre had already been staging fights and gatherings for more than forty years. Excavators later found traces of a small shrine to Nemesis, goddess of fate, tucked against the arena wall; it would not gain its familiar stone-faced shape for another 150 years.
properties.image_credit: Silchester Roman amphitheatre · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Calleva as a town of the Atrebates tribe in Britain, the settlement where this amphitheater stood just outside the town walls.

properties.notes: Calleva's civic heart began as a timber forum-basilica raised around 85 CE, then was demolished and rebuilt entirely in masonry under Hadrian; coin evidence dates the new stone hall to the 130s. That means the footings and column bases visible today did not yet exist on 11 August 117, only its wooden predecessor did. A bronze eagle recovered from the earlier building's floor in 1866 later inspired a well-known novel.

Builders raised this soaring wall of brick-banded stone around 150 CE as part of Viroconium's vast civic baths, and at seven meters tall it remains the largest freestanding fragment of Roman masonry anywhere in Britain. Work on the baths complex only began after Hadrian took the throne, and this section was not finished for another three decades, so it did not exist when Trajan died on 11 August 117. Rows of square sockets still visible in the stonework mark exactly where Roman masons anchored their scaffolding as they built it.
properties.image_credit: The Old Work, Wroxeter · Jeff Buck, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Viroconium among the towns of the Cornovii in Britain, alongside Deva, giving its geographic coordinates.

properties.notes: An inscribed dedication slab found on site fixes the completion of Viroconium's forum to 129 or 130 CE, honoring the Cornovii tribe's new civic center. That date lands more than a decade after Trajan's death; on 11 August 117 this was still a construction site, not the colonnaded plaza that later anchored the fourth-largest town in Roman Britain. Fire swept through it later in the 2nd century, and it was rebuilt rather than abandoned; its stone footings still trace the building's outline against the Shropshire grass.
properties.image_credit: Forum column bases, Viroconium (Wroxeter Roman City) · Wikimedia Commons / geograph.org.uk (CC BY-SA 2.0)
properties.image_alt: Surviving column bases of the forum at Viroconium, Wroxeter

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Viroconium among the towns of the Cornovii in Britain, alongside Deva, giving its geographic coordinates.

properties.notes: Wroxeter's covered market hall rose alongside the town's great public baths as part of a single building programme that ran from the 120s into the 160s, replacing a row of timber shops that had fronted Watling Street since around 90 CE. None of this masonry market existed in 117 CE; Trajan was still emperor when merchants here traded out of wooden stalls, not a stone-colonnaded hall. Archaeologists spent decades, from the 1950s into the 1980s, tracing its full courtyard plan.

Around 200 CE, Viroconium's residents dug a bank-and-ditch circuit roughly 4 kilometers long around their town, built from earth and timber rather than faced in stone. No trace of any boundary defence existed when Trajan died in 117; for its first eight decades as a civilian town, Viroconium sat completely open. Historians read the later earthwork less as a response to any actual attack than as a statement of civic status, since no evidence of warfare near the town has ever surfaced.

One hundred and sixty-seven dry-stone granite arches stride across the valley to the Plaza del Azoguejo, rising to 28 meters without a drop of mortar holding the ashlars together — the postcard image of Roman Hispania. For decades textbooks dated it to Domitian's reign (c. 98 CE) on the strength of a reconstructed bronze inscription, but a 2016 re-analysis of foundation fill from three pillars turned up a Trajanic sestertius struck 112-116 CE sealed in the packing — proof that at least part of the structure was still under construction well into Trajan's final years. A foundation coin only fixes when building started, not when it finished, and aqueduct bridges this scale typically took years above the footings, so this map takes the strict reading: still rising, not yet complete, at the 117 CE snapshot.
