Beneath the old Jewish quarter, a 1990 excavation in Plaza de Guevara uncovered a colonnaded public space some 100 meters across, interpreted as part of a forum or a basilica flanking one — the only real hint of civic Roman Segovia beyond the aqueduct. Coverage of the dig dates the occupation broadly to the 1st or 2nd century CE; a Flavian date around municipal promotion under Vespasian's Latin Rights edict (73-74 CE) is plausible but not fixed by any tighter excavated terminus. Coordinates approximate the find neighborhood, not a surveyed point.

Under the paving of Segovia's Plaza Mayor, a 2010 dig by Arex Arqueologia hit an intact Roman living space behind the former Hotel Victoria — a beaten-earth floor, rammed-earth wall stubs, and fragments of painted plaster, stratified to the High Imperial period (1st-2nd century CE). Unglamorous next to the aqueduct, but real stratigraphy showing ordinary Segovians living in proper Roman houses on this hill well before 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: Placa Ramon Berenguer el Gran, Barcelona, Spain
properties.notes: Barcino's first wall was a mark of civic status for a brand-new Augustan colony, not a defense against any real threat — a modest stone ring about 9 meters high and 2-3.5 meters thick, dated to the colony's founding around 15-10 BCE. The much heavier, tower-studded circuit visitors associate with Roman Barcelona today is a late-3rd/early-4th-century response to Frankish and Alemannic raids, more than a century after this snapshot — only the earlier, plainer wall stood in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman wall tower, Plaça Ramon Berenguer, Barcelona (ancient Barcino) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving tower of the Roman city walls of Barcino at Plaça Ramon Berenguer, Barcelona

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Barcino, surnamed Faventia, among the coastal colonies of Hispania Tarraconensis.

properties.notes: Four startlingly tall, slender Corinthian columns still stand in a medieval courtyard atop Mont Taber, the hill on which Barcino's founders laid out their forum. Most sources place the temple in the Augustan founding period (c. 15-13 BCE), though the dedication to Augustus is, by Barcino's own admission, traditional rather than proven — the identification rests on the temple's prominence and style, not a surviving inscription, and at least one strand of scholarship credits its formalization to Tiberius after 14 CE. Either way it had been the colony's religious high point for well over a century by 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: Placa de la Vila de Madrid, Barcelona, Spain
properties.notes: Outside Barcino's walls, along a minor road, roughly seventy tombs survive — cupae, urns, and stelae for slaves, freedmen, and working people, in stark contrast to the marble temple up on Mont Taber. Roman law forbade burial within the walls, so anyone entering the city from this direction in 117 CE would have passed row upon row of these graves; the necropolis is documented in continuous use from the 1st through the 3rd century CE, comfortably bracketing the snapshot.
properties.image_credit: Via Sepulcral Romana, Barcelona (ancient Barcino) · Wikimedia Commons / MUHBA
properties.image_alt: Roman funerary monuments along the Via Sepulcral Romana, Barcelona

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Barcino, surnamed Faventia, among the coastal colonies of Hispania Tarraconensis.

properties.notes: A modest masonry line, nothing on Segovia's scale, ran about 11.3 kilometers overland from springs in the Montcada hills to keep the working colony supplied; a short stretch of arcading survives beside the medieval Archdeacon's House. An inscription ties construction to Trajan's reign (98-117 CE), meaning it had already been carrying water for some years by the 117 CE snapshot at the latest. A once-proposed second line from Collserola is now considered not Roman at all, per a recent academic reassessment — this Montcada aqueduct is Barcino's one confirmed Roman line.

At the crossing of Barcino's cardo and decumanus atop Mont Taber, the colony built its civic heart — courts, market stalls, and public business, packed into the space now covered by Barcelona's city and regional government buildings. General sources place construction between the 1st and 2nd centuries CE; a fragment of monumental Montjuic-stone paving recovered in a 2023-2025 excavation under a nearby hotel is described as contemporary with the colony's Augustan founding, though it is actively forcing archaeologists to rewrite the forum's exact orientation and footprint, so treat the layout as provisional even though the forum's existence by 117 CE is not in doubt.

Sixteen arches carried the Via Augusta across the Guadalquivir, tying Corduba into the road network of the whole province. Aulus Hirtius records a temporary wooden bridge built here by Caesar's forces during the civil war against Pompey's sons (49-45 BCE); the stone bridge that replaced it belongs to Augustus's reign, though the exact decade isn't fixed in the sources. Modern surveys show only two of today's sixteen arches are genuinely Roman fabric (the rest are medieval and later flood rebuilds), but the Augustan-era stone bridge itself had already stood for over a century by 117 CE.

properties.name_english: Roman Temple of Calle Claudio Marcelo
properties.notes: A hexastyle, pseudo-peripteral Corinthian temple on a grand terraced sanctuary anchoring the city's eastern edge, almost certainly tied to the provincial imperial cult of Baetica. Construction began under Claudius (41-54 CE) and was finished roughly forty years later under Domitian (81-96 CE) — a fixture of the Corduban skyline for a full generation by Trajan's death. Rediscovered only in 1951 during expansion of the town hall.
properties.image_credit: Roman Temple of Calle Claudio Marcelo, Córdoba · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving columns of the Roman temple on Calle Claudio Marcelo, Córdoba

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: States that Corduba was founded by Marcellus, was settled from the outset with picked Romans and native Iberians, and was the first Roman colony sent to the region.

properties.modern_location: Plaza de Jeronimo Paez, Cordoba, Spain
properties.notes: One of the largest theatres anywhere outside Italy, seating roughly 15,000 in the city Augustus made capital of Baetica. The core structure dates to the Augustan period (before 5 BCE), with decoration extending into the Julio-Claudian era — a mature, well-established civic monument by Hadrian's day. Known only from 19th-century epigraphy until 1990s excavation beneath the modern archaeological museum rediscovered its foundations.

The original defensive circuit dates to the mid-2nd-century-BCE Republican foundation under M. Claudius Marcellus, enclosing about 48 hectares with limestone curtain walls and semicircular towers. When Augustus refounded the city as Colonia Patricia, capital of Baetica, the walled area was expanded to roughly 78 hectares. Surviving stretches near Puerta de Almodovar still show the coursed Roman masonry; by 117 CE the expanded Augustan-era walls had stood for well over a century.

properties.modern_location: Calle San Alvaro / Calle Gongora area, Cordoba, Spain
properties.notes: Corduba's civic heart began as a plain rammed-earth plaza under the Republic before Augustus paved it in stone; not content with one forum, the city added a second, more lavish square nearby — the so-called Forum Novum or Forum Adiectum — late in Augustus's reign or early under Tiberius. Both spaces were long-established fixtures by Hadrian's accession. The exact intra-city footprint of the Forum Novum is not precisely pinned down in available sources; this coordinate is an approximation from described street intersections, lower-confidence than the dating.

properties.name_english: Roman Mausoleums of Puerta de Gallegos
properties.modern_location: Jardines de la Victoria, Cordoba, Spain
properties.notes: Two monumental cylindrical tombs, each roughly 13 meters across, once flanked the Via Augusta where it left the city for Hispalis — funerary showpieces for a wealthy Corduban family, their design apparently borrowed directly from Italian mausolea. The North Mausoleum is dated to Tiberius's reign (14-37 CE), well over a century before Hadrian, and both would still have greeted travelers on the road out of the city in 117 CE. Rediscovered by archaeological test pits only in 1993.
properties.image_credit: Roman funerary mausoleums of Puerta de Gallegos, Córdoba · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman mausoleums at Puerta de Gallegos, Córdoba

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: States that Corduba was founded by Marcellus, was settled from the outset with picked Romans and native Iberians, and was the first Roman colony sent to the region.

properties.name_english: Flavian Forum and Imperial Cult Precinct of Conimbriga
properties.notes: Conimbriga's civic center had two lives before Hadrian ever took the throne: first an Augustan-era forum with the usual senate house, law court, and shops, then a wholesale Flavian-era demolition and rebuild that turned the space into a dedicated sanctuary of the imperial cult, stripped of its civic furniture. Either way, some form of monumental forum precinct had stood at the heart of the town for well over a generation by 117 CE. Coordinates use the general site location; a forum-specific sub-site coordinate was not found in sources consulted.

Water traveled some 3.5 kilometers from a spring at Alcabideque, partly on a raised arcade whose surviving arches are among the most photographed features of the site today. Built around 10 BCE as part of Augustus's investment in the town, it was already mature, functioning infrastructure by Hadrian's day, feeding the forum's fountains and later the bath complexes. Coordinates mark the Alcabideque source rather than the in-town arcade, the point with the most precisely documented location.

properties.name_english: House of the Fountains (Casa dos Repuxos)
properties.notes: The single most photographed house at Conimbriga — a mansion built around a formal garden threaded with fountain jets, its floors covered in some of the finest figural mosaics in Roman Iberia. A genuine dating trap: a plainer house occupied this plot from the early 1st century CE, but the fountain garden and famous mosaics that define the 'House of the Fountains' are dated by Portuguese excavation scholarship (Correia et al.) to the third quarter of the 2nd century through the early 3rd century CE — decades after Hadrian's accession, with some tourist sources pushing it as late as the Severan period. No reading puts the celebrated mansion before 117 CE. It was itself demolished, along with much of this quarter, when the town's defensive wall went up around 300 CE.

One of the largest domestic complexes excavated at Conimbriga, this peristyle mansion took its main form under the Flavian emperors (69-96 CE), replacing an earlier, less well-understood building on the plot. By 117 CE it had likely stood for a generation or more as one of the town's grander private residences — the private bath suite it is often pictured with was a later addition at the end of the 2nd century, and the house was substantially reworked again once the town wall was pushed through this district around 300 CE.

A second known dating trap for Conimbriga: for the whole of its 1st- and 2nd-century golden age, including 117 CE, the town had no defensive circuit at all — an open, confident settlement. Multiple independent sources agree the roughly 1,500-meter stone wall visitors see today, which cuts straight through the House of the Fountains and other houses (its stone quarried from their demolition), only went up hastily around the end of the 3rd century as frontier anxieties grew, abandoning the outer residential quarters. No earlier wall phase is attested.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Conimbriga, Portugal · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman ruins at Conimbriga including the city's defensive walls

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Conimbriga among the towns of Lusitania in his account of the region beyond the Durius river.

properties.notes: The largest bath complex in the town, fed by the aqueduct running down from Alcabideque, generally dated to the end of the 1st century CE — consistent with the town's other known Flavian-era building campaigns (forum, House of Cantaber). By Hadrian's accession this bathhouse would have been a well-worn fixture of daily civic life. Documentation pinning down its construction phase is thinner than for the town's flagship monuments, hence the lower confidence.

One of the largest Roman theatres ever built in Hispania, a 6,000-seat concrete-and-marble bowl loosely modeled on Rome's Theatre of Marcellus. Work began under Tiberius (14-37 CE) and was completed and refined under Claudius (41-54 CE). It stayed in use for centuries and declined only in the 3rd century, so it was certainly standing and functioning in 117 CE, giving the frontier colonia its taste of the capital's comedies and pantomimes. Lay forgotten under the old Jewish quarter until a chance 1972 building excavation on Calle Veronica brought it back to light.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes Caesaraugusta as a tax-exempt colony on the Ebro, formerly the town of Salduba, serving 55 peoples of the surrounding region.

properties.modern_location: Plaza de la Seo, Zaragoza, Spain
properties.notes: Augustus founded the colonia around 14 BCE for veterans of the Cantabrian Wars; the forum, including its cryptoporticus — the vaulted substructure that leveled the site's slope down to the Ebro — dates to that foundation phase. New colonnades were added under Tiberius and Claudius in the 1st century CE, but the core structure was already in place well before 117 CE and remained the civic center where the colony did business, worshipped, and posted its laws under Trajan and Hadrian.
properties.image_credit: Forum Museum of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: In-situ remains of the Roman forum of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes Caesaraugusta as a tax-exempt colony on the Ebro, formerly the town of Salduba, serving 55 peoples of the surrounding region.

properties.modern_location: Calle San Juan y San Pedro, Zaragoza, Spain
properties.notes: A porticoed thermal pool complex built early in the Julio-Claudian era (Caligula/Claudius, c. 37-54 CE), replacing an earlier set of 1st-century-BCE public latrines demolished to make way for it. By Trajan and Hadrian's time it had been operating for the better part of a century and would keep going for two more before closing in the 4th century. Coordinates are estimated from the museum's street address; no source gave precise GPS figures.
properties.image_credit: Museum of the Public Baths of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman public baths of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes Caesaraugusta as a tax-exempt colony on the Ebro, formerly the town of Salduba, serving 55 peoples of the surrounding region.

properties.notes: A working river quay on the calm inside bend of the Ebro, just downstream of the forum, that took in wine, salted fish, marble, and jewelry from the coast and sent wheat, timber, iron, and hides back the other way. Founded alongside the colony at the end of the 1st century BCE, it was still one of the busiest river ports in Hispania under Trajan and Hadrian, and stayed active until roughly the mid-6th century CE.
properties.image_credit: River Port Museum of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman river port structure of Caesaraugusta, Zaragoza

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes Caesaraugusta as a tax-exempt colony on the Ebro, formerly the town of Salduba, serving 55 peoples of the surrounding region.

properties.modern_location: Torreon de la Zuda, Zaragoza, Spain
properties.notes: A defensive circuit roughly 3 kilometers around almost certainly enclosed the colony from soon after its Augustan founding — traces of opus caementicium from this earliest phase survive bonded into the rear face and foundations of the standing wall. But the fabric actually visible today near the Torreon de la Zuda and Calle del Coso is a major rebuild dated to the second half of the 3rd century into the 4th, well after 117 CE. Map this as the earlier, largely non-surviving Augustan-Tiberian phase, not the handsome ashlar-faced monument a visitor sees today.

A very recent (March 2026) find at the corner of Coso and Calle Espartero: a concrete arcade that carried Huerva river water across the old Coso ravine into the colony while also functioning as a bridge. Press coverage dates it to the colony's earliest decades (roughly Augustan-Tiberian). Flagged low confidence — the identification is preliminary, not yet peer-reviewed, no source gives precise coordinates beyond the street corner, and no disuse date is known.

Merida's most iconic Roman monument: an elevated aqueduct bridge of alternating brick and granite, its distinctive cross-shaped piers rising up to 25 meters, originally spanning roughly 830 meters across the Albarregas valley (37 arched piers survive). Fed by the Proserpina reservoir five kilometers north, it carried water into Emerita Augusta and is generally dated to the 1st century CE, though the exact phasing (Augustan vs. later Julio-Claudian, with a possible later repair) is debated among specialists.
properties.image_credit: Los Milagros Aqueduct, Mérida · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Records that Augustus, after the Cantabrian War, discharged his older soldiers and let them found the city of Emerita Augusta in Lusitania.

properties.notes: A second, less famous aqueduct into Emerita Augusta, drawing from a catchment northeast of the city (Casa Herrera, Valhondo, Las Tomas) rather than from Proserpina, and supplying among other things the baths near the civic forum. Built toward the end of the 1st century CE, crossing the Albarregas gorge on a raised arcade — only three massive buttressed pillars of the Roman structure survive today, since a 16th-century rebuild mostly replaced it along the same line. Some sources tie its ultimate source to the Cornalvo reservoir, though period evidence more directly names the local catchment.
properties.image_credit: San Lázaro Aqueduct, Mérida · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving arches of the Roman San Lázaro Aqueduct, Mérida

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Records that Augustus, after the Cantabrian War, discharged his older soldiers and let them found the city of Emerita Augusta in Lusitania.

properties.notes: Built alongside the founding of Emerita Augusta in 25 BCE as the colony's crossing of the Guadiana, this granite bridge is one of the longest surviving bridges from antiquity — sources give figures around 755-792 meters and roughly 60 arched spans, partly owing to a period causeway over floodplain reaches. Repaired and partly rebuilt many times over two millennia, including major 17th-century flood repairs, but its Augustan-era piers and much of its original alignment survive; it remained the city's principal river crossing into the modern era.
properties.image_credit: Roman Bridge (Puente Romano) over the Guadiana, Mérida · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman bridge over the Guadiana river at Mérida

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Records that Augustus, after the Cantabrian War, discharged his older soldiers and let them found the city of Emerita Augusta in Lusitania.

properties.notes: Spanning the Marecchia (ancient Ariminus) at Ariminum, this five-arch bridge of Istrian stone was begun under Augustus in 14 CE and completed and dedicated under Tiberius in 21 CE, as recorded by its own dedicatory inscription naming both emperors. It marked the starting point of the Via Aemilia and connections onward toward Aquileia, cementing Ariminum's role as a road hub. Remarkably durable — it survived antiquity, the Middle Ages, and even reported German demolition charges in the Second World War, and still carries traffic today.
properties.image_credit: Richard Wilson, "Il Ponte di Tiberio", 1750 · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 18th-century oil painting by Richard Wilson depicting the Ponte di Tiberio at Rimini

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: The dedicatory inscription carved on the bridge's parapets, commemorating its construction by Augustus and completion by Tiberius.

properties.modern_location: Near Garrovillas de Alconetar, Caceres Province, Spain
properties.notes: A roughly 300-meter segmental-arch bridge carrying the Via de la Plata across the Tagus, distinctive for its flat, shallow arches — a sophisticated design often linked stylistically to Trajan's engineer Apollodorus of Damascus, and generally dated on that basis to the early 2nd century CE. Distinct from the map's existing 'Turmulus' road-station entry, which sat beside the bridge as a mansio/checkpoint. Its remains were physically relocated about 6 kilometers in 1970 during construction of the Alcantara reservoir; coordinates here mark the relocated site, not the original crossing point.

Designed by Trajan's chief engineer Apollodorus of Damascus and built in just two years (103-105 CE) to move Roman forces across the lower Danube for the Second Dacian War, this was for over a millennium the longest arch bridge ever built — roughly 1,135 meters long, twenty masonry piers up to 19 meters high carrying wooden arches spanning about 38 meters each. At the exact moment this map is frozen, its wooden superstructure was almost certainly still standing: Cassius Dio records that Hadrian had it dismantled shortly after becoming emperor, so its destruction falls right at or just after 11 August 117 CE. The twenty masonry piers survived far longer and remain traceable archaeologically today.
properties.image_credit: Trajan's Bridge over the Danube, reconstruction · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Scholarly reconstruction drawing of Trajan's timber-and-stone bridge across the Danube

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Describes the stone-piered bridge Trajan built across the Danube for his Dacian campaigns, detailing its twenty piers and the engineering work of Apollodorus of Damascus.

properties.notes: A 140-meter granite bridge over the Tamega carried the road linking Bracara Augusta (Braga) and Asturica Augusta (Astorga) through Aquae Flaviae, a spa town whose thermal springs made it a municipium under Vespasian. Two inscribed columns stand on the bridge: an earlier one (79 CE) honoring Vespasian and Titus, and a Trajanic column of 104 CE recording that the local populi of the surrounding conventus paid for and dedicated the bridge — a rare direct epigraphic record of provincial communities funding Roman infrastructure. Aquae Flaviae sat in the Conventus Bracaraugustanus of Hispania Tarraconensis in 117 CE; the later separate province of Gallaecia was not split off until after Diocletian.
properties.image_credit: Roman Bridge of Chaves · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: The Padrao dos Povos, a dedicatory inscription set up at the bridge naming ten local Gallaecian civitates that contributed to its construction, dated to Vespasian's reign.

properties.notes: A roughly 2.1-hectare cohort fort built in timber and earth around 80 CE under Vespasian or Titus, sited on a spur south of the Danube overlooking the river's bend and the mouths of the Naab and Regen — decades before the famous stone legionary fortress of Legio III Italica was founded 700 meters north of here, in 179 CE, well after this map's snapshot. A vicus with a bathhouse grew up around it. The garrison unit at 117 CE isn't securely identified: Cohors III Britannorum equitata is only epigraphically attested from 153 CE, so an earlier unit (possibly Cohors II Aquitanorum) is a plausible but unconfirmed occupant under Trajan and Hadrian. Sources also disagree on whether the defenses had already been rebuilt in stone by 117 or were still timber-and-earth, though continuous occupation through that date is well established. The fort and its vicus were destroyed in the Marcomannic Wars, c. 170-175 CE.

One of the largest Roman theatres north of the Alps, roughly 116 meters across with a 42-meter stage front and seating for about 10,000. An earlier timber theatre likely stood here from the early 1st century CE, tied to annual funerary games in honor of Drusus; the monumental stone structure whose remains survive today went up under Domitian (81-96 CE). Rediscovered in 1884 during railway construction but not correctly identified until 1914-16, then comprehensively excavated in 1998-99 under a parking area — it stayed in active use through the 4th century, when it was finally stripped for stone to build the shortened late-Roman city wall.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre of Mogontiacum, Mainz · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Describes soldiers of the First, Fourth, and Twenty-Second legions marching to relieve the besieged fortress of Mogontiacum during the Batavian revolt.

properties.notes: A towering, elaborately carved Jupiter column dedicated by the civilian canabae community of Mogontiacum to Jupiter Optimus Maximus for the emperor's wellbeing. Epigraphic and prosopographic evidence — including the tenure of governor P. Sulpicius Scribonius Proculus — dates its erection to c. 65-67 CE, plausibly commemorating Nero's survival of the Pisonian conspiracy. One of the oldest and most elaborate Jupiter columns known from the Germanic provinces; it was eventually toppled and deliberately buried (rediscovered in nearly 2,000 fragments in 1904-05), but nothing points to that happening before 117 CE, so it should still have been standing at the snapshot.
properties.image_credit: Great Mainz Jupiter Column · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Reconstructed Great Mainz Jupiter Column on display in the Landesmuseum Mainz

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: The column's dedication, set up by the canabae community of Mogontiacum to Jupiter Best and Greatest for the health of Nero.

properties.notes: A major fixed bridge across the Rhine linking the legionary fortress and civilian settlement at Mogontiacum to the fort of Castellum Mattiacorum on the far bank. An initial pontoon or timber crossing existed from around 11 BCE, but the permanent bridge — some 21 stone piers spanning roughly 400 meters — is generally dated to c. 71 CE, in the early Flavian period after the Batavian Revolt, when Rome moved to secure the crossing permanently. It remained standing into the early 5th century, well beyond 117 CE. Some popular accounts credit Domitian, but the stone construction is more consistently dated to 71 CE under Vespasian.

A nearly 20-meter masonry cenotaph raised in 9 BCE by the Mogontiacum garrison in honor of Nero Claudius Drusus, who died from a riding accident that year returning from a campaign beyond the Elbe. Originally faced in marble, it carried a commemorative inscription reportedly composed by Augustus himself, and anchored the annual Drusus memorial games held at Mogontiacum for generations. The core masonry survives to this day, later repurposed as a medieval watchtower within the citadel, making its presence at the 117 CE snapshot essentially certain.
properties.image_credit: Cenotaph of Drusus (Drususstein), Mainz Citadel · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Describes the monument the army raised at Mogontiacum in honor of Drusus, around which soldiers ran a ceremonial race each year while the communities of Gaul performed annual rites.

properties.notes: A roughly 9-kilometer aqueduct built in the Flavian period (69-96 CE) to carry spring water from Finthen to the legionary fortress and settlement at Mogontiacum, an estimated 30,000-plus liters a day for the two resident legions. Its final approach crossed the steep Zahlbach valley on arcades up to 30 meters high — the tallest known Roman aqueduct arcade north of the Alps — of which 58-59 tapering pillar cores still stand along the street 'An den Romersteinen.' A Flavian-era work with no attested destruction before the early empire, it was almost certainly still functioning in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct of Mogontiacum, Zahlbach valley, Mainz · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving piers of the Roman aqueduct of Mogontiacum in the Zahlbach valley, Mainz

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Names Mogontiacum as a Roman legionary base on the Rhine during the Batavian revolt of 69-70 CE, the city this aqueduct supplied with water.

properties.notes: Immediately outside the fortress walls, a civilian settlement grew up to house soldiers' families, veterans, traders, and craftsmen dependent on the garrison. Excavations across three campaigns recovered roughly 20,000 finds — coins, bronze jewelry, glassware, roof tiles, butchered animal bone — attesting to potters, innkeepers, and metalworkers living beside the fort. Occupation runs continuously from the second half of the 1st century through the end of the 3rd, so by 117 CE, under Legio I Minervia, the canabae would have been a dense, well-established quarter.
properties.image_credit: Bathing building of the vicus bonnensis (Roman canabae), Bonn · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of a Roman bathing building in the civilian settlement outside the Bonna fortress

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Names Bonna as the winter camp of the First legion, where Batavian rebels confronted the Roman garrison during the revolt of Civilis.

properties.name_english: Vicus of Bonna at the Gronau
properties.notes: A second, larger civilian settlement, distinct from the canabae hugging the fortress walls, developed further upstream along the Rhine in the area of modern Gronau. Excavations there uncovered five timber-and-stone strip houses roughly 10 by 30 meters with street-facing shopfronts, alongside evidence of coin counterfeiting, craft production, and tavern life. The exact founding date isn't precisely fixed in the excavation reports, but the settlement was clearly flourishing by the early 2nd century, a plausible feature of the Trajanic-Hadrianic townscape around Bonna.

A public bath complex served the civilian vicus rather than the garrison itself. Excavation seasons in 2021-2022, building on 19th- and early-20th-century observations of walls at the same site, exposed roughly 1,200 square meters of the complex — cold and hot rooms, plunge pools, drains, hypocaust underfloor heating, and furnace rooms, with one hypocaust found exceptionally intact, floor tiles still resting on their pilae stacks. No source pins down an exact construction year, so while a bathing establishment on this spot by 117 CE is plausible given the vicus's growth, the precise Trajanic-era date isn't independently confirmed.

properties.name_english: Roman river landing stage of Bonna
properties.notes: Excavations in 2010-2011 at the southern edge of the canabae uncovered a Roman landing site on the Rhine bank: a shallow, gravel-surfaced slope onto which vessels could be beached and unloaded directly, with evidence the bank was artificially reinforced to let up to five ships land at once. A modest installation rather than a monumental stone harbor, reflecting Bonna's role as a supply point on the Rhine transport corridor overseen by the Classis Germanica, headquartered downriver at Cologne. A separate tradition (Florus) credits Drusus with building an actual bridge at Bonna around 11 BCE, but modern historians dispute whether this crossing ever existed beyond a temporary Augustan-era pontoon, and no archaeological remains of a bridge have been confirmed — so it is not represented here as a standing 117 CE structure.

properties.name_english: Roman cemetery south of the Bonna fortress
properties.notes: Along the road leaving Bonna to the south, a cemetery serving both garrison and civilian settlement was already in use by the mid-1st century CE — the tombstone of Quintus Petilius Secundus, a 25-year-old legionary of Legio XV Primigenia (garrisoned at nearby Xanten) who died in 65 CE, was recovered here, showing the site predates even Legio I Minervia's arrival. Grave goods, sarcophagi, and dozens of inscribed tombstones from this and related Bonn cemeteries are now held in the Rheinisches Landesmuseum Bonn. The same burial ground later became sacred to the cult of the martyrs Cassius and Florentius, whose veneration eventually gave rise to the church that became Bonn Minster — a Roman cemetery directly shaping the medieval and modern city.

ancient_sources.author: Tacitus
ancient_sources.note: Names Bonna as the winter camp of the First legion, where Batavian rebels confronted the Roman garrison during the revolt of Civilis.

properties.modern_location: beneath Nezavisimost Square, central Sofia, Bulgaria
properties.notes: Trajan's engineers paved this stretch of the Singidunum-to-Byzantium highway with stone during the Dacian Wars of 101-106 CE to move legions north through the Balkans. Serdica's promotion to municipium in 106 CE rode on the same military logistics this road carried. It ran straight through the city as its main east-west artery and was still Serdica's principal thoroughfare on the day Trajan died in 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: near the former TZUM department store, central Sofia, Bulgaria
properties.notes: Costoboci raiders sacked Serdica around 170 CE during the Marcomannic Wars, and Marcus Aurelius's engineers answered by raising the town's first stone circuit, four gates and all, finishing by 180 CE. This first fortification predated the far larger Constantinian-era wall tourists walk today, but it still rose six decades after Trajan's death in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman wall remains, Sofia (ancient Serdica) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Arena di Serdica Hotel, Budapest Street, Sofia, Bulgaria
properties.notes: Serdica's amphitheater rose in the late 3rd century under Diocletian and was completed under Constantine I, its oval measuring 60 by 43 meters just outside the city walls. It sat atop an earlier, ill-dated theater that Gothic raiders had already wrecked. A hotel foundation dig accidentally rediscovered it in 2004. Every phase of it postdates Trajan's death in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Serdica, Sofia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Evgeni Paunov
ancient_sources.ref: Minerva: The International Review of Ancient Art & Archaeology 19 (May-June 2007), pp. 40-41
ancient_sources.note: Discusses the 2004 rescue excavation of the amphitheater beneath the Arena di Serdica hotel and the coin/artifact evidence dating its construction to the late 3rd-early 4th century under Diocletian and Constantine, long after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.modern_location: Presidency courtyard, Dondukov Boulevard, Sofia, Bulgaria
properties.notes: Constantine's building program raised this domed red-brick hall as part of a Roman bath complex in the early 4th century, making it the oldest standing building in Sofia today. It later hosted sessions of the Council of Serdica in 343 CE after conversion to a church. Nothing about it predates Hadrian's accession, let alone Trajan's death in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Rotunda of St George, Sofia, part of Serdica's Roman baths · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Bogdan Filov
ancient_sources.work: Софийската църква „Св. Георги" (The Sofia Church of St. George)
ancient_sources.note: The excavation studies that first documented the hypocaust and brick construction identifying the Rotunda's original phase as a Roman bath building of the early 4th century, under Constantine, well after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: A grand thermal bath complex rose south of Serdica's agora, its hypocaust floors and a sizeable pool coming to light during 2010-2012 metro excavations beneath today's St Nedelya Square. Archaeologists date the build to the late 2nd or early 3rd century, part of the city's post-Trajanic construction surge. That places it decades after the 117 CE snapshot, even on ground Trajan's own municipium had already claimed.

properties.modern_location: Bulbank building site, central Sofia, Bulgaria
properties.notes: A temple dedicated to Heracles once stood beneath what is now Sofia's Bulbank building, one of several cult sites excavators have traced in ancient Serdica alongside a shrine to Zeus Hypsistos. No excavation report ties its construction to a specific decade, and Serdica's other dated temples cluster in the building boom that followed Trajan's reign. Absent a confirmed date, it's treated as outside the 117 CE snapshot rather than assumed early.

Epirote builders carved this theatre into the acropolis slope around the middle of the 3rd century BCE, and its stone seats still bear manumission inscriptions freeing slaves at the adjoining shrine as early as 163 BCE. Romans kept the building in active use through the imperial period, later tying part of its structure into the neighboring bath complex. By 117 CE it had anchored the city's festivals for nearly four centuries.
properties.image_credit: Theatre of Butrint, Albania · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aeneas landing at Buthrotum and finding it ruled by the Trojan Helenus, who had taken the Greek city and kingdom once held by Pyrrhus.

properties.notes: Epirotes founded this healing sanctuary to Asclepius at the foot of the acropolis around 300 BCE, and worshippers left more than 300 votive offerings in a hidden chamber behind its rear wall. Roman colonists later rebuilt the small temple, enlarging it to the west and north and roofing it in brick-faced concrete tied into the theatre above. The cult kept drawing pilgrims well past 117 CE, its festivals filling the theatre next door.
properties.image_credit: Prytaneion and Sanctuary of Asclepius, Butrint, Albania · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aeneas's visit to Buthrotum (Butrint), ruled by the Trojan exiles Helenus and Andromache as a miniature replica of Troy. Describes the city, not the sanctuary of Asclepius.

properties.notes: Augustus's veteran colonists paved over Butrint's Hellenistic agora to lay out this forum, a roughly 20-by-72-meter plaza — the only excavated forum known from ancient Epirus. Julius Caesar had first eyed the site for settlement in the 40s BCE, a plan Cicero's letters show his friend Atticus fought to keep off his own nearby land. By 117 CE the forum anchored a thriving colonia in the freshly created province of Epirus.
properties.image_credit: Forum (Agora) of Butrint · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the forum/agora area of the ancient city of Butrint

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Cicero writes repeatedly to his friend Atticus about Atticus's estate near Buthrotum, lobbying against Julius Caesar's plan to plant a veteran colony there that threatened to confiscate Atticus's land.

properties.notes: Epirote builders raised Butrint's fortification circuit in four distinct phases across the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, using smoothed polygonal blocks on the acropolis and massive rectangular ashlar courses around the lower town. Archaeologists label these phases Butrint I through IV, the last dated to the 3rd century BCE. Roman colonists inherited the walls rather than rebuilding them, and the same fortifications still encircled the city when Hadrian took power in August 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Lion Gate in the city walls of Butrint, Albania · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aeneas landing at Buthrotum and finding it ruled by the Trojan Helenus, who had taken the Greek city and kingdom once held by Pyrrhus.

properties.notes: Augustus's veteran colonists built this bathhouse after 31 BCE, complete with a hypocaust-heated calidarium, a semicircular plunge pool, and a frigidarium floored in a black-and-white geometric mosaic. Underfloor pillars called pilae carried hot air from a furnace beneath the heated rooms. A further renovation in brick-faced concrete followed in the mid-2nd century CE, after this snapshot, but the original Augustan bathhouse was already decades old and in daily use when Hadrian became emperor.

ancient_sources.author: Virgil
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aeneas landing at Buthrotum and finding it ruled by the Trojan Helenus, who had taken the Greek city and kingdom once held by Pyrrhus.

properties.notes: Augustus's colonists built this 4-kilometer aqueduct to carry spring water from near modern Xarre across the Vrina plain on an arcade and over the Vivari Channel into the city. It ran continuously for over four centuries, finally failing in the late 4th or early 5th century CE. By 117 CE it had already been feeding Butrint's new bathhouse and fountains for close to a century and a half.

Where the Augustan aqueduct's arcade reached the city after crossing the Vivari Channel, engineers built this nymphaeum as both a monumental public fountain and a distribution tank feeding Butrint's water network. It marked the point where spring water piped four kilometers from the hills near Xarre finally reached the colony's streets. The structure had been supplying the city's fountains and baths for roughly a century and a half by the time Hadrian took the throne in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum of Butrint, Albania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A wealthy patron named Junia Rufina transformed a natural spring near the Lion Gate into a monumental public well, dressing it in stone walls and brick arches and dedicating it with a Greek inscription calling herself "friend of the Nymphs." Its brick-faced concrete matches other buildings from a citywide renewal that researchers tie to Hadrian's own tour of Epirus in 132 CE — about fifteen years after the 117 CE snapshot this map captures, so the well did not yet exist when Hadrian took the throne.

This lavish waterfront mansion took its name from three shell-shaped alcoves framing a grand dining room, added when the house was rebuilt into a palatial form around 400 CE. It grew out of an ordinary Roman townhouse of the 2nd or 3rd century CE, itself centuries later than this map's 117 CE snapshot. Workers finished the roof and fitted window frames but never laid the floors, apparently abandoning the project as Butrint's lake level rose.
properties.image_credit: Triconch Palace, Butrint · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Viminacium Archaeological Park, Stari Kostolac, Serbia
properties.notes: Legionaries and townsfolk at Viminacium first watched games in a timber amphitheatre raised outside the fortress during Trajan's reign, its arena floor packed with sand over a 55 by 45 meter oval. Trajanic coins turned up in its earliest levels. Stone-and-timber rebuilding that folded the arena into the city walls came later, at the end of the 2nd century, well after this snapshot. Excavators found bear and camel bones from its animal hunts.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Viminacium, Serbia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Viminacium Archaeological Park, Stari Kostolac, Serbia
properties.notes: A bathhouse stood within the canabae hugging the legionary fortress from around the time Legio VII Claudia's stone camp went up, giving soldiers a steam bath with under-floor heated pools. Excavators found lanterns proving night bathing was practiced here. The building visitors see today, with its mosaic floors and six ornamented pools, reflects later 2nd-4th century remodeling that postdates this snapshot — only its earlier military-scale core belongs to 117.

properties.modern_location: South of Viminacium Archaeological Park, Stari Kostolac, Serbia
properties.notes: Two adjoining cemeteries, Vise Grobalja and Pecine, grew up along Viminacium's southern approach from the mid-1st century onward, with cremation and inhumation practiced side by side from the start. Rescue digs since 1977 have logged over 10,700 graves and 7,000 coins between the two fields alone. By 117 the necropolis had already been in continuous use for roughly six decades, filled with modest cremation urns and the first brick-vaulted family tombs.
properties.image_credit: Necropolis at Viminacium, Serbia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ptolemy
ancient_sources.note: Lists Viminacium among the towns of Moesia Superior.

properties.modern_location: Viminacium Archaeological Park, Stari Kostolac, Serbia
properties.notes: The trapezoidal underground tomb visitors descend into today, its walls covered in fresco painting blending Eastern and classicizing styles, is dated by art-historical analysis to around the start of the 4th century. That places it nearly two centuries after this map's snapshot, so it does not belong on the 117 CE map despite being Viminacium's best-known burial monument. Its scale shows how much grander the necropolis became under the later empire.

properties.modern_location: Viminacium Archaeological Park, Stari Kostolac, Serbia
properties.notes: Geophysical survey and digging since 2020 exposed a forum with tribunal, portico and heated rooms tied to Viminacium's life as a chartered town rather than a bare legionary base. That charter, elevating Viminacium to municipium, is usually dated to 117 or 117-118 under Hadrian — but Hadrian only took the throne on 11 August 117, so a forum built to serve a fresh municipium almost certainly rose just after this map's exact snapshot moment, not before it.

properties.modern_location: Confluence of the Mlava and Danube, near Stari Kostolac, Serbia
properties.notes: Viminacium sat at the meeting of the Mlava and the Danube and hosted a river fleet detachment guarding this stretch of the limes, its officer titled praefectus classis at Viminacium. Excavated warship timbers, one hull carrying a ram, ran 15 to 22 meters long. The fortress and its river squadron were already established here well before 117, giving Legio VII Claudia a working harbor at its doorstep.

Roman forces occupied the Nisava valley crossing by the late 1st century CE, after subduing the Dardanian tribes, planting a fortified camp on the hill later built over by the Ottoman-era Nis Fortress. This early garrison controlled the valley long before Naissus had any civic charter, holding the junction where roads split toward the Danube, the Adriatic, and Thrace. No detailed excavated plan of this earliest Roman-period fort has been published, so its exact 117 CE footprint is inferred rather than mapped.

Naissus stood where roads met and split four ways: north to Viminacium and Singidunum, west toward the Adriatic, south to Thessalonica, and east through Remesiana to Serdica and beyond. The Via Militaris backbone linking these routes was substantially built up under Trajan, putting a functioning road station here by 117 even though the town itself had no city charter yet. Travelers relied on it as a stopover for lodging and remounts on the long haul between the Danube and the Balkan interior.

properties.name_english: Naissus Civic Center and City Baths
properties.notes: A 22-hectare walled civic quarter with a forum, temple, basilica and a 775 square meter city bath was uncovered in 1987-88 campaigns, but Naissus only reached municipium status under Marcus Aurelius or later, decades after this map's 117 CE moment. At the snapshot date Naissus was still a road station without this civic architecture. Its later fame as Constantine's birthplace belongs to this post-117 town, not the site as it stood in 117.

properties.modern_location: old town area, Sremska Mitrovica, Serbia
properties.notes: Legio XIII Gemina raised Sirmium's first rampart, a stretch of earth and timber fronted by a ditch, when the settlement won status as Colonia Flavia Sirmium under the Flavian emperors. Masons rebuilt the circuit in stone by the early 2nd century as the colony grew into the city Trajan chose as capital of Pannonia Inferior around 103. Its later Tetrarchic replacement lies to the south, encasing the 4th-century imperial palace instead.
properties.image_credit: Fired-brick city rampart ruins, ancient Sirmium, Serbia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Colonia Flavia Sirmium's forum anchored the young colony's civic core, its colonnades carrying Corinthian capitals carved between the Flavian decades and the early 2nd century, modeled on workshops across the Adriatic in Dalmatia. This was the square where the colony's magistrates conducted business just as Trajan was naming Sirmium capital of Pannonia Inferior around 103.

properties.name_english: Beneficiarii Station and Shrine of Jupiter, Sirmium
properties.modern_location: northwestern rampart area, Sremska Mitrovica, Serbia
properties.notes: Beneficiarii consulares, soldiers detached to staff a road checkpoint outside Sirmium, dedicated stone altars to Jupiter Optimus Maximus at a shrine along the city's northwestern rampart. More than eighty such altars have been recovered from the site, the earliest limestone examples carved around 100 CE. The station was already active when Trajan made Sirmium capital of Pannonia Inferior, and officers kept adding altars there for over a century afterward.

properties.name_english: Eastern and Western Necropoleis of Sirmium
properties.notes: Two large cemeteries flanked Colonia Flavia Sirmium outside its walls, holding family tombs of ordinary colonists rather than soldiers. Cremation was the standard rite through the 2nd century, before inhumation gradually replaced it from the later 3rd century on. These burial grounds were already in active use when Trajan elevated Sirmium to capital of Pannonia Inferior, decades before the city's famous Tetrarchic-era Christian basilica cemeteries developed nearby.

properties.name_english: River Harbor and Fleet Station on the Sava
properties.notes: Sirmium's landings on the Sava served the Classis Flavia Pannonica, the river fleet that patrolled the waterway 45 Roman miles downstream to its Danube junction at Taurunum. Pliny the Elder recorded Sirmium as capital of the Sirmienses and Amantini beside the confluence of the Bacuntius and Sava. The harbor's position where roads from Italy, Dalmatia, and the Danube frontier converged was a central reason Trajan chose Sirmium as capital of Pannonia Inferior in 103.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Sirmium as the town of the Sirmienses and Amantini near the confluence of the Bacuntius and Sava rivers, 45 miles upstream from Taurunum where the Sava meets the Danube.

properties.modern_location: Solin, Croatia, around Porta Caesarea, Salona archaeological park
properties.notes: Massive limestone blocks ringed Salona's old town, the urbs vetus, by the 2nd century BCE, long before Rome made the city a colony. In 47 BCE the walls proved their worth: defenders posed wives and children atop the ramparts to fake round-the-clock watch, then broke a Pompeian siege under Marcus Octavius in a single sortie. Stretches of that original circuit still framed the eastern gate in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Porta Caesarea, city walls of Salona (Urbs Vetus), Solin · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Augustan-era Porta Caesarea gate in the city walls of Salona

ancient_sources.author: Hirtius (attrib.)
ancient_sources.note: Describes the 47 BCE siege of Salona by the Pompeian commander Marcus Octavius, repelled by the town's Caesarian defenders using its walls and a coordinated night sortie.

properties.modern_location: Solin, Croatia, eastern edge of the Salona archaeological park
properties.notes: Augustus's engineers raised this gateway in large opus quadratum limestone blocks in the last years of his reign, giving Salona a ceremonial threshold into its old town. Two octagonal towers flanked a wide central carriageway plus two side passages for pedestrians. It stood in exactly this form in 117 CE, a full century before any later aqueduct piping was routed across its top.
properties.image_credit: Porta Caesarea, Salona, Croatia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes the siege of Salonae by Marcus Octavius, in which the citizens built wooden towers, armed their slaves, and used women's hair for catapult ropes to hold out until relieved.

properties.notes: Salona's forum measured 45 by 70 meters and rose as the city was promoted to Roman colony and capital of Dalmatia around the turn of the millennium. It anchored civic life here for four centuries straight, housing magistrates, temples and market stalls for the fastest-growing city on the eastern Adriatic. By 117 CE it had already served Dalmatia's governors for more than a century.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Salona as the seat of a conventus (judicial assize) for the Delmatae, whose fighting men were organized into 342 decuriae, underscoring the city's role as an administrative hub centered on its forum.

properties.notes: Salona's theatre measured 65 by 58 meters and seated around 3,500 spectators on stone benches near the forum. It went up in the decades after Augustus elevated the city to colonial status, giving Roman drama and pantomime a permanent home in Dalmatia's new capital. Danish excavators mapped its plan in the 1920s, confirming an early Imperial build well predating the city's amphitheatre.

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes the siege of Salonae by Marcus Octavius, in which the citizens built wooden towers, armed their slaves, and used women's hair for catapult ropes to hold out until relieved.

properties.modern_location: Vrilo Jadra spring near Klis, Croatia, running to Salona
properties.notes: Augustus's engineers channeled the Jadro spring's karst water 3,850 meters downhill to Salona, sizing the line for a city of just 15 hectares. Two centuries later the same channel was still watering a metropolis nearly five times that size, before Avar and Slav raiders finally silenced it in the 7th century. In 117 CE the line had already run without a major rebuild for roughly a century.
properties.image_credit: Aqueduct of Salona, Croatia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes the siege of Salonae by Marcus Octavius, in which the citizens built wooden towers, armed their slaves, and used women's hair for catapult ropes to hold out until relieved.

properties.modern_location: Solin, Croatia, northwestern end of the Salona archaeological park
properties.notes: Salona's amphitheatre rose only in the second half of the 2nd century, around 170 CE, roughly half a century after our snapshot date. Set partly into the hillside, its elliptical arena measured about 65 by 40 meters and the auditorium held some 17,000 spectators, folded directly into the city's fortifications. A visitor to Salona in 117 CE would have crossed open ground here, decades before construction began.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Salona, Croatia · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Caesar
ancient_sources.note: Describes the siege of Salonae by Marcus Octavius, in which the citizens built wooden towers, armed their slaves, and used women's hair for catapult ropes to hold out until relieved.

properties.modern_location: Solin, Croatia, eastern quarter of the Salona archaeological park
properties.notes: Salona's largest public baths, the Great Thermae, rose in the eastern quarter no earlier than the late 2nd century, decades after our 117 CE snapshot. The finished complex packed three separate frigidaria plus a caldarium, tepidarium and a massage room called the unctorium into one riverside block. A visitor touring Salona in 117 CE would have found this entire stretch of the city still undeveloped ground.

properties.modern_location: Mostine district, Split, Croatia, near Solinska cesta, toward Salona
properties.notes: Excavators working ahead of a shopping-center expansion at Mostine, on Split's edge toward Salona, uncovered a 2,000-square-meter villa rustica with stone walls still standing 1.5 meters high. Stone channels, a cistern and an oil press mark it as a working farm that shipped olive oil to Salona, just a few kilometers away. Archaeologists trace its founding to as early as the 1st century CE, making it the strongest documented Roman presence on the Split site nearly two centuries before Diocletian's palace.

Thessalonica's civic square sat here since a 60 BCE inscription honored public buildings on the spot, continuing a modest Roman-period marketplace through the 1st century CE. The grand two-terraced marble forum tourists see today was not yet built. In 117 CE this was still a working but architecturally unremarkable agora at the junction of the Via Egnatia and the road to the acropolis.

The two-terraced forum with its cryptoporticus, Caryatid stoa, twin baths, mint and odeon was an Antonine-to-Severan building program, completed only around 200-210 CE. It stood for three centuries afterward as the city's civic heart, but at the moment of the 117 CE snapshot it simply did not exist yet — the site's most famous ruin is a genuine dating trap.
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum, Thessaloniki, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Cicero
ancient_sources.note: Written by Cicero from Thessalonica during his exile in 58 BCE, recording his stay in the city. Not a description of the forum itself.

properties.name_english: Sanctuary of Sarapis, Isis and Anubis
properties.modern_location: Near Dioikitiriou Square, western Thessaloniki, Greece
properties.notes: Egyptian merchants and residents built this sanctuary to Sarapis, Isis and Anubis in the 3rd century BCE, and it remained active for over four centuries. Excavated after a 1917 fire tore through the neighborhood, it yielded a dedicatory stoa, a small prostyle temple, pebble mosaics and cult inscriptions. By 117 CE it had already served Thessalonica's Egyptian-cult community for some 350 years.

properties.name_english: Temple of Roma and Augustus, Thessalonica
properties.notes: Thessalonica added the goddess Roma to its pantheon in the 1st century BCE and gave her a dedicated priesthood alongside a new temple to Augustus, attested by inscriptions and coinage showing Julius Caesar and Augustus as divine. As capital of Macedonia since 146 BCE, the city embraced the imperial cult early and enthusiastically. By 117 CE the cult had been running continuously for well over a century.

Gnaeus Egnatius drove this great highway through Macedonia in the 140s BCE, linking Dyrrhachium on the Adriatic to Byzantium 700 Roman miles away, and Thessalonica was its single most important station. The road ran along the city's north edge as the main east-west artery, carrying legions, governors and traders for centuries. By 117 CE it had already carried imperial traffic for over 250 years.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Traces the route of the Via Egnatia eastward from Apollonia through Macedonia to Thessalonica and beyond, naming the city as one of the road's principal waypoints.

properties.notes: Cassander sited his new city on the Thermaic Gulf in 315 BCE precisely for its natural harbor, and the port grew into one of the busiest on the Aegean's northern rim under Roman rule. It anchored the western end of the overland Via Egnatia route to Byzantium, moving grain, timber and goods between the Aegean and inland Macedonia. In 117 CE it was still Macedonia's primary maritime gateway.

properties.modern_location: Ano Poli, city center perimeter, Thessaloniki, Greece
properties.notes: Cassander's original fortification circuit went up with the city's founding in 315 BCE, but the long Roman peace let it decay: by the mid-1st century CE the walls were already described as ruinous and unmaintained. Macedonia's demilitarized status under Rome made rebuilding unnecessary until the Gothic siege of 253/4 CE finally forced a full overhaul. At the 117 CE snapshot Thessalonica was effectively an unwalled city.

properties.modern_location: Egnatia and Dimitriou Gounari Streets, Thessaloniki, Greece
properties.notes: This eight-pier triumphal arch celebrated Galerius's victory over Persia in 298 CE and was raised as part of his new imperial palace complex between 298 and 305 CE. It postdates the 117 CE snapshot by nearly two centuries and belongs to a different city — a later imperial tetrarchic capital, not the Antonine-era provincial seat this map captures.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Galerius (Kamara), Thessaloniki · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Acts of the Apostles
ancient_sources.note: Records Paul and Silas passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia to reach Thessalonica, where they found a synagogue, naming the city where this arch was later built.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the founding of Thessalonica by Cassander, who settled the population of some twenty-six smaller towns of the Thermaic Gulf into the new city and named it for his wife.

properties.modern_location: Nicopolis archaeological site, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: Augustus enclosed his new Victory City with a polygonal circuit stretching roughly 5,000 meters, built within the first five years after the city's founding. The walls used a poured-concrete core faced in brick, thickening from 2.5 meters along the curtain to 4.6 meters at the five gates. They read more as a statement of Roman order than a real defensive necessity, since the victory at Actium had already made the region safe.
properties.image_credit: City walls of ancient Nicopolis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Nicopolis, founded by Augustus to commemorate his victory at Actium, and its sanctuary of Apollo Actius. Describes the city's foundation, not its walls.

properties.modern_location: Michalitsi Hill, north of Nicopolis, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: Octavian raised this trophy on the hill where his own camp had stood before the battle, dedicating it two years after crushing Antony and Cleopatra's fleet at Actium in 31 BCE. A 70-meter stone podium held roughly 35 bronze rams stripped from the captured warships, wedged into carved niches alongside 1,100 sculpted marble panels of naval and Amazon battle scenes. By 117 CE it had stood as Rome's founding monument to the Augustan peace for nearly a century and a half.
properties.image_credit: Victory Monument of Augustus, Nicopolis, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Describes Augustus founding Nicopolis after his victory at Actium and decorating the site of his camp with captured naval trophies, dedicating the monument to Neptune and Mars.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the sacred precinct above Nicopolis holding this victory monument, adorned with warships captured from the fleet of Antony and Cleopatra.

properties.modern_location: South slope of the Apollo sanctuary hill, Nicopolis, Greece
properties.notes: Built in Augustus's initial wave of public works, the theatre blended Greek and Roman technique, its cavea running up the natural hillside on one side and on built stone vaulting on the other. It hosted the dramatic and musical competitions of the Actia games alongside civic assemblies. The original Augustan structure was already a working venue during the years Epictetus's students filled Nicopolis to hear him lecture.
properties.image_credit: Theatre of Nicopolis, near Preveza · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Arrian
ancient_sources.note: Arrian records that he took down Epictetus's lectures as a young student attending his school at Nicopolis around 108 CE, under Trajan, presenting them as near-verbatim notes rather than his own composition.

properties.modern_location: Nicopolis archaeological site, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: This smaller covered theatre went up alongside the main theatre, stadium and gymnasium in Augustus's founding building program for the new Victory City. It served musical contests tied to the Actia festival and smaller civic gatherings that didn't need the main theatre's capacity. Its Augustan core was already a century and a half old by 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: Nicopolis archaeological site, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: Built into a hillside with unusual rounded ends at both extremities, this stadium held the athletic and equestrian contests of the Actia games that Augustus founded in 27 BCE to rival the Olympics in prestige. Its north bank alone seated an estimated 10,000 spectators every four years when the Panhellenic-tier games came around. By 117 CE it had hosted roughly 36 celebrations of the Actia.

Cassius Dio records that Augustus fortified his victory camp and ran walls down to connect it to Comarus, the outer harbor on the open Ionian side, distinct from the calmer Ambracian Gulf anchorage. This gave the new city dual sea access — sheltered gulf trade on one side and open-water shipping on the other. It functioned as Nicopolis's working port for the whole of the early empire.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Describes Octavian fortifying his victory camp above Actium and connecting it by walls down to the harbor of Comarus, part of the founding of Nicopolis.

properties.modern_location: Louros River to Nicopolis, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: This roughly 50-kilometer channel carried water from the Louros River springs down an 80-meter elevation drop to the growing city, but its actual build date is unresolved: estimates range from the Augustan or Neronian 1st century to as late as Hadrian's reign in the 2nd century. Because a credible reading places its construction at or after 117 CE, it is marked not-yet-built here rather than assumed early.
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct of Nicopolis, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Northeast of the Nicopolis archaeological site, near Preveza, Greece
properties.notes: This large bathing complex, with its natatio pool, frigidarium, tepidarium, caldarium and surviving hypocaust, dates on architectural grounds to the reign of Septimius Severus around the turn of the 3rd century CE. That places its construction roughly eight decades after the 117 CE snapshot — a straightforward dating trap despite being the best-preserved bath structure on the site today.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Augustus resettling the depopulated Epirote cities into the single city of Nicopolis, named for his victory at Actium.

properties.modern_location: Mycenae archaeological site, Mykines, Argolis, Greece
properties.notes: The Lion Gate stood as the monumental entrance to a citadel already abandoned for over a thousand years by 117 CE, its two lionesses flanking a column above a lintel weighing roughly 20 tons. Roman-era travelers came specifically to marvel at it as a relic, believing only the mythical Cyclopes could have set such stones. No Roman structure occupied the site; visitors found only silent Bronze Age ruins reached by a shepherd's path.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Lion Gate and remaining wall circuit as the work of the Cyclopes, among the ruins of Mycenae; mentions being led to the site by local shepherds.

properties.image_credit: Lion Gate, Mycenae, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Mycenae archaeological site, Mykines, Argolis, Greece
properties.notes: This beehive-shaped royal tholos tomb had already stood empty for well over a millennium by 117 CE, its corbelled dome rising nearly 13.5 meters above the entrance passage. Pausanias described it and similar structures near Mycenae as the underground treasure-chambers of Atreus and his sons, a detail that shows the tomb's true funerary purpose had been forgotten by his era. No priesthood or cult tended the site; it survived purely as an object of local legend and antiquarian curiosity.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Refers to "subterraneous buildings of Atreus and his sons, in which their treasures were deposited" among the ruins of Mycenae — the tholos tombs, misunderstood as treasuries rather than graves.

properties.image_credit: Gate of the Treasury of Atreus, Mycenae · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_english: Hellenistic Temple on the Acropolis of Mycenae
properties.modern_location: Mycenae acropolis summit, Mykines, Argolis, Greece
properties.notes: Built on the crown of the Mycenae acropolis in the early 3rd century BCE by Argive settlers who briefly revived the hilltop as a village, this small temple to Athena or Hera outlasted the settlement itself. The village was abandoned not long after, and by the time Pausanias toured the site around 150 CE he found it already in ruins with no functioning cult. Only scant foundations survive today, and no evidence points to Roman-period restoration or worship here.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: States plainly that Mycenae was already in ruins by the time of his visit, without describing an active temple on the acropolis.

properties.notes: Carved into the slope below the Spartan acropolis around 30-20 BCE under the patronage of the Augustan-era dynast Gaius Julius Eurycles, this theatre gained its permanent two-story marble stage building as a personal gift from Emperor Vespasian in 78 CE. By 117 CE it stood as Sparta's grandest public building, its Corinthian-order skene bearing an inscribed architrave naming its imperial donor. The stone cavea and finished marble stage were both firmly in place well before Hadrian's accession.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Notes tombs opposite the theatre, including that of Leonidas, and describes annual speeches and a Spartans-only contest held there.

properties.image_credit: Ancient theatre of Sparta, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: East bank of the Eurotas River, Sparti, Laconia, Greece
properties.notes: This riverside sanctuary of Artemis Orthia had stood on the same spot since the Archaic period, its temple rebuilt in the 2nd century BCE around an altar left untouched from far earlier. In 117 CE it remained Sparta's living heritage attraction, where boys underwent a ritualized flogging contest before the goddess's wooden cult image, said to grow unbearably heavy if the whip-bearers showed mercy. Visitors came to witness the spectacle even before any permanent seating existed.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Gives the origin myth of the scourging ritual at the altar of Artemis Orthia and describes the wooden cult statue known as Lygodesma.

properties.image_credit: Remains of the Temple of Artemis Orthia, Sparta · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name_english: Roman Grandstand at the Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia
properties.modern_location: East bank of the Eurotas River, Sparti, Laconia, Greece
properties.notes: This horseshoe-shaped stone grandstand was built to seat spectators watching the ritual flogging of Spartan youths before the altar of Artemis Orthia, but not until after 225 CE, over a century past this snapshot. Its concrete platform even reused older inscribed fragments as building rubble. In 117 CE, spectators at the same ritual still stood or found informal vantage points, since no permanent seating yet existed — this is the structure most tourist guides show today when picturing Roman Sparta, but it postdates Hadrian's reign by decades.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Describes the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia at Sparta and the ritual flogging of youths at the altar there, said to have replaced an earlier custom of human sacrifice after quarrels among the founding villages.

properties.notes: This nearly 200-meter marble double stoa framed the southern end of Sparta's agora, but construction dates to roughly 125-150 CE, tied to renovation work by the Spartan grandee Gaius Julius Eurycles Herculanus. Herculanus only began his senatorial career after Hadrian's 117 CE accession sponsored his entry to Rome's Senate, placing this building's rise squarely after our snapshot. A visitor to Sparta's agora in 117 CE would have found an older, unmonumentalized public square rather than this colonnaded showpiece.

properties.modern_location: Acropolis of Sparta, Sparti, Laconia, Greece
properties.notes: Crowning the modest acropolis of Sparta since the early 6th century BCE, this temple to Athena took its name from the bronze plating that once lined its interior walls with mythological scenes. It remained a functioning civic sanctuary through the Roman period, sitting at the symbolic heart of the city's religious life alongside the agora. Its most famous historical association is grim: the Spartan general Pausanias reportedly starved to death after taking refuge inside its precinct centuries earlier.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Describes the sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos on the Spartan acropolis and its bronze-relief decoration depicting mythological scenes.

properties.image_credit: Sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos, Sparta, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This Doric limestone temple crowned a pine-covered ridge on Aegina's east coast, its 32 surviving columns marking one of the best-preserved Archaic sanctuaries in Greece. Built around 500 BCE to replace an earlier wooden shrine lost to fire, it honored the local goddess Aphaia. Worship here had faded by the late Hellenistic period, but the building itself still stood intact when Trajan died, its famous pediment sculptures still in place a century before scavengers pried out its bronze clamps.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Mentions the sanctuary on Aegina and identifies Aphaia with the Cretan goddess Britomartis-Diktynna, without describing the temple in detail.

properties.image_credit: Temple of Aphaia, Aegina, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This Doric temple stood on the fortified acropolis hill overlooking Aegina's main harbor, built around 520 BCE on a site inhabited since the Bronze Age. Eleven columns ran along its length in local limestone, with pediments carved in Parian marble. The sanctuary and its surrounding walls, altar, and enclosure survived through the Roman period, only being pulled down for building material centuries later when the hill became a small Christian settlement. A single column still standing today gave the site its modern name, Kolona.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Describes Apollo's temple in the city of Aegina and a naked wooden cult image of native workmanship.

properties.image_credit: Column of the Temple of Apollo at Kolona, Aegina · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A square white-marble enclosure roughly 30 meters on a side stood in the most prominent part of Aegina's town, marking the legendary tomb of the hero Aeacus. Old olive trees grew inside it around a low altar that doubled as his grave, with carved reliefs at the entrance showing the Greek envoys who once begged Aeacus to end a drought. The nearby barrow of his son Phocus, capped with a single rough stone, stood right beside it. This civic monument to Aegina's founding hero remained a fixture of the town when Trajan died.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Describes the quadrangular marble enclosure, the altar-tomb of Aeacus, its relief carvings, and the adjacent barrow of Phocus.

properties.notes: Aegina's waterfront held two harbors side by side: a commercial port used since the Bronze Age and a walled military harbor with ship sheds for triremes, described by ancient visitors as the island's secret port. Combined installations once stretched along roughly 1,600 meters of coastline, testament to Aegina's centuries as a naval power. By Trajan's death the harbors still stood but carried a fraction of their old traffic, as the island's economy had shifted toward farming and small trades.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Notes the principal harbor near the temple of Aphrodite and a second, hidden harbor near the theater used for warships.

properties.notes: A theater rose above Aegina's shore on a scale ancient visitors compared to the famous theater at Epidaurus, with a stadium laid out just behind it. Both stood near the town's secret harbor, part of the cluster of public buildings on the headland. No record survives of Roman-era renovation here, unlike the lavishly rebuilt theaters of Corinth or Athens, suggesting the complex simply endured from its Classical construction into the 2nd century CE as a fading but intact civic landmark.

ancient_sources.author: Pausanias
ancient_sources.note: Describes a theater on Aegina rivaling Epidaurus's in size, with a stadium situated behind it.

ancient_sources.author: I.Aphrodisias 2007
ancient_sources.note: The complex's own dedication reads "to Aphrodite, the Divine Augusti, and the People," naming the local family who paid to build it.

properties.notes: Two prominent local families funded this temple to Aphrodite and the Julio-Claudian emperors between 20 and 60 CE. A 90-meter processional avenue ran between two three-story porticoes covered in marble relief panels of gods, emperors, and conquered peoples. By 117 CE it had stood finished and in active use for over half a century. Excavators uncovered it only in 1979.
properties.image_credit: Sebasteion, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (seat reservations)
ancient_sources.work: Topos inscriptions cut into the stadium benches
ancient_sources.note: Rows of seats are labeled "place of..." for specific trade guilds, including tanners, goldsmiths, and gardeners, showing how the stadium's seating was parceled out by guild.

properties.notes: Built in the later 1st century CE, this marble stadium ran 270 meters long with 30 tiers of seats for 30,000 spectators, closed at both ends unlike a typical Greek stadium. Its slightly elliptical sides sharpened every sightline. Inscribed seats reserved blocks for the goldsmiths' and tanners' guilds. Athletes still ran, jumped, wrestled, and threw the discus here in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Stadium, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: I.Aphrodisias 2007, 8.5
ancient_sources.work: Stage-building dedication of C. Julius Zoilos
ancient_sources.note: An inscription cut into the stage building records that Zoilos, a freedman of Augustus who returned home wealthy, personally paid for the stage, its proscenium, and all its decoration.
