properties.notes: Gaius Julius Zoilos, a freedman of Octavian who returned home rich and powerful, paid for this theatre's elaborate three-story marble stage building before 28 BCE and dedicated it to Aphrodite and the people. Carved into the slope of the acropolis mound, it seated several thousand for Greek-style drama and civic assembly. It had already stood for well over a century when Hadrian became emperor.
properties.image_credit: Aphrodisias Theatre, stage inscription · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A cluster of small rooms behind the Bouleuterion where Aphrodisian marble was carved into portraits and gods sent across the empire. Excavators found part-finished statues abandoned mid-carving alongside older pieces brought in for repair. Sitting on its own seam of fine white and blue-grey marble, the city ran a formal sculpture school whose signed work turns up as far as Rome. It was already a working atelier well before 117 CE and stayed active into the late 4th century.
properties.image_credit: Sculptor's workshop, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Also called the Portico of Tiberius, this was Aphrodisias's second public square, laid out in the early 1st century CE under Tiberius. Recent excavation found it functioned as an urban park rather than a bare marketplace, with a long ornamental pool, fountains, and rows of planted trees behind its colonnades. It was already nearly a century old by the time Hadrian took the throne.
properties.image_credit: South Agora and pool, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The largest roofed public hall in the city center, spanning three full city blocks. Its decoration and a surviving dedication place its completion in the late 1st century CE, roughly a generation before Hadrian's reign began. Centuries later, once Aphrodisias became a provincial capital, the building may have served as the governor's administrative seat, but in 117 CE it was still a civic law-court-and-commerce hall.

This ornate ceremonial gate of sixteen Corinthian columns, blue-and-white marble, and pediments carved with Eros and Nike figures marked the processional entrance to the sanctuary of Aphrodite. Stylistically Antonine to Severan, it was built around 200 CE, roughly eighty years after Trajan's death, so it did not yet exist in 117 CE. Toppled by earthquakes, it was rebuilt stone-for-stone from original blocks in 1991.
properties.image_credit: Tetrapylon, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Charlotte Roueché and R. R. R. Smith (eds.)
ancient_sources.work: Aphrodisias Papers 3: The Setting and Quarries, Mythological and Other Sculptural Decoration, Architectural Development, Portico of Tiberius, and Tetrapylon
ancient_sources.ref: Journal of Roman Archaeology Supplementary Series 20, 1996
ancient_sources.note: NYU excavation-team study of the Tetrapylon's architectural development, dating it stylistically to the Antonine-Severan era (c. 200 CE), roughly eighty years after the 117 CE snapshot.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription series (bath architecture)
ancient_sources.work: Dedicatory inscriptions naming Hadrian Olympios and Panhellenios
ancient_sources.note: Inscriptions carved into the bath complex name Hadrian with two of his special titles, dating the building to well after this map's 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: A monumental marble bath complex dedicated to the emperor Hadrian, who reigned from August 117 CE. Construction began after his accession, so the block was still occupied by older shops and houses on the day Trajan died. This is a textbook post-117 dating trap: 'Hadrianic' at Aphrodisias always means built under Hadrian, not before him.
properties.image_credit: Baths of Hadrian, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (statue base)
ancient_sources.work: Honorific base for L. Antonius Claudius Diogenes Dometeinos
ancient_sources.note: A statue base at the council house's entrance honors a prominent local citizen, tying his family's name to a building raised well after 117 CE.

properties.notes: Aphrodisias's city council chamber, seating roughly 1,750 people and doubling as a concert odeon, was funded by Attalos son of Dometeinos around 200 CE, a generation-plus after Hadrian's death, let alone Trajan's. In 117 CE the site behind the Sebasteion where it stands had not yet been built up this way. It was later refurbished around 390 CE by the Roman governor of Caria.
properties.image_credit: Bouleuterion, Aphrodisias · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A fissure at the foot of the Temple of Apollo that vents carbon dioxide heavy enough to kill sparrows and bulls on contact, worshipped as a literal gate to the underworld of Pluto and Kore. Strabo, writing before 24 CE, described throwing sparrows in and watching them drop dead while the eunuch priests of Cybele walked through unharmed. Pilgrims and sacrificial bulls kept coming until the 4th century CE, long after it was already ancient in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Plutonium (Pluto's Gate), Hierapolis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Plutonium's lethal vapor, killing sparrows and bulls thrown in while priests of Cybele entered unharmed.

properties.notes: The oldest religious building in the city, raised on this podium not long after Eumenes II of Pergamon founded Hierapolis around 190 BCE, and standing directly beside the toxic Plutonium cave. The catastrophic earthquake of 60 CE under Nero shattered the Hellenistic sanctuary along with much of the city. What tourists walk through today is a 3rd-century CE Severan rebuild reusing the old blocks, so the temple was likely still a ruin, not a standing shrine, on the day Trajan died in 117 CE.

The earthquake of 60 CE flattened the original Hellenistic theatre; the cavea and stage building standing today were rebuilt under the Flavian emperors in the following decades, replacing an earlier theatre slightly to the northeast. A gallery inscription records further work done under Hadrian after 117 CE, and Septimius Severus redecorated the stage front a century later, but the Flavian-era structure itself was already complete and in use well before Trajan's death.
properties.image_credit: Theatre of Hierapolis, scaenae frons · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: At 200 by 130 meters, this marble-paved square ranked among the largest agoras anywhere in Asia Minor and served as the city's commercial heart, ringed by a two-story stoa with Ionic and Corinthian colonnades. Its west side and eastern basilica-stoa were built during the reign of Hadrian, who took the throne in August 117 CE, so the monumental agora seen today postdates the snapshot even though Hierapolis had earlier marketplaces on the same general site.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (architrave block)
ancient_sources.work: Dedicatory inscription, Nymphaeum of the Tritons
ancient_sources.note: An inscription carved into the fountain's architrave dates the monument to over a century after this map's 117 CE snapshot - it did not yet exist at the time.

properties.notes: One of the longest monumental fountains in the Roman world, stretching 60 meters along the colonnaded main street. An inscription on its architrave dates it firmly to the reign of Severus Alexander, around 222 to 235 CE, roughly a century after Trajan's death. It replaced whatever more modest water feature stood on Frontinus Street in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum of the Tritons, Hierapolis · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The blinding-white cascade of mineral pools below the city, built up over hundreds of thousands of years by calcium-laden hot springs, was the reason Hierapolis existed at all. Strabo recorded that the water hardened into stone so fast that channels dug for it turned into solid stone dams within a season. The same springs fed the city's baths and were credited with the sacred power that made the Plutonium cave next door an entrance to the underworld.
properties.image_credit: Travertine pools, Pamukkale · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Hierapolis water as petrifying so readily that irrigation channels became solid stone dams.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (gate facade, Latin and Greek)
ancient_sources.note: A bilingual inscription records that the Roman governor Sextus Julius Frontinus built the gate and dedicated it to Domitian, whose name was later chiseled out after his assassination.

properties.notes: A monumental triple gate flanked by two round towers, dedicated to Domitian by Sextus Julius Frontinus, proconsul of Asia, around 84 to 86 CE. It opened onto Frontinus Street, the city's 14-meter-wide colonnaded main artery running north-south through its center. Already three decades old and a fixed civic landmark by the time Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Frontinus Gate, Hierapolis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (theatre seating block)
ancient_sources.work: Seat reservation, "Place of the Jews, who are also called God-fearers"
ancient_sources.note: One row of theatre seats carries a carved label reserving that block for the local Jewish community - direct evidence of who sat where in Roman Miletus.

properties.notes: A Hellenistic theatre reborn as one of Roman Asia's biggest stages. Trajan's engineers spent his whole reign rebuilding it to hold 15,000 spectators, triple the old Greek capacity, with a three-story columned stage front. By 117 CE the vast Roman cavea dominated the skyline above the Theatre Harbor.
properties.image_credit: Theatre of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Miletus's chief civic sanctuary, sacred to Apollo Delphinios since the city's earliest days. An open courtyard ringed by Doric colonnades doubled as the state archive, holding over 150 inscribed decrees and treaties. The city's chief magistrates, the prytaneis, governed from offices inside its walls. Still the ritual heart of the city in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Delphinion of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Miletus's foundation, harbors, and civic institutions in Roman-era Ionia.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (architrave)
ancient_sources.work: Dedication by Timarchos and Herakleides for King Antiochus IV Epiphanes
ancient_sources.note: The council house's own architrave inscription records two Milesian brothers arranging for the Seleucid king to fund the building as a gift to the city's gods and people.

properties.notes: The council house where Miletus's civic assembly met, a gift from a foreign king rather than the city itself. Dedication inscriptions on its architrave name the donor as the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, reigning 175-164 BCE. A colonnaded courtyard and monumental gateway led into a roofed auditorium seating around 1,500 councilors. Still in active civic use under Roman rule in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Bouleuterion of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A monumental fountain house paid for by Marcus Ulpius Traianus, governor of Asia and father of the future emperor Trajan, around 79-80 CE. Its facade rose in tiers of columns and statue niches modeled on a theatre's stage front, marking the terminus of the aqueduct bringing water down from the southern hills. Already decades old and fully functioning when Trajan himself, its founder's son, visited Miletus in 117 CE. A third story was added later, under Gordian III.
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: At roughly 164 by 196 meters, the largest agora ever built in the Greek world, framing the city's civic and commercial life. Roman-period builders enclosed it further with new gateways at its corners, including an elaborate monumental market gate. By 117 CE it had been the beating commercial heart of Miletus for over three centuries, still ringed by shaded stoas full of merchants. Coordinates are approximate, estimated from the excavated city plan.
properties.image_credit: Agora of Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Two marble lions once flanked the mouth of Miletus's busiest port, a chain strung between them to seal the harbor in wartime. One lion's inscribed base declared it stood guard over the public harbor. Citizens raised a victory monument nearby after Pompey crushed the pirates in 67 BCE, later rededicating it to Augustus for his win at Actium. Coordinates are approximate, marking the harbor entrance near the theatre.

ancient_sources.author: Chariton
ancient_sources.note: Early Roman-era novel referencing a Milesian harbor, thought to correspond to the Lion Harbor.

properties.notes: The processional road out of Miletus's southeast gate, lined by an elegant Ionic colonnade, that led pilgrims 17 kilometers south to the oracle sanctuary at Didyma. Statues of seated priests and sphinxes once lined its route. In 117 CE it was still walked each year in festival processions honoring Apollo. Coordinates are approximate, marking the Ionic Stoa at its city-side start.
properties.image_credit: Ionic Stoa, Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Miletus's largest bathhouse, built and funded decades after Trajan's death by Faustina the Younger, wife of emperor Marcus Aurelius, around the mid-to-late 2nd century CE. Its three great halls held frigidarium, tepidarium, and caldarium beneath soaring vaults. In 117 CE this whole quarter of the city was still open ground; the empress who gave it her name would not even be born for another decade.
properties.image_credit: Sculpture from the Faustina Baths, Miletus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Armin von Gerkan and Fritz Krischen
ancient_sources.work: Thermen und Palaestren (Milet: Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen und Untersuchungen seit dem Jahre 1899, Band I, Heft 9)
ancient_sources.note: German Archaeological Institute excavation report on the Faustina Baths, establishing the mid-to-late 2nd century CE construction date under Faustina the Younger, decades after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: One of the largest Ionic temples ever built, begun around 300 BCE under Seleucid patronage but never finished in antiquity. By 117 CE only the Hellenistic cella and part of its colonnade stood complete, work having stalled generations earlier as Seleucid funding dried up. The gigantic double-cella Roman rebuild, wrapping the whole structure in a forest of new columns and adding an imperial-cult chamber beside Artemis's own, did not begin until Hadrian's reign after 117.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Artemis, Sardis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the fall of Sardis to Cyrus the Great after a fourteen-day siege. Describes the city's capture, not this temple.

properties.notes: "A thousand hills" of royal Lydian burial mounds spread across the plain north of Sardis, raised for kings including Gyges and Alyattes centuries before Rome ever ruled Asia. The tomb of Alyattes alone measures 355 meters across and rises 61 meters, one of antiquity's largest funerary monuments and already ancient when Herodotus described it. Still a famous landmark of the region in 117 CE, over 600 years after it was raised.
properties.image_credit: Tomb of Alyattes, Bin Tepe · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the tomb of Alyattes at Sardis, built by the market-traders, craftsmen, and prostitutes of the city.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription (Marble Court architrave)
ancient_sources.work: Dedication to Julia Domna, Caracalla, and Geta
ancient_sources.note: A monumental inscription dedicates the Marble Court's upper story to the emperor's family - Geta's name was later erased after his murder - about a century after this map's 117 CE snapshot.

properties.name_english: Sardis Roman Gymnasium and Bath Complex
properties.notes: A vast bath-gymnasium covering over 5.5 acres, its famous Marble Court raised under Lucius Verus around 165 CE and lavishly rebuilt for the imperial cult in 211-213 CE under Julia Domna's patronage. In 117 CE none of this stood yet; only bare ground and perhaps early foundation work occupied the site decades before the emperors whose names it would later honor were even born. Coordinates are approximate.
properties.image_credit: Bath-Gymnasium complex at Sardis · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The grandest ancient synagogue found outside Israel, its hall able to seat a thousand worshippers under mosaic floors and marble-paneled walls. It was carved out of rooms inside the Roman bath-gymnasium complex, work usually dated to the late 3rd century CE at the earliest, though a Jewish community is attested at Sardis for centuries before that. In 117 CE the building did not yet exist; the space was still part of an unbuilt bathhouse. Coordinates are approximate.
properties.image_credit: Sardis Synagogue · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A steep citadel rising some 300 meters above the plain, once called by Polybius the strongest fortress in the world. Croesus's Lydian kings ruled from its heights until Cyrus's Persian troops famously scaled its supposedly unclimbable cliffs by night in 546 BCE. Rome inherited it peacefully in 133 BCE, and its ancient walls still crowned the city when Trajan died in 117 CE. Coordinates are approximate, marking the fortified hilltop above the lower city.
properties.image_credit: Acropolis of Sardis · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the Persian capture of the Sardis acropolis under Cyrus in 546 BCE, scaled at an unguarded cliff.

properties.modern_location: Sart Cayi, Sart, Salihli, Manisa, Turkey
properties.notes: A modest stream off Mount Tmolus that ancient writers credited with making Lydia's kings the richest men on earth. Herodotus wrote that its gold-bearing sands ran straight through the middle of the Sardis marketplace, and legend held King Midas washed away his golden touch in its waters. Excavators found 6th-century BCE workshops here for refining electrum into pure gold and silver. The dried placer deposits were long exhausted by 117 CE, but the river and its legend still ran through the city.

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: States that the river Pactolus, carrying gold dust from Mount Tmolus, flowed through the middle of the Sardis marketplace.

properties.notes: Nicaea's showcase theatre held roughly 10,000 spectators across a three-story, 24-meter cavea built on vaulted arches instead of a hillside, a rare flat-ground design in Anatolia. Governor Pliny the Younger inspected the unfinished building around 111 CE and found its walls already cracking and sinking, despite more than 10 million sesterces spent. He recommended tearing it down; Trajan told him to use his own judgment on the spot. Construction pressed on regardless.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Reports to Trajan that Nicaea's unfinished theatre, already costing over 10 million sesterces, showed severe cracking and subsidence.

ancient_sources.author: Trajan
ancient_sources.note: Tells Pliny to decide on the spot whether to complete or demolish the half-built theatre.

properties.notes: Nicaea's public gymnasium had burned down, and the city rebuilt it far larger than before even as the theatre project next door ran badly over budget. Pliny reported the spending to Trajan around 111 CE, and the emperor waved it through, remarking that Greek cities could never resist a gymnasium. No excavation has pinned down the building's footprint beneath modern İznik. This marks an approximate city-center placement for a documented but unlocated project.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Reports that Nicaea's fire-damaged gymnasium was being rebuilt on a larger scale, with a considerable sum already spent.

ancient_sources.author: Trajan
ancient_sources.note: Approves continuing the gymnasium's reconstruction, remarking that Greek cities are devoted to their gymnasia.

properties.notes: Nicaea's Hellenistic walls, raised under King Lysimachus around 300 BCE, had largely disappeared by the Roman period. The Flavian emperors rebuilt the circuit from scratch in the later 1st century CE, laying out an irregular pentagon nearly 5 kilometers around with four new marble gates dedicated by the provincial governor. Little of what visitors photograph at Lefke Gate today is this Roman fabric, since most standing stonework was rebuilt again centuries later under Byzantine emperors.
properties.image_credit: Dick Osseman · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

properties.notes: Nicaea sat inland on Lake Ascania with no direct sea access, so its trade leaned on a harbor built out from the city's eastern shore. Observers have reported extensive stone foundations visible through the clear, shallow water, substantial enough to suggest real quay infrastructure rather than a simple landing. No excavation has published a construction date for the site. This marks an approximate placement along the ancient shoreline for a documented but undated harbor.

An inscription found along its route names Hadrian as dedicatee, dating the standing arches east of İznik's Lefke Gate to his reign rather than Trajan's. About 1.5 kilometers of the channel is still visible on the ground, though the masonry was rebuilt repeatedly under later Byzantine and Ottoman rulers, and a geophysical survey found a fault line warping its foundations. Hadrian only became emperor the day Trajan died, so this aqueduct almost certainly rose just after our snapshot.

Nicomedia burned through more than 5 million sesterces on two separate aqueduct schemes, both abandoned half-built, before Pliny arrived as governor. He reported the waste to Trajan around 112 CE and asked Rome for a qualified engineer to find who was responsible. A two-story arcaded aqueduct still stands north of İzmit at Üçtepeler, traditionally linked to the working system finally completed under Pliny's own supervision. Byzantine and Ottoman repairs show it stayed in use for centuries.
properties.image_credit: Carole Raddato · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Reports that Nicomedia had wasted 3,329,000 sesterces on one abandoned aqueduct and 2,000,000 more on a second, and asks for an engineer from Rome.

ancient_sources.author: Trajan
ancient_sources.note: Orders an inquiry into who was responsible for wasting so much money on the Nicomedia aqueducts.

properties.notes: Nicomedia's residents were expanding their forum with a grand new wing when a small, unconsecrated shrine to the Mother of the Gods stood in the way. Pliny asked Trajan whether it could simply be moved, since the temple predated Roman rites of consecration. Trajan approved without hesitation, and the expansion moved forward around 112 CE, giving Nicomedia a larger civic square within a few years of Trajan's death. Coordinates mark an approximate city-center placement.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Reports that Nicomedia's new forum, under construction beside the old one, was obstructed by an unconsecrated shrine of the Mother of the Gods.

ancient_sources.author: Trajan
ancient_sources.note: Grants permission to relocate the temple to make way for the new forum.

properties.name_latin: Fossa a Lacu Sophone ad Mare
properties.modern_location: İzmit, Turkey (between Lake Sapanca and the Gulf of İzmit)
properties.notes: Pliny proposed cutting an 18-mile canal from Lake Sophon, today's Lake Sapanca, down to the sea at Nicomedia, hoping to cut the cost of hauling marble, timber, and produce into the city. Locals told him the lake sat 40 cubits above sea level, so he asked Trajan to send a surveyor before digging began. Trajan told him to borrow an engineer from Calpurnius Macer, governor of Lower Moesia. No ancient source records the canal being dug, and no trace of it survives, so it is marked unbuilt here.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Proposes a canal from Lake Sophon to the sea to ease transport of stone, timber, and produce to Nicomedia, and asks for a leveling engineer.

ancient_sources.author: Trajan
ancient_sources.note: Directs Pliny to request a surveyor from Calpurnius Macer, governor of Lower Moesia.

properties.notes: In 29 BCE Octavian let Bithynia's Greeks dedicate a temple to Roma and himself at Nicomedia, one of the empire's first two imperial-cult temples. It became the meeting hall of the Bithynian koinon, the provincial assembly running the emperor's cult. Eight Corinthian columns and an entablature reading 'to Rome, the Senate, the People, Augustus' survive only on coin dies; the building itself has never been excavated. A major earthquake struck Nicomedia in 120 CE, three years after our snapshot.

A violent fire tore through Nicomedia around 112 CE, gutting private houses and reaching the city's Gerusia hall even though a street separated it from where the blaze started. Pliny blamed the damage on a total lack of firefighting equipment and asked Trajan to authorize a 150-man brigade of tradesmen. Trajan refused, worried any organized group in Bithynia would turn into a political faction. Whether the hall was ever rebuilt went unrecorded before Trajan died, so it is marked destroyed here.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Reports a fire at Nicomedia that destroyed many houses and the Gerusia's hall, and requests permission to form a 150-man firefighting guild.

ancient_sources.author: Trajan
ancient_sources.note: Refuses the guild, fearing any association in Bithynia would become a political faction.

properties.notes: The same fire that gutted Nicomedia's Gerusia hall around 112 CE also destroyed the city's temple of Isis, evidence the Egyptian cult had a real foothold in Roman Bithynia. Pliny listed it among the fire's public losses and pushed for a firefighting guild to prevent a repeat. Trajan turned the guild down, and no source records the temple being rebuilt before his death. Its exact location within Nicomedia is unknown, so this marker is an approximate city-center placement.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Younger
ancient_sources.note: Lists the temple of Isis among the public buildings destroyed in Nicomedia's fire.

properties.notes: Attalus II of Pergamon ringed his new harbor city with defensive walls when he founded Attaleia around 150 BCE, cutting the cliff-top site off from the plain behind it. Roman builders thickened and repaired long stretches after Rome absorbed the city in 133 BCE, adding towers that still shape Kaleiçi's street grid. By 117 CE the walls had guarded the harbor for well over two centuries. Cut stone from this circuit still climbs the cliff above the marina beneath later Byzantine and Seljuk rebuilding.
properties.image_credit: Kale Kapısı, a surviving gate of Antalya's old city walls · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: States that Attaleia was founded by Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamon.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo describes Attaleia as a city founded by King Attalus II Philadelphus of Pergamon, who also had the harbor's entrance narrowed on his own orders.

properties.notes: Attalus II picked this half-moon cove beneath the cliffs because it was the only sheltered anchorage on an otherwise harborless stretch of the Pamphylian coast. Roman engineers reinforced its breakwater with massive cut-stone blocks, some still visible underwater today. Grain, timber, and Pamphylian goods moved through its roughly 100-meter basin for more than two centuries before 117 CE. The same harbor, now a yacht marina, has stayed in continuous use for over two thousand years.
properties.image_credit: The Roman-era harbor of Antalya · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription series (gate facade, gilded bronze letters)
ancient_sources.note: Two dedications to Hadrian once carried gilded bronze letters spelling out his adoptive father Trajan's name - surviving fragments are now scattered across museums in Vienna, Berlin, London, and Oxford.

properties.notes: Antalya raised this triple-arched marble gate to honor Emperor Hadrian's visit to the city in 130 CE, more than a decade after Trajan's death. Two square towers flank three coffered arches that once carried a full second story and a row of honorific statues, now lost. It survives as the only one of the old city's original gates still standing intact. On 11 August 117 CE this gate did not yet exist and Hadrian had not yet even become emperor.
properties.image_credit: Hadrian's Gate, Antalya · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Builders raised this Corinthian temple in Attaleia around 130 CE, the same year Hadrian's Gate went up to mark the emperor's tour of the city. Byzantine Christians later converted it into a church for the Virgin Mary, and Seljuk Turks topped it with a minaret that eventually snapped off in a storm, giving the ruin its modern name, the Broken Minaret. Its original dedication is disputed, with some accounts linking it to Serapis. Like the nearby Hadrian's Gate, it postdates Trajan's death by over a decade and had not been built on 11 August 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Kesik Minare, the Broken Minaret, originally a Roman temple · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Builders raised this stone tower where Antalya's old walls meet the sea cliffs, starting on a square Roman base later rebuilt into the cylindrical form still standing today. Historians debate whether Rome built it as a tomb, a harbor watchtower, or both, since Roman-era graves have turned up nearby. Byzantine engineers later topped it with a beacon, turning a tomb into a working lighthouse. Most surveys date its construction broadly to the 2nd century CE, most plausibly the decades after Trajan's death, so it most likely had not yet risen at the snapshot moment.
properties.image_credit: Hidirlik Tower, Antalya · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Inscription series (statue bases, Latin and Greek)
ancient_sources.note: Every statue base in the gate's horseshoe courtyard names the wealthy local benefactress Plancia Magna, who paid to renovate the old Hellenistic gate and fill it with statues of gods, ancestors, and the imperial family.

properties.notes: Perge's founders raised two round defensive towers flanking the city's southern gate in the 3rd century BCE, standing three stories over a horseshoe courtyard cut into the fortification line. The towers had already watched over the city for more than four centuries by 117 CE. A wealthy priestess named Plancia Magna would later fill the courtyard with imperial statues and a triple arch, but that remodeling began only after Hadrian took the throne. On 11 August 117 CE the bare Hellenistic towers, without her later decoration, were what stood here.
properties.image_credit: The Hellenistic round towers of Perge's city gate · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Perge's Hellenistic founders enclosed the city with a wall studded with rectangular towers at even intervals across the 3rd century BCE, a circuit the city never needed to fully rebuild afterward. The eastern and western stretches still stand largely as built, running from the acropolis mound down toward the plain. Only the southern wall received a Roman-era addition, and that came in the 2nd century, decades after Trajan's reign. By 117 CE the Hellenistic walls had guarded Perge for roughly four centuries, one of Pamphylia's best-preserved fortification circuits today.
properties.image_credit: The Hellenistic eastern wall of Perge · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Livy
ancient_sources.note: Recounts the Roman commander Gnaeus Manlius Vulso's visit to Perge and its temple of Artemis during his 189 BCE campaign in Asia Minor. Describes the city, not its walls.

properties.notes: The Aspendos-born architect Zenon, son of Theodorus, designed this theatre for two wealthy brothers who funded its construction around the mid-2nd century CE, decades after Trajan's death. Its stage building still rises unbroken to the top of the seating bank, the best-preserved example of that design anywhere in the Roman world, and it still hosts performances today. Roughly 15,000 spectators could fill its curved rows in antiquity. On 11 August 117 CE, Aspendos was still generations away from cutting the first stone for this theatre.
properties.image_credit: The Roman theatre of Aspendos · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Aspendos as an Argive foundation on the Eurymedon river, calling it a considerable city of Pamphylia. A description of the city, not the theatre.

ancient_sources.author: Inscription series (7 statue bases)
ancient_sources.work: Victory dedications of Attalos I to Athena Nikephoros
ancient_sources.note: A run of statue bases set up in the temple square records King Attalos I dedicating his early victories over the Galatians and rival Hellenistic generals to Athena Nikephoros.

properties.notes: Pergamon's rulers built this Doric temple on a terrace above the great theatre around 300 BCE, the oldest sanctuary standing on the acropolis. Philetaerus and his Attalid successors dedicated it to Athena Polias Nikephoros, 'bringer of victory,' and lined its stoas with captured Galatian shields as war trophies. The Library of Pergamon rose directly beside it, so scholars worked within sight of the goddess's own shrine. By 117 CE the sanctuary had anchored Pergamon's religious life for roughly four centuries, its columns among the oldest stonework on the hill.
properties.image_credit: The Temple of Athena, Pergamon acropolis · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Pergamon's earliest known cult site, this open-air sanctuary to Demeter and her daughter Kore occupied a long terrace on the acropolis's southern slope, reaching back to the 4th century BCE. Philetaerus, founder of the Attalid dynasty, and his mother Boa rebuilt its Ionic temple and altar in the early 3rd century BCE, decorating the marble frieze with carved bulls' skulls. Women of the city gathered here yearly for torchlit rites echoing the Eleusinian mysteries, on stone benches still visible today. By 117 CE the sanctuary had served Pergamon's women for over four centuries.
properties.image_credit: The Sanctuary of Demeter, Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Roman builders raised this immense brick temple directly over the Selinus River in Pergamon's lower city, engineering a hidden double bridge nearly 200 meters wide just to carry the water beneath its foundations. Dedicated to the Egyptian gods Serapis and Isis, its main hall ranks among the largest Roman-era religious buildings surviving anywhere in the Greek world. Its brick construction and sculptural style point to the first half of the 2nd century CE, most likely under Hadrian rather than Trajan. On 11 August 117 CE this temple almost certainly did not yet exist.
properties.image_credit: Red Basilica (Kızıl Avlu), Bergama · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Flavius Josephus
ancient_sources.note: Josephus records that King Herod Agrippa I lavishly rebuilt Berytus with a theatre, an amphitheatre, porticoes, and baths, funding extravagant games to inaugurate them.

properties.notes: Augustus's veterans built these baths in the heart of Colonia Berytus during the 1st century AD. Bathers moved through four heated chambers warmed by a hypocaust, where furnaces pushed hot air beneath the floor through rows of terracotta pillars. The complex sat between the forum and the sea, serving the colony's Roman citizens for generations. Archaeologists uncovered the ruins in 1968, buried under Beirut's modern city center.
properties.image_credit: Roman bath Beirut lebanon 026 · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

properties.notes: Augustus turned Berytus into a full Roman colonia in 14 BC and raised a forum at its civic core. A 99-meter basilica with a Corinthian portico of polychrome stone lined its north side, built within the colony's first Roman century. Veterans of two legions settled here, turning a Phoenician port into a Latin-speaking showcase of empire. Its granite columns still stand near Beirut's Place de l'Etoile.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Berytus's destruction by Tryphon and its Roman refoundation as a colonia settled with legionary veterans.

properties.notes: Berytus laid its Cardo Maximus out as the north-south spine of the Roman colony, later dressing it in imported grandeur. Under Trajan, workers raised red granite columns quarried at Aswan in Egypt, spaced 2.5 meters apart on carved pedestals. The colonnaded street ran roughly 100 meters from the forum toward the harbor, sheltering pedestrians under a continuous portico. Five re-erected columns still mark its crossing with the Decumanus in downtown Beirut.

Berytus built a hippodrome for chariot racing soon after Augustus founded the colony, first raising its stands and starting gates in timber. Excavators traced a central barrier, seating banks, and gate foundations across a 3,500-square-meter track near the ancient harbor. Masons rebuilt the venue in stone as the city grew through the 2nd century AD. Later writers ranked it among the finest racing circuits of the Roman Levant.

Berytus grew around a natural harbor Phoenician sailors had used for over a thousand years before Rome arrived. After Augustus settled veterans there in 14 BC, Roman engineers deepened the basin and extended its seawalls to handle heavier trade. The port anchored the colony's economy, moving grain, timber, and goods along the Levantine coast. It stayed the city's commercial lifeline for centuries under Roman rule.

ancient_sources.author: KAI 15 and KAI 16 (Bodashtart inscriptions)
ancient_sources.work: Building and restoration dedication of King Bodashtart
ancient_sources.note: Phoenician inscriptions carved into the temple's own podium blocks record that King Bodashtart, and later his son and heir Yatonmilk, expanded and restored the sanctuary of Eshmun.

properties.notes: Sidon's king Eshmunazar II founded this healing sanctuary to the god Eshmun beside the Awali River around 500 BC. Later Phoenician kings expanded it with monumental staircases, votive thrones, and sacred pools fed by the YDLL spring. Under Roman rule the sanctuary gained a colonnaded approach, a nymphaeum, and an inn for pilgrims seeking cures. Worshippers kept visiting the site for more than a thousand years, into the 8th century AD.
properties.image_credit: Eshmun Bab columns · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sidon's kings carved two vast rock-cut burial chambers into the hills south of the city, reachable only through vertical shafts. The tombs held 21 sarcophagi spanning Egyptian, Greek, Lycian, and Phoenician styles, sealed away since the late 4th century BC. Among them lay the Alexander Sarcophagus, a 15-ton limestone masterpiece carved with battle scenes of Alexander the Great. The chambers stayed hidden underground for over two thousand years, until workmen broke into them in 1887.
properties.image_credit: Alexander Sarcophagus, Istanbul Archaeological Museums · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Sidon as a major Phoenician city renowned for glassmaking and dyed textiles, the city whose royal burial ground this necropolis belongs to.

ancient_sources.author: CIS I 3 / KAI 14
ancient_sources.work: Royal Phoenician funerary inscription of King Eshmunazar II
ancient_sources.note: The sarcophagus lid bears a long Phoenician inscription in which King Eshmunazar II recounts his lineage and building works and pronounces a curse against anyone who disturbs his burial.

properties.notes: Sidon's own King Eshmunazar II was buried in a black stone sarcophagus inscribed with a lengthy Phoenician royal epitaph. Workers found the tomb at Magharat Abloun, a rock-cut necropolis southeast of the city, in January 1855. The inscription cursed any future violator of the grave and recorded the king's grants of land from the Persian crown. The sarcophagus lay sealed in Sidon's necropolis for roughly two thousand years before its rediscovery.
properties.image_credit: Eshmunazar II sarcophagus, Louvre · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Generations of Sidonian dye workers crushed millions of murex sea snails along the shoreline, piling the broken shells into hills still visible today. Extracting a few drops of purple-red dye from each mollusk's gland made Tyrian purple worth more than its weight in gold. Workshops operated near Sidon's harbor and kept running straight through the Roman period. The mounds south of the later Sea Castle remain the clearest physical trace of the ancient purple trade.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes the murex shellfish and the extraction of purple dye, the industry that produced Sidon's shell mounds.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes sand carried to Sidon from the nearby coast and fused into glass, reflecting the city's fame as a Phoenician manufacturing center.

properties.notes: Sidon built one of Phoenicia's oldest working harbors, sheltered by the offshore islet of Zire and a sandstone ridge along its northern shore. Sailors had used the anchorage for well over two thousand years by the time Rome absorbed the city into the province of Syria. Roman engineers extended a 230-meter mole and reshaped the basin with heavier stonework during their occupation. The harbor kept Sidon's glass, timber, and purple-dye trade flowing across the Mediterranean.

Alexander the Great's engineers built this half-mile mole of stone, timber, and rubble from the abandoned mainland town of Ushu to break the naval defenses of island Tyre during his 332 BCE siege. Centuries of silt piling against the mole steadily widened it into a true isthmus, permanently fusing the once-island city to the coast. By 117 CE Roman Tyre stood on a broad peninsula built entirely on Alexander's foundation, its main landward road running straight over ground his army had won. The causeway remains visible today as the very shape of modern Tyre's isthmus.
properties.image_credit: Alexander at the Siege of Tyre · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Arrian
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Macedonian army building the mole from stone, timber, and rubble taken from the abandoned mainland city.

properties.notes: Ancient writers called Tyre's north-facing harbor the Sidonian Harbor, or Port of Astronoe, and it worked as the city's main commercial port straight through the Roman period. Strabo and Arrian, writing in the first and second centuries CE, both describe Tyre as a city with two harbors, this one enclosed and defensible against enemy fleets. Merchant ships loaded grain, cedar timber, and Tyre's famous purple-dyed cloth from its quays. Archaeologists have traced ancient breakwater foundations beneath the modern fishing harbor of Sour, which still occupies roughly the same spot.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes Tyre's mole and its two harbors, one closable, the other called the Egyptian harbor.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Strabo describes Tyre as having two harbors, an enclosed northern "Sidonian" harbor and an open southern one he explicitly calls the "Egyptian" harbor.

properties.notes: Tyre's southern harbor opened toward Egypt and carried the city's direct trade link to Alexandria's grain and papyrus. A stone breakwater discovered in 2019, built in the same style as Tyre's Iron Age Phoenician moles, once guarded its mouth. By the Roman period part of the basin had silted up and the reclaimed land was used for a monumental bath complex, but the port itself stayed active. Byzantine tombstones later even name local 'murex fishermen of the Egyptian port,' proving the harbor still functioned centuries after 117 CE.

Tyre gave its name to Tyrian purple, the violet-red dye pressed from the crushed glands of thousands of murex sea snails and prized as antiquity's costliest color. Shell mounds many meters deep, still visible along Tyre's shoreline, mark centuries of industrial-scale crushing and dyeing. Producing a single gram of dye took as many as twelve thousand mollusks, and under Rome the color became the exclusive mark of imperial rank, worth more than its weight in gold. By 117 CE Tyre's dye works had already supplied kings and emperors for well over a thousand years.
properties.image_credit: Bolinus brandaris, the spiny dye-murex used for Tyrian purple · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Describes the murex snail and the process of extracting and dyeing with Tyrian purple.

properties.name_english: Thrones of Astarte Sanctuary, Ain Baal
properties.notes: At the spring sanctuary of Ain el-Baal south of Tyre, Phoenician worshippers carved stone 'thrones of Astarte,' flanked by winged, cherub-headed lions, as offerings to the city's chief goddess. One inscribed throne excavated here, dated to the Hellenistic period, now stands in Beirut's National Museum. The shrine sat beside the same springs that fed Tyre's own water supply, tying worship of Astarte directly to the city's lifeline. These open-air Phoenician shrines carried on through the Roman period, when Astarte still appeared on Tyre's civic coinage.
properties.image_credit: Throne of Astarte from the region of Tyre, Hellenistic period · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Tyre's hippodrome at the Al-Bass necropolis was one of antiquity's largest, nearly 480 meters long with tiered seating for tens of thousands of chariot-race spectators. It rose alongside a monumental triumphal arch and a new aqueduct as part of a building program tied to Emperor Hadrian's tour of the eastern provinces around 130 CE, when Tyre was elevated to metropolis status. Hadrian succeeded Trajan only in August 117 CE, so this entire ceremonial complex postdates the snapshot by more than a decade. In 117 CE the approach road to Al-Bass was still an ordinary Roman-period thoroughfare, not yet the grand racing venue later tourists know.
properties.image_credit: Roman Hippodrome, Tyre, Lebanon · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL III 14149
ancient_sources.work: Roman milestone recording construction of the Via Nova Traiana
ancient_sources.note: This Trajanic milestone records the new road built from Bostra to the Red Sea after Rome turned the former Nabataean kingdom into the province of Arabia, with Bostra as the road's starting point for mile-counting.

properties.notes: Trajan ordered this new imperial highway built immediately after annexing the Nabataean kingdom, running 267 miles south from Bostra through Petra to the Red Sea port of Aila. Governor Gaius Claudius Severus oversaw the work, and dated milestones show the road substantially finished by 111 CE, just three years before the 117 CE snapshot. The Via Nova Traiana replaced the old caravan King's Highway with a paved, garrisoned Roman route and fixed Bostra permanently as Arabia Petraea's northern gateway and the province's chief military and trade artery.

This triple-arched gateway marked Bosra's eastern approach while the city was still a Nabataean caravan capital, decades before Trajan's legions arrived. Its carved stonework follows Nabataean decorative taste even though its arched form already matched Roman fashion current across the region. The gate opened onto a 300-meter paved processional road leading into Bosra's sacred precinct. Still standing when Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE, it kept welcoming caravans and travelers into the new provincial capital straight through Trajan's reign.
properties.image_credit: Nabataean Doorway and Arch at Bosra, Syria · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Dushara was the chief god of the Nabataean pantheon, and Bosra's temple to him anchored a sacred precinct of three temples reached by a monumental arch and a colonnaded processional road. Built while Bosra served as the Nabataean kingdom's northern royal seat under King Rabbel II, the temple was already old by the time Trajan's officials arrived in 106 CE. Romans elsewhere equated Dushara with Dionysus, but at Bosra his cult and shrine carried on largely unchanged through the new province's first decade of Roman rule.

Beside the temple of Dushara, Bosra's sacred precinct held a second shrine to Ba'al-Shamin, 'Lord of the Heavens,' a sky god worshipped across the Nabataean and wider Semitic world. The temple formed part of an interconnected religious complex sharing the precinct's processional road and monumental gate, showing the layered pantheon Nabataean Bosra maintained before Roman annexation. When Trajan made Bosra capital of Arabia Petraea in 106 CE, this temple and its neighbors were already generations old, handing the new Roman provincial capital a religious skyline it inherited entirely from its Nabataean past.

Bosra's black basalt theatre, one of the best-preserved Roman theatres anywhere, seated roughly seventeen thousand people around a stage over forty-five meters wide. Some sources link its start to Trajan's reign, but the fuller weight of archaeological scholarship places its monumental construction in the second quarter to second half of the 2nd century CE, after Trajan died in August 117. At the 117 CE snapshot Bosra was an eleven-year-old provincial capital still built mostly of inherited Nabataean structures; its famous theatre almost certainly did not yet stand in the form visitors see today.
properties.image_credit: Roman Theatre in Bosra · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Bulla Regia's civic forum covered more than 1,000 square meters and organized the whole Roman townscape after Vespasian granted the city municipium status. Colonnaded porticoes lined every side, backed by a Capitol and a temple to Apollo. Archaeologists uncovered it in a five-year dig starting in 1949. In 117 CE this was still a modest civic square, not yet ringed by the grander facades later wheat wealth would add.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the forum at Bulla Regia, Tunisia

properties.notes: The Capitol crowned the west side of Bulla Regia's forum, a podium roughly 16 meters long dedicated to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. Hadrian's reign funded its construction after the town won colonial status and the name Colonia Aelia Hadriana Augusta Bulla Regia. Steps once led worshippers up to a triple cella overlooking the civic square below. Trajan died on 11 August 117, before ground broke on this temple.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Side view of the Capitol podium at Bulla Regia

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Names Bulla Regia among the free towns of the African interior.

properties.notes: North of the forum stood a temple of Apollo built as three joined sanctuaries, its cult statue of Apollo playing the cithara now displayed at the Bardo Museum. Excavators cleared the site in 1906, finding a cella whose floor was relaid in colored opus sectile stone. That marble paving dates to the early third century, a full century after Trajan died. The temple's earlier core may be older, but no firm pre-117 construction date survives.
properties.image_credit: Historic 1906 excavation photograph via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Temple of Apollo at Bulla Regia photographed shortly after its 1906 excavation

ancient_sources.author: AE 2005, 1690
ancient_sources.note: A later votive altar to Isis Augusta dedicated by P. Aelius Privatus and his wife Cocceia Bassa in fulfillment of a vow, set up before the temple podium after the original construction.

properties.notes: A small temple to Isis stood beside where Bulla Regia's theater would later rise, built in the 1st century against the line of an older Numidian wall. Seven steps climbed to its podium, leading through a pronaos into a cella flanked by six columns on each side. Roman builders repaired the shrine decades after Trajan's reign, well past this map's snapshot. By 11 August 117 this modest temple had already stood for generations.
sources: Institut National du Patrimoine (INP) Tunisia: Bulla Regia

properties.notes: Bulla Regia's covered market measured just 12 by 13 meters yet packed in a dozen shop stalls, six facing north and six south around a portico. Builders raised it in the third century, giving the town a dedicated food market separate from the open forum. An apse on one side likely held a shrine or the market office. Trajan had been dead for more than a century when the first stallholder set up here.

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Bulla Regia as a free town (liberum oppidum) of Numidia. A geographic notice, not a description of the macellum.

properties.notes: Bulla Regia's theater rose under co-emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, its cavea eventually spanning a 60 by 50 meter footprint. Marble statues of both emperors once stood near the stage and are now in the Bardo Museum. A fourth-century remodel added the orchestra's surviving mosaic of a bear. Ground broke on this theater roughly 45 years after Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Aerial view of the ruined Roman theatre at Bulla Regia, Tunisia

ancient_sources.author: Pliny the Elder
ancient_sources.note: Lists Bulla Regia as a free town (liberum oppidum) of Numidia. A geographic notice, not a description of the theatre.

ancient_sources.author: ILAfr 454
ancient_sources.note: Praises Julia Memmia for the extraordinary magnificence of the baths she funded for the city's beautification and public health.

properties.notes: Bulla Regia's largest bathing complex takes its name from Julia Memmia, daughter of a local consul, who funded its construction in the early third century. Bathers moved through a gymnasium, changing rooms, and a vaulted frigidarium. Excavators clearing the site between 1909 and 1924 uncovered a shell-shaped mosaic decorating one apse. Trajan's empire had already given way to the Severan dynasty by the time these baths opened.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Memmian Baths at Bulla Regia

properties.notes: The House of Amphitrite is one of Bulla Regia's semi-subterranean mansions, its lower rooms sunk underground and lit by a small open courtyard to escape the summer heat. A triclinium floor there carries a mosaic long nicknamed for Amphitrite, though scholars now read it as Venus rising from the sea flanked by tritons and fish. The house belongs to the 2nd-3rd century building boom that made Bulla Regia famous. Construction began decades after Trajan's death in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Marine Venus mosaic nicknamed Amphitrite, House of Amphitrite, Bulla Regia

properties.notes: The House of the Hunt paired a colonnaded peristyle of 19 by 13 meters above ground with a sunken underground suite for the hottest months. Eight ornamented pillars with hexagonal openings held up its underground hall to shed weight from the vault. A hunting mosaic added to the property in the 4th century gave the house its name. Builders broke ground here roughly a century after Trajan's reign ended in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Underground peristyle court of the House of the Hunt, Bulla Regia

properties.notes: The House of the Fisherman held a compact underground suite lit by a small courtyard fountain, its plan mirroring the larger House of the Hunt next door. One small room preserves a mosaic of a fisherman working the water. Late Roman owners later swallowed up a public street to fuse this house with its neighboring insula. None of this existed yet on the day Trajan died in August 117 CE.

properties.name_english: Alexandria Uprising of the Kitos War
properties.notes: Jewish rebels under Lukuas overran Alexandria in 116 CE after the Roman governor fled, burning the tomb of Pompey and torching temples across the city. An initial clash saw Alexandria's Greek population routed before they regrouped and killed the Jews trapped inside the city. Trajan dispatched his top general Marcius Turbo with a fleet, cavalry, and infantry to retake Egypt. By August 117 Turbo had crushed the revolt and driven its survivors toward Judaea.

ancient_sources.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Jewish uprising against the Greeks of Alexandria and Trajan's dispatch of Marcius Turbo with land and sea forces.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Jewish revolts across Cyrenaica, Egypt, and Cyprus during Trajan's reign and their suppression.

properties.image_credit: O. Von Corven, 19th-century engraving, via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century engraving imagining the grand public buildings of ancient Alexandria

properties.notes: Ptolemy IV built this mausoleum around 215 BCE to hold Alexander's body alongside the Ptolemaic kings. Julius Caesar wept before the glass coffin in 48 BCE, and Augustus broke off part of the mummy's nose reaching in to touch its crown in 30 BCE. Caligula later took its breastplate to wear at gladiator shows. In 117 CE the tomb still stood where the Canopic Way crossed the Street of the Soma, a required stop for visiting emperors.

ancient_sources.author: Suetonius
ancient_sources.note: Describes Augustus viewing Alexander's body and accidentally breaking off part of the nose.

properties.image_credit: 19th-century engraving · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century reconstruction drawing of Alexander the Great's funeral catafalque, based on Diodorus's description, en route to his tomb in Alexandria

properties.notes: Alexandria's Gymnasium ran for over a stadium, more than 180 meters, of colonnades along the city's central avenue. Strabo called it the most beautiful of all the city's public buildings, its courtyards shaded by groves and hosting the law courts as well as athletics. Alexandrian youths trained here for citizenship status that carried real legal weight under Roman rule. It remained a working civic center through Trajan's reign.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Calls the Gymnasium the most beautiful of Alexandria's buildings, with porticos over a stadium in length.

properties.image_credit: Historical map · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Map of Ptolemaic Alexandria showing the ancient city's districts and monuments including the Gymnasium

properties.notes: Alexander's architect Dinocrates laid out this street as the city's east-west spine when Alexandria was founded in 331 BCE. Colonnaded along its full length and roughly 30 meters wide, it ran from the Gate of the Sun to the Gate of the Moon, passing the Gymnasium, the Soma, and the theater. Strabo marveled at how straight and grand it was for a working thoroughfare. By 117 CE it had carried imperial processions and daily market traffic for over four centuries.
properties.image_credit: Engraving by L.F. Cassas, 1784 · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 1784 engraving of the Canopic Street (Canopic Way) in Alexandria by Louis-Francois Cassas

properties.notes: Alexandrians built this artificial cone-shaped hill as a shrine to Pan, reachable by a spiral path winding to its summit. Strabo climbed it around 25 BCE and described a full panoramic view over the entire city from the top. A park surrounded it, and the grounds doubled as a pleasure garden for Alexandrians. The mound still rose over the district later called Kom el-Dikka in 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Paneum as an artificial mound shaped like a fir cone, climbed by a spiral path, with a view over the whole city.

properties.image_credit: Historical map · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Map of Hellenistic and Roman Alexandria showing the ancient city's monuments and topography including the Paneum

properties.notes: Strabo described the Poseidium as a temple projecting like an elbow from the Emporium into the Great Harbor, a sacred landmark for ships entering port. Mark Antony built his retreat, the Timonium, right beside it after his defeat at Actium in 31 BCE. Priests here blessed the merchant fleets carrying Alexandria's grain toward Rome. The temple still marked the harbor entrance when Trajan's fleet sailed for the Parthian campaign.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Poseidium as a temple on a promontory projecting from the Emporium into the harbor.

properties.image_credit: Historical map · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Map of ancient Alexandria showing the Great Harbor area where the Poseidium stood

properties.notes: The Emporium was Alexandria's customs house and commercial exchange, where Egyptian grain, glass, and papyrus were weighed, taxed, and loaded onto Mediterranean ships. It sat directly on the Great Harbor between the Poseidium and the naval docks. Egypt alone supplied roughly a third of Rome's grain dole by Trajan's reign, and it all passed through buildings like this one. In 117 CE its warehouses and quays remained the busiest waterfront in the empire's second city.
properties.image_credit: Historical map · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Map of Ptolemaic Alexandria showing the harbor district including the Emporium

properties.notes: Alexandria faced two waterfronts at once: the Mediterranean to the north and Lake Mareotis to the south, linked to the Nile by canal. Strabo judged the lake harbor even richer than the sea harbor, since it handled the entire flow of Egyptian grain, wine, and glass coming downriver. Warehouses, glass workshops, and vineyards lined its shore for kilometers. The lake port still moved Nile cargo into the city's granaries when Trajan died in 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Strabo
ancient_sources.note: States that the harbor on Lake Mareotis was richer than the sea harbor.

properties.image_credit: Photo by Amr Fayez · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Modern photo of Lake Mariout (ancient Lake Mareotis) near Alexandria, Egypt

properties.notes: Alexandria's Great Synagogue, called the Diplostoon for its double colonnade, was so vast that an attendant waved a flag to cue the congregation's response because voices couldn't carry to the back. The Talmud held that whoever had not seen it had never seen the glory of Israel in exile. Alexandria's Jewish community, among the largest in the ancient world, worshipped here for over three centuries. Roman forces under Marcius Turbo destroyed it in 116 CE while crushing the Kitos War revolt, less than a year before Trajan died.

ancient_sources.author: Babylonian Talmud
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Alexandrian synagogue as a great double-colonnaded basilica with seventy-one golden seats.

properties.notes: Two of Alexandria's five alphabetically named districts, most prominently the Delta quarter in the northeast, housed the largest Jewish community outside Judaea. Philo, writing around 38 CE, described a population dense enough to fill whole neighborhoods with synagogues, workshops, and self-governing courts. By August 117 CE this quarter's Jewish population had been massacred and its institutions gutted, the toll of the previous year's Kitos War revolt and its Roman suppression under Marcius Turbo.
properties.image_credit: Historical photograph, 1898 · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 1898 photograph of the Jewish quarter (historic Delta Quarter) in Alexandria, Egypt

properties.notes: Villagers raised this limestone temple to Pnepheros and Petesouchos, two local forms of the crocodile god Sobek, with roots reaching back to the first century BCE. Nero's reign saw it formally rededicated to the same pair of gods. Mummified crocodiles have been found in its inner sanctuary, matching the sacred-animal cult practiced across Faiyum temples. The temple stayed in active use well past 117 CE, into the fourth century.

A second, larger limestone temple stood at the settlement's north end, built in the early Roman period in a purely Egyptian style with only its corner columns showing Greco-Roman influence. Unlike the South Temple it carries almost no relief decoration, an unusually plain design for a Faiyum cult building. It anchored the northern end of Karanis's temple precinct throughout the height of the Roman Empire, including in 117 CE.

Granary C123 was built in the first century CE to hold Karanis's wheat surplus before shipment down the Nile. University of Michigan excavators recovered 37 papyrus documents from inside it between 1928 and 1931, records tracking who deposited grain and when. Fayum villages like Karanis fed the Roman grain dole, and buildings like this one formed the first link in that supply chain. The granary was still receiving harvests when Trajan died in August 117 CE.

Karanis's mudbrick houses survived so completely, some still roofed, that they preserve entire room layouts, wall niches, and storage bins intact. The two-story House of the Banker points to real wealth built up inside this farming village. University of Michigan excavators pulled thousands of papyri directly from trash heaps and floor fill inside these houses between 1924 and 1935. The desert climate preserved everyday Roman-Egyptian domestic life here better than almost any other site in the empire.
properties.image_credit: Photo by Roland Unger · Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
properties.image_alt: Well-preserved mudbrick ruins at the Karanis archaeological site

properties.notes: Karanis households built at least six dovecotes, mudbrick towers up to two stories tall lined with nesting jars, some attached to houses and others run as standalone businesses. The two largest towers together housed around 1,250 birds. Villagers sold the squabs as a delicacy and the manure as fertilizer for land the Nile flood couldn't reach, and Roman tax collectors levied a specific tax on every productive nest. These pigeon-houses operated at Karanis from the first century BCE through the fourth century CE, squarely spanning 117 CE.

Karanis's Roman bath held a large plastered room with a brick bench running around the walls and a smaller alcove holding the tub itself, its painted wall decoration still visible when excavators uncovered it. Public baths were a hallmark of Roman provincial life, reaching even a farming village deep in the Faiyum. Its construction is generally placed in the second century CE, most likely after Trajan's reign in 117 CE. The dry site preserved its roof and painted plaster far better than most Roman baths anywhere in the empire.

Cyrene's largest temple was an octastyle Doric giant begun around 500 BCE, larger in floor area than the Parthenon. Its cella once held a colossal marble Zeus modeled on the Olympian original. Jewish rebels tore through the sanctuary in 115 CE, snapping columns and gutting the roof in the opening violence of the Kitos War. On the day Trajan died the ruin still stood untouched, its rebuilding under Hadrian still years away.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Standing columns of the Temple of Zeus at Cyrene

ancient_sources.author: Eusebius
ancient_sources.note: Describes the Jewish revolt of 115-117 CE that devastated Cyrene under Trajan. A citywide account of the destruction, not a description of the Temple of Zeus itself.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: Records the scale of the killing in Cyrene during the same revolt. A citywide account, not a description of this temple.

properties.notes: Two springs below the acropolis cliff marked, in myth, where Apollo carried off the nymph Cyrene and fathered the city's founder. Herodotus and Pindar both praised this water, and Greeks built their sacred quarter around it from the 7th century BCE. Jewish rebels burned the temple here in 115-116 CE during the Kitos War. By Trajan's death in August 117 CE the terraces stood scorched, though the spring still ran.

ancient_sources.author: Herodotus
ancient_sources.note: Mentions the spring of Apollo at Cyrene.

ancient_sources.author: Eusebius
ancient_sources.note: Names the temple of Apollo among those torn down by Jewish rebels at Cyrene.

properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Temple of Apollo at Cyrene

properties.notes: Cyrene's open civic square held the tomb of Battos, the city's 7th-century BCE founder, and a monument to the naval victory at Actium. Shops and long colonnaded stoas ran along its sides while assemblies and trials filled the open ground between. The square had served as Cyrene's political heart for more than 700 years by the time Trajan died in August 117 CE. Fires from the 115-116 CE Jewish revolt had scorched its porticoes only months before.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the agora at Cyrene

properties.notes: A 2nd-century BCE gymnasium on Cyrene's acropolis ridge was rebuilt under Augustus into a Doric-colonnaded court honoring the deified Caesar. A civil basilica went up alongside it under the later Flavian emperors, turning the complex into the city's second forum. Jewish rebels badly damaged the Caesareum in the destruction of 115-116 CE. It still lay in ruins when Trajan died in August 117 CE, awaiting Hadrian's restoration.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the gymnasium-Caesareum complex at Cyrene

properties.notes: A bath complex rose on the northwest edge of the Sanctuary of Apollo during Trajan's reign, its hypocaust floors still visible today. Bathers here numbered among the last Cyreneans to enjoy the sanctuary before the Jewish revolt convulsed the city in 115-116 CE. The baths were among the newest buildings standing in Cyrene when Trajan died in August 117 CE. Hadrian later enlarged and restored them.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman Baths of Trajan within the Sanctuary of Apollo, Cyrene

properties.notes: Cyrene's acropolis crowned the western ridge where Greek colonists from Thera first settled around 630 BCE, holding the old royal palace and the spring feeding the Sanctuary of Apollo below. Augustus's proconsul Lucanius Proculus restored its buildings in the early 1st century CE. The hilltop had anchored the city for more than 700 years by the time Trajan died in 117 CE. Violence from the recent Jewish revolt had reached its slopes only months earlier.

A small roofed theatre stood tucked behind the Stoa of Hermes and Herakles at the edge of Cyrene's agora, built for council business and public readings rather than the spectacles staged at the city's larger theatre. Its compact covered form let meetings continue through Cyrenaica's rainy winters. The odeon had served the agora quarter for generations by August 117 CE, when Trajan died with the empire at its largest extent.

A Roman-period forum stood in Cyrene's civic center, named for Proculus, the official credited with building or restoring it. Over a hundred free-standing Doric columns lined its rectangular court, with a small temple at the center and a basilica along one side. Merchants and magistrates used the space daily as Cyrene's second marketplace and law court. It stood exactly as built when Trajan died in August 117 CE.

Terraces cut into a ravine south of Cyrene's walls, in the Wadi Bel Ghadir valley, held the sanctuary of Demeter and Persephone, founded around 600 BCE and built up across three sloped levels. Pig bones, lamps, and terracotta figurines left by generations of worshippers came out of its soil by the thousand. Jewish rebels tore down this temple along with five others across the city during the revolt of 115-116 CE. It lay wrecked and unrepaired when Trajan died in August 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: Eusebius
ancient_sources.note: Names the temple of Demeter among those destroyed by Jewish rebels at Cyrene.

properties.name_english: Cyrene Revolt of the Kitos War
properties.notes: In 115-116 CE Cyrene's Jewish community rose against Rome under a leader named Lukuas, tearing down the temples of Apollo, Artemis, Hecate, Demeter, Isis, and Pluto. Cassius Dio put the death toll at 220,000 non-Jewish residents of the city and region. Quintus Marcius Turbo, sent by Trajan, crushed the revolt through 117 CE, leaving Cyrene a burned, half-empty city. Hadrian later funded its rebuilding with confiscated rebel property.

ancient_sources.author: Cassius Dio
ancient_sources.note: States that 220,000 people were killed in Cyrene during the revolt, describing atrocities committed by the rebels.

properties.notes: Apollonia served as Cyrene's outport from the city's founding, its anchorage sheltered behind a long stone breakwater built into the Mediterranean. Roman fleets used the harbor as a naval base guarding the Cyrenaican coast. Coastal subsidence has since dropped the ancient harbor works nearly 4 meters underwater, so much of what Roman sailors walked on in 117 CE now lies submerged and visible only through clear water.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View of the ancient port ruins at Apollonia, Cyrenaica

properties.notes: A Greek theatre with rows cut into the hillside outside Apollonia's walls had entertained the port town since the 3rd century BCE. Domitian's engineers added a new stone stage building late in the 1st century CE, updating the old Hellenistic cavea for Roman tastes. The theatre still stood in full use facing the sea when Trajan died in August 117 CE.

Massive Hellenistic fortification walls ran along Apollonia's shoreline, raised to guard the harbor town from the 4th century BCE onward. They enclosed the city through the Roman conquest of Cyrenaica and stood unbreached through Trajan's reign. In August 117 CE these walls still marked the edge of Roman Apollonia, centuries before Byzantine engineers rebuilt them on a grander scale.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Hellenistic defensive walls at Apollonia, Cyrenaica

properties.notes: A bathhouse rose on Apollonia's waterfront under Hadrian, just after Trajan's death, and was later restored under Caracalla. Its ruins still stand today beside the ancient harbor mole. In August 117 CE this stretch of shore held only older buildings; Hadrian's baths were still years from being built.

Tombs cut into the hills around Apollonia held generations of the port city's dead, including rock-hewn hypogea reused for centuries after their first burials. Rescue excavations in 2012 uncovered three such hypogea and twenty rectangular tombs, some floored in mosaic. The cemetery had already served Apollonia for hundreds of years by the time Trajan died in 117 CE.

Apollonia's oldest religious building was a Doric temple raised outside the city walls, identified by excavators as the port town's first pagan shrine. Greek settlers built it not long after founding Apollonia around 630 BCE. The temple had stood watch over the approach to the harbor for more than seven centuries when Trajan died in August 117 CE.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII 26609
ancient_sources.note: The pagus and civitas of Thugga thank L. Marcius Simplex for donating the Capitol; companion bases at the same find-spot honor his father and brother.

properties.notes: The Capitol crowned Thugga's forum with a temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, dedicated in 166 CE under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Byzantine soldiers later built it into their fortress wall, which is why six of its Corinthian columns still stand 12 meters tall today. In 117 CE this corner of the forum held only open pavement. The temple that made Dougga famous was still half a century away.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Rome consecrated this hilltop temple to Saturn in 195 CE, but the ground had been sacred for centuries before that. Excavators found a Punic sanctuary to Baal Hammon underneath, its votive pits packed with neo-Punic stelae from the 2nd century BCE. The Romans renamed the god rather than abandon the site. In 117 CE the old Punic shrine still stood; Saturn's temple was 78 years away.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Dougga's theatre seated 3,500 people and was paid for entirely by one local priest, Publius Marcius Quadratus, who dedicated it in 168-169 CE. Carved into the hillside below the future Capitol site, it still hosts a summer festival today. In 117 CE that hillside was bare rock. Marcus Aurelius had not yet even become emperor.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL
ancient_sources.note: The theatre's dedicatory inscription recording that Publius Marcius Quadratus built it for his hometown at his own expense in AD 168-169, celebrated with games and public distributions.

properties.notes: The Licinii family funded these winter baths for Thugga under Caracalla, around 212-217 CE, nearly a century after Trajan's death. Bathers moved through vaulted halls floored in geometric mosaic before a later inscription under Gallienus recorded repairs. In 117 CE this stretch of the lower town was still open ground with houses, no bathhouse in sight.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Thugga raised this triumphal arch in 228 CE to thank Alexander Severus for imperial favor, framing the road toward Carthage. It formed one of the town's grandest gateways for travelers arriving from the coast. In 117 CE, 111 years earlier, that road ran past open fields with no arch standing over it.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: PETRAE epigraphic database (Institut Ausonius, Université Bordeaux Montaigne)
ancient_sources.work: Record for the dedicatory inscription of the Arch of Alexander Severus, Thugga (Dougga)
ancient_sources.ref: petrae.huma-num.fr, record for Thugga/Dougga (CIL VIII, Africa Proconsularis series)
ancient_sources.note: Critical edition of the arch's dedicatory inscription, which names Alexander Severus and fixes the monument's erection to 228 CE, more than a century after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: Septimius Severus elevated Thugga to a municipium, and the town answered in 205 CE with this triumphal arch on its western approach. The dedication doubled as thanks for the town's new civic status. In 117 CE Thugga was still just a civitas of mixed Numidian and Roman citizens, 88 years from that promotion.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The triumphal Arch of Septimius Severus at Dougga, Tunisia

properties.notes: Built between 222 and 235 CE under Alexander Severus, this temple wrapped a curved portico of two dozen columns around a shrine to Juno Caelestis, the Romanized form of the Punic moon goddess Tanit. It ranks among the best-preserved temples in Roman Africa. In 117 CE the hillside it occupies was empty ground, more than a century before construction began.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL
