ancient_sources.note: The temple's dedicatory inscription recording its construction and dedication to Caelestis Augusta by Quintus Gabinius Rufus Felix Beatianus.

ancient_sources.author: ILAfr 558
ancient_sources.note: Thugga's earliest dated inscription, recording the paving of the forum and the ground before the Temple of Caesar, plus an altar of Augustus, an early temple of Saturn, and an arch, funded by L. Postumius Chius and his sons.

properties.notes: Thugga's forum served as the town's civic heart from the early Roman empire onward, a compact square of roughly 924 square meters ringed by porticoes. A Numidian-era temple to King Masinissa, dedicated in 139 BCE, lies buried beneath its paving. By 117 CE the forum had already anchored daily business for generations, decades before the Capitol rose across its northern edge.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The Roman forum area at Dougga, Tunisia

properties.notes: Thugga's covered market opened in 54 CE, a colonnaded courtyard of shops ending in an apse where a statue of Mercury watched over trade. Merchants sold meat, fish and produce here for centuries. By 117 CE the macellum had already served the town for 63 years, one of its oldest standing public buildings.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A small temple to Mercury stood at the northern edge of Thugga's forum, its rectangular cella flanked by two curved exedrae. It belongs to the same late-2nd-century building phase as the neighboring Square of the Winds, raised between 180 and 192 CE under Commodus. In 117 CE that corner of the forum held no temple at all, just open pavement.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Temple of Mercury at Dougga, Tunisia

properties.notes: Dougga built this small semicircular temple to Pietas Augusta, Imperial Piety, in the 2nd century CE along the street linking the theatre to the Capitol. Two columns and two pilasters framed its curved facade. In 117 CE that stretch of street ran past ordinary houses; the temple was still generations away.
properties.image_credit: Photo via Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: The semicircular Temple of Pietas Augusta at Dougga, Tunisia

properties.notes: Utica's forum grew unusually large after Rome made the city its first African provincial capital in 146 BCE, following Carthage's destruction. Cato the Younger crossed this square in April 46 BCE before withdrawing to end his own life rather than accept Caesar's clemency. Excavators found the pavement rebuilt across some four centuries of continuous use. By 117 CE it had already anchored the city's civic life for 263 years.

ancient_sources.author: Plutarch
ancient_sources.note: Describes Cato's final days and suicide at Utica in April 46 BCE, in the city where this forum stood.

properties.notes: Utica's amphitheatre was cut into a hillside south of the forum, part of a wave of public building that transformed the city in the 2nd century CE. It joined a theatre, grand baths and a possible circus as the Roman colony reached its height under Hadrian. In 117 CE that hillside was still undeveloped slope; the amphitheater lay years in the future.

Utica built an open-air theatre within its Roman grid after Octavian made the city a municipium in 36 BCE. A second, larger theatre would eventually rise on a nearby hillside in the 2nd century CE. By 117 CE this first theatre had already entertained Utica's residents for about 137 years.

Utica's extensive baths expanded to monumental scale during the 2nd-century building boom that also gave the city its amphitheater. Bathers moved through halls faced with Proconnesian marble shipped in from across the Mediterranean. In 117 CE that marble hall did not exist yet; the baths as they stand were still ahead under Hadrian's patronage.

The House of the Cascade takes its name from a marble-lined pool where water spilled through a fountain in a Roman townhouse built in the 1st century CE. Its floor mosaics of fishing cupids and tritons predate similar scenes elsewhere in Roman Africa by a full century. Archaeologists still count it among the best-preserved private houses at Utica. By 117 CE the house had stood for decades, its cascade still running for a wealthy Uticensian family.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The House of the Grand Oecus was the largest private residence excavated at Utica, its formal reception hall opening onto a garden pool. Wealthy owners occupied it for more than 400 years, from the early empire into late antiquity. Mosaics of fish and dolphins hint at an owner tied to the maritime trade running through Utica's harbor. In 117 CE the house was already an established fixture of the city's elite quarter.

Utica's harbor served ships for centuries before the Mejerda River's silt pushed the coastline more than 10 kilometers away, stranding the ancient port far inland. Phoenician sailors had used this anchorage since at least the 8th century BCE, making it older than Carthage's own harbor by tradition. French engineer A. Daux first traced its quays in 1869. In 117 CE the harbor still opened directly onto the Mediterranean, moving grain for Rome's African province.

Utica's Punic-period cemeteries, known as Ile and La Berge, held cremation burials dating from the 7th to the 5th century BCE. Grave goods and urns recovered here document the city's earliest Phoenician settlers, generations before Carthage rose to prominence nearby. The burial grounds fell out of use long before Rome's arrival. By 117 CE this necropolis had already lain abandoned for roughly 400 years, buried beneath the Roman colony above it.

properties.name_english: Legionary Fortress of Legio III Augusta
properties.notes: Emperor Vespasian settled Legio III Augusta into a single permanent fortress here in 75 CE after decades split across smaller Numidian outposts. The camp anchored Rome's desert frontier for over fifty years while veterans retired to farms in the surrounding territory. In August 117 CE the legion still called Theveste home; only under Hadrian did it march west to a new fortress at Lambaesis.

properties.name_english: Forum of the Colonia of Theveste
properties.notes: Trajan raised Theveste from legionary settlement to chartered Roman colonia, folding retired soldiers and their farms into full civic status. A forum anchored the new city, seating the magistrates who governed the Tebessa plain. By August 117 CE the colonia was not yet twenty years old, its public buildings modest next to the marble city that later generations built.

Built in the early 3rd century CE under the Severan dynasty, this Corinthian temple rises nine meters on a raised podium and survives today as one of the best-preserved Roman temples in Algeria. Its facade still stands almost complete, a rarity for North African religious architecture. In 117 CE the ground where it rose was still open space inside the young colonia, nearly a century before construction began.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII.1 7094-7098
ancient_sources.note: Five inscriptions across the arch's attic dedicated to the deified Septimius Severus, to Julia Domna, and to Caracalla.

properties.notes: A local prefect named Gaius Cornelius Egrilianus funded this four-fronted triumphal arch by testamentary bequest, and the city dedicated it in 216 CE to Caracalla, Julia Domna, and the deified Septimius Severus. Carved reliefs of Oceanus, Minerva, and the personification of the city still survive on its faces. Byzantine builders later folded the arch into their city wall as a gate. In 117 CE this monument did not yet exist.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Caracalla, Tébessa (ancient Theveste) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Builders raised Theveste's amphitheater on the left bank of the Wadi Zarour in the 4th century CE, seating crowds for games on the edge of the colonia. Its arena floor and lower seating tiers still survive among the town's Roman ruins today. In August 117 CE this ground stood empty, two centuries before construction began here.

properties.name_english: City Walls and Citadel of Theveste
properties.notes: Justinian's general Solomon rebuilt Theveste behind a massive square citadel wall in the early 6th century, studded with twelve towers and four gates. Roman column drums scavenged from older buildings were built directly into the new Byzantine masonry. The older Arch of Caracalla was absorbed into this wall as a gate. In 117 CE no fortification ring yet enclosed the young colonia.

A sprawling Christian basilica complex grew up at Theveste honoring Crispina, a Numidian noblewoman beheaded near the city in 304 CE for refusing to sacrifice to the emperors. A mosaic inscription dates its central shrine to 350 CE, with further wings added into the 5th century, making it one of the largest basilica complexes in Roman North Africa. In 117 CE neither her cult nor any building here yet existed.

Numidian kings built this hillside sanctuary to Baal-Hammon just south of Cirta, and under Massinissa's long 2nd-century-BCE reign it grew rich enough that worshippers left behind nearly a thousand carved votive stelae. Rome later folded the god into the cult of Saturn, and Latin dedications joined the older Punic ones on the same hill. By 117 CE the sanctuary had already stood for generations as one of Numidia's great religious sites.

Numidian kings fortified Cirta's rock plateau with an embossed ashlar rampart long before Rome arrived, exploiting cliffs that drop over 200 meters into the Rhumel gorge on three sides. Roman Cirta inherited these defenses after Caesar's veteran Publius Sittius settled his men here in 46 BCE, founding the Colonia Sittianorum. Stretches of the ancient walling still stand inside the old citadel today. In 117 CE these walls still guarded one of Numidia's most naturally defensible cities.

Roman engineers carried water into Cirta from the spring at Ain Bou Merzoug, crossing the 200-meter-deep Rhumel gorge on a masonry bridge whose fragmentary arches still stand in the valley below the old town. No inscription records its exact building year, and estimates for its date range across the 2nd century CE. Because the construction date cannot be pinned down with confidence, this entry is flagged as not yet standing at the 117 CE snapshot.

Thuburbo Maius rebuilt its civic forum in 161 CE, laying out a square colonnaded on three sides with shops behind the portico. A wide staircase at its north end climbed straight up to the new Capitol. Its paving stones still show the wear of two centuries of foot traffic. In 117 CE this ground held only an earlier, smaller square, not the piazza that survives today.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Colonnaded forum ruins at Thuburbo Maius

properties.notes: Under Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, Thuburbo Maius raised a Capitol in 168 CE on a monumental podium reached by a broad flight of stairs from the forum. Excavators found a sandaled marble foot from a cult statue of Jupiter, estimated at 7.5 meters tall. Carved inscriptions on the building name both emperors alongside Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. In 117 CE this hillside stood empty, more than fifty years before ground was broken.
properties.image_credit: Capitolium of Thuburbo Majus · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Pauline Cuzel
ancient_sources.work: Thuburbo Maius et Carthage sous le Haut-Empire
ancient_sources.note: Epigraphic study reconstructing the Capitolium's long dedicatory inscription from recovered marble fragments (preserved in the Bardo Museum), naming Marcus Aurelius and Commodus and dating the temple's dedication to 168 CE, decades after the 117 CE snapshot.

properties.notes: A round temple ringed by a peristyle and closed off by four apses honored Mercury, patron of the merchants who passed through Thuburbo Maius on the inland road linking Carthage to Numidia. It rose next to the Capitol under Marcus Aurelius, in the second half of the 2nd century CE. Its circular plan set inside a square precinct is almost unique among Roman temples in Africa. In 117 CE the site was open ground; Mercury's temple was still decades from being built.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Thuburbo Maius built its Winter Baths in the 2nd century CE, after Hadrian raised the town to municipium status and gave its citizens a rank worth building for. The complex covered 1,600 square meters and opened onto a public square where two streets crossed. Columns of reddish marble quarried at distant Simitthus framed its entrance. In 117 CE Hadrian had not yet become emperor, and this bath block did not exist.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The larger of Thuburbo Maius's two bathhouses, the Summer Baths spread across roughly 2,800 square meters of cold, warm, and hot rooms fed by three large cisterns. Records show the complex already needed restoration by 136 CE, placing its original construction in the early 2nd century. Emperor Constantius II rebuilt it again in 361 CE to revive the aging town. Its exact founding year was never recorded, so it is marked absent from the 117 CE map.

In 225 CE, Petronius Felix and his sons paid for a colonnaded exercise yard wedged between the two bathhouses of Thuburbo Maius. Wrestlers, boxers, and pankration fighters trained under its Corinthian portico before crossing into the Summer Baths next door. An inscription on site still credits the Petronii family by name. In 117 CE this courtyard was more than a century away from being built.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: ILAfr 271
ancient_sources.note: Records P. Petronius Felix, ex-tribune and primipilaris, and his sons building the palaestra at their own expense, with distributions made to the town's decurions and officials at its dedication.

properties.notes: Thuburbo Maius built a covered market beside its forum during the town's 2nd-century building boom, giving merchants stalls under a colonnade a short walk from the Capitol. Fragments of its mosaic floor still show the produce once sold there. It served the same trade route that funded the nearby Temple of Mercury. No precise construction year survives, so it is marked absent from the 117 CE map out of caution.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Thuburbo Maius worshipped Baal Hammon on a hill above the town long before Rome arrived; the standing Roman temple that replaced the Punic shrine dates only to the 2nd or 3rd century CE, when the old god was renamed Saturn. Its hilltop position gave the sanctuary a commanding view over the entire settlement below. The renaming pattern repeated at towns across Roman Africa. In 117 CE a Punic-style shrine still occupied this spot, not the Roman temple whose walls survive.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Southeast of the Summer Baths, Thuburbo Maius kept a small porticoed sanctuary to Baalat, a Punic goddess who was chief deity of Byblos in Phoenicia. The shrine shows how thoroughly Carthaginian religion outlasted Carthage in inland Africa. Its surviving colonnaded form dates to the Roman imperial period, in the 2nd or 3rd century CE. In 117 CE this exact structure had not yet been built, though the cult it served was already centuries old.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sufetula's forum opened onto a rarity among Roman towns: three separate temples built side by side, one each for Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, instead of a single shared Capitol. Bridges linked the three raised cellae so priests could cross between them without stepping down to ground level. The complex belongs to Sufetula's 2nd-century building boom, after the town grew wealthy on olive oil. In 117 CE this forum was a smaller Flavian-era square; the triple temple was still decades away.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Three adjoining Roman temples of the Sufetula Capitol

properties.notes: A triple-arched gateway framed the entrance to Sufetula's forum, dedicated in 139 CE to Emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Stonecutters left its four Corinthian column shafts unsmoothed, evidence the arch was never fully finished. It is the one structure at Sufetula whose date historians can fix with certainty, thanks to its own inscription. In 117 CE Antoninus Pius was an unknown senator, and this arch was 22 years from being built.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: in situ dedicatory inscription
ancient_sources.work: attic inscription, Arch of Antoninus Pius
ancient_sources.note: The arch's own (heavily worn) attic inscription carries Antoninus Pius's imperial titulature; it is the only monument at Sufetula whose construction date is fixed by its own text rather than by excavation alone.

properties.notes: Cut into a slope above the Oued Sbeitla, Sufetula's theatre seated roughly 3,500 spectators for plays and civic gatherings. Archaeologists date its standing remains to the 2nd century CE, with rebuilding recorded in the 3rd. It shared its hillside neighborhood with the town's Great Baths, just to the west. In 117 CE Sufetula was still a young Flavian municipium with no stone theatre standing.

East of the forum, Sufetula built a paired bathing complex with separate summer and winter suites linked by a mosaic-floored palaestra measuring 27 by 17 meters. Cruciform hot rooms sat on raised brick piers with clay ducts piping heat beneath bathers' feet. Construction continued into the early 3rd century CE, well after the town's Antonine growth. In 117 CE none of this bathing complex had been built.

At the edge of Sufetula stands the Triumphal Arch of the Tetrarchy, raised for Diocletian and his three co-emperors around 293 CE. It ranks among the best-preserved tetrarchic arches in North Africa, still framing the road into the ruined city. It commemorated the four-way power-sharing system Diocletian built to stabilize the empire after decades of crisis. In 117 CE this arch was over 175 years from being built, and the tetrarchy did not yet exist even as an idea.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Watchtower Wp 1/1 marked the caput limitis, the exact point where the Upper Germanic frontier left the Rhine and struck out overland toward the Taunus hills. Soldiers raised the first wooden tower here under Domitian, planting post number one of a chain that would eventually run more than 550 kilometers to the Danube. From its post above the river a sentry watched both boat traffic on the Rhine and the road climbing away from the crossing. Later garrisons rebuilt the tower in stone, but the site kept its role as the anchor point of the entire Upper Germanic-Raetian frontier.

ancient_sources.author: Historia Augusta
ancient_sources.note: Describes Hadrian separating Roman territory from barbarian lands in regions without a river boundary by driving great timber stakes into the ground and binding them into a continuous palisade, the building program to which this stretch of the Germanic limes belonged.

properties.notes: Roman soldiers cut watchtower Wp 10/15 out of the Odenwald forest in 98 CE, the year Trajan's engineers opened the building phase that carried a patrol road and its towers through the hills above Vielbrunn. The wooden tower rose about twelve meters over the tree line, tall enough to relay a signal along a forested ridge where sightlines ran short. It anchored a newly cleared stretch of the frontier road that let couriers move faster than the terrain would otherwise allow. Archaeologists later used the excavated tower base as the model for a full-scale timber reconstruction on the same spot.

ancient_sources.author: Historia Augusta
ancient_sources.note: Describes Hadrian separating Roman territory from barbarian lands in regions without a river boundary by driving great timber stakes into the ground and binding them into a continuous palisade, the building program to which this stretch of the Germanic limes belonged.

properties.notes: A second watchtower, Wp 10/16, stood barely half a kilometer from its neighbor at Im Oberen Haspel, part of the dense chain of posts the Roman army planted along the Odenwald frontier road. Its garrison watched a stretch of forest where the hills broke direct sightlines between the larger stations, closing a gap in the signal chain. Excavators found the telltale mound of its collapsed wooden tower along with the low ring bank that once surrounded it. The tower belonged to the same building push that Trajan's engineers carried through the Odenwald in the frontier's opening decade.

The watchtower on the Kahler Buckel held the northernmost post on this stretch of the Odenwald limes, standing 530 meters up on a bald summit that gave its garrison a clear line of sight in every direction. A dedication tablet recovered during excavation let archaeologists fix the date of one of its building phases precisely, a rarity among the frontier's hundreds of otherwise anonymous towers. A copy of that inscription now stands on the site while the original is kept in the Badisches Landesmuseum in Karlsruhe. Three superimposed sets of foundation walls, uncovered by excavation, mark where successive towers rose on the same spot.

Watchtower Wp 10/35 stood in the Klosterwald forest, one link among roughly ninety towers the Roman army raised along the Odenwald limes between the Main and Neckar rivers. Like its neighbors it began as a wooden post spaced about 709 meters from the next tower in the chain, close enough to keep constant visual contact along the forested ridge. Soldiers rebuilt it in stone as the frontier matured. Its excavated foundation still marks the site today, a short walk from the better-known tower at Kahler Buckel.

The watchtower known as Vogelbaumhecken took its name from the hedge-lined clearing where Roman surveyors set it along the Odenwald limes. Its garrison stood roughly midway between the towers at Kahler Buckel and Vielbrunn, filling a gap along several kilometers of forested frontier. Excavation uncovered the mound of its collapsed wooden tower and the shallow ditch that once ringed it. The post went up during the early second-century building campaign that gave the Odenwald line its full chain of towers.

Watchtower Wp 10/11 stood on the Sellenplatte above Lützelbach, one of the northern posts on the Odenwald stretch of the limes. Its crew watched a forested section of frontier where the patrol road climbed between the forts at Seckmauern and Würzberg. The tower began in timber and earth, following the pattern of nearly every post the Roman army raised along this line in the frontier's first decades. Its foundation mound still survives in the forest, visible today to hikers following the marked Limes trail.

The watchtower at Schneidershecke guarded a bend in the Odenwald limes near Mudau, its garrison watching the forest below for movement along the frontier. Roman engineers set it into a chain of towers running the line at intervals of a few hundred meters, close enough that a lit beacon or a shout could carry from post to post. The tower began as a wooden structure typical of the frontier's earliest building phase before a later rebuilding in stone. Its buried foundations still lie under the forest floor near the modern hiking route that traces the ancient patrol road.

Watchtower Wp 10/21, known locally as In der Heumatte, held a post on the Odenwald limes between the forts at Hesselbach and Würzberg. Its crew relayed signals along a stretch of frontier where dense forest cut sightlines down to a few hundred meters at a time. The tower started as timber and turf, part of the wave of construction Trajan's army pushed through the Odenwald in the frontier's opening decades. Twentieth-century surveys first mapped its mound and surrounding ditch when archaeologists traced the full course of this limes sector.

The watchtower in the Breitenbrunner Bannholz forest carried a double footprint: a substantial mound from its original timber tower plus the rubble of a stone successor built twenty meters to the north. It stood on the Odenwald limes near Breitenbrunn, part of the chain linking the forts at Würzberg and Hesselbach. Roman troops raised the first wooden tower here during the early second-century push that opened the Odenwald frontier under Trajan. Its paired remains make it one of the more legible tower sites on the entire Odenwald line.

The stone watchtower on the Gaulskopf stood 397 meters up in the Taunus hills, about three kilometers from the fort at Kapersburg it helped to guard. Rebuilt as a full-scale reconstruction in 1926, it survives today as one of the best-restored towers anywhere on the frontier. Its garrison held sightlines across the eastern Hintertaunus and out over the Wetterau plain below. The tower belonged to the wave of posts Trajan's army raised along this stretch of the limes as the frontier hardened into a permanent line.

Watchtower Wp 4/103 stood in the Eckartshäuser Unterwald forest south of what is now Limeshain-Rommelhausen, one link in the Wetterau chain of the Upper Germanic limes. Excavators could still trace both its wooden and stone tower sites side by side in the terrain, a rare look at how a single post was rebuilt over time. The first timber tower went up around 100 CE as Trajan's army pushed the Wetterau frontier into permanent form. A reconstructed stone tower, raised to a height of 11.46 meters and inaugurated in 2013, now marks the spot using construction methods drawn directly from the excavation.

ancient_sources.author: Historia Augusta
ancient_sources.note: Describes Hadrian separating Roman territory from barbarian lands in regions without a river boundary by driving great timber stakes into the ground and binding them into a continuous palisade, the building program to which this stretch of the Germanic limes belonged.

properties.notes: Watchtower Wp 3/15 stood beside the cohort fort at Zugmantel on the western Taunus ridge, close enough that its garrison could relay a signal to the fort gates in moments. It formed part of the timber palisade and ditch system that ran the length of this limes sector, fifty meters of which survive in reconstruction today. The tower watched the frontier road as it crossed the forested high ground above what is now Taunusstein-Orlen. Its post dates to the early phase of frontier building that Trajan's engineers carried out along the Taunus crest.

The watchtower on the Pulverberg above Sayn kept watch over the Brexbach valley from a wooded summit east of the Rhine. Local preservationists rebuilt its tower in 1912, one of the earliest Limes reconstructions anywhere in Germany, using the debris mound of the original as their guide. Roman soldiers built the first post here as part of the frontier's push inland from the Rhine in the early second century. Hikers today reach it by the Saynsteig trail, which climbs the same ridge the tower once watched.

Watchtower Wp 10/14 stood an der Döllchenschneise, a forest ride on the Odenwald limes near the fort at Hainhaus. Its garrison kept the chain of signal posts unbroken along a stretch of frontier where dense woodland cut sightlines short. The tower began as timber during the early second-century push that opened the Odenwald line, part of the same building campaign attested at neighboring posts. Records show the post stayed in use until about 159 CE, when the frontier here was eventually abandoned and the line pulled forward.

Didymoi guarded a well on the road linking Koptos to the Red Sea port of Berenike, its garrison keeping caravans of incense, spices, and quarry workers moving safely across 380 kilometers of open desert. Soldiers under Vespasian built the fort around 77 CE, giving traders and imperial convoys alike a defended place to rest and water their animals. Excavators recovered thousands of ostraca here, the daily paperwork of a small desert garrison, covering duty rosters, supply requests, and private letters home. The fort's mudbrick walls and corner towers still stand at Khashm el-Menih, rising from the gravel plain much as they did when Roman troops manned them.

ancient_sources.author: I.Did.
ancient_sources.note: The fort's foundation dedication, recording the construction of the hydreuma, praesidium, and cistern under the prefect Iulius Ursus in the ninth year of Vespasian (AD 76/77).

properties.notes: Krokodilo stood on the Koptos-Myos Hormos road at El-Muwayh, one of ten fortified stations spaced along the route that carried Red Sea trade goods inland to the Nile. Soldiers built the fort under Vespasian as part of a security program that put a defended well within a day's march of the next, letting caravans cross the desert without running dry. More than 150 ostraca recovered from its rubbish dumps recorded the daily military correspondence passing between the fort's small garrison and its neighboring posts. Its intramural cisterns, still visible in the ruins, let the garrison store water through the driest stretches of the year.

ancient_sources.author: O.Krok. 1–151
ancient_sources.work: military ostraca: correspondence and a daily duty journal
ancient_sources.note: Greek and Latin ostraca excavated at the fort include an official day-by-day journal of its routine covering 8 February–28 March 109 CE, naming Krokodilo directly as the writing post.

properties.notes: Maximianon secured a well at El-Zarqa on the road between Koptos and Myos Hormos, giving the Red Sea trade route a fortified stop roughly a day's march from Krokodilo. Its garrison, part of the chain of praesidia the Roman army built along this desert corridor, watched over caravans carrying goods bound for the Nile and beyond. Excavation of the site recovered ostraca detailing the unit's daily routine, from work rosters to requests for supplies sent up the line. The fort's square mudbrick walls, worn by nearly two thousand years of desert wind, still trace the outline of the original garrison post.

properties.modern_location: Qasr el-Banat, Red Sea Governorate, Egypt
properties.notes: Qasr el-Banat held a well on the Koptos-Myos Hormos road where travelers had already been watering their animals for over a century before Roman soldiers built a fortified station on the spot. Its garrison gave the desert crossing a defended stop between the quarries and ports of the Red Sea coast and the markets of the Nile valley. The praesidium's stone-and-mudbrick walls enclosed barracks, a well, and storage space for the small unit posted there. Today the ruins sit a short distance from the modern road that still roughly follows the ancient route.

Xeron Pelagos took its name, 'the dry sea,' from the flat, wind-scoured plain where the Roman army built it between the forts of Dios and Phalakron on the road to Berenike. Its garrison kept watch over one of the loneliest stretches of the desert route, where the absence of any landmark had given the station its name. Archaeologists excavating the site between 2010 and 2013 recovered the postal register of the fort's curator, a rare survival that names the soldiers who passed through the post. The excavated walls at Feisaleya now stand exposed to the same open plain that once made the station's name fitting.

Compasi sat on the Koptos-Berenike road roughly 85 Roman miles from Koptos, a fortified well the naturalist Pliny the Elder recorded by name in his account of the route to the Red Sea. Soldiers under the prefect Iulius Ursus built it as part of a chain of praesidia that made the desert crossing to Berenike survivable for merchants and imperial cargo alike. Its garrison held one of the harder stretches of the road, in the sandy country now known as Wadi Dagbagh. The fort's remains still mark the well that gave travelers their reason to stop there.

Soldiers dedicated the fort at Dios in 116 CE, and the Latin inscription recording that date survived nearly two thousand years underground before excavators uncovered it in 2005. The praesidium guarded a well on the Koptos-Berenike road between the stations of Compasi and Xeron Pelagos, its garrison keeping the desert crossing open for the emerald and gemstone trade heading toward the Nile. Excavators also found a shrine inside the fort where soldiers left graffiti and consulted oracles, a rare window into the religious life of a small desert garrison. The dedication makes Dios one of the most precisely dated forts anywhere on Rome's eastern desert frontier.

ancient_sources.author: Itinerarium Antonini
ancient_sources.note: Lists this desert-road station as 'Iovis'; a Latin dedicatory inscription found at the fort in 2005 gives its foundation date as 115/116 CE, and ostraca recovered there call it Dios.

properties.notes: A great imperial olive estate stood in the Bagradas Valley, fifty kilometers from Carthage. In 116 CE, procurators of Trajan carved its farming rules onto stone for the tenant farmers who worked its fields, fixing exactly how much of each harvest went to Rome: a third of the grain, a third of the wine, a fifth of the olive oil. That inscription, the Lex Manciana of Henchir Mettich, remains the fullest surviving record of daily life on a Roman imperial farm.

ancient_sources.author: CIL VIII 25902
ancient_sources.note: A bronze/stone copy of estate regulations for the imperial estate Villa Magna Variana sive Mappalia Siga, setting out the coloni's right to work the estate's unused (subseciva) land under the lex Manciana.

properties.notes: A Roman farming estate rose on the hills above Lake Balaton in the 1st century CE. Its main house grew to 2,400 square meters, the largest known residence in the province of Pannonia. Guests crossed a mosaic floor of 62 square meters before reaching painted courtyards and workshop yards beyond. Excavators found it by accident in 1904, buried under a Hungarian wheat field.
properties.image_credit: Villa Romana Balaca, Nemesvamos, Hungary · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: tile stamp, Balácapuszta villa
ancient_sources.note: A stamped roof tile reading 'X VIKVS AVGVS' (vicus Augusti) recovered at the villa supports identifying the estate as part of an imperial (fiscal) property.

properties.notes: A Roman farmstead rose beside the Amber Road in the late 1st century CE, eleven kilometers from the fortress of Carnuntum. Over three centuries it grew into one of the largest estates north of the Alps, its floors eventually covered by 300 square meters of mosaic. Ammianus Marcellinus later called it Murocincta, the walled villa, where the future emperor Valentinian II sheltered in 375 CE after his father's sudden death.
properties.image_credit: Kaiservilla Bruckneudorf, Burgenland, Austria · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
ancient_sources.note: Describes the empress Justina and the infant Valentinian II staying at the imperial villa Murocincta when Valentinian I died nearby at Brigetio in November 375 CE — an estate widely identified with the excavated villa at Bruckneudorf.

properties.notes: A timber house went up inside the future civilian town of Carnuntum in the 1st century CE, decades before Hadrian granted the settlement its Roman city charter. Around 200 CE it was rebuilt in wood and stone, and by 300 CE the whole villa stood in stone alone. Archaeologists named it the Villa Urbana for the wealth its later owners piled into it. In 117 CE its walls were still just timber and thatch.

A vast rural estate rose west of Salzburg in the mid-1st century CE, its main house eventually stretching 220 meters, among the largest Roman villas found north of the Alps. Farmers, craftworkers and a wealthy household shared a courtyard that grew to nearly 9 hectares. Discovered by chance in 1815, its floor later yielded a mosaic of Theseus slaying the Minotaur, now held in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum.
properties.image_credit: Theseus Mosaic from the Roman villa at Loigerfelder near Salzburg, Kunsthistorisches Museum Vienna · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A farming estate rose near Radovljica in the first half of the 1st century CE, its main house holding seven rooms including a private bath suite. The caldarium's hypocaust and hot-water tank still show how its household warmed the mountain air below the Julian Alps. Buried and forgotten for centuries, the villa's stone footings resurfaced only in 2006.

A grand riverside residence rose at Zeugma on the Euphrates in the late 1st century CE, home to an officer or merchant grown wealthy on frontier trade. Its floors were later paved with mosaics of the nine Muses circling Calliope, goddess of epic poetry. The house stood until the Sasanian sack of the city in 252-253 CE. Archaeologists uncovered it only after 2007, just ahead of the rising waters of the Birecik Dam.

Wealthy Knossians built this domus beside the old Minoan palace in the 1st century AD, arranging reception rooms around a colonnaded peristyle court. Excavators uncovered eight mosaic floors here, three showing Dionysos and his followers in flowing color, behind walls once lined with marble paneling. By 11 August 117 CE the house stood roughly seventy years old and still hosted banquets under its wine god's gaze. An earthquake toppled it around 200 CE.

Ptolemais's governor lived behind this 165-meter colonnaded facade, raised under the last Ptolemies and fitted out with Roman-style rooms during the 1st century AD. A grand peristyle led to mosaic-floored dining halls where a Medusa mosaic guarded one threshold, alongside a private bath suite and separate women's wing. On 11 August 117 CE the palace still anchored the city beside its agora, a Hellenistic mansion wearing a fresh Roman face. Polish archaeologists began excavating it in 1937.
properties.image_credit: Palazzo delle Colonne, Ptolemais · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the colonnaded peristyle at the Palazzo delle Colonne in Ptolemais, Libya

properties.notes: A wealthy Roman raised this seaside villa near Tyndaris around 100 BCE, then remodeled its 53 rooms twice more under the early empire. Its frigidarium floor still carries a black-and-white mosaic of dolphins and swordfish chasing across the tiles, fed by baths piped from a spring the Romans dedicated to Venus. By 11 August 117 CE the villa had stood for over two centuries along the coastal road linking Tyndaris to Messina. Excavators brought it back to light in the 1950s.
properties.image_credit: Villa Romana di San Biagio, Terme Vigliatore · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the Roman villa of San Biagio at Terme Vigliatore, Sicily

properties.modern_location: Contrada Durrueli, Realmonte, Agrigento, Sicily, Italy
properties.notes: A landowner raised this seaside villa above Punta Grande in the 1st century AD, arranging guest rooms around a central peristyle floored in marble slabs and polychrome mosaic. Railway workers cutting a bed for the Castelvetrano-Porto Empedocle line found it by accident in 1907. A second wing with private baths was added in the 2nd century AD, expanding an estate that once ran this stretch of Agrigento's coast. On 11 August 117 CE the original villa had already welcomed guests for decades.
properties.image_credit: Villa Romana di Durrueli, Realmonte · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman villa of Durrueli overlooking the sea at Realmonte, Sicily

properties.notes: Six wealthy Ephesian families shared this hillside apartment block, built in the second quarter of the 1st century AD along Curetes Street. Each unit opened onto its own Corinthian-columned courtyard, floored with mosaics of Nereids riding hippocamps, beneath frescoed walls showing Eros figures and hunts. By 11 August 117 CE the terrace houses had sheltered Ephesus's leading families for some eighty years, and would stand for centuries more. Hermann Vetters led their excavation from 1960.
properties.image_credit: Terrace Houses, Ephesus · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated Roman terrace houses at Ephesus with peristyle courtyards and mosaic floors

ancient_sources.author: in situ inscriptions, Terrace House 2 (Dwelling Unit 6)
ancient_sources.note: Inscriptions found within the residence name its owner as Gaius Flavius Furius Aptus, a leading Ephesian citizen who served as alytarch (games president) of the city's Olympic festival.

properties.notes: An Aphrodisian family built this residence north of the Sebasteion in the early 1st century AD, centered on a monumental four-columned Ionic atrium. Later generations kept remodeling it, eventually adding an apsidal courtyard and a second colonnaded wing. On 11 August 117 CE the atrium already stood roughly a century old, home to a family prominent enough to build beside the city's temple to the emperors. Its famous marble shield portraits of philosophers came only in the 5th century.

Hippo Regius's seafront quarter held this colonnaded villa, named for a labyrinth-pattern mosaic laid into one of its floors. Successive owners repaved its rooms across four centuries, with the earliest phases dating to the 1st century AD beneath later mosaic layers. On 11 August 117 CE the villa looked out over Hippo's harbor, decades before Augustine's mother Monica would be born in the same city. Archaeologists still work out which mosaic belongs to which building phase.

A beneficiarii consularis post here policed road and tax traffic along the lower Sava from Trajan's reign onward. Excavators uncovered 84 votive altars in a single sanctuary in 1988, the largest cache of beneficiarius inscriptions found anywhere in the empire. Soldiers detached from the governor's staff at Sirmium dedicated most of the stones to Jupiter for a safe tour of duty. The station anchored security on Pannonia Inferior's busiest river corridor.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Sremska Mitrovica - The ruins of Imperial Palace of Syrmium.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Imperial Palace of Sirmium, Sremska Mitrovica · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: AE 1994, 1418
ancient_sources.note: One of more than eighty beneficiarius altars unearthed at the Sirmium statio in 1988 — the largest single cache of beneficiarii dedications ever found — this one set up by a beneficiarius consularis to Jupiter and the Genius loci.

properties.notes: A beneficiarii procuratoris post opened at Celeia under Trajan, guarding the road linking Italy to Noricum through the Atrans pass. Its earliest dated altar names a beneficiarius serving around 110 CE under the procurator Prifernius Memmius Apollinaris. The station ran without a break for half a century, with thirteen of Noricum's governors represented among its dedications. Soldiers here answered to the province's procurator rather than a legionary legate.
properties.image_credit: Roman city wall of Celeia (modern Celje) · Wikimedia Commons

ancient_sources.author: CIL III 5176
ancient_sources.note: Dedicated by C. Mustius Tettianus, a beneficiarius of the procurator Lisinius Sabinus, to Epona Augusta — one of roughly thirty beneficiarii inscriptions attesting the roadside statio at Celeia.

properties.notes: A beneficiarius consularis dedicated an altar at Virunum, the seat of Noricum's governor, around 120 CE. It stands as the only known beneficiarius inscription from a provincial capital among the early stationes network catalogued down to 150 CE. Virunum served as Noricum's administrative hub on the Zollfeld plain from the province's founding until the Marcomannic Wars. Nearby iron workings on imperial land gave the post's soldiers a tax role beyond simple road patrol.
properties.image_credit: Roman arena remains at Virunum, Zollfeld, Austria · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A beneficiarius consularis manned a statio beside the auxiliary fort at Acimincum, watching the Danube road upriver from Sirmium. Soldiers posted here answered to the governor of Pannonia Inferior rather than to the fort's own auxiliary commander. The post checked travelers and freight moving along the frontier highway between the legionary bases of the Danube limes. It formed one link in a chain of beneficiarius posts that the governor's staff strung along the river.
properties.image_credit: Stari Slankamen on the Danube, site of the Roman fort Acimincum, Serbia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A beneficiarius consularis held a statio at Campona, an auxiliary fort on the Danube road a short ride south of Aquincum. Trajan made Aquincum the seat of Pannonia Inferior's governor in 106 CE, and Campona's post gave that governor eyes on frontier traffic just downriver. Soldiers detached here from the governor's staff worked alongside the fort's own auxiliary cohort but answered up a separate chain of command. The post screened the approach to the new provincial capital.

A beneficiarius post at Ampelum, administrative seat of Rome's newly opened gold district, tracked wagons and workers through the Apuseni mountains after Trajan's conquest of Dacia in 106 CE. At least three beneficiarii of Legio XIII Gemina are attested serving the mining community at nearby Alburnus Maior. Immigrants from Dalmatia, Pannonia, and Noricum worked the gold seams under this military oversight. The post answered to the governor at Apulum, not a local mine official.

Trajan built a fort at Porolissum in 106 CE to guard the main pass through the Carpathians into newly conquered Dacia. Around 5,000 auxiliary troops transferred from Spain, Gaul, and Britain garrisoned the empire's new northern edge here. Beneficiarii detached from the governor's staff worked the road station at this crossing, the busiest gateway on the Dacian frontier. The fort later grew into the capital of the split-off province of Dacia Porolissensis.
properties.image_credit: The Praetorian Gate at the Roman fort of Porolissum, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: An auxiliary fort at Micia doubled as an administrative post, with a beneficiarius station and a likely customs checkpoint on the western Dacian limes. Troops arrived here as early as Trajan's Dacian Wars, guarding the road and river route toward Partiscum on the Tisza. The beneficiarius post let the governor's staff at Apulum watch river traffic and tax collection at this crossing on the Mures. Milestones found nearby later record repairs to the Apulum-Micia road into the 3rd century.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological findings at the amphitheatre of the Roman fort Micia, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Roman forces built the castra at Napoca in 105-106 CE during Trajan's second Dacian campaign, and a milestone from nearby Aiton dated 108 CE records the road linking it to Potaissa. Beneficiarii consularis staffed a statio here, one of only three city-based posts recorded anywhere in Roman Dacia. The settlement rose to municipium status only later, under Hadrian in 124 CE. In 117 CE it still functioned chiefly as a fresh military and road hub in the empire's newest province.
properties.image_credit: Roman ruins with hypocaust heating system in Cluj-Napoca, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: An auxiliary fort went up at Buciumi under Trajan to help hold the northwestern edge of newly conquered Dacia. Two infantry cohorts, I Brittonum and V Lingonum, later garrisoned the post as part of the limes Porolissensis defensive network. Scholars count Buciumi among Roman Dacia's frontier beneficiarius stations, screening approaches from the Upper Tisza basin alongside the fort at Samum. Decades of excavation since the 1960s have made it one of the best-documented forts in the province.
properties.image_credit: The Roman auxiliary fort (castra) of Buciumi, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A beneficiarii consularis statio operated at Teregova, on the road through the Banat borderland between Dacia and Moesia. The post sat along a route Roman engineers opened after Trajan's conquest of Dacia in 106 CE, in the hill country approaching the Iron Gates of the Danube. Soldiers detached from the governor's staff here checked travelers and freight moving between the two frontier provinces. Votive material recovered at the site confirms the station's presence on this border road.

Legionary troops garrisoned Burnum from the early Principate to the late 1st century CE, and soldiers from that garrison dedicated five surviving altars to Jupiter Optimus Maximus as beneficiarii. The fort sat on the road linking Aquileia to Dyrrachium, the shortest overland route from Italy to the Balkans. No structure of the beneficiarius post has ever been excavated; its existence is inferred from these votive stones. Traffic control on this corridor continued into Trajan's reign.
properties.image_credit: Arches of the principium at the Roman legionary camp of Burnum, Croatia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Trajan gave Rome's speculatores and frumentarii a permanent base on the Caelian Hill, the Castra Peregrina, gathering soldiers detached from provincial legions for courier and liaison duty. Speculatores carried official dispatches as mounted messengers, an early node in the empire's long-distance communications. Frumentarii based here moved between Rome and the provinces on courier business. The site later grew into a full headquarters under the Severan emperors.
properties.image_credit: The Caelian Hill, Rome, site of the Castra Peregrina courier barracks · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa rose around 108-110 CE as Trajan's new capital for conquered Dacia, replacing the old Dacian royal seat deeper in the mountains. Beneficiarii consularis staffed a station here, one of only three city-based beneficiarius posts recorded anywhere in Roman Dacia. A forum, amphitheater, and road network radiated out from this new colonia within a decade of the conquest. By 117 CE the city anchored Roman civil and military administration for the entire province.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre at Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: An auxiliary fort at Samum helped anchor the limes Porolissensis, the fortified line Trajan's army built to hold northwestern Dacia after the conquest of 106 CE. Scholars count it among Roman Dacia's frontier beneficiarius stations, paired with the fort at Buciumi nearby. Troops here watched the approaches from the Upper Tisza basin into Transylvania alongside a chain of smaller forts and watchtowers. The post stayed garrisoned through the following two centuries of Roman rule in the province.

A road station named Praetorium anchored traffic on the route linking Tibiscum to the Danube crossing near Dierna, opened as Trajan pushed into the Banat during the Dacian Wars. Scholars count Praetorium among the small number of beneficiarius posts placed directly on Dacia's main roads rather than at a city or fort. Its name, meaning headquarters or governor's station, marks it as an official waystation. The road it guarded fed troops toward the Iron Gates of the Danube.

A beneficiarii post watched over traffic on Trajan's Bridge, the 1,135-meter span that carried Roman legions across the Danube into Dacia in 105 CE. Soldiers detached from Legio V Macedonica pulled duty here, checking travelers and cargo at the empire's newest river crossing. Two of their altars survive, dedicated by men answering to the governor's staff rather than their own legion's officers. The station guarded the single busiest chokepoint on the entire Danube frontier.
properties.image_credit: The Roman castra of Drobeta, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Savaria doubled as home to Pannonia Superior's provincial archive and a beneficiarii consularis post under Trajan. A dated inscription places the station here alongside the tabularium provinciae, tying road security directly to the province's tax paperwork. Soldiers detached from the governor's staff processed records and travel documents in this Amber Road colony rather than at the legionary bases downriver. Few other Danubian stationes combined bureaucratic and security duties so visibly under one roof.
properties.image_credit: The reconstructed Iseum (Temple of Isis) at Savaria, Szombathely, Hungary · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: As capital of Dalmatia, Salona hosted the province's busiest beneficiarii post, with fourteen surviving dedications naming men posted to the governor's staff here, more than any other town in the province. Detachments rotated in chiefly from Legio I Adiutrix, XIV Gemina, and XI Claudia to handle security and paperwork for the entire governorship. A soldier posted here answered to the consular governor directly, bypassing his own legion's centurions. The post anchored a network of seventeen confirmed beneficiarii stations radiating from Salona along Dalmatia's interior roads.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of the Roman provincial capital Salona, Croatia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Viminacium served as Trajan's forward headquarters through both Dacian Wars, and its officium consularis kept a beneficiarii post busy processing the tax and travel traffic of an active war zone. Legio VII Claudia's fortress stood beside the provincial governor's seat, giving beneficiarii direct access to both military and civilian administration. One surviving altar records a soldier's promotion from a legate's beneficiarius to a full consular beneficiarius, a career step made at this very post. The station sat where the Danube road met the supply routes feeding two Dacian campaigns.
properties.image_credit: Archaeological site of Viminacium near Kostolac, Serbia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Siscia kept a beneficiarii consularis post running long after its legion marched off to the Danube frontier in the Flavian era. Soldiers such as Lucius Virilius Pupus dedicated altars here, filling the security gap left by departing troops at this Sava River crossing. The town's road-and-river junction made it a natural chokepoint for tax collection and travel control heading into the second century. Beneficiarii, river-fleet detachments, and passing units made up Siscia's visible Roman military presence for decades after the legion left.

Narona ran one of only three judicial assize centers in Dalmatia, and a governor's beneficiarius worked out of the town to keep the southern conventus running smoothly. A surviving altar to Jupiter records a soldier named Claudius Marcus who was promoted from optio straight into a consular governor's beneficiarius post here. The town sat at the head of the navigable Neretva, funneling river and road traffic from the coast into the Balkan interior. Its posting gave a handful of soldiers oversight of one of Dalmatia's three legal and administrative hubs.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Augustus (Augusteum) at Narona, Vid, Croatia · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Apulum housed Dacia's schola speculatorum, a dedicated barracks for the governor's courier-scouts built inside the fortress of Legio XIII Gemina. A building inscription lists three centurions and two cornicularii overseeing twenty serving speculatores alongside five veterans of the corps. These men carried dispatches and gathered intelligence for the governor's office rather than answering to their legion's own chain of command. The post anchored courier traffic for Dacia, the newest province Trajan had added to the empire.
properties.image_credit: Roman ruins of Apulum within the Alba Carolina Fortress, Alba Iulia, Romania · Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: A castrum and vicus stood at a sharp bend of the Danube's Moson branch, giving the post its name meaning 'at the bend.' It guarded the limes road between Carnuntum and Arrabona for over 300 years, into the 5th century. Local trade grew up behind its walls as craftsmen settled near the garrison. Its foundations lie today beneath the town's historic castle grounds.

An auxiliary camp for 1,000 men rose on a Celtic river-junction settlement under Claudius, guarding the mouth of the Rába. By the early 2nd century it held the ala Ulpia contariorum milliaria, the only double-strength cavalry unit in Pannonia Superior. Roman-era stonework still sits in the casemates of Győr's later castle. The fort anchored trade between the Danube frontier and the interior for four centuries.

Trajan's engineers raised a timber-and-earth fort roughly midway between Ad Flexum and Arrabona to close a gap in the limes road. Hadrian's visit to Pannonia in 124 CE prompted its rebuild in stone, with a near-perfect 99 x 99.5 meter square plan that later gave the post its name. Excavations exposed a corner tower and the right-hand gate. Its precise identification remains debated among archaeologists, but Barátföldpuszta is the leading candidate.

A castellum sat 6 kilometers east of the legionary base at Brigetio, watching the Danube where two small streams met the river. The 2nd-century Itinerarium Antonini recorded it under the name Azaum, drawn from the local Azali tribe. Rescue excavations in 1959-1960, forced by a hydroelectric project, uncovered its western gateway. A civilian settlement grew alongside the garrison to serve the Brigetio-Aquincum road.

Perched on Sánc-hegy hill on the Danube's right bank, this fort sat roughly 27 kilometers east of Brigetio along the limes road toward Aquincum. An 18th-century traveler, Richard Pococke, still found Roman bricks and wall foundations scattered across the site. Later quarrying and 18th-century conflict destroyed most of the visible structure. Aerial surveys today pick out its outline only as shadow marks in the fields.

A palisade camp measuring 124 by 147 meters went up here around the turn of the 2nd century, the first Pannonia Superior post south of the provincial border along the Danube Bend. The cohors II Alpinorum equitata, previously stationed at Cologne, later garrisoned the site before it was rebuilt in stone. Excavations begun in 1930 by Ákos Szalay have never resumed. Its outline is still visible in the terrain near Tahi today.

Built in the first years of the 2nd century, this 134 by 205 meter camp on the Danube Bend housed up to 1,000 soldiers behind double moats and square towers. Its name is thought to mean 'wolf camp.' The fully excavated principia and stone finds are now displayed in Szentendre's Ferenczy Károly Museum. Emperors Septimius Severus and Caracalla both later passed through the post on Danube campaigns.
properties.image_credit: Roman brick stamp from Ulcisia Castra, Szentendre · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman brick stamp excavated at Ulcisia Castra

properties.notes: The ala I Tungrorum Frontoniana, transferred from Aquincum, built the first palisade camp here under Domitian before it was rebuilt in stone as a 178 by 200 meter fort. Triple ditches and paired corner towers ringed its walls. A Mithraic relief turned up among the finds from its vicus, now buried under modern Nagytétény. The fort's eastern and southern gates remain visible on site today.
properties.image_credit: Site plan of the Campona fort, Nagytétény · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological site plan of the Campona Roman fort

properties.notes: An earth-and-timber fort went up on the Danube's west bank early in the 1st century, some 33 kilometers south of Aquincum according to the Itinerarium Antonini. Its stone rebuild came only after the Marcomannic Wars, around the turn of the 3rd century. A military vicus of merchants, craftsmen and soldiers' families grew up beside the camp, mixing with the local Celtic population. A well inside the principia has yielded some of the site's best-studied finds.

Named in Ptolemy's Geography, this Danube-bank camp held the cohors II Alpinorum until it handed over to the cohors III Batavorum around 117-120 CE. A tribune of the Batavian cohort dedicated an altar to the goddess Vagdavercustis, otherwise unknown in Pannonia. A Jupiter Dolichenus sanctuary went up just outside the fort's northwest corner after the Marcomannic Wars. A late Roman cemetery of some 20 graves was later cut into the abandoned camp itself.
properties.image_credit: Jupiter Dolichenus sanctuary at the Vetus Salina Roman fort site, Adony, Hungary · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Jupiter Dolichenus sanctuary associated with the Vetus Salina Roman fort

properties.notes: Excavations between 1999 and 2005 uncovered a fort garrisoned by the cohors VII Breucorum, whose stamped tiles make up roughly a quarter of all bricks found on site. A bronze miniature sword pendant, one of only 17 known from the entire Roman world, points to soldiers arriving from Germania Superior around 130-132 CE. Two barrack blocks built parallel to the fort wall were traced through several construction phases. A previously unrecorded gate design was uncovered here in 2000-2001.

An auxiliary garrison settled on Bottyán Hill during Claudius's reign, among the earliest forts on this stretch of the Danube limes. A military diploma recovered from the site confirmed decades of later excavation work here. Tolna County's only restored Roman ruin garden now opens the fort's foundations to visitors. It was named a protected heritage site and 'Tolna jewel' in 2020.
properties.image_credit: Aerial photograph of the Lussonium Roman fort site near Dunakomlod, Hungary · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Aerial view of the Lussonium Roman fort site on the Danube limes

properties.notes: Alta Ripa, 'the high bank,' held a link position in the chain of forts running down the Ripa Pannonica between Lussonium and Alisca. Its name described the site's raised position over the Danube floodplain. Centuries of river erosion have since swallowed most of its remains. It survives today chiefly through its listing in Roman itineraries as a fixed station on the frontier road.

Roman itineraries list this fort as 'Alisca ad latus,' set on the Báta stream south of Szekszárd on the Danube's right bank. An inscribed stone recorded soldiers likely lost when a unit shipped out to Moesia around 98-99 CE, pointing to a late-1st-century garrison. Its true location was long misplaced at Szekszárd's Kálvária hill before researcher Mór Wosinsky reassigned it to Őcsény. It filled the gap on the limes road between Lugio and Alta Ripa.
properties.image_credit: Roman sarcophagus from Alisca (Őcsény), Hungarian National Museum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman marble sarcophagus depicting Cupid and Psyche, found at Alisca

properties.notes: A tombstone from the site proves the cohors I Alpinorum was already garrisoned here by 17 CE at the latest, making Lugio one of the earliest inscribed Roman posts in eastern Pannonia. The camp sat on Várhegy, a fortified bluff rising 100 meters over a likely Danube crossing point. By the 2nd century the cohors VII Breucorum shared the site with a detachment of legio II Adiutrix. Most of the Roman-era finds now lie beneath the modern village.

This castellum and its attached vicus sat at Hajlokpart on the Danube, marking roughly where Pannonia Inferior's Hungarian limes sector gave way to its Croatian-Serbian continuation. A watchtower at nearby Sátorhely-Törökdomb extended its field of observation along the river. It formed a link in the unbroken line of forts, watchtowers and the limes road running the length of the Pannonian frontier. Little of the site has been excavated compared with neighboring forts.

Built near the Drava's confluence with the Danube in the 1st century CE, this fort at various times garrisoned the ala II Hispanorum Aravacorum and the ala I civium Romanorum. Stray finds of javelin heads and horse-harness pendants trace its cavalry garrison across the 1st and 2nd centuries. A 19th-century brickyard built directly over the site destroyed most of its structural remains. Ongoing riverbank erosion continues to eat away what is left.

Set on the loess plateau of Popino Brdo above the Danube, this was one of the most important bases on Croatia's stretch of the limes from the 1st century CE onward. A recovered Roman spatha, now held in the Zagreb Archaeological Museum, points to the sword-armed cavalry once quartered here. No systematic excavation has ever reached the fort itself, leaving its exact layout unrecovered. Stamped bricks and roof tiles remain the main record of its Roman garrison.

A necropolis dated to the first third of the 1st century CE, holding burials of auxiliary soldiers and their dependents, confirms an early Roman military presence on Ilok's hilltop. The fort itself was traditionally placed at the Gornji Grad but its precise footprint was never pinned down. Systematic digs between 2001 and 2007 turned up 3rd-century architectural remains nearby. Later builders recycled some of its stonework into the medieval fortress that replaced it.

Garrisoned by a cohors Alpinorum on the northern slopes of Fruška Gora, this fort doubled as a river port serving Sirmium downstream. Paired with the Onagrinum fort across the Danube at Begeč, it helped Rome control river traffic through the Srem region. Large bath buildings once filled the eastern half of its rectangular plateau site. A sizeable Roman cemetery still lies on the slope just east of the old ramparts.

At the Gradina site on a raised Danube bank, 1955 trenching found a 1st-century settlement layered beneath a later military camp and brick-built tombs. The ala I Augusta Ityraeorum, a cavalry unit originally raised in Syria, garrisoned the post. Coins recovered on site date use of the position back to the 1st century CE. Its Turkish-derived modern name, Surduk, references the cliffs overlooking the river.

This Danube fort sat roughly 16 kilometers south of Rittium, watching the river approach to Taurunum and the Sava confluence. Excavations have reached only limited parts of its defenses, but the distinctive shapes of its surviving towers help date separate building phases. The site remained under some form of occupation from the late Republic through the 7th century. Its Roman name survives directly in the modern village of (Novi) Banovci.

Rome absorbed this Celtic river town into Pannonia around 15 CE, turning its position at the Sava-Danube confluence into a naval base for the Classis Flavia Pannonica. Detachments of legio VII Claudia, based across the rivers at Singidunum, manned smaller units posted here. A Roman cemetery beneath Zemun's later Gardoš tower has yielded 3rd- and 4th-century graves. Neither the fort nor the fleet harbor itself has been pinned down archaeologically with certainty.

Positioned where the Great Morava river meets the Danube, this fortified customs post controlled river traffic and trade through the 1st to 4th centuries. Excavations between 1947 and 1949 identified three separate building phases at the site. Roman houses with painted walls and hypocaust heating were later uncovered in its civilian quarter. Marcus Aurelius eventually elevated the growing settlement to a municipium.
properties.image_credit: Margum excavation, 2011 · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 2011 excavation photograph of the Margum fort site

properties.notes: One of the largest forts on the Upper Moesian limes, this 200 by 150 meter camp went up on a hilltop overlooking a Danube crossing in the late 1st century. Trajan's army is thought to have used a pontoon bridge here to launch its invasion of Dacia, a crossing depicted at the opening of the reliefs on Trajan's Column in Rome. Builders quarried local green shale for its walls and towers. Justinian later shrank the fort to a 50 by 60 meter fortification in its northeast corner.
properties.image_credit: Lederata archaeological site · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Archaeological remains at the Lederata fort site

properties.notes: Rome folded this Thracian-Dacian settlement at the mouth of the Pek river into Moesia Superior in the 1st century CE, garrisoning it with troops of legio VII Claudia. It administered the nearby Aeliana Picensia mining district and gave its name to the local Pincenses community recorded by Ptolemy. A 2nd-century marble funerary relief of Achilles dragging Hector around Troy's walls survives from the site. A matching fortification stood across the river to cover the opposite bank.

Vicus Cuppae rose at the western edge of the Iron Gates gorge right at the turn of the 2nd century CE, administered from Viminacium as a stop on the road toward Nicomedia. It housed the praefectus of legio VII Claudia's frontier command in this section of the Danube. The post's Roman-era ruins were later built over by the medieval Golubac Fortress that now dominates the site. Repeated 6th- and 7th-century raids eventually emptied the settlement out.

Domitian rebuilt this fort's original earth-and-timber walls in stone in 87 CE, just before his own Dacian War, giving it a 134 by 126 meter footprint. It stood as one link in the tightly spaced chain of forts guarding the Iron Gates section of the Moesian limes. A full restoration followed in the later 3rd century, and semicircular corner towers were added in the 4th. Archaeologists later found an early Christian basilica built within its walls.

Built under Tiberius and Claudius on cliffs above the Danube, this fort was destroyed during Domitian's Dacian War and rebuilt in 100 CE at nearly double its original 1-hectare size for Trajan's own campaign. Detachments from four Moesian legions rotated through alongside the cohors VI Thracum and cohors V Gallorum. The Tabula Traiana, an inscribed slab commemorating Trajan's canal cut through the Iron Gates in 101 CE, was found 150 meters from its walls. It remains one of the best-excavated forts on the entire Moesian limes.
properties.image_credit: Remains of Diana Fort at Karataš, rebuilt for Trajan's Dacian campaign · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Stone wall remains of the Roman fort Diana on the Danube bank at Karataš, Serbia

properties.notes: Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus built this 112 by 120 meter fort in 103 CE to guard the southern end of his new Danube bridge, at the time the longest in the Roman world. Crossing the bridge required passing through fortified camps at both ends. A bronze head from a statue of Trajan, once mounted at the bridge entrance, was recovered here and now sits in Belgrade's National Museum. Thick sections of the camp's ramparts still stand above ground today.
properties.image_credit: Wall remains of the Pontes fort, Kostol (Kladovo) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Surviving wall remains of the Pontes Roman fort

properties.notes: Three successive fortifications on this stretch of the Danube, spanning the 1st through 6th centuries, made Egeta one of the longest-used military sites on the Iron Gates limes. By the 2nd century it housed the cohors I Cretum along the road linking Viminacium to Aquae. Excavations recovered cult objects tied to the Syrian god Jupiter Dolichenus from a shrine on site. Its large civilian settlement has since been repeatedly flooded by the Danube.

A Roman military base and arsenal grew up on the Danube's right bank in the 1st century, serving as a supply point during Trajan's Dacian Wars. Trajan raised its status to a full Roman colony after his 106 CE victory over Decebalus, naming it Colonia Ulpia Traiana Ratiaria. It later became the seat of a provincial governor and the base of legio XIII Gemina. The site lies 2 kilometers west of the modern village of Archar.

A Roman road station and fort rose on the site of an older Thracian settlement, with the stone fortress itself built at the start of the 2nd century as part of Ratiaria's administrative district. Its pentagon-shaped circuit, roughly 4 hectares in area, carried round towers at each angle. A 1986-1990 excavation by the Lom Museum of History uncovered its structure in detail, and a later rescue dig found the western gate. Bulgaria declared the site a monument of national importance in 1971.
properties.image_credit: Remains of the Roman fort (castra) of Almus, Lom, Bulgaria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Excavated remains of the Roman fort of Almus at Lom, Bulgaria

properties.notes: Its name means 'port of sixty ships,' and Domitian made it headquarters of the Classis Flavia Moesica river fleet around 85 CE before Trajan's Dacian conquest shifted the fleet base to Noviodunum. A temple to Apollo and the principia headquarters building were later uncovered on site. A 7-meter stretch of fortress wall from a later Diocletianic rebuild still stands in Ruse today. The Roman city was finally destroyed by Avar and Slavic raids after 596 CE.
properties.image_credit: Inscription fragment from Sexaginta Prista · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Roman inscription fragment from the Sexaginta Prista fort

properties.notes: Acumincum guarded a Danube bend where routes from beyond the Tisza reached the river, anchoring the Pannonian limes between Rittium and Taurunum. The Flavian-era fort first held Cohors I Britannica equitata, then Cohors I Campanorum civium Romanorum, whose tile stamps still turn up in the soil. A 1955-1957 excavation traced the Roman wall buried beneath a medieval fortress built directly over it. Soldiers there worshipped Jupiter Dolichenus, whose carved reliefs surfaced centuries later.

Augustus's legions raised a castrum here beside a Berber village named Auzia, planting one of the earliest Roman garrisons in central Mauretania Caesariensis. Tacitus recorded the post as the Castellum Auziense, headquarters for the district commander during the Tacfarinas war. A civilian vicus grew up alongside the fort on the road roughly 150 kilometers southeast of Icosium, and by 117 CE both fort and settlement anchored Rome's inland frontier. Septimius Severus later elevated the town to colonia status as Colonia Septima Aurelia Auziense, decades after Trajan's reign.
properties.image_credit: Aqueduct of Sour El-Ghozlane (ancient Auzia), Algeria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the Roman aqueduct at Sour El-Ghozlane, ancient Auzia

properties.notes: Roman engineers laid out this quadriburgium fort in 122 CE on the Nova Praetentura road linking Numidia to Mauretania Tingitana, roughly 100 kilometers south of Icosium. Its first garrison, the Cohors II Sardorum, watched the frontier zone between Auzia and the Chelif valley. A civilian vicus grew up around the walls and lasted until Berber raiders destroyed it under Aurelian more than a century later. Rapidum's foundation date falls five years after Trajan's death, so on 11 August 117 CE the site was still open ground.

Tigava Castra guarded a river crossing on the road between Oppidum Novum and Malliana in central Mauretania Caesariensis, two Roman miles from the separate civilian town of Tigava. Ptolemy's Geography and the Antonine Itinerary both list the post as a fixed stop on the province's road network. An amphitheater later rose in the garrison town that grew up around the fort's walls. No surviving inscription records the year the camp itself was raised, though its place in the province's early road system points to an origin well before the second century.

Zaraï stood on the pre-desert frontier of Numidia at the edge of the Hodna range, where Legio III Augusta and its auxiliaries extended Rome's road network under Trajan. Funerary inscriptions from the site name a soldier of the Cohors VI Commagenorum and a standard-bearer of the Cohors I Flavia Equitata, confirming a garrison town rather than a mere market stop. Emperor Hadrian personally inspected an auxiliary cohort at Zaraï on 7 July 128 CE while touring the African provinces. A later customs post here recorded a detailed tariff of tolls on livestock, hides, and slaves crossing between the desert and the coast, one of only a handful of complete Roman customs schedules to survive.

Diana Veteranorum took its name from the retired soldiers of Legio III Augusta whom Trajan settled here on land grants in Numidia's high plains. The colony sat 90 kilometers southwest of Cirta and anchored a chain of veteran settlements meant to hold the frontier without full-time garrisons. A monumental arch and other public buildings rose over the following decades as the post grew from a military settlement into a proper town. On 11 August 117 CE its founding veterans, granted land under Trajan's own settlement scheme, still worked those fields.
properties.image_credit: Triumphal arch at Diana Veteranorum (Zana), Algeria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Ruins of the triumphal arch at Diana Veteranorum, Zana, Algeria

properties.notes: Mascula rose on the northern slope of the Aurès at 1,200 meters, guarding the route into the mountains where Numidia met the pre-desert. Trajan's army built the post, and a cohort of Lusitanian auxiliaries held its walls alongside detachments of Legio III Augusta. The fort controlled the most important pass giving Roman Numidia access to the far side of the range. Mascula grew into a full colonia only later in the second century, well after this map's snapshot.

Mesarfelta rose in the second half of the first century CE as a fortified Roman-Berber post on the northern approach to the Aurès massif. Ditches and earthworks of the later Fossatum Africae ran north from here toward Thubunae, tying the post into a chain of watchpoints that tracked seasonal herding across the frontier. Hadrian gave the settlement an amphitheater for its games decades after this map's snapshot. Archaeologists still debate whether Mesarfelta's ruins lie at El-Outaïa or at one of several other candidate sites near the Aurès foothills, so its exact position on this map is approximate.

Emperor Claudius folded this Atlantic gateway into the new province of Mauretania Tingitana in 42 CE, raising a Roman stronghold above the harbor across the strait from Baelo Claudia in Spain. Local fishermen salted and exported tunny from these waters, feeding a trade that tied the fort to ports throughout the western Mediterranean. Roads ran overland from here to both Tingis and Volubilis, linking the coastal garrison to the rest of the province's network. The post took its name, Ad Septem Fratres, from seven hills visible along this stretch of coast.

Roman troops built an 80-meter-square castellum at Tamuda in the mid-first century CE, garrisoning a site the Mauretanian Berbers had already held since the third century BCE. Governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus campaigned through this stretch of the Tingitana coast in 42 CE, the same years the fort's earliest phase took shape. The camp sat on the Martil river six kilometers from where Tétouan stands today, guarding the approach to the coast from the interior. Excavators found the fort's walls overlying the older Mauretanian town, itself built up over centuries before Rome arrived.
properties.image_credit: Northern gate of the Roman military camp at Tamuda, Morocco · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Remains of the northern gate of the Roman military camp at Tamuda, Morocco

properties.notes: Thubunae sat astride the road linking the Aurès forts to Nicivibus, a river crossing important enough that Rome garrisoned it through much of the province's history. A single surviving milestone on that road carries the abbreviated name '[a Thu]bonis,' one of the few inscriptions to confirm the site by its Roman name. Archaeologists trace the earliest Roman-period occupation to the first century CE, though the settlement did not gain municipium status until Septimius Severus's reign nearly a century later.
